tests.title: Review the documented communication needs and external connections
tests.obj: Find undocumented external services and places where users can set an external location the server connects to.
steps: Ask for the document of all communication needs, including external services.
List the outbound hosts seen in traffic captures or egress logs.
Find features where a user supplies a URL, host or webhook.
Compare the list with the document.
tests.ex: tcpdump -i any -nn 'dst net not 10.0.0.0/8' -w egress.pcap; review egress firewall logs
tests.exp: All external services and user-supplied destinations are documented.

tests.title: Review connection limits and resource management for each backend service
tests.obj: Find missing limits, time-outs and retry rules that cause denial of service when a backend is slow.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Ask for the documented connection pool limits, time-outs and retry rules per service.
Read the configuration of each service client and compare it with the document.
Slow down one backend in a test system and watch the application behavior.
Fill the connection pool in a test system and check for graceful handling and recovery.
tests.ex: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=10000 db; compare pool settings in app config
tests.exp: Documented limits exist and match the configuration. The application degrades safely and recovers.

tests.title: Make sure backend components authenticate with individual, least-privilege accounts
tests.obj: Find shared, uncontrolled or default service credentials, and over-privileged service accounts.
steps: List service-to-service links: APIs, middleware, databases, queues.
Check how each link authenticates: service account, short-term token, or certificate.
Check that no link uses a shared static password or default credential such as root/root.
Review the privileges of each account and compare them with what the link needs.
tests.ex: psql -c '\du'; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa; try admin/admin on the management port
tests.exp: Each link uses its own account or token with least privilege. No default credentials work.

tests.title: Make sure the server can contact only an allowlist of external systems
tests.obj: Find servers that can send requests to any destination and so allow SSRF and data theft.
steps: Find the egress allowlist at the application, web server or firewall level.
Use a feature that fetches a URL and give it an internal address and a non-listed host.
Try a redirect from an allowed host to a blocked host.
From the server shell, in a test system, try to reach a non-listed external host.
tests.ex: curl -s 'https://example.com/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/'; curl -s 'https://example.com/fetch?url=https://allowed.example/redirect?to=http://127.0.0.1'
tests.exp: The server reaches only allowlisted systems. Requests to others fail.

tests.title: Make sure responses return only the fields that the client needs
tests.obj: Find objects that expose internal or sensitive fields that the client does not need.
steps: Compare the fields shown in the UI with the fields in the API or page response.
Look for password hashes, tokens, internal IDs, role flags and personal data.
Compare responses for different roles and for unauthenticated requests.
Check nested objects and GraphQL fields.
Look in the code for DTOs or field selection on the server.
tests.ex: jq 'keys' response.json; Burp Logger++ filter on JSON; compare with UI
tests.exp: Responses contain only the fields required by the function. The server selects fields, not the client.

tests.title: Test for mass assignment on create and update actions
tests.obj: Find actions that bind extra request fields to protected object properties such as role or owner.
steps: Find create and update requests that send a JSON, XML or form body.
Add extra fields such as role, isAdmin, balance, ownerId and id.
Send the request and read the object back.
Check the code for an allowlist of fields or a DTO per action.
tests.ex: curl -s -X PATCH https://example.com/api/me -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"x","role":"admin","isAdmin":true}'
tests.exp: Fields that are not part of the action are ignored or rejected. Protected properties do not change.

tests.title: Check strict typing and strict comparison to stop type confusion
tests.obj: Find loose type handling that leads to type juggling and logic bypass.
steps: Send arrays, objects, null, booleans and numeric strings where a string is expected.
Send 0, "0", "0e123" and true in comparison fields such as tokens and passwords.
Look in the code for loose comparison operators on security values.
Check that input types are enforced before use.
tests.ex: curl -s https://example.com/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"user":"admin","password":true}'; semgrep --config p/php
tests.exp: The application rejects wrong types and uses strict comparison for security decisions.

tests.title: Test JavaScript code for prototype pollution
tests.obj: Find merge and assignment code that lets a user set properties of Object.prototype.
steps: Send JSON with __proto__, constructor and prototype keys to endpoints that merge input.
Send the same in query strings and form fields.
Check whether a later request shows a changed property.
Search the code for recursive merge functions and object literals used as maps.
tests.ex: curl -s -X POST https://example.com/api/settings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}}'; ppfuzz or DOM Invader
tests.exp: User input cannot change the prototype. The code uses Map or Set, or safe merge functions.

tests.title: Test for HTTP parameter pollution
tests.obj: Find parameters that the application, proxy and WAF read in different ways.
steps: Send the same parameter twice in the query string, and in the body and the query together.
Send the same name in a cookie and a header.
Look at which value each component uses and compare the results.
Check that the framework takes one defined source.
tests.ex: curl -s 'https://example.com/transfer?to=alice&to=mallory'; curl -s -d 'amount=1&amount=1000' https://example.com/pay
tests.exp: The application handles duplicate parameters in a defined way, and a WAF or proxy sees the same value.

tests.title: Review documented resource-demanding functions and the defenses against overload
tests.obj: Find expensive functions with no limits that an attacker can use to take the service down.
pre: Do not run load tests on production. Get written approval.
steps: Ask for the list of functions that need much time or memory, for example search, export, upload and report.
Check the documented defenses: rate limits, quotas, queues, timeouts and caching.
Send a few requests at a normal rate and increase the load slowly on a test system.
Test large uploads, large request bodies and slow connections.
Check that the response time stays below the time-out of the client.
tests.ex: slowhttptest -c 1000 -H -u https://example.com/; k6 run load.js; curl --limit-rate 10 -T bigfile https://example.com/upload
tests.exp: Resource-demanding functions are documented and protected by limits. The service stays available under load.

tests.title: Review shared objects in multi-threaded code for thread safety
tests.obj: Find race conditions on caches, files and in-memory objects that more than one thread uses.
steps: Find shared mutable objects: caches, singletons, static fields and files.
Check that thread-safe types or locks protect them.
Send many parallel requests that change the same object.
Run a race detector or thread sanitizer on the tests.
tests.ex: go test -race ./...; java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions with thread-safety analyzers; Burp Turbo Intruder parallel requests
tests.exp: Shared objects are accessed safely. Parallel requests do not corrupt data.

tests.title: Test for time-of-check to time-of-use gaps
tests.obj: Find checks of state or permission that are not atomic with the action that follows.
steps: Find checks of existence, permission or balance followed by an action.
Send the same request many times in parallel, for example a coupon or a transfer.
Look for results that break the check, such as a second use.
Check that the check and action are one atomic operation, for example one database transaction or file operation.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder single-packet attack; curl --parallel --parallel-max 30 -d 'code=SAVE10' https://example.com/redeem?[1-30]
tests.exp: The check and the action are atomic. Parallel requests cannot break the check.

tests.title: Review lock use and fair resource allocation against deadlock and starvation
tests.obj: Find locks that cause deadlock and pools that starve low-priority work.
steps: Review the code for lock order, retry loops and locks that outside code can change.
Check that lock logic stays in the code that owns the resource.
Check thread pool settings and queue priorities.
Load the system with mixed work and look for tasks that never run.
tests.ex: jstack <pid> | grep -A5 'deadlock'; py-spy dump --pid <pid>
tests.exp: Locks are used in a consistent order and are not stuck. Low-priority work finishes in a reasonable time.

tests.title: Look for default and vendor accounts and passwords
tests.obj: Finds default administrator accounts and known vendor passwords that still work.
pre: Do not run on production without owner approval.
steps: Identify the software and version from the response headers and login page.
Find the vendor default accounts in the manual and in default-credential lists.
Try each default pair on every login page, including admin consoles.
Try admin, root, sa and system with blank, admin and password values.
Make sure the build does not contain hard-coded or test accounts.
tests.ex: nuclei -u https://target -tags default-login ; hydra -C default-creds.txt target https-post-form '/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=Invalid'
tests.exp: No default, hard-coded or test account can log in. Default accounts are removed or disabled before production.

tests.title: Check the account lockout and throttle on failed logins
tests.obj: Finds missing or weak lockout that allows online password guessing.
pre: A test account that you can afford to lock.
Do not run on production.
steps: Send three wrong passwords. Then send the correct password and note the result.
Repeat with four and five wrong passwords and note when the account locks.
Wait five, ten and fifteen minutes. Send the correct password after each wait.
Look at the failed-login counter: make sure it follows the account and not only the IP address.
If the lockout is client side, turn off JavaScript and send the requests with a proxy.
Compare with the lockout rule in the security documentation.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder, null payload x 10, resource pool: 1 concurrent request, delay 2000 ms, POST /login with the test user and a wrong password; then send the correct password.
tests.exp: The application locks or delays the account after a small number of failures, as documented. The counter follows the account. A valid user is not locked out for long.

tests.title: Test distributed brute force, password spray and credential stuffing
tests.obj: Finds protection that counts failures only per IP address and so misses spread-out attacks.
pre: Only use accounts that you are allowed to test.
Do not run on production.
steps: Prepare a list of known test user and password pairs and a list of common passwords.
Send each pair from a different source IP address using proxies or VPN endpoints.
Send one common password against many test accounts (password spray).
Look for account lockout, CAPTCHA, delay or MFA step-up in the responses.
Check if the application warns the user or the administrator about the attack.
tests.ex: ffuf -w pairs.txt:USERPASS -X POST -d 'username=USERPASS&password=PASS' -u https://target/login -x socks5://127.0.0.1:9050 ; Burp Intruder cluster bomb for the spray case.
tests.exp: The application detects attacks that span many IP addresses and accounts. It applies account-based controls such as step-up, delay or block, and it raises an alert.

tests.title: Try to bypass the CAPTCHA on login and recovery
tests.obj: Finds CAPTCHA checks that the server does not enforce, so automated guessing still works.
steps: Send the login request with the CAPTCHA parameter removed.
Send the request with a wrong CAPTCHA value and with an empty value.
Send the same solved CAPTCHA response in two requests.
Clear the cookies and see if the CAPTCHA is skipped.
Look in the alt text, file name and hidden fields for the answer.
Try the mobile or API endpoint for the same function.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: delete the 'g-recaptcha-response' parameter, then replay an old valid token; compare the status codes.
tests.exp: The server checks every CAPTCHA response, accepts it once, and rejects missing or wrong values. All endpoints enforce it. The CAPTCHA does not replace the lockout.

tests.title: Check that the account unlock process is not weak
tests.obj: Finds unlock links or answers that an attacker can guess or reuse to unlock an account.
pre: Test account that you can lock.
Do not run on production.
steps: Lock a test account. Start the unlock process.
Examine the unlock link or code: length, randomness and lifetime.
Use the unlock link twice.
Try to unlock another account by changing the user parameter.
Make sure the unlock process has its own rate limit.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: GET /unlock?user=victim&token=<token>, replay twice, then change user=other.
tests.exp: The unlock token is random, single use and short lived. An attacker cannot unlock an account that is not theirs. The process is rate limited.

tests.title: Read the documentation for anti-automation controls
tests.obj: Finds missing or incomplete documentation of rate limit, anti-automation and adaptive controls.
pre: Access to the security documentation and configuration.
steps: Get the security documentation for authentication.
Find the rules for rate limit, lockout and adaptive response against credential stuffing and brute force.
Make sure the document gives the thresholds and configuration values.
Make sure the document explains how malicious account lockout is prevented.
Compare the documented values with the real configuration.
tests.ex: Review the security design document and the gateway or WAF rate-limit configuration; record the threshold, window and lockout time.
tests.exp: The documentation defines the controls, their values, and how they prevent malicious lockout. The real configuration matches it.

tests.title: Read the documentation of all authentication pathways
tests.obj: Finds authentication pathways that are not documented with their required strength.
pre: Access to the security documentation.
steps: List every way to log in: web form, API, mobile, SSO, support channels and admin consoles.
Get the documentation for authentication.
Make sure each pathway is in the document with its controls and strength.
Make sure the document says the controls must be the same on all pathways.
tests.ex: Build a table: pathway, factors, rate limit, MFA, session type. Compare to the design document.
tests.exp: All authentication pathways are documented together with the controls and strength that every pathway must enforce.

tests.title: Look for undocumented or weaker authentication pathways
tests.obj: Finds alternative channels or endpoints with weaker authentication than the main login.
steps: Find other channels: mobile site, old API versions, staging hosts, partner sites and call centre.
Read robots.txt, sitemap.xml and the help pages for links to them.
Try the same account on each channel.
Compare lockout, MFA, password reset and TLS on each channel with the main login.
Send the same login to each API version and look for missing checks.
tests.ex: ffuf -w hosts.txt -u https://FUZZ.target/login ; curl -i https://m.target/myaccount/ ; curl -i https://target/api/v1/login vs /api/v2/login
tests.exp: Every channel and API version enforces the same authentication strength. No undocumented pathway exists.

tests.title: Try to bypass the authentication schema
tests.obj: Finds protected pages that can be reached by parameter changes, forced browsing or injection in the login.
pre: Do not run on production without owner approval.
steps: Request each protected page without a session.
Change values such as authenticated=no to authenticated=yes in URLs, cookies and hidden fields.
Skip the second step of a multi-step login and request the final page.
Try SQL injection payloads in the user and password fields.
Look at the session ID values for predictable patterns.
tests.ex: curl -i 'https://target/page.asp?authenticated=yes' ; sqlmap -u https://target/login --data 'user=a&pass=b' --level 3 --batch
tests.exp: Protected pages need a valid server-side session. Client-side values do not change the result. Login input is not injectable.

tests.title: Check password comparison for type and length flaws
tests.obj: Finds loose hash comparison, magic hashes and logins that accept a wrong password of the right length.
pre: Source code access for the code part.
steps: Log in with a wrong password that has the same length as the real one.
Set a password whose hash starts with 0e and digits. Log in with a different 0e hash password.
In PHP code, look for == in hash and token checks.
Send a wrong-type value, such as true or an array, in place of the password or token.
tests.ex: Test hashes: md5('240610708') and md5('QLTHNDT') both start with 0e; try each as the password for an account that holds the other. grep -rn '== md5\|== sha1' src/
tests.exp: The application accepts only the exact password. It uses strict, constant-time comparison with fixed types.

tests.title: Check the remember me function and stored credentials
tests.obj: Finds remember me tokens or stored credentials that stay valid too long or can be read.
steps: Log in with remember me turned on.
Look in cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage for passwords or encoded credentials.
Decode every stored value and look for user names or passwords.
Make sure the token expires and the server can revoke it.
Check that login forms can not be framed or auto-submitted from another site.
tests.ex: Browser DevTools > Application tab; echo '<value>' | base64 -d ; curl -I https://target/login | grep -i x-frame-options
tests.exp: The browser holds no password or reversible credential. The remember me token is random, expires, and the server can revoke it.

tests.title: Check that the browser cache does not keep private pages
tests.obj: Finds sensitive pages that the browser stores or shows again after logout.
steps: Log in and open pages with sensitive data.
Log out and press the Back button.
Look at the Cache-Control header on every authenticated response.
Search the browser cache directory for sensitive values.
Repeat with a mobile User-Agent.
tests.ex: curl -sI -b 'session=<id>' https://target/account | grep -i cache-control ; ZAP passive scan rule 'Re-examine Cache-control Directives'
tests.exp: Authenticated responses with sensitive data have Cache-Control: no-store. The Back button after logout does not show private data.

tests.title: Check that users get notice of suspicious sign-in events
tests.obj: Finds missing alerts for unusual or partly successful sign-in events.
pre: Test mailbox.
steps: Sign in from a new device and a new location.
Fail the second factor with the correct password.
Sign in successfully after several failures.
Look at the notices: message, email and recent-login page.
tests.ex: Log in with curl using a different User-Agent and X-Forwarded-For through a VPN; then read the mailbox of the test user.
tests.exp: The user gets a notice for each suspicious event with time, device and place. The notice does not leak data of other users.

tests.title: Check that email is not an authentication factor
tests.obj: Finds designs that use email as a sole or additional factor for high assurance.
steps: Read the authentication design and the login flow.
Find any step that uses an emailed code or link as a factor.
Make sure email is not used as a single factor or as a second factor.
tests.ex: Log in with a test user and record each prompt in Burp; mark any step that sends a code to an email address.
tests.exp: Email is not used as a single or second authentication factor at the L3 level. Stronger factors are used.

tests.title: Check notices after changes to authentication details
tests.obj: Finds missing notices after password reset or email and user name change.
pre: Test mailbox.
steps: Reset the password of a test user.
Change the email address and the user name.
Read the messages that the old and the new address receive.
Make sure the messages do not contain the password or a secret.
tests.ex: Use a mail catcher such as MailHog: POST /account/email new=a@b.test, then list the messages for the old address.
tests.exp: The user gets a notice after each change to authentication details. The notice goes to the old address as well. It contains no secrets.

tests.title: Check that one IdP cannot spoof a user of another IdP
tests.obj: Finds account linking by email or user ID alone, which lets a second IdP take over an account.
pre: Two IdPs or a test IdP that you control.
steps: List the IdPs that the application supports.
Create an account at one IdP with the same email and user ID as a victim of another IdP.
Log in to the application through that IdP.
Examine if the application links the session to the victim account.
Read the code for the account key: it must be IdP ID plus user ID.
tests.ex: Register user victim@corp.test at a test IdP; log in with 'Login with IdP-B' and compare the resulting account ID.
tests.exp: The application identifies users by IdP ID plus the IdP user ID. It does not link accounts by email or name alone.

tests.title: Check that SAML and JWT assertion signatures are required
tests.obj: Finds assertions that the application accepts without a valid signature.
steps: Decode the SAMLResponse or the ID token and note the signed parts.
Remove the signature and send the message.
Change the NameID or a claim and keep the old signature.
Sign the message with a different key.
Move the signature between Response and Assertion.
tests.ex: Burp SAML Raider: remove signatures, modify NameID, re-sign with a cloned self-signed certificate, then forward the SAMLResponse to /saml/acs.
tests.exp: The application rejects unsigned assertions and any assertion with a bad signature. It uses only the signed data.

tests.title: Check that SAML assertions cannot be replayed
tests.obj: Finds assertions that the service provider accepts more than once.
steps: Log in through SAML and capture the SAMLResponse.
Log out. Send the same SAMLResponse again.
Send it twice inside the validity time.
Check the Conditions: NotOnOrAfter and OneTimeUse.
tests.ex: curl -i -X POST https://target/saml/acs --data-urlencode 'SAMLResponse=<captured>' -d 'RelayState=/' (send twice).
tests.exp: The service provider accepts each assertion ID only once in its validity period and rejects repeats, also after logout.

tests.title: Check that the application uses IdP authentication strength data
tests.obj: Finds functions that need strong or recent login but do not check what the IdP reports.
steps: Find functions that need MFA or a recent login.
Log in with a weak method at the IdP.
Call those functions and look at the response.
Read the code for checks of the acr, amr and auth_time claims.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <id_token> to read acr, amr, auth_time; then call the sensitive endpoint with a session from a password-only login.
tests.exp: The application checks the strength, method and age of the login from the IdP data before it allows the function.

tests.title: Check SAML conditions: audience, recipient, issuer and time
tests.obj: Finds service providers that do not enforce the Conditions and Subject data of an assertion.
steps: Change the Audience to another service provider.
Use the assertion before NotBefore and after NotOnOrAfter.
Change the Recipient so it does not match the ACS URL.
Send a response for an InResponseTo ID that this service did not issue.
Send a response with a different Issuer.
tests.ex: SAML Raider: edit Conditions/AudienceRestriction and SubjectConfirmationData/@Recipient, re-sign with the test IdP key, post to the ACS endpoint.
tests.exp: The service provider rejects each changed or expired assertion. It checks Audience, Recipient, Issuer, validity and InResponseTo.

tests.title: Test SAML signature wrapping and NameID parsing
tests.obj: Finds parser flaws that let an attacker place unsigned identity data next to a valid signature.
steps: Copy the signed Assertion to a new place and add a changed assertion.
Use a NameID such as user@example.com plus an XML comment and .attacker.com.
Add a second Assertion for another user.
Check if attributes can set roles or groups without a limit.
Look for XSLT in the signature transforms.
tests.ex: SAML Raider XSW 1-8 attacks; NameID test value: user@example.com<!---->.attacker.com
tests.exp: The service provider reads identity only from the element whose signature it checked. Comments and extra assertions have no effect. Role attributes are limited.

tests.title: Check SAML RelayState, IdP-initiated login and logout
tests.obj: Finds open redirects, login CSRF and unsigned logout in SAML flows.
steps: Change RelayState to an external URL and log in.
Send an unsolicited response without an earlier request.
Log out at the service provider. Look at the LogoutRequest signature.
Use the old session cookie after logout.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: POST /saml/acs RelayState=https://evil.example/ ; replay the session cookie after SLO.
tests.exp: RelayState allows only expected values. Unsolicited responses are accepted only if this is documented. Logout ends the session and uses signed messages.

tests.title: Check protection of certificates used for authentication assertions
tests.obj: Finds trusted certificates that an attacker can change.
pre: Server or configuration access.
steps: Find where the service stores the IdP or device certificates.
Look at the file and database permissions.
Try to change a certificate with a low-privilege account.
Check for integrity protection, such as a signed store or read-only mount.
tests.ex: ls -l /etc/app/trust/ ; icacls C:\app\trust ; review the keystore ACL and backup access.
tests.exp: Only privileged administrators can change trusted certificates. Changes are detected or logged.

tests.title: Check the challenge nonce of cryptographic authentication
tests.obj: Finds short or repeated challenge nonces in WebAuthn or certificate authentication.
steps: Start 1000 login challenges and save each nonce.
Look at the nonce length. It must be at least 64 bits.
Look for repeated values.
Make sure the server stores and checks the challenge for one login only.
tests.ex: for i in $(seq 1000); do curl -s https://target/webauthn/challenge | jq -r .challenge; done | sort | uniq -d
tests.exp: Each challenge is at least 64 bits long, unique, and valid for one login only.

tests.title: Check that authentication events are logged and alerted
tests.obj: Finds missing logs for failed logins and lockouts, which hides attacks.
steps: Cause failed logins, a lockout and a password reset.
Read the application and security logs.
Make sure the log has time, source, account and result.
Make sure passwords and tokens are not in the log.
Check that repeated failures raise an alert.
tests.ex: grep -iE 'login failed|locked' /var/log/app/auth.log | tail ; grep -i 'password=' /var/log/app/*.log
tests.exp: All failed logins, lockouts and resets are logged and reviewed. Alerts exist for attack patterns. Logs hold no secrets.

tests.title: Read the authorization rules for functions and data
tests.obj: Finds missing rules for who may use which function and which data.
pre: Access to documentation.
steps: Get the authorization documentation.
Make sure it lists function-level rules by consumer permission.
Make sure it lists data-specific rules by resource attribute.
Compare five rules with real behavior.
tests.ex: Build a role-to-endpoint matrix from the document, then replay it with Autorize or ZAP Access Control Testing.
tests.exp: The documentation defines function-level and data-specific access rules. The application follows them.

tests.title: Read the field-level access rules
tests.obj: Finds missing rules for who may read or write each field.
pre: Access to documentation.
steps: Get the authorization documentation.
Make sure it defines read and write rules for each sensitive field.
Look for rules that depend on object state, such as status.
Compare with the API schema.
tests.ex: Compare the OpenAPI schema (readOnly, writeOnly) with the documented field matrix.
tests.exp: Field-level read and write rules are documented, including state-dependent rules.

tests.title: Read the contextual and environmental decision rules
tests.obj: Finds missing rules for time, place, IP and device in access decisions.
pre: Access to documentation.
steps: Get the authentication and authorization documentation.
Find the attributes used: time, location, IP address and device.
Make sure the document lists thresholds and actions: allow, challenge, deny, step-up.
tests.ex: Review the risk engine rules and the design document side by side.
tests.exp: The attributes, risk thresholds and actions are documented for authentication and authorization decisions.

tests.title: Test function-level access for each role
tests.obj: Finds functions that users can call without explicit permission.
steps: Map all functions and admin pages for each role.
Log in as a low role. Call the functions of a higher role with a proxy.
Call the same requests with no session.
Change HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.
Compare every response with the response of the allowed role.
tests.ex: Burp Autorize: set the low-privilege cookie and browse as admin; or POST /admin/addUser (userID=fakeuser&role=3) with a user cookie.
tests.exp: Only roles with explicit permission can use each function. Others get 401 or 403 for every method.

tests.title: Test forced browsing without a session
tests.obj: Finds pages and operations that need no login.
steps: Collect all URLs from crawl, JavaScript and API docs.
Request each URL without a session.
Request admin and internal paths.
Check the files in storage buckets that hold uploads.
tests.ex: ffuf -w urls.txt -u https://target/FUZZ -mc 200,204,301,302,403 ; ZAP: Access Control Testing add-on with an unauthenticated context.
tests.exp: Non-public URLs return 401 or redirect to login. Stored private files are not public.

tests.title: Test privilege escalation by parameter and profile changes
tests.obj: Finds hidden fields, groups or conditions that a user can change to gain privileges.
steps: Look for group, profile, role and flag fields in requests, hidden fields and responses.
Change a value, such as profile=SysGuest to SysAdmin.
Change the group ID or order ID to one outside your group.
Try to add yourself to a higher role.
tests.ex: POST /user/viewOrder.jsp groupID=grp002&orderID=0001 from a grp001 user; also change <input name='profile' value='SysAdmin'>.
tests.exp: The server does not trust client values for role, group or privilege. A user cannot raise their own privilege.

tests.title: Test field-level access and mass assignment
tests.obj: Finds objects where users can read or write fields they should not.
steps: Compare the fields in responses for different roles.
Add extra fields such as role, isAdmin and balance to update requests.
Change read-only fields.
Check fields that depend on state, such as status.
tests.ex: curl -X PATCH https://target/api/users/me -b 'session=<user>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"role":"admin","isAdmin":true}'
tests.exp: Users cannot read or write fields without permission. Unknown and protected fields are ignored or rejected.

tests.title: Test adaptive access controls at login and during a session
tests.obj: Finds contextual controls that apply only at login or not at all.
steps: Read the documented context rules.
Log in from a new device and an unusual place.
Change the IP, device or time during an active session.
Check the action: step-up, deny or revoke.
tests.ex: Move the test session to a different VPN country and call a sensitive endpoint.
tests.exp: Context rules apply when a session starts and during the session, with the documented action.

tests.title: Check that authorization is enforced on the server
tests.obj: Finds access control that exists only in client-side code.
steps: Find controls hidden in JavaScript or by CSS.
Call hidden admin URLs with curl.
Remove or change client-side checks with a proxy.
Send API calls that the UI never makes.
tests.ex: curl -i https://target/app/admin_getappInfo -b 'session=<user>'
tests.exp: The server decides access on every request. Changes in client code do not change the result.

tests.title: Check that permission changes apply at once
tests.obj: Finds tokens or caches that keep old permissions after a change.
steps: Log in as a user and keep the session or token.
Remove a role from the user as administrator.
Call a function of that role at once.
Check the lifetime of the token or cache.
tests.ex: curl -i -H 'Authorization: Bearer <old jwt>' https://target/api/admin/report right after the role is removed.
tests.exp: A permission change takes effect at once. If not, there is a control that alerts on the action and reverts it.

tests.title: Check that back-end calls use the original user permissions
tests.obj: Finds services that act with their own rights on behalf of a user.
steps: Map the calls between internal services for one user action.
Call the action with a low-privilege user token.
Look at the token that the second service gets.
Check that the second service enforces the user rights.
tests.ex: Trace with a proxy or service mesh logs: compare the Authorization headers on hop 1 and hop 2.
tests.exp: Services pass on the user identity and apply the user permissions. No service acts as a confused deputy.

tests.title: Test tenant isolation in multi-tenant applications
tests.obj: Finds operations that affect other tenants.
steps: Create two tenants with a user in each.
Use IDs, names and tokens of tenant A in requests as a user of tenant B.
Change a tenant header or subdomain value.
Check search, export and bulk functions.
tests.ex: curl -b 'session=<tenantB user>' -H 'X-Tenant-ID: tenantA' https://target/api/invoices
tests.exp: A user can never read or change data of another tenant.

tests.title: Check layers of control on administrative interfaces
tests.obj: Finds admin interfaces that rely only on network location.
steps: List admin interfaces.
Reach them from a trusted network with a low role.
Check for ongoing identity checks, device posture and risk analysis.
Check that network location alone is not enough.
tests.ex: curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' https://target/admin ; review the admin gateway policy.
tests.exp: Admin access needs several layers: continuous identity checks, device posture and risk analysis. Network location is never the only factor.

tests.title: Test bypass with special request headers
tests.obj: Finds access control that trusts headers such as X-Original-URL or X-Forwarded-For.
steps: Send a blocked admin URL with X-Original-URL set to it, with a harmless request path.
Do the same with X-Rewrite-URL.
Add X-Forwarded-For, X-Client-IP and X-Remote-Addr with 127.0.0.1, ::1 and RFC1918 addresses.
Try IPv4-mapped IPv6 values.
tests.ex: curl -i https://target/ -H 'X-Original-URL: /admin' ; curl -i https://target/admin -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1'
tests.exp: Header values do not change the path or the client identity. The blocked page stays blocked.

tests.title: Test directory traversal and file inclusion in file parameters
tests.obj: Finds parameters that read files outside the allowed folder.
steps: Find parameters that name files, templates or pages, also in cookies.
Send ../ sequences with 3 to 8 levels.
Send encoded forms: %2e%2e%2f, double encoding and backslashes.
Try an absolute path and a remote URL.
On Windows, try UNC paths and trailing characters.
tests.ex: ffuf -w LFI-Jhaddix.txt -u 'https://target/index.php?file=FUZZ' -fs <size> ; curl 'https://target/getUserProfile.jsp?item=../../../../etc/passwd'
tests.exp: The application accepts only expected file names. Traversal and remote includes are rejected after full decoding.

tests.title: Check URL path matching in authorization rules
tests.obj: Finds rules that use partial string matching on URLs.
steps: Read the code for startswith, endswith, contains and indexOf on paths.
Send encoded, double-slash and dot-segment paths to protected URLs.
Try different case and trailing characters.
tests.ex: curl -i 'https://target//admin' ; curl -i 'https://target/%2e%2e/admin' ; curl -i 'https://target/admin;.css'
tests.exp: Authorization uses the normalized path and exact rules. Encoded paths and dot segments do not skip a check.

tests.title: Check deny by default and checks on every request
tests.obj: Finds new or unlisted routes and methods that have no access control.
steps: List all routes from the code or API description.
Find routes with no access rule.
Call them without rights, using POST, PUT and DELETE too.
Check that one shared mechanism enforces checks on every request.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'permitAll\|@PermitAll\|skip_authorization' src/ ; compare the OpenAPI paths with the security config.
tests.exp: Access is denied when no rule matches. Every request goes through the same authorization check, including AJAX and API calls.

tests.title: Check logging and alerts for access control failures
tests.obj: Finds access control failures that nobody sees, and automated abuse that is not limited.
steps: Send 20 forbidden requests.
Read the logs for each failure.
Check for an alert after repeated failures.
Check for a rate limit on API and controller access.
tests.ex: for i in $(seq 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -b 'session=<user>' https://target/admin; done; grep 403 /var/log/app/access.log | tail
tests.exp: Access control failures are logged. Repeated failures raise an alert. API and controller access has a rate limit.

tests.title: Test forged requests that skip the frontend workflow
tests.obj: Finds backend endpoints that accept forged requests without the checks the frontend enforces.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Observe HTTP traffic for guessable or sequential values, such as an incrementing transaction ID.
Observe for hidden fields or parameters indicating debug or development functionality.
Submit a forged request directly to the backend endpoint, skipping the frontend screens.
Guess or change a hidden field value, such as a discount flag, and resubmit.
tests.ex: Change a hidden field senior_discount=false to senior_discount=true and resubmit directly to the checkout endpoint
tests.exp: The backend independently re-derives discounts, prices and flags and rejects requests that were not produced by the real workflow.

tests.title: Test non-editable and hidden fields for integrity bypass
tests.obj: Finds hidden, read-only or dropdown-bound fields that the server trusts without re-validation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Capture a request containing a hidden field, a disabled form control, or a value shown only in a dropdown.
Submit the request with that field changed to a value not offered by the interface.
Submit a value for a field that only an administrator should be able to set.
Check whether application logs can be modified by submitting crafted log-bound input.
tests.ex: Change a hidden price=20.00 field to price=0.01, or a role dropdown value to a role never shown to this user
tests.exp: The server treats hidden and non-editable fields as untrusted and revalidates every value against the business rule.

tests.title: Test time-dependent processes for information leakage and race windows
tests.obj: Finds processing time differences that leak information or create a window to exploit a transaction.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a process whose completion time might depend on a secret, such as login or password reset.
Measure and compare response time for valid and invalid inputs across many requests.
Identify a time-sensitive transaction, such as a price quote with an expiry, and test extending it past the expected window.
tests.ex: Automated timing script sending repeated login attempts with valid and invalid usernames, comparing mean response time
tests.exp: Response time does not depend on whether input is valid, and time-sensitive transactions are strictly bound to their stated window server-side.

tests.title: Test functions that should set a hard limit on repeated use
tests.obj: Finds coupon, bonus or similar functions missing a server-side limit on how many times they can run.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a function documented or expected to run only once or a limited number of times per user.
Call the function repeatedly, for example reapplying a one-time discount code.
Check whether the limit is enforced per account, per session or globally as required.
tests.ex: Reapply the same one-time discount code repeatedly in separate checkout requests
tests.exp: The limit on the number of times a function can be used is enforced server-side and cannot be bypassed by repeating the request.

tests.title: Test multi-step workflows for step skipping and reordering
tests.obj: Finds workflows that can be completed out of order or with required steps skipped entirely.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Map every step of a multi-step workflow and the request associated with each step.
Call a later-stage endpoint directly without completing the earlier required steps.
Replay or reorder captured requests to reach an unauthorized or unintended state.
Submit a status or phase parameter with an invalid, future, or unauthorized value.
tests.ex: Call the order-fulfillment endpoint directly without a preceding confirmed-payment step; replay step 3 before step 2
tests.exp: The server tracks workflow state itself and rejects a request for any step whose prerequisites were not completed in order.

tests.title: Test transactional operations for atomic all-or-nothing behavior
tests.obj: Finds multi-step business transactions that can be left in a partially applied state.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a business operation composed of multiple writes, such as a transfer that debits one account and credits another.
Interrupt the operation partway, for example by closing the connection after the first write.
Check whether the operation rolls back completely or leaves an inconsistent partial state.
tests.ex: Terminate the connection immediately after the debit step of a funds transfer and check both account balances afterward
tests.exp: The business operation runs inside a transaction that either completes in full or rolls back to the prior correct state.

tests.title: Test limited-quantity resources for double-booking
tests.obj: Finds booking or allocation logic missing a locking mechanism for a limited resource.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a limited-quantity resource, such as a seat, slot or inventory item.
Send two or more concurrent requests to reserve the same resource.
Check whether more reservations succeed than the resource actually has capacity for.
tests.ex: Fire 20 concurrent requests for the last available seat using a tool such as Turbo Intruder or ffuf with -c
tests.exp: A business-logic-level lock or atomic conditional update prevents more reservations than the resource has capacity for.

tests.title: Test high-value flows for required multi-user approval
tests.obj: Finds high-value or safety-critical business actions that a single user can complete alone.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify high-value flows, such as a large monetary transfer or an access-level change.
Try to complete the flow with a single compromised account and no second approver.
Check whether the application requires a second, independent approval for the action.
tests.ex: Submit a large fund transfer as a single authenticated user with no second approval step triggered
tests.exp: High-value business flows require a second, independent approval before the action takes effect.

tests.title: Test functions for anti-automation and rate-limit controls
tests.obj: Finds application functions reachable at excessive volume without a rate limit or anti-automation control.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify functions that could be abused by automation, such as a search, coupon check or export.
Send a high volume of requests to the function using an automated tool.
Check whether the application applies a rate limit, CAPTCHA or account lock after excessive use.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://target/api/coupon?code=FUZZ -w codes.txt -t 50 and observe whether throttling begins
tests.exp: The application enforces a rate limit or anti-automation control before quota exhaustion, data exfiltration or denial-of-service can occur.

tests.title: Test transaction submission timing against expected human speed
tests.obj: Finds workflows missing a check for unrealistically fast, automated transaction submission.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a multi-step flow with a timing assumption, such as filling a form or confirming a purchase.
Automate the flow to complete every step far faster than a human could.
Check whether the application detects and blocks the unrealistic timing.
tests.ex: Automated script submitting a multi-field form in under 200 milliseconds, repeated across many sessions
tests.exp: The application detects submissions faster than realistic human timing and blocks or challenges them.

tests.title: Test active defenses against combined application misuse
tests.obj: Finds applications that take no defensive action after a user sends many clearly malicious requests.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Send a sequence of mild then increasingly malicious probes: an invalid ID, a tick character, a verb change.
Continue probing with a blatant SQL injection or XSS payload.
Observe whether the application changes behavior, such as adding delays, extra authentication, or blocking the session.
tests.ex: Sequence: /file?id=999 -> /file?id=' -> change GET to POST -> duplicate a parameter -> submit ' OR 1=1-- and watch for a defensive response
tests.exp: The application detects the pattern of misuse and responds with increased scrutiny, delays, or a block rather than processing every request normally.

tests.title: Test payment quantity and price fields for business logic tampering
tests.obj: Finds checkout logic that trusts client-supplied quantity, price or currency values.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Add an item to the basket and intercept the add-to-basket or checkout request.
Change the quantity to a negative number and resubmit.
If a price or currency field is present, change it to a lower value or another currency.
If a secure hash or encrypted field protects the transaction, try submitting the request without it.
tests.ex: item_id=1&quantity=-5 ; item_id=1&quantity=5&price=0.01 ; currency=XXX where USD is expected ; strip the secure_hash parameter entirely
tests.exp: The server re-derives price, quantity and currency from trusted data server-side and rejects a request without a valid integrity hash.

tests.title: Test discount codes for guessability and stacking abuse
tests.obj: Finds discount code systems with guessable codes, no brute-force protection, or unsafe stacking.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Try common discount code patterns such as TEST10 or the company name.
Submit many sequential or incremented codes to check for brute-force protection.
Apply more than one discount code to the same order and check whether they stack below cost.
tests.ex: code=TEST10 ; code=SORRY10 ; try sequential codes SAVE01..SAVE99 ; apply two valid codes to the same basket
tests.exp: Discount codes are unpredictable, rate-limited against brute force, and cannot be stacked to push the price below cost.

tests.title: Test payment race conditions and double-spend windows
tests.obj: Finds payment flows vulnerable to a race between a check and a write on a balance or stock value.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a payment or balance operation with a check-then-act pattern, such as spending a gift card balance.
Send multiple concurrent requests that use the same balance or the same one-time resource.
Check whether more value or resource is consumed than the balance actually allows.
tests.ex: Fire 20 concurrent gift-card redemption requests against a balance that should cover only one redemption
tests.exp: The balance check and debit run inside a single atomic transaction or a conditional update, so concurrent requests cannot overdraw it.

tests.title: Test redirect parameters for open redirect
tests.obj: Finds client-side redirect logic that sends a user to an attacker domain from an unvalidated parameter.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find client-side code that reads a redirect target from the URL hash, query string or a parameter.
Submit an external domain as the redirect target and confirm the browser navigates there.
If plain domains are blocked, try the javascript: scheme in the same parameter.
tests.ex: https://target/?#www.malicious-example.invalid ; https://target/?#javascript:alert(document.cookie) ; redir=https://malicious-example.invalid
tests.exp: Redirect destinations are checked against an allowlist of trusted hostnames before navigation, and dangerous schemes are rejected.

tests.title: Test CORS configuration for overly permissive origin handling
tests.obj: Finds CORS responses that reflect an arbitrary origin or allow the null origin with credentials.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Send a request with an attacker-controlled Origin header to each API endpoint.
Check whether Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflects the submitted origin or returns a wildcard.
If credentials are used, check whether Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true alongside a reflected or null origin.
Test a crafted subdomain, for example target.com.attacker.com, against a regex-based allowlist.
tests.ex: Origin: https://attacker.example ; Origin: null (from a sandboxed iframe) ; Origin: https://example.com.attacker.com against regex /\.example.com$/
tests.exp: The server allows only an explicit allowlist of trusted origins, never reflects an arbitrary or null origin together with credentials.

tests.title: Test clickjacking protections with an embedding iframe
tests.obj: Finds pages that can be framed by another origin and tricked into unintended clicks.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Create a test page that loads the target in an iframe.
Load the test page in a browser and confirm whether the target renders inside the frame.
Check the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive and the X-Frame-Options header on the response.
Repeat the test with JavaScript disabled to rule out a frame-busting script as the only defense.
tests.ex: <iframe src="https://target" width="400" height="400"></iframe> ; check header Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
tests.exp: The response sets frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options so the page cannot be framed by an untrusted origin, even with JavaScript disabled.

tests.title: Test WebSocket origin checks and transport security
tests.obj: Finds WebSocket endpoints that accept connections from any origin or run over unencrypted ws.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify WebSocket usage from the client source or the browser network panel.
Try to open a WebSocket connection from a different origin and check if the server accepts it.
Check whether the endpoint uses the wss scheme instead of plain ws.
Fuzz WebSocket messages for the same injection classes used on normal HTTP input.
tests.ex: new WebSocket("wss://target/socket") opened with a forged Origin header from a separate test page
tests.exp: The server validates the Origin header on the handshake, enforces wss, and treats WebSocket input with the same injection controls as HTTP.

tests.title: Test postMessage handlers for origin and input validation
tests.obj: Finds window message listeners that trust the sender origin or the message content without checks.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review client-side code for a message event listener and note how it checks event.origin.
From an attacker page, send a postMessage with an origin check bypass, for example a domain containing the expected substring.
Send a message with an unexpected structure or an invalid, non-JSON payload and check if the handler discards it.
Send a message containing an embedded script and check if it is evaluated as HTML.
tests.ex: iframe1.contentWindow.postMessage(payload,"*") from https://www.owasp.org.attacker.example to pass an indexOf(".owasp.org") check
tests.exp: The receiving handler checks the full origin string with strict equality, discards invalid-syntax messages, and treats data as untrusted text.

tests.title: Test browser storage for sensitive data and injection risk
tests.obj: Finds localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB entries holding sensitive data or session tokens.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Open developer tools and list all keys and values in localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB.
Check whether any value is a session token, password or other sensitive data.
Trigger a stored or reflected XSS proof-of-concept and confirm it can read these values.
tests.ex: for(let i=0;i<localStorage.length;i++){console.log(localStorage.key(i),localStorage.getItem(localStorage.key(i)))}
tests.exp: No session token or sensitive data is stored in localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB; session tokens use HttpOnly cookies instead.

tests.title: Test same-origin JavaScript resources for cross-site script inclusion
tests.obj: Finds a script resource that leaks sensitive data when included cross-origin as a classic script tag.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify script resources that return sensitive data as a global variable, JSONP or an array literal.
From an attacker-controlled page, include the script with a script tag while the victim session cookie is sent.
Read the resulting global variable or array prototype from the attacker page and confirm the leaked data.
tests.ex: <script src="https://target/internal/api.js"></script> then read window.secret from the attacker page
tests.exp: Sensitive endpoints require a non-GET method or a custom header, are not valid JavaScript, and set a restrictive SameSite cookie.

tests.title: Test window.open links for reverse tabnabbing
tests.obj: Finds links opened in a new tab that can redirect the original tab through window.opener.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find links or window.open calls that open user-controlled or third-party URLs in a new tab.
Check the HTML source for the rel attribute on target="_blank" links.
Open the link and confirm whether the opened page can set window.opener.location.
tests.ex: <script>window.opener.location="https://malicious-example.invalid";</script> in the page opened by a user-supplied link
tests.exp: Every link that opens a new tab sets rel="noopener noreferrer" or the browser default behavior is relied on and confirmed.

tests.title: Test cookie attributes for Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
tests.obj: Finds session or sensitive cookies missing the Secure, HttpOnly or correct SameSite attribute.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Log in and inspect the Set-Cookie header for every session or sensitive cookie.
Confirm the Secure attribute is present and the cookie uses the __Host- or __Secure- prefix.
Confirm the HttpOnly attribute is present on cookies not needed by client-side script.
Confirm the SameSite attribute matches the purpose of the cookie.
tests.ex: curl -I https://target/login then inspect Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict
tests.exp: Every session cookie sets Secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value, and uses a __Host- or __Secure- prefix.

tests.title: Test cookie size limit handling
tests.obj: Finds application behavior when a cookie name and value exceed the browser storage limit.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Set a cookie whose name and value combined exceed 4096 bytes.
Reload the page and check whether the browser stored and sent the oversized cookie.
Confirm the application still functions correctly when the cookie is dropped.
tests.ex: document.cookie = "big="+"A".repeat(4100)
tests.exp: Cookies stay under 4096 bytes combined, and the application degrades safely if a browser drops an oversized cookie.

tests.title: Test HSTS header presence and configuration
tests.obj: Finds missing or weak Strict-Transport-Security headers that allow protocol downgrade.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request the site over HTTPS and inspect the Strict-Transport-Security response header.
Confirm max-age is at least one year and includeSubDomains is present if subdomains use HTTPS.
Check whether the domain is present on the HSTS preload list.
tests.ex: curl -I https://target then check for Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
tests.exp: Every HTTPS response sets Strict-Transport-Security with a max-age of at least one year and includeSubDomains where applicable.

tests.title: Test Content-Security-Policy header strength
tests.obj: Finds a missing CSP or a CSP that lacks object-src, base-uri or a strict script source list.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request a page and inspect the Content-Security-Policy header or meta tag.
Confirm object-src and base-uri are set to none.
Confirm script-src uses nonces, hashes or an allowlist rather than unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval.
Try the earlier reflected XSS payloads again with the CSP active to confirm it blocks execution.
tests.ex: curl -I https://target then check Content-Security-Policy: object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; script-src 'nonce-RANDOM'
tests.exp: The CSP sets object-src none, base-uri none, and restricts scripts with nonces, hashes or a narrow allowlist, blocking injected inline scripts.

tests.title: Test response headers for MIME sniffing and referrer leakage
tests.obj: Finds missing X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy headers that leak data or allow MIME confusion.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request several response types and inspect the X-Content-Type-Options header.
Navigate from a page containing sensitive query parameters to an external link and inspect the Referer sent.
Confirm a Referrer-Policy header or meta tag restricts what is sent cross-origin.
tests.ex: curl -I https://target then check X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
tests.exp: Every response sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and a Referrer-Policy that avoids leaking sensitive URL data to third parties.

tests.title: Test Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy on document responses
tests.obj: Finds document responses missing Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, allowing tabnabbing and frame counting.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request the main HTML document and inspect the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header.
Confirm the value is same-origin or same-origin-allow-popups as the application requires.
Open the page from an attacker tab using window.open and check whether window references leak.
tests.ex: curl -I https://target then check Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
tests.exp: HTML document responses set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy to same-origin or same-origin-allow-popups.

tests.title: Test CORS preflight enforcement for sensitive actions
tests.obj: Finds sensitive endpoints reachable by a simple cross-origin request that skips the CORS preflight.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a sensitive endpoint relied on to be protected by the CORS preflight mechanism.
Send the request cross-origin using only CORS-safelisted headers and a simple content type to avoid a preflight.
Check whether the server processes the request despite not seeing an OPTIONS preflight.
tests.ex: fetch("https://target/api/transfer",{method:"POST",credentials:"include",headers:{"Content-Type":"text/plain"},body:"amount=100"}) from an attacker page
tests.exp: Sensitive endpoints require a custom header or a method that cannot be sent without a CORS preflight, or validate Origin and Content-Type strictly.

tests.title: Test state-changing endpoints for unsafe HTTP methods
tests.obj: Finds sensitive functionality reachable with a safe HTTP method such as GET.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify state-changing functionality, such as a delete or transfer action.
Resend the action using the GET method instead of POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
Check the Sec-Fetch-* request headers the server receives and whether it validates them.
tests.ex: GET /api/account/delete?id=123 HTTP/1.1 sent instead of the original DELETE request
tests.exp: Sensitive functionality rejects safe HTTP methods and validates Sec-Fetch-* headers to block cross-origin navigation or resource loads.

tests.title: Test that unrelated applications share a hostname insecurely
tests.obj: Finds separate applications hosted on the same origin that weaken same-origin policy isolation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify whether unrelated applications or trust levels are hosted under the same scheme, host and port.
Check whether a lower-trust application can set cookies or access storage visible to the higher-trust application.
Review hostname-based cookie scoping for each application.
tests.ex: Compare cookie Domain and Path scoping between https://target/app1 and https://target/app2 sharing one origin
tests.exp: Applications with different trust levels are hosted on separate hostnames so cookies and storage do not cross between them.

tests.title: Test externally hosted client-side assets for Subresource Integrity
tests.obj: Finds externally hosted scripts, styles or fonts loaded without an integrity attribute.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List every script, link and font tag that loads from an external host or CDN.
Check each external tag for an integrity attribute with a matching hash.
Confirm the asset is versioned and static rather than a mutable or latest-tag URL.
tests.ex: <script src="https://cdn.example/lib.js" integrity="sha384-HASH" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
tests.exp: Every externally hosted static asset is versioned and loaded with a matching Subresource Integrity hash, or hosted internally.

tests.title: Test for use of unsupported or insecure client-side technology
tests.obj: Finds pages that still rely on retired plugin technologies such as Flash, Silverlight or Java applets.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review page source and network requests for plugin object or embed tags.
Check for Flash, Silverlight, ActiveX, NACL or Java applet content types.
Confirm the application functions fully without any retired plugin technology.
tests.ex: grep -riE "application/x-shockwave-flash|silverlight|activex|applet" against page source and asset list
tests.exp: No page relies on Flash, Silverlight, ActiveX, NACL or Java applets to function.

tests.title: Test browser security feature fallback behavior
tests.obj: Finds applications that behave unsafely when an expected browser security feature is unsupported.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review documentation or the application for expected browser security features such as CSP or HSTS support.
Use a browser or a developer tools override that disables one expected feature, such as CSP enforcement.
Confirm the application warns the user or blocks access rather than continuing silently without protection.
tests.ex: Disable CSP enforcement in browser devtools or use a legacy user agent, then load the application
tests.exp: The application warns the user or blocks access when a browser does not support an expected security feature, as documented.

tests.title: Test authenticated resource embedding across origins
tests.obj: Finds authenticated images, scripts or documents that an attacker page can embed or load.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an authenticated resource such as an image, video or script that is loaded while a session cookie is set.
From an attacker page, embed the resource URL and check whether it loads using the victim session.
Inspect the response for a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header and Sec-Fetch-Dest validation.
tests.ex: embedded on an attacker page while the victim is logged in
tests.exp: The server validates Sec-Fetch-* headers or sets a restrictive Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy so other origins cannot load authenticated resources.

tests.title: Test query parameters for HTTP Parameter Pollution
tests.obj: Finds inconsistent handling of duplicate parameter names that can bypass validation or filters.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Submit a request with a parameter name duplicated with two different values.
Compare the response to the single-parameter baseline to see which value the server and front-end filter used.
Repeat with a duplicated parameter inside a JSON body if the endpoint accepts JSON.
tests.ex: https://target/?mode=guest&search_string=kittens&search_string=puppies ; JSON: {"search_string":"kittens","search_string":"puppies"}
tests.exp: The application and any filter in front of it handle duplicate parameters consistently and no security check can be bypassed by duplication.

tests.title: Review the network infrastructure configuration and known server vulnerabilities
tests.obj: Find open ports, outdated servers and weak network rules around the application.
pre: Do not run vulnerability scripts on production without approval.
steps: Get the list of ports that the application needs from the owner.
Scan the hosts with Nmap and compare the open ports with the list.
Run Nuclei or Nikto and check each version-based finding by hand.
Review security groups, firewall and container network rules for rules that are wider than the list.
Look at the admin interfaces of the infrastructure for default credentials.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p- 192.0.2.10; nuclei -u https://example.com -severity medium,high,critical; nikto -h https://example.com
tests.exp: Only needed ports are open. Components are patched. Network rules follow the change-controlled port list.

tests.title: Remove default, sample and debug functionality from production
tests.obj: Find sample applications, debug modes, debug endpoints and test code that remain in the production deployment.
steps: Request known sample paths such as phpinfo.php, /swagger-ui, /actuator/env and framework welcome pages.
Trigger an application error and look for stack traces, local variables or an interactive debugger.
Look for DEBUG, FLASK_DEBUG and similar settings in the effective runtime configuration.
Check GraphQL introspection and source maps in production builds.
Review container images for sample files, build-time secrets and debug environment variables.
Compare installed modules and features with the list of required functions.
tests.ex: curl -si https://example.com/actuator/env; curl -si https://example.com/phpinfo.php; nuclei -u https://example.com -tags exposure,debug,misconfig
tests.exp: No sample, test or debug functionality is reachable. Debug mode is off in all components. Only required functionality is deployed.

tests.title: Make sure documentation and monitoring endpoints are not exposed
tests.obj: Find API documentation, health and metrics endpoints that are open to users who do not need them.
steps: Request /swagger.json, /openapi.json, /api-docs, /graphql, /metrics, /health and /actuator without credentials.
Request the same paths with a low-privilege account.
Look in robots.txt and JavaScript files for more documentation paths.
Read the content of each reachable endpoint for internal host names and secrets.
Compare the result with the list of intended public endpoints.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://example.com/FUZZ -w api-docs-wordlist.txt -mc 200,401,403; curl -si https://example.com/openapi.json
tests.exp: Documentation and monitoring endpoints need authentication and are limited to the intended network, or they do not exist.

tests.title: Find old, backup and unreferenced files and unsafe file extension handling
tests.obj: Find backup copies, include files, archives and dumps that the web server serves in readable form.
steps: Request common suffixes on known files: .bak, .old, .orig, .save, .swp, .inc, .zip and the tilde suffix.
Request archives and dumps such as backup.zip, db.sql, .env and terraform.tfstate on the web root.
Check how the server handles unknown and sensitive extensions in each directory.
Try Windows 8.3 short names where the host runs Windows.
Check cloud storage that holds static files for forgotten artifacts.
Look at the server configuration for the allowed file extensions.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://example.com/FUZZ -w raft-medium-files.txt -e .bak,.old,.zip,.sql,.inc,.env,~ -mc 200; nuclei -u https://example.com -tags backup,config
tests.exp: The web tier serves only files with approved extensions. No backup, dump or include file is reachable.

tests.title: Make sure source control metadata is not deployed or reachable
tests.obj: Find .git, .svn and similar folders that expose source code and history.
steps: Request /.git/HEAD, /.git/config, /.svn/entries and /.hg/ on the web root and on each subpath.
If a response is valid, dump the repository with a safe tool and look for secrets in the history.
Check the deployed file tree and the container image for these folders.
Check that the application process cannot read these folders.
tests.ex: curl -si https://example.com/.git/HEAD; git-dumper https://example.com/.git ./dump && trufflehog git file://./dump
tests.exp: Source control folders do not exist in the deployment, or the server and the application cannot read them.

tests.title: Make sure directory listing is disabled
tests.obj: Find directories where the server shows a file index to users.
steps: Request each directory path found during the crawl with and without a trailing slash.
Request upload, static, backup and log directories.
Look for index pages such as Index of or Directory listing for.
Review the server configuration for the autoindex or Options Indexes setting.
tests.ex: curl -s https://example.com/static/ | grep -iE 'index of|directory listing'; nikto -h https://example.com -Tuning 2
tests.exp: The server returns 403 or 404 for directories without an index file. No file list is shown.

tests.title: Find admin interfaces and check them for weak exposure and default credentials
tests.obj: Find infrastructure and application admin consoles that are reachable by the wrong users or use default credentials.
steps: Enumerate admin paths for the framework with a wordlist, and on alternative ports.
Look at source comments and documentation for admin links.
Check consoles such as Actuator, Kubernetes Dashboard, Jenkins, Portainer and database UIs.
Try the documented default credentials of each product, within the rules of engagement.
Make sure each console is not reachable from the public internet and uses TLS.
Make sure setup wizards cannot run again.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://example.com/FUZZ -w admin-panels.txt -mc 200,301,302,401,403; nmap -p 8080,8443,9000,10250,2379 192.0.2.10
tests.exp: Admin interfaces are not public, need strong authentication and TLS, and have no default credentials.

tests.title: Make sure only needed HTTP methods work and method override is blocked
tests.obj: Find enabled methods such as PUT, DELETE, CONNECT and WebDAV, and method override that bypass access control.
steps: Send OPTIONS and read the Allow header.
Send each method from the list, and an unknown method, to each key path.
Send PUT to upload a test file and DELETE on a test file in a safe location.
Try X-HTTP-Method-Override and the _method parameter on a protected action.
Repeat the checks through the CDN or proxy and directly on the origin.
Send the request with a mixed-case method name.
tests.ex: curl -si -X OPTIONS https://example.com/; curl -si -X FOO https://example.com/; nmap -p443 --script http-methods --script-args http-methods.url-path=/ example.com
tests.exp: Only the methods that the application supports are accepted. Other methods get 405 or 501 and unused methods are blocked.

tests.title: Make sure the HTTP TRACE method is not supported
tests.obj: Find TRACE or TRACK support that echoes requests and leaks headers.
steps: Send a TRACE request with a custom header to the host.
Send a TRACK request to the host.
Repeat on every HTTP service and port found.
tests.ex: curl -si -X TRACE -H 'X-Test: 1' https://example.com/; nmap -p443 --script http-trace example.com
tests.exp: The server rejects TRACE and TRACK with 405 or 501 and does not echo the request.

tests.title: Review file and directory permissions on host, container and cloud storage
tests.obj: Find files, secrets and volumes that have wider permissions than needed.
steps: List permissions of web root, config, key, log, upload and temp directories with namei and ls -l.
Look for world-writable files and files owned by root that the web user can change.
Inspect the container image for root user and wide file modes.
Review Kubernetes securityContext, Secret defaultMode and hostPath mounts.
Review bucket ACLs and IAM bindings for public grants.
tests.ex: namei -l /var/www/app/config; find /var/www -perm -o+w -type f; docker inspect --format '{{.Config.User}}' app:latest
tests.exp: Files and secrets have least-privilege permissions. The web process cannot write to code or configuration.

tests.title: Find subdomain takeover through dangling DNS records
tests.obj: Find DNS records that point to external services that no longer exist and that an attacker can claim.
steps: Enumerate subdomains with subfinder and keep names with CNAME, NS or MX records.
Run subzy and the Nuclei takeover templates on the list.
Resolve each hit with dig and compare the page with the can-i-take-over-xyz fingerprint.
Check expired domains used in CNAME records.
Do not claim the resource. Report the finding.
tests.ex: subfinder -d example.com -silent | subzy run --targets /dev/stdin; nuclei -l subs.txt -t http/takeovers/; dig CNAME dev.example.com
tests.exp: No DNS record points to an unclaimed or expired resource.

tests.title: Check cloud storage for public access, weak signed URLs and old versions
tests.obj: Find buckets and containers that allow public listing, write access, long-lived signed URLs or exposed old object versions.
steps: Find bucket URLs in page source and responses.
Request the bucket root unauthenticated and look for a file list.
Try an unauthenticated write to the bucket.
Review ACL and policy for AllUsers and AuthenticatedUsers grants.
Check signed URL expiry, scope and tampering of path and query.
Check versioning for objects that were deleted but still readable.
tests.ex: curl -si https://BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/; aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket BUCKET; S3Scanner scan -b BUCKET
tests.exp: Buckets are private except for intended public assets. Signed URLs are short-lived and scoped. Deleted data is not readable.

tests.title: Test path confusion between proxy, cache, WAF and application
tests.obj: Find path variants that bypass access control or cache rules because components read the path in different ways.
steps: Take a protected path and request it with a trailing slash, other case and double slash.
Request it with dot segments and encoded separators such as %2f.
Add a static extension such as /none.js to a dynamic path and look at the cache headers.
Compare status code and body for each variant against the original.
Review the route rules in the application for loose regular expressions.
tests.ex: for p in /user/dashboard/ /User/Dashboard //user/dashboard /user%2Fdashboard /user/dashboard/none.js; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$p %{http_code}\n" https://example.com$p; done
tests.exp: All path variants give the same access-control result. Dynamic pages are not cached by extension.

tests.title: Check that security controls do not depend on client-controlled feature flags
tests.obj: Find feature flags and kill switches that let a user turn off a security control or that fail open.
steps: Find feature flags in JavaScript bundles, API responses and cookies.
Change the flag values in the client and send the request again.
Call the hidden function with a user that has no right, and look for server-side authorization.
Block the flag service and look at how the application behaves.
Read flag configuration for internal names and user segments.
List old flags that are no longer toggled.
tests.ex: grep -rEi 'featureflag|flags\.|launchdarkly|unleash' ./static/*.js; curl -s https://example.com/api/flags
tests.exp: The server enforces authorization without regard to flag state. A failed flag service gives the safe default.

tests.title: Make sure clients cannot override proxy headers or spoof the client IP
tests.obj: Find headers such as X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP and X-User-ID that a user can set and that the application trusts.
steps: List the headers that the proxy or load balancer sets for the application.
Send the same headers with other values directly from the client.
Send X-Forwarded-For with a spoofed address and look at the logs and the rate limit.
Add the header name to the Connection header and look for stripped headers.
Look at the proxy configuration for headers that it overwrites or removes.
tests.ex: curl -si -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' -H 'X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1' -H 'X-User-ID: 1' https://example.com/admin; curl -si -H 'Connection: close, X-Auth-User' https://example.com/
tests.exp: The proxy overwrites or removes these headers from clients. The application uses the real client IP for logs and rate limits.

tests.title: Review the cross-domain policy files of legacy rich clients
tests.obj: Find legacy crossdomain.xml and clientaccesspolicy.xml files that allow untrusted domains.
steps: Request /crossdomain.xml and /clientaccesspolicy.xml.
Look for wildcard domain entries.
Remove the files if no legacy client needs them.
tests.ex: curl -si https://example.com/crossdomain.xml; curl -si https://example.com/clientaccesspolicy.xml
tests.exp: Policy files do not exist, or they list only trusted domains.

tests.title: Review the key management policy and the cryptographic inventory
tests.obj: Find missing key lifecycle rules and an incomplete list of keys, algorithms and certificates.
steps: Ask for the key management policy and compare it with NIST SP 800-57.
Look for rules on key generation, distribution, storage, rotation, compromise and destruction.
Ask for the cryptographic inventory of keys, algorithms and certificates.
Make sure the inventory states where each key may and may not be used.
Make sure each shared secret is known to at most two parties and each private key to one.
tests.ex: Document review checklist: policy exists, lifecycle covered, inventory current (date), owner named, key-use limits stated.
tests.exp: A current policy and inventory exist, cover the full lifecycle, and limit key sharing and use.

tests.title: Find all cryptography in use and check the migration plan
tests.obj: Find unknown cryptographic use and a missing plan for post-quantum change.
steps: Run a cryptographic discovery scan of source code and dependencies.
List encryption, hashing and signing operations and compare them with the inventory.
