Ask for the documented migration plan to post-quantum algorithms.
Check that the plan names owners and dates.
tests.ex: semgrep --config p/insecure-transport --config p/crypto ./src; cbomkit or CycloneDX CBOM export of the repository
tests.exp: Discovery covers all cryptographic use, the inventory matches, and a migration plan exists.

tests.title: Make sure industry-validated cryptographic libraries are used
tests.obj: Find custom algorithms and unvalidated implementations.
steps: Search the code for hand-written encryption, hash or random functions.
List the cryptographic libraries and their versions.
Check that each library is maintained and, where needed, validated, for example FIPS 140.
Check that hardware acceleration uses vendor libraries.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'xor|rot13|custom.*(cipher|encrypt)' ./src; npm ls | grep -i crypto; pip list | grep -i crypt
tests.exp: Only maintained, industry-validated libraries do cryptographic operations. No custom algorithms exist.

tests.title: Check crypto agility of algorithms, key lengths and keys
tests.obj: Find hard-coded algorithms that the owner cannot change quickly after a break.
steps: Find where algorithms, key lengths, rounds and modes are set.
Check that configuration or one module changes them without a code rewrite.
Do a test change of one algorithm in a test system.
Check how the application replaces keys and certificates.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'AES|SHA|RSA|PBKDF2' ./src | wc -l; review config for algorithm settings
tests.exp: The team can swap algorithms, key sizes, keys and certificates by configuration or in one place.

tests.title: Make sure all cryptographic primitives give at least 128 bits of security
tests.obj: Find weak keys and algorithms such as DES, RC4, 1024-bit RSA, SHA-1 and 160-bit EC.
steps: Search code and configuration for MD4, MD5, RC2, RC4, DES, Blowfish and SHA-1.
Check the key sizes: RSA 3072 bits or more, EC 256 bits or more, AES 128 bits or more.
Scan the server for weak primitives in TLS and SSH.
Check PBKDF2 iteration counts.
tests.ex: grep -rEniw 'md4|md5|rc2|rc4|des|3des|blowfish|sha-?1' ./src; nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p443 example.com; semgrep --config p/crypto
tests.exp: No primitive has less than 128 bits of security. Deprecated algorithms are not used.

tests.title: Make sure secret comparisons and cryptographic operations are constant-time
tests.obj: Find short-circuit comparisons that leak secrets through timing.
steps: Find comparisons of MACs, tokens, hashes and passwords in the code.
Check that they use constant-time functions such as hmac.compare_digest or MessageDigest.isEqual.
Measure response time for guesses with a correct and a wrong prefix, many times.
tests.ex: grep -rEn '==\s*.*(hmac|token|signature|digest)' ./src; python3 timing_probe.py https://example.com/api/verify
tests.exp: No timing difference exists between correct and wrong prefixes. Comparisons use constant-time functions.

tests.title: Make sure cryptographic failures give no padding oracle
tests.obj: Find decryption code that shows different errors for padding failure, which lets an attacker decrypt data.
steps: Find encrypted values sent to the client: cookies, hidden fields, tokens, URL parameters.
Decode them and check for a block length that fits 8 or 16 bytes.
Change one bit of the cipher text, and the last block, and send the value back.
Compare status code, body, length and time of the three states: valid, garbled, padding error.
Check in the code that the integrity check (HMAC or AEAD) runs before decryption.
tests.ex: padbuster https://example.com/page.aspx 'Dg6W8OiWMIdVokIDH15T/A==' 16 -encoding 0; Burp Intruder on the last bytes of the value
tests.exp: The application gives one uniform answer for any failure. An integrity check rejects changed data before decryption.

tests.title: Make sure insecure block modes and padding schemes are not used
tests.obj: Find ECB mode, unauthenticated CBC and PKCS#1 v1.5 padding.
steps: Search for ECB, CBC and PKCS1Padding in the code and configuration.
Check that RSA encryption uses OAEP and signatures use PSS.
Check that SSH and other protocols do not use CBC.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'ECB|PKCS1Padding|RSA/ECB|AES/CBC|NoPadding' ./src; semgrep --config p/crypto
tests.exp: No ECB or PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding is used. AEAD modes are the default.

tests.title: Make sure only approved ciphers and modes such as AES-GCM are used
tests.obj: Find ciphers or modes that are not approved.
steps: List every cipher and mode used for data at rest and in transit.
Compare the list with the approved algorithm list of the organization or NIST.
Check that data uses authenticated encryption, for example AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'Cipher.getInstance|createCipheriv|AESGCM|ChaCha20' ./src
tests.exp: Only approved ciphers and modes are used, with authenticated encryption by default.

tests.title: Make sure encrypted data is authenticated and encrypt-then-MAC is used
tests.obj: Find encrypted data that an attacker can change without detection.
steps: Find where encrypted data is stored or sent to the client.
Change bytes of the cipher text and submit it.
Check that the change is detected and rejected.
If encryption and MAC are separate, check that the MAC is made over the cipher text.
tests.ex: python3 -c 'import base64;d=bytearray(base64.b64decode("<token>"));d[20]^=1;print(base64.b64encode(d).decode())'
tests.exp: Changed cipher text is rejected. Authenticated encryption or encrypt-then-MAC is used.

tests.title: Make sure nonces and initialization vectors are unique for each key
tests.obj: Find IV or nonce reuse and predictable IVs.
steps: Find the code that creates an IV or nonce.
Check that it uses a CSPRNG or a safe counter for the mode.
Encrypt the same plain text twice and compare the output.
Check that one IV is never used twice with one key.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'IvParameterSpec|iv\s*=|nonce\s*=' ./src; compare two encryptions of the same value
tests.exp: Each encryption uses a new IV or nonce that fits the mode. Equal plain texts give different cipher texts.

tests.title: Make sure only approved hash functions are used
tests.obj: Find MD5, SHA-1 and other banned hashes in security use, and hashes that are not collision resistant.
steps: Search the code for MD5, SHA-1 and CRC used in security checks.
Check signature, HMAC and KDF code for approved hashes.
Check that digests used for signatures or integrity are at least 256 bits where collision resistance is needed.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'MessageDigest.getInstance|hashlib\.(md5|sha1)|createHash\(.(md5|sha1)' ./src; semgrep --config p/crypto
tests.exp: Only approved hash functions, with enough output length, are used. MD5 is not used for any cryptographic purpose.

tests.title: Check password hashing and key derivation settings
tests.obj: Find passwords that are stored with fast hashes or too few iterations, and weak password-based key derivation.
steps: Find where passwords are hashed and where keys are made from passwords.
Check for Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with current parameters.
Check that each hash has a random salt.
In a test copy, look at the hash format in the database.
Check that passwords are not used directly as encryption keys.
tests.ex: psql -c 'select password from users limit 3'  (hash prefix: $argon2id$, $2b$, $pbkdf2); hashcat --example-hashes
tests.exp: Passwords use Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with current work factors and unique salts.

tests.title: Make sure non-guessable values use a CSPRNG with 128 bits of entropy
tests.obj: Find tokens, IDs and secrets that come from weak random number generators.
steps: Find code that makes tokens, reset links, keys, nonces and session values.
Search for Math.random, rand, java.util.Random and UUID v1 or v4 used as secrets.
Collect 1000 tokens and look at length and patterns.
Check that the generator works under load and is not reseeded with weak seeds.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'Math\.random|java\.util\.Random|rand\(|random\.random' ./src; Burp Sequencer on the token
tests.exp: All security values come from a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits of entropy. Weak generators are not used.

tests.title: Check key generation and signature algorithms
tests.obj: Find insecure key generation and algorithms for signatures.
steps: Find where keys are made: RSA, EC and symmetric keys.
Check that generation uses approved algorithms and a CSPRNG.
Check RSA keys for known weak patterns.
Check signature algorithms and key sizes in use.
tests.ex: openssl rsa -in key.pem -text -noout | head -3; ssh-keygen -l -f key.pub
tests.exp: Keys come from approved generation methods. Signatures use approved algorithms and sizes.

tests.title: Check key exchange algorithms and parameters
tests.obj: Find weak Diffie-Hellman parameters and key exchange that enable adversary-in-the-middle attacks.
steps: List key exchange methods in TLS and other protocols.
Check that groups are approved: x25519, secp256r1 or ffdhe2048 or larger.
Check for entity authentication in each key exchange.
tests.ex: testssl.sh -f example.com; nmap --script ssl-dh-params -p443 example.com
tests.exp: Key exchange uses approved algorithms with safe parameters and authenticates the peers.

tests.title: Review memory protection and data minimization for sensitive data in use
tests.obj: Find sensitive data that stays in memory longer than needed and is not encrypted at once.
steps: Read the design for memory encryption of sensitive data.
Check how long keys and plain text stay in memory.
Check that the application keeps the minimum data during processing.
Check that data is encrypted as soon as possible.
tests.ex: Design review; core dump and heap dump review for secrets: strings core.dump | grep -i 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY'
tests.exp: Sensitive data in use is limited and protected, and it is encrypted again as soon as possible.

tests.title: Make sure no hard-coded, default or checked-in cryptographic keys exist
tests.obj: Find keys in source code, repositories, images or configuration that an attacker can read.
steps: Scan the repository and its history with trufflehog or gitleaks.
Search for PEM headers, hex keys and JWT secrets in code, configs and images.
Check for the default keys of frameworks and products.
Check that each environment uses different keys.
tests.ex: trufflehog git file://. --only-verified; gitleaks detect -v; grep -rEn 'BEGIN (RSA |EC )?PRIVATE KEY' .
tests.exp: No cryptographic key is in source, history, images or default configuration. Each environment has its own keys.

tests.title: Review the classification of sensitive data and its protection requirements
tests.obj: Find sensitive data that is not classified and levels that have no documented protection rules.
steps: Ask for the data classification and the list of protection levels.
List the data the application creates and processes, including Base64 values and JWT payloads.
Compare the list with the classification and find unclassified data.
Check that each level has rules for encryption, integrity, retention, logging, access and privacy.
tests.ex: Document review: data inventory vs classification table; decode JWT payloads and Base64 fields found in traffic.
tests.exp: All sensitive data is classified and each level has documented protection rules.

tests.title: Make sure sensitive data is not sent in the URL
tests.obj: Find API keys, tokens and personal data in URLs, which logs, proxies and referrers store.
steps: Walk through the application with a proxy and list all URLs with query strings.
Look for tokens, keys, passwords, session IDs and personal data in URLs.
Look at the Referer header sent to third parties.
Look at server and proxy access logs for such URLs.
tests.ex: zap-baseline.py -t https://example.com; grep -E '[?&](token|key|password|session)=' access.log
tests.exp: Sensitive data goes only in the request body or header fields, never in the URL.

tests.title: Make sure sensitive data is not kept in server-side caches
tests.obj: Find load balancers, CDNs and application caches that store sensitive responses.
steps: Request a sensitive page with a session, then request it with no session or another session.
Look at the cache headers and the Age, X-Cache and CF-Cache-Status headers.
Review CDN, reverse proxy and Redis or Memcached cache rules.
Check that cached sensitive data is purged after use.
tests.ex: curl -si -H 'Cookie: session=A' https://example.com/account; curl -si https://example.com/account | grep -iE 'age|x-cache|cache-status'
tests.exp: Sensitive responses are not stored by shared caches, or the cache purges them after use.

tests.title: Make sure sensitive data is not sent to untrusted third parties
tests.obj: Find trackers, analytics and third-party scripts that receive sensitive data.
steps: Record the requests to third-party hosts in the developer tools.
Look at the URL, headers and body of each request for personal or sensitive data.
List third-party scripts and check how they are loaded and what they can read.
Check consent rules for the data that is sent.
tests.ex: Browser DevTools Network filter 'third-party'; mitmproxy -s log_third_party.py; Blacklight scan
tests.exp: No sensitive data is sent to trackers or untrusted third parties. Only the listed data goes to approved parties.

tests.title: Check that data protection controls follow the documented protection level
tests.obj: Find sensitive data whose real protection differs from its documented level.
steps: Pick samples of each protection level.
Check encryption, integrity checks, retention, logging and access control for each sample.
Compare each result with the documented requirement.
tests.ex: Sample review table: data item, level, required control, observed control, gap.
tests.exp: Real controls match the documented requirements for each protection level.

tests.title: Make sure caches store only expected content types and non-sensitive responses
tests.obj: Find caches that store sensitive, dynamic or wrong-type responses, or serve another file for a missing one.
steps: Request a non-existent static path and check for 404 or 302 and not another file.
Request a dynamic page with a static extension, for example /account/x.css, and look at cache headers.
Check that cache rules use the content type and not only the path.
Request the page from a second client and compare.
tests.ex: curl -si https://example.com/account/none.css -H 'Cookie: session=A'; curl -si https://example.com/account/none.css
tests.exp: Caches store only the expected type of resource. Sensitive dynamic content is not cached. Missing files give 404 or 302.

tests.title: Make sure responses contain only the minimum sensitive data and mask values
tests.obj: Find responses and pages with more sensitive data than the function needs.
steps: Compare data shown in the UI with data in the response for key pages.
Look for full card numbers, IDs, tokens and hashes in responses.
Check that the UI masks values unless the user asks to see them.
tests.ex: Burp: compare rendered page and JSON; jq 'paths' on the response to list all fields
tests.exp: Responses return the minimum data. Sensitive values such as card numbers are partly masked.

tests.title: Check retention and automatic deletion of sensitive data
tests.obj: Find sensitive data that stays after its retention period.
steps: Ask for the retention schedule for each data class.
Check that deletion jobs or database rules exist and run.
Find records older than the schedule in a test or production copy.
Delete a test record and check backups, caches and storage versions.
tests.ex: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created < now() - interval '7 years';  review lifecycle rules of buckets
tests.exp: Old sensitive data is deleted on schedule, with proof, including copies and versions.

tests.title: Make sure metadata is removed from user-submitted files
tests.obj: Find uploaded files that keep GPS, author and device data.
steps: Upload an image that has EXIF GPS data and a document with author data.
Download the stored file from another account or the public URL.
Read the metadata with exiftool.
Check that the user gave consent if metadata stays.
tests.ex: exiftool -gps:all -author uploaded.jpg
tests.exp: Stored files have no sensitive metadata unless the user agreed.

tests.title: Make sure the client clears authenticated data when the session ends
tests.obj: Find DOM, storage and cache data that stays in the browser after logout or timeout.
steps: Log in, open sensitive pages, then log out.
Look at localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, Cache API and the DOM.
Use the Back button and look for sensitive pages.
Check for the Clear-Site-Data header on the logout response.
Test again with the server not reachable.
tests.ex: curl -si -X POST https://example.com/logout -H 'Cookie: session=A' | grep -i clear-site-data; DevTools > Application > Storage
tests.exp: No authenticated data stays in the client after the session ends. Clear-Site-Data or client code clears it.

tests.title: Check anti-caching headers on sensitive responses
tests.obj: Find sensitive pages that browsers may cache.
steps: Request pages with sensitive data after login and read Cache-Control, Pragma and Expires.
Make sure Cache-Control: no-store is set. no-cache alone is not enough.
Log out, then use the Back button and look for the cached page.
Check API responses and file downloads too.
tests.ex: curl -sI https://example.com/account -H 'Cookie: session=A' | grep -iE 'cache-control|pragma|expires'
tests.exp: All sensitive responses send Cache-Control: no-store. The browser shows no cached page after logout.

tests.title: Make sure browser storage holds no sensitive data except session tokens
tests.obj: Find sensitive data in localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and cookies.
steps: Use the application for the main functions.
Read all keys and values in localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and cookies.
Look for personal data, API keys, JWTs with personal data and passwords.
Check that cookies with tokens are the only secrets.
tests.ex: DevTools > Application; chrome-devtools evaluate: JSON.stringify(localStorage)
tests.exp: Browser storage holds no sensitive data. Only session tokens are allowed, in protected cookies.

tests.title: Make sure sensitive data is encrypted at rest
tests.obj: Find stored sensitive data in clear text, such as databases, files and backups.
steps: Find where sensitive data is stored: database, files, object storage, backups, logs.
Check encryption at rest at the storage and the application level.
Check that keys are stored apart from the data.
Check that data not needed is not stored.
tests.ex: aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].StorageEncrypted'; aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket BUCKET
tests.exp: All sensitive data at rest is encrypted with managed keys that are separate from the data.

tests.title: Review remediation time frames for vulnerable third-party components
tests.obj: Find missing or weak rules for how fast vulnerable libraries and components must be updated.
steps: Ask for the documented remediation time frames by risk level.
Check that the rules cover libraries, frameworks, runtimes, the OS and containers.
Check that a process tracks advisories for the components in use, for example CVE, OSV and vendor feeds.
Look at the last three vulnerability fixes and compare the real time with the rule.
tests.ex: Document review; osv-scanner -r . ; dependency-check --scan . --format JSON
tests.exp: Documented time frames exist, cover all component types, and past fixes met them.

tests.title: Check the component inventory (SBOM) and the trust of package sources
tests.obj: Find unknown components, transitive dependencies and untrusted package repositories.
steps: Generate or request an SBOM for each release, with direct and transitive dependencies.
Compare the SBOM with the lock files and the deployed artifact.
Check that all components come from defined, trusted and maintained repositories.
Check that client-side libraries are in the inventory.
tests.ex: syft dir:. -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json; cdxgen -o bom.json .; grype sbom:sbom.json
tests.exp: A current SBOM covers all components and their sources. Every component comes from a trusted repository.

tests.title: Find components with known vulnerabilities, outdated or unsupported versions
tests.obj: Find components that break the update time frames or that have known CVEs.
steps: Identify component versions from banners, JavaScript comments, file names and package files.
Scan server-side dependencies with a software composition analysis tool.
Scan client-side libraries with retire.js.
Check support status and end-of-life dates for the OS, runtime, server and database.
Check each finding by hand against the real version.
tests.ex: retire --js --outputformat json; trivy fs --scanners vuln .; osv-scanner -r .; nuclei -u https://example.com -tags cve,tech
tests.exp: No component is vulnerable, unsupported or past the documented update time frame.

tests.title: Make sure dependencies come from the expected repository (dependency confusion)
tests.obj: Find internal package names that a public repository can supply, and unpinned dependency sources.
steps: List the internal package names and the repository settings in npm, pip, Maven and NuGet.
Check that the public registry has no package with an internal name.
Check that scoped registries or index settings force the internal repository.
Check that lock files pin versions and hashes.
tests.ex: npm config get registry; pip config list; cat .npmrc pip.conf; npm view @company/internal-lib
tests.exp: All dependencies, including transitive ones, resolve from the expected repository. Lock files pin them.

tests.title: Check integrity of downloaded code, packages and third-party scripts
tests.obj: Find code that the application loads or installs without a signature or integrity check.
steps: List external scripts and styles in the pages.
Check for Subresource Integrity attributes with the crossorigin setting.
Check that package installs use signatures or hashes, and the lock file is used.
Check that auto-update and plugin download features check signatures.
Check mappings of company sub-domains to external providers.
tests.ex: curl -s https://example.com | grep -oE '<script[^>]+src=[^>]+>' | grep -v integrity; npm ci --ignore-scripts; pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt
tests.exp: External code is loaded only with integrity checks or signatures, and from trusted sources.

tests.title: Make sure serialized data from clients is signed or integrity-checked
tests.obj: Find serialized objects, cookies and state that the client can change and the server trusts.
steps: Find serialized objects, view-state values and state cookies in requests.
Change a value and send the request again.
Replay an old value after a state change.
Check that a signature or MAC protects the data, and that the server does not deserialize untrusted data.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: edit the serialized value; ysoserial or marshalsec for Java test payloads in a lab
tests.exp: The server rejects changed or replayed serialized data. It does not deserialize unsigned client data.

tests.title: Review documented risky components and dangerous functionality and their protections
tests.obj: Find risky libraries and dangerous functions with no documentation and no isolation.
steps: Ask for the list of risky third-party components and dangerous functionality.
Find use of eval, system commands, deserialization, XML parsers and file conversion.
Check that each item has sandboxing, containerization or network-level isolation.
Compare the list with a code scan result.
tests.ex: semgrep --config p/default ./src; grep -rEn 'eval\(|exec\(|Runtime.getRuntime|pickle.loads' ./src
tests.exp: Risky components and dangerous functionality are documented and have extra protection.

tests.title: Make sure errors return a generic message without stack traces or internals
tests.obj: Find error output that shows stack traces, queries, paths, versions, keys or tokens.
steps: Send wrong types, missing parameters, long values and special characters to every input.
Send malformed JSON and XML bodies and invalid HTTP requests.
Request missing files and folders.
Look at the response body and headers for stack traces, SQL, paths, versions and secrets.
Look at error responses that return status 200.
Check that debug pages and consoles are off.
tests.ex: ffuf -u 'https://example.com/page?id=FUZZ' -w fuzz-errors.txt -mc 500; curl -si 'https://example.com/api/item/%00'; zap-baseline.py -t https://example.com
tests.exp: Unexpected or security-sensitive errors return a generic message and a correlation ID. No internal data is visible.

tests.title: Make sure web server and framework use custom error pages
tests.obj: Find default server and framework error pages that identify the product and version.
steps: Request random missing paths and forbidden folders.
Send a request that breaks the HTTP rules, such as a wrong version or a very long line.
Compare the pages with the known default pages of Apache, Nginx, IIS and the framework.
Look at the configuration for custom error pages and a global error handler.
tests.ex: curl -si https://example.com/nonexistent-$(date +%s); printf 'GET / HTTP/9.9\r\n\r\n' | openssl s_client -quiet -connect example.com:443
tests.exp: The application uses custom error pages and a central error handler. No default product page is shown.

tests.title: Make sure the application degrades safely when an external resource fails
tests.obj: Find applications that crash, hang or expose data when a dependency is down.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Block, slow down or break one dependency at a time in a test system.
Look at the user response and the application state.
Check for circuit breakers, time-outs and graceful degradation.
Check that the application recovers when the dependency returns.
tests.ex: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t timeout -a timeout=0 backend; iptables -A OUTPUT -d <dep-ip> -j DROP
tests.exp: The application keeps working in a safe reduced mode, gives a generic error, and recovers by itself.

tests.title: Make sure the application fails closed and rolls back on errors
tests.obj: Find fail-open paths where an error lets a request or transaction pass.
steps: Make a validation, authorization or payment step fail with an exception in a test system.
Check that the request is denied and not processed.
Interrupt a multi-step transaction in the middle and check the state of the data.
Check that partial changes are rolled back.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: send input that raises an exception in the validator; interrupt the second step of a transfer with a dropped connection
tests.exp: Errors lead to denial and complete rollback. No transaction is processed after a failed check.

tests.title: Check for a last-resort error handler that catches all exceptions
tests.obj: Find code paths with no global handler that lose error data or stop the process.
steps: Find the global exception handler in the framework configuration.
Raise an unhandled exception in a test route and in a background job.
Check that the process stays up, the error is logged, and the user gets a generic message.
Search the code for empty catch blocks and generic exceptions.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'catch\s*\(\s*(Exception|Throwable)|except\s*:|catch\s*\{\s*\}' ./src
tests.exp: A central handler catches all unhandled exceptions, logs them and keeps the process available.

tests.title: Review documentation for permitted upload types, extensions and size
tests.obj: Confirms upload features document the allowed file types, extensions, maximum size and safety handling.
steps: Request the application design documentation for each upload feature.
Check that permitted file types, extensions and maximum unpacked size are documented.
Check that the documentation states how a detected malicious file is handled.
tests.ex: Review upload feature specification for the stated allowlist, size limit and malicious-file handling
tests.exp: Every upload feature documents its permitted types, extensions, size limit and how malicious files are handled.

tests.title: Test file upload size limits for denial of service
tests.obj: Finds upload endpoints that accept files larger than the application can safely process.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an upload endpoint and its stated size limit.
Upload a file just under, at, and over the stated limit.
Upload a very large file and monitor server resource use and response time.
tests.ex: curl -F "file=@bigfile_1gb.bin" https://target/upload and monitor CPU, memory and response time
tests.exp: The server enforces the documented size limit before processing and rejects oversized files without resource exhaustion.

tests.title: Test file type validation against extension, Content-Type and magic bytes
tests.obj: Finds uploads validated only by extension or Content-Type instead of actual file content.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify how the upload feature checks file type: client-side script, Content-Type header, or extension.
Upload a file with a disallowed extension renamed to an allowed one, keeping its original magic bytes.
Upload a file with an allowed extension but a Content-Type header for a disallowed type.
Upload a polyglot or mismatched-signature file to see if magic byte checks are enforced.
tests.ex: Rename shell.php to shell.jpg while keeping PHP content, and set Content-Type: image/jpeg on a PHP file
tests.exp: The server validates the true file content, including magic bytes, against the expected type for every upload, not only the extension or header.

tests.title: Test compressed file uploads for decompression bomb limits
tests.obj: Finds archive extraction that does not cap uncompressed size or file count before extracting.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an upload or import feature that accepts a compressed file such as zip, gz, docx or odt.
Create an archive with an extreme compression ratio, for example a zip bomb.
Create an archive containing an extremely large number of files.
Upload each archive and monitor storage and resource use during extraction.
tests.ex: Create a 42.zip-style nested zip bomb or a zip with 100000 tiny files, then upload and monitor disk and CPU use
tests.exp: The application checks the uncompressed size and file count against a maximum before extracting any archive.

tests.title: Test per-user file and storage quota enforcement
tests.obj: Finds upload features missing a per-user limit on file count or total storage.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify the stated quota for file count and total storage size per user.
Upload files repeatedly as a single user until the stated quota should be reached.
Confirm whether the application rejects uploads once the quota is exceeded.
tests.ex: Loop curl -F "file=@1mb.bin" https://target/upload past the documented per-user quota and check for rejection
tests.exp: The application enforces a per-user file count and storage quota and rejects uploads once the quota is exceeded.

tests.title: Test archive uploads for symlink inclusion
tests.obj: Finds archive extraction that preserves symbolic links pointing outside the intended directory.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Create a symbolic link to a sensitive file, for example /etc/passwd.
Package the symlink into an archive and upload it.
Check whether the extracted symlink is preserved and whether reading the linked file discloses its content.
tests.ex: ln -s /etc/passwd link.txt; tar -czf malicious.tar.gz link.txt; upload malicious.tar.gz and request link.txt
tests.exp: The extraction process rejects or strips symbolic links unless an explicit allowlist of symlink targets is enforced.

tests.title: Test image upload for pixel flood attacks
tests.obj: Finds image processing features missing a maximum pixel dimension check.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an image upload feature that processes or resizes images server-side.
Create an image file with an extreme pixel width and height but a small file size.
Upload the image and monitor memory and CPU use during processing.
tests.ex: Craft a PNG with declared dimensions of 65000x65000 pixels and a tiny compressed size, then upload it
tests.exp: The application rejects images above a maximum pixel size before decoding or processing them.

tests.title: Test uploaded files for malicious content and web shells
tests.obj: Finds upload features missing malware scanning that would allow a web shell or malware to be stored and executed.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an upload feature and the folder files are stored in.
Upload the EICAR anti-malware test file and confirm it is detected and quarantined.
If the server may execute uploaded code, upload a minimal web shell with a random filename and request it directly.
Remove the web shell immediately after confirming execution.
tests.ex: Upload the EICAR string X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H* ; then upload a minimal <?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?> shell with a random name
tests.exp: Uploaded files are scanned for malware and files stored in a public folder are never executed as server-side code.

tests.title: Test archive extraction for zip slip path traversal
tests.obj: Finds archive extraction code that writes entries to attacker-chosen paths outside the target directory.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a feature that extracts an uploaded archive, such as zip, on the server.
Create an archive containing an entry with a path traversal sequence in its name.
Upload the archive and check whether a file is written outside the intended extraction directory.
tests.ex: zip test.zip base ../../../traversed to create an entry whose name escapes the target directory on extraction
tests.exp: The extraction code validates each entry path against the target directory and ignores or rejects path traversal sequences.

tests.title: Test served filenames for validation and Content-Disposition handling
tests.obj: Finds downloads that trust a client-submitted filename for the response or storage path.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a download or export feature that accepts a filename from the client, including in JSON or a URL parameter.
Submit a filename containing path traversal characters or an unexpected extension.
Check that the response sets a safe Content-Disposition filename regardless of the submitted value.
tests.ex: filename=../../etc/passwd submitted in a JSON body or URL parameter to a download endpoint
tests.exp: The server ignores or strictly validates a client-submitted filename and always sets its own safe filename in Content-Disposition.

tests.title: Test served filenames for header and injection safety
tests.obj: Finds filenames reflected in response headers or email attachments without encoding against injection.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Upload a file whose name contains CRLF sequences or special characters.
Download the file and inspect the Content-Disposition header for injected header fields.
If files are emailed as attachments, check the attachment filename for the same encoding.
tests.ex: filename="normal.txt\r\nX-Injected: true" uploaded then downloaded to inspect the response header
tests.exp: Served filenames are encoded or sanitized following RFC 6266 so they cannot inject headers or break document structure.

tests.title: Test files from untrusted sources for antivirus scanning
tests.obj: Finds files obtained from third parties or users that are served without malware scanning.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify files obtained from an untrusted source, such as a partner feed or a public upload area.
Confirm whether an antivirus or content-scanning step runs before the file is made available to other users.
Upload the EICAR test file through the untrusted-source path and confirm detection.
tests.ex: Upload the EICAR string through a partner-integration or public upload path and confirm it is scanned before being served
tests.exp: All files from untrusted sources are scanned by an antivirus engine before being served to other users.

tests.title: Test rejection of unexpected file types at upload
tests.obj: Finds upload features that accept file types outside the documented allowlist.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review the documentation for file types the feature should reject.
Prepare files of disallowed types, including an HTML file containing a script and an executable.
Upload each disallowed file type and confirm it is rejected, not merely hidden from the UI.
tests.ex: Upload a .jsp, .exe and an HTML file containing <script>alert(1)</script> to an image-only upload feature
tests.exp: The server rejects every file type outside the documented allowlist, independent of any client-side check.

tests.title: Check that abuse cases exist for each business feature
tests.obj: Finds features that nobody reviewed for misuse, so generic security requirements stay unclear.
steps: Ask for the list of features and the list of abuse cases.
Make sure each abuse case has a unique identifier, the affected feature and an attack description.
Make sure each abuse case is marked technical or business and has a business risk rating.
Make sure the workshop had business, risk, pentest, technical and QA roles.
tests.ex: Spreadsheet with FEATURES, ABUSE CASES and COUNTERMEASURES sheets; CAPEC and OWASP Testing Guide as attack lists
tests.exp: Each feature has abuse cases with identifier, type and risk rating. The list comes from a documented review.

tests.title: Check that selected abuse cases become requirements and are validated
tests.obj: Finds abuse cases that never reach the specification or whose countermeasures nobody tests.
steps: Take five selected abuse cases.
Make sure each appears as a security requirement or an acceptance criterion in the feature.
Look in the design notes and code for a reference to the abuse case identifier.
Make sure an automated test, a SAST rule or a manual check validates each countermeasure.
Make sure the penetration test scope lists the abuse cases.
tests.ex: grep -rn "ABUSE_CASE_" src/ docs/ tests/
tests.exp: Each selected abuse case has a requirement, a code or design reference and a repeatable validation.

tests.title: Test rate-limit key design for login and recovery endpoints
tests.obj: Find rate limits that an attacker passes by changing the IP address, the username form or the request timing.
steps: Find out which keys the limit uses: IP, session, username or a mix.
Send many attempts against one username from many source IP addresses.
Send many usernames from one source IP address.
Change the username case and add spaces or encoding to reach a new bucket.
Add X-Forwarded-For and similar headers with new values.
Send attempts at the end and the start of a time window.
Make sure the limit answer is a generic 429 without detail.
tests.ex: ffuf or Burp Intruder with a rotating X-Forwarded-For; one username with 50 attempts from proxies; compare 429 bodies
tests.exp: Separate limits apply per username and per source. Header changes and username variants do not reset the counters. Bursts at window edges are blocked.

tests.title: Test signup, card testing and inventory flows for velocity limits
tests.obj: Find business flows that let bots create fake accounts, test stolen cards or hold stock.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List the flows at risk: signup, low-value purchase, cart hold and coupon check.
Create many accounts with one device and one email domain.
Try many small payments with different test card numbers.
Add items to the cart and keep them without payment.
Look for limits, verification steps and queues in each flow.
Look at the logs for alerts on these patterns.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder on POST /signup and POST /checkout in a test environment; review the fraud alerts
tests.exp: Each flow has velocity limits per identity, device and payment data. Cart holds expire. The team gets alerts for the patterns.

tests.title: Test unkeyed request inputs for web cache poisoning
tests.obj: Find request inputs that change a cached response but are not part of the cache key.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find cached pages with the response headers Age, X-Cache or CF-Cache-Status.
Add a cache buster to the URL so that only you see the test entry.
Send unkeyed inputs one at a time, such as X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme and a body on a GET request.
Look for the value in links, redirects, JSON and response headers.
Request the same URL without the extra input and look for the changed response.
Remove the test entry from the cache after the test.
tests.ex: curl -s "https://target/?cb=123" -H "X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example"; then curl -s "https://target/?cb=123" | grep evil; Burp Param Miner
tests.exp: Unkeyed inputs do not change a cacheable response. Forwarded headers are trusted only from the proxy, and the cache key holds every input that changes the output.

tests.title: Review CDN and proxy cache rules against the origin cache policy
tests.obj: Find CDN or proxy rules that override origin headers and cache sensitive, error or redirect responses.
steps: List the cache rules of the CDN and reverse proxy.
Look for rules that override Cache-Control, or that cache by file extension, path or status code.
Check the cache policy of error pages, redirects and authentication responses.
Make sure Vary: Cookie is not the only control for personalized pages.
Make sure the URL normalization is the same at the CDN, the proxy and the origin.
Test the purge function for one key or one route group.
tests.ex: CDN configuration export; curl -sI of /login, /404, /redirect and /account with and without cookies
tests.exp: Cache rules follow an allowlist of routes. No rule makes a personalized response public. Purge works for a narrow scope.

tests.title: Check that the secure code review process covers baseline and diff reviews
tests.obj: Finds missing or weak security review of new applications and of code changes.
steps: Ask for the secure code review procedure.
Make sure it defines baseline reviews for new applications, major releases and legacy onboarding.
Make sure it defines diff-based reviews for pull requests.
Make sure reviewers get the threat model, earlier findings and a list of high-risk functions before the review.
Take three recent pull requests. Make sure a security-focused review is on record.
tests.ex: Procedure document; gh pr list --state merged --limit 20 --json number,reviews
tests.exp: A written procedure defines both review types and their inputs. Recent changes have a security-focused review on record.

tests.title: Review the code for high-risk patterns by scan and by hand
tests.obj: Finds hard-coded secrets, unsafe functions and injectable queries that tools alone may miss.
steps: Search the source for hard-coded secrets such as password, api_key and secret assignments.
Search for unsafe functions such as eval, exec, innerHTML and document.write.
Search for queries built with string concatenation.
Read each hit and decide if user-controlled data can reach it.
Use SAST findings to rank the areas for manual review.
tests.ex: grep -riE "password\s*=|api_key\s*=|secret\s*=" src/; grep -rE "eval\(|exec\(|innerHTML|document\.write" src/; grep -rE "SELECT.*\+|executeQuery.*\+" src/
tests.exp: No hit is exploitable. Each hit has a decision on record. Hard-coded secrets are absent.

tests.title: Trace data from sources to sinks across trust boundaries in the code
tests.obj: Finds places where untrusted data reaches a sink without validation, encoding or authorization.
steps: List the sources: user input, file uploads, API calls, database reads and environment variables.
List the sinks: database queries, file writes, output rendering, logs and external APIs.
Follow each source through validation, transformation and business logic to its sink.
Make sure each trust boundary has input validation and output encoding.
Make sure sensitive data has protection that fits its classification at each step.
tests.ex: Data flow notes per feature; CodeQL or Semgrep taint rules to find source-sink paths
tests.exp: Every path from an untrusted source to a sink has validation or encoding at the trust boundary. Sensitive data stays protected.

tests.title: Test origin checks with Origin, Referer and Sec-Fetch-Site headers
tests.obj: Find state-changing endpoints that accept requests from another site because the server does not check the request origin.
steps: List the state-changing requests that use cookie authentication.
Replay each request with an Origin header from an attacker site.
Replay each request with Origin: null and with the Origin header removed.
Replay each request with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site and a foreign Referer header.
Look for a safe method such as GET that changes state.
Make sure the server does not allow the literal null origin or a partial host match.
tests.ex: curl -b "session=<id>" -H "Origin: https://evil.example" -H "Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site" -X POST https://target/account/email -d "email=a@b.test"; also test Origin: https://target.evil.example
tests.exp: The server rejects cross-site requests that change state. It checks the Origin header, uses Referer only as a fallback, and does not trust null or a partial match.

tests.title: Test that anti-CSRF tokens are bound to the session and are random
tests.obj: Find CSRF tokens that an attacker can predict, reuse, or use with another account.
steps: Collect anti-CSRF tokens from several sessions and users.
Look at the tokens for patterns, such as a user ID, an email address, or a time value.
Use a valid token of user A in a request of user B.
Use a token from before logout or login in a new session.
Look for tokens in URLs, Referer headers, and logs.
Send the token in a different place, such as a query parameter, and in an empty form.
tests.ex: Burp Sequencer on the token; repeat a POST with the token of another session; compare token values with Burp Comparer
tests.exp: Each token is unique per session, secret and unpredictable. The server rejects a token of another session, an old token, and an empty token. Tokens are not in URLs.

tests.title: Test double-submit cookie tokens for forgery from a subdomain
tests.obj: Find double-submit CSRF defenses where an attacker can set the token cookie and a matching request value.
steps: Find out if the CSRF token is a cookie value that is copied into the request.
Check if the token is signed (HMAC) and tied to the session.
Set an own cookie with a chosen token value from a sibling subdomain or over HTTP, in a test environment.
Send a request with the same chosen value in the cookie and in the header.
Check if the cookie uses the __Host- prefix and no Domain attribute.
tests.ex: Set-Cookie: csrf=attacker; Domain=example.com from a test subdomain, then POST with X-CSRF-Token: attacker
tests.exp: The server rejects a token that it did not issue for this session. The token cookie cannot be set from another subdomain.

tests.title: Test login and other pre-session forms for cross-site request forgery
tests.obj: Find login forms that accept a forged request, which lets an attacker sign the victim in to an attacker account.
steps: Open the login form without a session and look for a CSRF token.
Submit the login request from a page on another origin, in a test environment.
Check if the victim then works in the attacker account and saves private data there.
Do the same for the sign-up and password reset forms.
tests.ex: Host an HTML form that posts attacker credentials to https://target/login and open it in a browser that has no session
tests.exp: The login and pre-session forms need a CSRF token or an origin check. A forged login request fails.

tests.title: Test client-side code for request forgery from URL and DOM inputs
tests.obj: Find client-side CSRF where attacker input in the URL or the DOM makes the page send a state-changing same-origin request.
steps: Search the JavaScript for request calls that build the URL or body from location, hash or postMessage data.
Put path traversal and extra parameters in the input, such as ../ and &action=delete.
Open a crafted link as the victim and watch the network requests.
Check if the request carries the CSRF token and the session cookie.
tests.ex: https://target/app#/profile/..%2f..%2fadmin%2fdelete ; use browser DevTools network tab and grep the bundle for fetch(
tests.exp: Client-side code does not build request targets from untrusted input without allowlist checks. The server still checks the token and the origin of each state-changing request.

tests.title: Review database server hardening and default content
tests.obj: Find database servers with default accounts, sample data, risky functions or weak host settings.
pre: Read access to the database configuration.
steps: List the database engines and versions and compare them with the vendor security baseline.
Look for default accounts and sample databases.
Look for risky features: xp_cmdshell, CLR, the FILE privilege and database links.
Make sure the service runs as a low-privilege operating system user.
Make sure the management tools need authentication, HTTPS and network limits.
Make sure backups are encrypted and have restricted permissions.
tests.ex: SQL Server: SELECT name,value_in_use FROM sys.configurations WHERE name IN ('xp_cmdshell','clr enabled'); MySQL: SHOW GRANTS; SELECT user,host FROM mysql.user;
tests.exp: No default account or sample database remains. Risky features are off. The service has low privilege, and backups and management tools are protected.

tests.title: Review application database accounts, permissions and encrypted connections
tests.obj: Find application database accounts with too many rights, shared credentials or unencrypted connections.
steps: List the database accounts of each application and environment.
Make sure each account serves one application and each environment has its own database and account.
Make sure no account is root, sa or SYS, owns the schema or has administrative rights.
Compare the granted rights with the needed rights, at table, column or view level.
Make sure each account connects only from the allowed hosts.
Make sure the server needs TLS and the client checks the server certificate.
Make sure the connection string is not in source code.
tests.ex: psql: \du+ ; SELECT grantee,table_name,privilege_type FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE grantee='<app>'; SHOW ssl;
tests.exp: Each application uses its own least-privilege account. Connections use TLS with certificate checks. Credentials are outside the source code.

tests.title: Check that a user cannot reuse a recent password
tests.obj: Find password change and reset flows that accept a password that the user used before.
pre: A test account and the password policy.
steps: Read the password policy for the rule on password reuse and the number of stored old passwords.
Change the password to a new value, and then change it back to the old value.
Use the password reset flow to set the old password again.
Change the password to a variation of the old value, such as a new digit at the end.
Make sure the history holds hashes and not plain text.
tests.ex: Test account: change Passw0rd-A to Passw0rd-B, then back to Passw0rd-A, in the change form and in the reset form
tests.exp: The application rejects a recent password in the change flow and in the reset flow, as the policy says. The history holds only hashes.

tests.title: Review isolation, logging and monitoring around code that deserializes data
tests.obj: Find deserialization features that run with high privilege and without logs, which makes abuse hard to limit and to detect.
steps: Find the code and services that deserialize data from clients or other systems.
Check the type allowlist and the integrity check that apply before the object is created.
Check that the deserializing component runs with low privilege, for example in a temporary container.
Check the network rules for inbound and outbound connections of that component.
Send a malformed serialized object and look in the log for the failure.
Look for an alert on repeated deserialization failures from one client.
tests.ex: Search the code for readObject, pickle.loads, unserialize and BinaryFormatter; check container securityContext and egress rules; send a corrupted object
tests.exp: Deserializing components run with low privilege and limited network access. Failures are logged and repeated failures raise an alert.

tests.title: Review code and services that run with elevated privileges
tests.obj: Find components that hold high privileges longer than needed, which makes any flaw in them more severe.
steps: List the services and code paths that run as root, administrator or with raised capabilities.
Find out why each one needs the privilege and which step uses it.
Check that the code raises privilege just before that step and drops it as soon as the step ends.
Check that user input is not processed while the privilege is active.
Check the process owner and capabilities at run time.
tests.ex: ps -eo user,pid,cmd | grep -v "^<app_user>"; getpcaps <pid>; Windows: Get-Process -IncludeUserName; review setuid or impersonation calls in the code
tests.exp: Elevated privilege is held only for the step that needs it. The application runs as a low-privilege account for all other work.

tests.title: Test email address normalization for duplicate and look-alike accounts
tests.obj: Find identity flows that treat one email address in different ways, which allows duplicate, merged or spoofed accounts.
steps: Register an account with a mixed-case domain and then register again with a lowercase domain.
Register with a different case in the local part and with plus tags and dots.
Register with a Cyrillic or other look-alike character in the local part and in the domain.
Use the variants in login, password reset and account linking and look at which account answers.
Make sure the stored address keeps the original form and the comparison policy is the same in every flow.
tests.ex: user@Example.com vs user@example.com; usеr@example.com (Cyrillic e); user+tag@example.com; xn-- punycode domain
tests.exp: The application applies one documented comparison policy in all flows. Look-alike and equivalent addresses cannot take over or merge with another account.

tests.title: Test email ownership verification and the email change workflow
tests.obj: Find flows that let an attacker use or take over an account with an email address that the attacker does not own.
steps: Register and try to use the account before you open the verification link.
Examine the verification tokens for randomness, single use, and expiry.
Change the email address and check that the new address needs confirmation before it becomes active.
Check that the old address gets a notice and that re-authentication is needed.
Change the address in the request to another user address and look at the result.
Look in logs for full addresses and for tokens in URLs.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater on POST /account/email; compare token values from three registrations; open the same link twice
tests.exp: The account stays inactive until the address is verified. Tokens are random, single-use and expire. A change needs re-authentication and confirmation, and the old address gets a notice.

tests.title: Review browser extension permissions, manifest and update path
tests.obj: Find extensions that ask for too many permissions, run weak policies or load code that nobody reviewed.
pre: The extension package.
steps: Read manifest.json and list the permissions, host permissions and content script matches.
Remove each permission that no feature needs.
Look for optional permissions where full access is not always needed.
Look at content_security_policy.extension_pages and make sure scripts load from the package only.
Search the code for remote scripts and eval-like calls.
Make sure updates come from the extension store and that the dependencies are audited.
tests.ex: unzip ext.crx -d ext; jq .permissions,.host_permissions,.content_security_policy ext/manifest.json; npm audit
tests.exp: The manifest asks only for needed permissions and a strict policy. The extension loads no remote code, and the dependencies have no known vulnerabilities.

tests.title: Test extension message handlers for sender validation
tests.obj: Find extension code that accepts messages from web pages or other extensions and runs privileged actions.
pre: The extension package and a test browser profile.
steps: List the runtime.onMessage and onMessageExternal handlers, and the externally_connectable settings.
Send a message from a web page through the content script with a new action name.
Send a message from another extension or a different frame.
Check that the handler tests sender.id and sender.origin and allows only known actions and fields.
Check that the handler does not use message data in innerHTML or eval.
tests.ex: DevTools console on a test page: chrome.runtime.sendMessage("<ext-id>",{action:"getToken"}); grep -R "onMessage" ext/
tests.exp: The handlers check the sender and allow only listed actions with validated fields. A web page cannot start a privileged action or run script.

tests.title: Test extension storage, data transfer and display of sensitive data
tests.obj: Find extensions that keep secrets in storage, send data in clear text or show data where a web page can read it.
pre: The extension package and a test browser profile.
steps: Look at chrome.storage and localStorage content after use and look for tokens and personal data.
Search the code for hard-coded keys.
Record the network traffic of the extension and make sure it uses HTTPS only.
Check if the extension adds sensitive data to the DOM of web pages.
Check if the extension shows data in a popup, options page or side panel instead.
Check the privacy notice and the opt-out for data collection.
tests.ex: DevTools Application tab; mitmproxy with the browser profile; grep -R "apiKey\|secret" ext/
tests.exp: The extension keeps no secrets in storage or code. All traffic uses HTTPS. Sensitive data shows only in extension UI that page scripts cannot read.

tests.title: Check the inventory and risk assessment of legacy applications
tests.obj: Finds unknown or unassessed legacy applications that keep running.
steps: Ask for the inventory of legacy applications.
Make sure each entry has the version, production date, configuration, owner and end-of-life status.
Make sure each entry has a risk assessment and a threat model.
Make sure the assessment states the data handled, known vulnerabilities, business impact and pivot risk.
tests.ex: Asset inventory export; compare with network scan results
tests.exp: Every legacy application is in the inventory with version, owner and a current risk assessment.

tests.title: Check access restrictions around a legacy application
tests.obj: Finds legacy applications that anyone on the network can reach or use with high-risk features.
steps: Find the network location of the application. Make sure it sits in a restricted subnet.
Make sure IP allow-lists or a gateway limit who can connect.
Scan the hosts. Make sure only needed ports are open.
Make sure only authenticated users can use it, by the application or by an IdP.
Make sure high-risk features are off for users who do not need them.
tests.ex: nmap -sV -p- HOST; curl -i https://HOST/ without credentials
tests.exp: Only needed ports are open and only allowed users and networks reach the application. Unused risky features are off.

tests.title: Check scanning, patching and compensating controls for legacy applications
tests.obj: Finds legacy applications with known vulnerabilities and no plan to patch or contain them.
steps: Make sure a vulnerability scan of the application and its hosts runs on a schedule.
Take the last scan results. Make sure each finding has a patch or a recorded compensating control.
Make sure patch priority uses the risk of the application.
For findings with no patch, make sure the control, an owner and a review date exist.
tests.ex: nessus or qualys scan report; patch ticket history
tests.exp: Scans run regularly. Each finding has a patch or a compensating control with an owner and a review date.

tests.title: Check monitoring and incident response for legacy applications
tests.obj: Finds legacy applications whose attacks go unseen because logs do not reach the security tools.
steps: Find how application logs reach the security monitoring system.
If the format is not supported, look for a converter or a script that reports indicators of compromise.
Make sure network traffic of the legacy environment is monitored for anomalies.
Make sure the incident response plan lists the legacy application as a priority system.
tests.ex: SIEM search for the legacy host; incident response plan
tests.exp: Legacy logs or indicator reports reach the monitoring system. The incident response plan names the system as a priority.

tests.title: Check the maintainability and migration plan of legacy applications
tests.obj: Finds legacy applications that nobody can fix or replace.
steps: Ask who can troubleshoot and reconfigure the application. Make sure at least two people can.
Make sure troubleshooting guides exist for common failures.
Read the migration plan. Make sure it has steps, an expected completion date and an owner.
Make sure the plan covers budget, expertise and urgency from the risk profile.
tests.ex: Runbooks; migration plan document
tests.exp: More than one person can maintain the application. A migration plan with steps, date and owner exists.

tests.title: Test micro-frontend iframe sandbox and message sender checks
tests.obj: Find embedded features that run with the privileges of the host page or accept messages from a wrong sender.
steps: List the micro-frontends and how the host loads each one: script, component or iframe.
Look at the iframe sandbox attribute of each less-trusted feature.
Make sure allow-scripts and allow-same-origin are not both set for a same-origin frame.
Send a message from another frame of the same origin and from a sandboxed frame with origin null.
Make sure the receiver checks event.origin, event.source and the message type and fields.
Make sure a message cannot start a privileged action without a server-side check.
tests.ex: DevTools console: frames[1].postMessage({type:"setRole",role:"admin"},"*"); grep the bundle for addEventListener("message"
tests.exp: Less-trusted features run in sandboxed frames on a separate origin. Receivers check the exact origin, the source window and the message contract, and do not trust null.

tests.title: Review how the host loads remote micro-frontend code
tests.obj: Find remote code loading where an attacker or a compromised remote can change the running host application.
steps: List all remote entry URLs and the place where each URL is set.
Make sure the URLs come from host configuration and not from a query parameter or user input.
Make sure each remote uses HTTPS and an immutable, reviewed release.
Make sure Subresource Integrity covers the entry script and the dynamic chunks.
Make sure the Content-Security-Policy allows only the approved remote origins.
Make sure the shell and each remote have separate deployment credentials.
tests.ex: grep -R "remoteEntry" dist/; check webpack ModuleFederation config; curl -sI of the Content-Security-Policy header
tests.exp: Only approved HTTPS remotes at fixed releases load. Integrity and CSP controls cover the dynamic chunks. Deployment credentials are separate.

tests.title: Test passkey registration for account binding and recent authentication
tests.obj: Find passkey enrollment that lets an attacker add a credential to the account of a victim.
pre: A test account with WebAuthn support or a virtual authenticator.
steps: Add a passkey with a long-lived session and make sure the application asks for recent re-authentication.
Start registration as user A and send the response from user B.
Change the user ID or account value in the registration request.
Send the registration request from another site and make sure CSRF checks block it.
Look for rate limits and a notice to the user after enrollment.
tests.ex: Burp: intercept POST /webauthn/register/finish and change the userId; replay the options request without a fresh login
tests.exp: The server asks for recent authentication, uses the account from its own ceremony state and ignores an account identifier from the client. The user gets a notice.

tests.title: Test WebAuthn ceremony checks for challenge, origin and user verification
tests.obj: Find a relying party that accepts a replayed, forged or wrong-scope passkey response.
pre: A virtual authenticator.
steps: Capture a valid registration and a valid sign-in response with a virtual authenticator.
Replay the sign-in response and make sure the server rejects the used challenge.
Wait until the challenge expires and send the response.
Change the type, the origin and the RP ID hash in the client data and send it again.
Use a registration challenge in a sign-in and a challenge of one account for another account.
Clear the user verification flag where the policy needs it.
tests.ex: Chrome DevTools WebAuthn panel (virtual authenticator); Burp Repeater on /webauthn/authenticate/finish
tests.exp: The server accepts only an unused and unexpired challenge of the right ceremony and account. Type, origin, RP ID and flags must match the policy. A used response fails.

tests.title: Test passkey management, revocation and the last credential
tests.obj: Find credential management that allows silent changes or leaves a revoked passkey valid.
pre: A test account with two passkeys.
steps: Open the passkey management page and look at the data shown, such as name and last use.
Remove a passkey and use it to sign in again.
Try to add or remove a passkey without recent re-authentication.
Try to remove the last sign-in method.
Make sure the user gets a notice when a passkey is added or removed.
Look at the audit log for enrollment, use and revocation events.
tests.ex: Virtual authenticator in Chrome DevTools; sign in with a removed credential ID
tests.exp: A removed passkey stops working at once. Changes need recent authentication, send a notice, and are logged. The last method cannot be removed without a safe recovery path.

tests.title: Test account recovery and fallback paths for bypass of passkey login
tests.obj: Find recovery or fallback methods that are weaker than the passkey and let an attacker take over the account.
pre: A test account with a passkey and a recovery email.
steps: List all recovery and fallback methods for an account with a passkey.
Fail a passkey sign-in and look for a silent fallback to a password, SMS or email code.
Start recovery with only email access and look at what the user gets.
Make sure recovery codes are single-use and hashed, and that the user can create new ones.
After recovery, look at the sessions and the old credentials, and make sure the user gets a notice.
tests.ex: Use the forgot password and lost device flows with a test mailbox; compare the steps with the passkey sign-in
tests.exp: Recovery is not weaker than the passkey for high-risk accounts. Recovery codes work once. Recovery ends old sessions and the user gets a notice.

tests.title: Test payment gateway return and callback handling for spoofing
tests.obj: Find checkout flows that mark an order as paid because of a forged return URL or callback.
pre: A gateway sandbox account.
steps: Find the return URL and the callback URL that the gateway uses.
Call the return URL with a changed status, amount and order ID.
Send a callback with no signature and with a wrong signature.
Send a valid callback twice and look for a second fulfillment.
Send a callback with a different amount or currency than the order.
Check that the server asks the gateway API for the payment status before it fulfills the order.
Check that the server calculates the order total again from trusted data.
tests.ex: curl "https://target/checkout/return?order=1001&status=paid&amount=0.01"; replay the gateway callback with curl --data-binary
tests.exp: Only a verified server-to-server callback with matching order, amount and currency completes an order. Return URL values are not trusted. A repeated callback has no second effect.

tests.title: Test that policy decision errors and timeouts deny access
tests.obj: Find enforcement points that allow a request when the policy decision service fails, times out or returns unusable output.
pre: A test environment where the decision service can be stopped.
steps: Find the enforcement points and the policy decision service that each one calls.
Stop the decision service or block the network path to it, in a test environment.
Send requests to protected operations and look at the result.
Return a slow, empty or malformed answer from a decision service test double.
Send a batch decision request with one missing item result and look at that item.
Look for a gateway setting that allows traffic when authorization fails.
tests.ex: Block the PDP port with iptables; curl -i https://target/api/admin/users; check Envoy ext_authz failure_mode_allow
tests.exp: Every protected operation is denied when a valid decision is not available. A missing or invalid item in a batch is denied.

tests.title: Test list, search, export and count paths for authorization filters
tests.obj: Find collection endpoints that return or count objects that the user may not access, even when single-object reads are safe.
pre: Two users with different data access.
steps: List the endpoints that return collections: list, search, export, count and aggregate.
Call each endpoint as a low-privilege user and as a user of another tenant.
Compare the returned items, the total count and the facets with the allowed items.
Add filter and sort parameters with unusual operators and field names.
Use a returned identifier in an update or delete request.
Stop the policy service and look at the collection result: a missing filter must not mean all items.
tests.ex: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <userB>" "https://target/api/orders?limit=1000&sort=-created"; GET /api/orders/count; GET /api/orders/export.csv
tests.exp: Collection paths return and count only the objects that the user may access. Unsupported filters and missing policy output are denied. A listed item does not authorize later changes.

tests.title: Review how authorization policy and data reach the decision points
tests.obj: Find policy distribution that lets old rules stay active, accepts unsigned policy or leaves decision APIs open.
steps: Find who may change each policy and attribute, and the maximum delay for a change to take effect.
Change a role or revoke a permission and measure the time until each decision point denies access.
Look for signature checks on policy bundles before activation.
Try to load an unsigned or old policy bundle in a test environment.
Make sure the decision and policy administration APIs need authentication and tenant scope.
Make sure a decision point with missing or old data denies the affected operations.
tests.ex: opa run --server --verification-key key.pem ...; curl http://pdp:8181/v1/policies without credentials
tests.exp: Policy changes reach all decision points within the set delay. Only signed and approved bundles load. Old data or a missing bundle leads to deny. Policy APIs need authentication.

tests.title: Check that an automated authorization matrix runs on every release
tests.obj: Find access rules that break over time because no automated test checks them against the documented matrix.
steps: Find the authorization matrix: roles, resources and actions in a machine-readable file.
Make sure every service and route in the application appears in the matrix.
Run the matrix tests and look for each allowed and each denied combination.
Add a new route without a matrix entry and make sure the pipeline fails or alerts.
Make sure the tests cover horizontal, vertical and cross-tenant access and use two accounts per role.
Make sure the pipeline stops the release when a test fails.
tests.ex: CI job output; pytest or Newman suite generated from authz-matrix.yaml with expected 200/403 for each role
tests.exp: A machine-readable matrix drives automated tests in the release pipeline. New routes without an entry fail the build. A failed test stops the release.

tests.title: Test post-quantum hybrid key exchange, fallback and dual signature checks
tests.obj: Find deployments where post-quantum protection is not used, is silently dropped, or where one of two signatures is enough.
pre: A test client that supports hybrid key exchange.
steps: Open the connection from real clients through the proxy, the gateway and the back end.
Look at the negotiated key exchange group of each connection.
Block the post-quantum group at the client and look for a silent retry with classical algorithms where PQC is required.
Send a signature object where one of two required signatures is missing or wrong.
Test the handshake time and the limits for certificate, message and field sizes.
Look at logs and alerts for connections that use classical algorithms only.
tests.ex: openssl s_client -connect target:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -brief; curl --curves X25519MLKEM768 -v https://target; wireshark ClientHello
tests.exp: Required paths use the hybrid exchange and fail without a silent classical retry. Both signatures must be valid. Classical-only use is logged and approved as an exception.

tests.title: Test database tenant isolation with the request role and pooled connections
tests.obj: Find shared-table tenant isolation that fails because of a privileged database role, missing policies or a reused connection.
pre: Two tenants with test data.
Read access to the database role settings.
steps: List the tables that hold tenant data and the isolation method for each, such as row-level security.
Read the database role of the request path. Make sure it is no superuser and has no BYPASSRLS attribute.
Make sure every tenant table has a policy that is enforced.
Send requests for tenant A and then tenant B over the same pooled connection.
Send a request with no tenant context and look at the result.
tests.ex: psql: SELECT rolname,rolsuper,rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='<app_role>'; SELECT relname,relrowsecurity,relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN (<tables>)
tests.exp: The request role cannot bypass row security. Each tenant table has an enforced policy. Tenant context does not carry over between pooled requests, and a missing context denies access.

tests.title: Test cache keys for tenant and user scope
tests.obj: Find application caches that serve one tenant data to another tenant because the key has no tenant context.
steps: List the caches in use and the key format of each.
Make sure each key of tenant data holds the tenant identifier and the other inputs that change the result.
Fill the cache as user A of tenant A, then request the same object ID as tenant B.
Use the same user ID in two tenants and compare the cached results.
Make sure the request is authorized before a cached value is read.
tests.ex: redis-cli --scan --pattern "*" | head; compare keys such as prefs:42 and tenantA:prefs:42
tests.exp: Keys of tenant data hold the tenant identifier. A cached value never goes to another tenant. Shared entries live in a documented global namespace.

tests.title: Test background jobs and queue messages for tenant context
tests.obj: Find asynchronous work that runs with a tenant identifier from the message that nobody authorized.
steps: List the queues and job types that process tenant data.
Send a message to the queue with the tenant identifier of another tenant, in a test environment.
Check if the consumer authenticates the producer and authorizes the action again.
Look at idempotency keys and retry state and check that they are scoped by tenant.
Flood the queue as one tenant and measure the delay for another tenant.
tests.ex: Publish a job JSON with a changed tenant_id to the test broker; compare the job result and the audit log
tests.exp: The consumer trusts only authenticated producers and checks the action again. Idempotency keys and retries are per tenant. One tenant cannot starve the others.

tests.title: Test file storage and signed URLs for tenant isolation
tests.obj: Find object storage where one tenant can read, change or delete the objects of another tenant.
steps: List how tenant files are named and which bucket, key prefix or policy keeps tenants apart.
Request the object key of tenant A as a user of tenant B.
Change the tenant part of a path with ../ and with a similar tenant name prefix.
Make sure a signed URL covers one object, one action, and a short time.
Check if the client tenant metadata is trusted for authorization.
tests.ex: curl -b "session=<tenantB>" https://target/files/tenants/acme/report.pdf ; try tenants/acme-corp/ and tenants/acme/../acme-corp/
tests.exp: The server authorizes the exact tenant, object and action for each request. Prefixes are not a boundary. Signed URLs are narrow and expire.

tests.title: Test tenant offboarding, data deletion and backup restore
tests.obj: Find tenant lifecycle gaps that leave access or data after offboarding, or that mix tenants in a restore.
pre: Two test tenants and a backup test plan.
steps: Offboard a test tenant.
Make sure the sessions, API keys and tokens of the tenant stop working at once.
Look for tenant data left in caches, object versions, exports and replicas.
Check that deletion of the tenant prefix does not match other tenants, such as tenants/acme and tenants/acme-corp.
Restore one tenant from a shared backup and look for the data of other tenants.
Try a restore request as an unauthorized operator.
tests.ex: Use the tenant admin API to delete tenant "acme" in a test environment; then replay its API key and list the storage prefixes
tests.exp: Offboarding stops all tenant access and removes data by the retention policy. Other tenants are not affected. A restore adds only data of the target tenant and needs authorization.

tests.title: Test tenant-aware rate limits and shared resource quotas
tests.obj: Find shared services where one tenant can use all capacity and slow down the other tenants.
steps: Find the shared resources: API, queue, worker pool, connection pool and storage.
Check if the limits have the tenant identity as one dimension.
Send a high request rate as tenant A and measure the response time for tenant B.
Make sure the limit counters work across all application instances.
Make sure throttled responses use HTTP 429 and Retry-After.
tests.ex: ab or k6 with tenant A token at the limit rate while tenant B runs a steady request every second; compare latency
tests.exp: The tenant A load does not change the service for tenant B. Limits are per tenant and apply on every instance.

tests.title: Check the system model with data flows and trust boundaries
tests.obj: Finds systems whose threat model is missing, out of date or without trust boundaries.
steps: Ask for the data flow diagram or a comparable system model.
Make sure it shows trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities.
Compare the diagram with the real system. Look for missing components and flows.
For cloud systems, make sure the model shows IAM roles, managed services, storage and the shared responsibility split.
tests.ex: Data flow diagram in a format that the team can update, such as a threat model file in the repository
