tests.obj: Finds APIs that rely on the client to send steps in the right order.
steps: Write down the steps of a flow, for example create, pay, approve and ship.
Capture the request of each step.
Send a later step without the earlier steps. Replay and reorder steps.
Change status or step values and reuse tokens from other steps.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater and Sequence of requests; Postman collection with a changed order; example: POST /orders/<id>/ship before payment.
tests.exp: The server checks the state of the flow on every request. Out-of-order calls, replays and changed states are rejected.

tests.title: Race parallel requests against single-use functions
tests.obj: Finds single-use limits, such as coupons or votes, that fail when requests run at once.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Find functions that must run once or a few times, such as coupons, votes and invites.
Send many identical requests at the same time.
Count how many succeeded.
Compare with the limit.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater send group in parallel; Turbo Intruder race-single-packet-attack template; curl --parallel.
tests.exp: The function succeeds as many times as the limit allows. The server uses locks or atomic updates.

tests.title: Check that B2B and developer APIs have the same anti-automation controls
tests.obj: Finds machine-to-machine APIs that skip the protection of the public client.
steps: List the APIs for partners, developers and machines.
Compare the controls of these APIs with the controls of the web client for the same flow.
Run the scripted flow test against the partner API.
Check the keys, quotas and alerts for each partner.
tests.ex: Postman collection of the partner API; comparison table of controls; review of the quota settings in the API gateway.
tests.exp: Partner APIs have quotas, keys per client and alerts. The controls are not weaker than those of the public client.

tests.title: Check the detection of scripted misuse and the response
tests.obj: Finds systems that do not detect or log non-human use of sensitive flows.
steps: Run a script on a sensitive flow with a very short time between steps.
Look for changes in responses, blocks, captcha or extra logins.
Check the logs and alerts for the script.
Read the incident process for the alerts.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder; log search for the test source IP; review of the WAF or bot rules.
tests.exp: The system detects non-human speed and device patterns on sensitive flows. It logs the events and sends an alert.

tests.title: Bypass login and OTP limits with batched requests
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL APIs where many login or OTP tries fit in one HTTP request.
pre: Use a test account.
steps: Send a JSON array of several login mutations in one request.
Send one query that holds many aliased login mutations.
Check if the rate limit and the lock out count each operation or each request.
Check if batched requests work for sensitive operations.
tests.ex: InQL batch attack; graphql-cop (test for batching and alias overloading); Burp request: [{"query":"mutation{login(...)}"},{...}].
tests.exp: Rate limits and lock outs count each operation. Sensitive operations cannot run in batches, and the batch size has a limit.

tests.title: Bypass resource limits with batched expensive mutations
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL endpoints where batched requests skip request limits and size checks.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Find a costly mutation, such as an image upload or an export.
Send the mutation many times in one array or with many aliases.
Watch the CPU, memory and time of the server.
Check the limit for the number of operations in a request.
tests.ex: graphql-cop; Burp request with 100 aliases of uploadPic; load graph of the test host.
tests.exp: The server limits the number of operations per request and the cost of a request. Total work per client is bounded.

tests.title: Bypass a query denylist with aliases
tests.obj: Finds access rules that block field names by text match and so miss aliased fields.
steps: Send a query for a blocked field and confirm the block.
Send the same field with an alias.
Send it with changed space characters, fragments and variables.
Check where the access rule runs: at the text level or at the resolver.
tests.ex: InQL; Burp GraphQL Raider; query { a: adminUsers { id } } compared with query { adminUsers { id } }.
tests.exp: Access is enforced in the resolvers by role. Aliases, fragments and space characters do not change the result.

tests.title: Test object access by ID, node fields and edges in GraphQL
tests.obj: Finds queries that return objects of other users by ID or through relations.
steps: Run a query for an object ID of user B as user A.
Use the node and nodes fields with IDs of user B.
Reach the same object through a relation from an object of user A.
Repeat with mutations that delete or change an object of user B.
tests.ex: InQL scan; graphql-path-enum; query { user(id: "<idB>") { name email } }; mutation deleteReports with an ID of user B.
tests.exp: Every resolver, edge and node checks that the caller may access the object. Another user's ID returns an error or null.

tests.title: Call privileged mutations and queries as a lower role
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL operations for admins that other roles can call.
steps: Get the schema from a test environment. List all mutations and queries.
Mark the ones that need a role, such as deleteUser and promoteUser.
Call each marked operation with a lower role and without a token.
Check mutations and subscriptions too.
tests.ex: InQL; mutation { deleteUser(id: "12345") { success } } with a token of a normal user.
tests.exp: Operations for higher roles return an authorization error for lower roles and for anonymous clients.

tests.title: Look for sensitive fields in the schema and in mutation results
tests.obj: Finds types and mutation results that expose private fields of other objects.
steps: Read the schema for fields such as passwordHash, apiKey, ssn, role and recentLocation.
Query these fields as a normal user.
Call mutations that return objects, such as reportUser. Read the returned fields.
Compare the fields with the fields that the client needs.
tests.ex: InQL; query { __type(name: "User") { fields { name } } }; GraphQL Voyager to view types.
tests.exp: Types expose only fields the caller may read. Mutation results hold no private fields of other users.

tests.title: Check query timeouts, pagination and amount limits
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL APIs without a time limit or a cap on list sizes.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Send a query that asks for a very large list size.
Send a costly query and measure the time before the server stops it.
Check that list fields use pagination with a maximum.
Check the timeout in the resolver and in the HTTP server.
tests.ex: graphql-cop; Burp request with first: 99999999; timing in Burp Logger.
tests.exp: List sizes have a server-side maximum. Queries stop after a set time at the application and at the HTTP layer.

tests.title: Test GraphQL arguments and custom scalars for injection
tests.obj: Finds resolvers that pass arguments to SQL, OS or other interpreters without checks.
steps: List arguments of type String and custom scalars such as DateTime.
Send injection test strings for SQL, NoSQL, OS command and XSS in each argument.
Read errors and response data for changes.
Check that the schema uses enums, input types and length limits.
tests.ex: InQL; sqlmap with a GraphQL request file (-r); query { dogs(namePrefix: "a'") { name } }.
tests.exp: Arguments are checked against strict types and allowlists. Resolvers use safe query methods. Test strings do not change the result.

tests.title: Test if GraphQL arguments reach an older REST API unchecked
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL layers that forward arguments to old APIs and use the rights of the GraphQL node.
steps: Find GraphQL fields that call an older REST or internal API.
Send an ID argument with path parts, for example 1/delete.
Check if the call reaches another route or object of the old API.
Check if the old API sees the user rights or the rights of the GraphQL node.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater with id variable values such as "1/delete" and "1?admin=true" on a test system.
tests.exp: The GraphQL layer validates arguments and passes them in a safe way. The old API gets the rights of the caller.

tests.title: Check GraphQL errors, debug mode and schema tools in production
tests.obj: Finds GraphQL servers that return stack traces, debug data or schema tools.
steps: Send invalid queries, wrong types and a query that fails in a resolver.
Read the error body for traces, paths and SQL text.
Look for debug flags, GraphiQL and Playground on the host.
Check the error format against the documentation.
tests.ex: graphql-cop; InQL; curl -d '{"query":"{ x }"}' https://api.example/graphql.
tests.exp: Errors are generic. Stack traces and debug mode are off in production, and schema tools are not reachable.

tests.title: Check that gRPC services use TLS and mutual TLS
tests.obj: Finds gRPC ports that accept plain text or clients without a certificate.
steps: Connect to each gRPC port without TLS.
Check the TLS version and cipher suites.
For service-to-service calls, connect without a client certificate.
Check the life time and the rotation of certificates.
tests.ex: grpcurl -plaintext host:50051 list; testssl.sh host:443; openssl s_client -connect host:443.
tests.exp: Production gRPC accepts only TLS 1.2 or newer. Service-to-service calls need a client certificate with a short life.

tests.title: Check that gRPC reflection is off in production
tests.obj: Finds gRPC servers that list all services and messages to any client.
steps: Call the reflection service on each production gRPC port.
List the services, methods and message types.
Check for internal or admin methods in the list.
Check the option in the server code.
tests.ex: grpcurl host:443 list; grpcurl host:443 describe <service>; grpcui for exploration.
tests.exp: Reflection is off in production, or only authorized clients can use it.

tests.title: Check authentication on every gRPC method, also for streams
tests.obj: Finds methods, mostly stream methods, that no authentication interceptor covers.
steps: List all methods, also stream methods, with the proto files.
Call each method without metadata credentials.
Call each method with an expired token.
Read the server code for the interceptors and check unary and stream registration.
tests.ex: grpcurl -d '{}' host:443 pkg.Service/Method without the authorization header; review of grpc.UnaryInterceptor and grpc.StreamInterceptor.
tests.exp: Every protected method returns UNAUTHENTICATED without a valid credential. Stream methods have an interceptor too.

tests.title: Test method-level and object-level authorization in gRPC
tests.obj: Finds gRPC methods and message IDs that any authenticated client can use.
steps: Call each method with tokens of different roles.
Check for PERMISSION_DENIED for methods the role may not use.
Change object IDs in messages to IDs of another user.
Check that denials are logged.
tests.ex: grpcurl -H 'authorization: Bearer <userToken>' -d '{"userId":"<idB>"}' host:443 pkg.Admin/DeleteUser
tests.exp: Each method checks the role of the caller. Object IDs in messages are checked against the owner. Failures return PERMISSION_DENIED and are logged.

tests.title: Test protobuf field validation and message size limits
tests.obj: Finds gRPC servers that trust field types and accept very large messages or streams.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Send values at the edge of range, empty, over length and with injection test strings.
Send a message over the size limit in both directions.
Send a stream with many messages or a very long run time.
Check the maximum messages per stream and the session time.
tests.ex: grpcurl -d @ < big.json host:443 pkg.Service/Method; ghz load tool in a test environment; fuzz with protobuf-aware tools.
tests.exp: The server validates every field for business rules. It rejects oversize messages and ends streams that pass the message and time limits.

tests.title: Check rate limits and deadlines for gRPC calls
tests.obj: Finds gRPC services without limits per client or without call deadlines.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Send many unary calls from one client. Look for RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.
Open many streams from one client.
Send a call without a deadline and a slow call.
Check the client and the server timeout settings.
tests.ex: ghz --rps 500 --total 5000 host:443; grpcurl -max-time 1; review of the limiter and stream interceptor.
tests.exp: The service limits calls and streams per client. Server-side deadlines end slow calls.

tests.title: Check gRPC errors, status codes and credential placement
tests.obj: Finds detailed errors and credentials in message fields.
steps: Send invalid messages and read the status and the error text.
Look for stack traces and internal names.
Check that credentials travel in metadata and not in message fields.
Check the token life time.
tests.ex: grpcurl -v ... to see the status and trailers; review of proto files for password and token fields.
tests.exp: Errors are generic and use the right status codes. Credentials are in metadata. Tokens are short lived.

tests.title: Compare the inventory of API hosts with the exposed hosts
tests.obj: Finds API hosts that are not in the inventory or whose purpose is unclear.
steps: Get the inventory of API hosts with environment, network exposure and version.
List hosts from DNS, certificate logs, the cloud account and the gateway.
Compare the two lists.
Write down hosts that have no owner, no environment or no version.
tests.ex: subfinder -d example.com | httpx -title -tech-detect; amass enum -passive; crt.sh query; cloud API listing of gateways.
tests.exp: Every exposed API host is in the inventory with environment, audience and version. No host is unknown.

tests.title: Find old, beta and undocumented API versions and test them
tests.obj: Finds retired or test versions that run with weaker controls.
steps: Change the version in the path, header or host: v1, v2, beta, internal, test.
Search archives and old documents for retired endpoints.
Send the same request to each version that answers.
Compare the authentication, authorization and limits with the current version.
tests.ex: waybackurls api.example.com | grep -E '/v[0-9]'; gau; ffuf -u https://api.example/FUZZ/users -w versions.txt.
tests.exp: Retired versions are off. Each version that runs has the same security controls as the current version.

tests.title: Compare controls on non-production hosts with production
tests.obj: Finds beta, staging or test hosts that run the same API without the protection of production.
pre: Test only the hosts that are in scope.
steps: Find the staging, beta and test hosts of the API.
Repeat a rate limit test and a login brute force test on each host.
Check the gateway, WAF and authentication of each host.
Check which data these hosts hold.
tests.ex: ffuf against beta.api.example.com/password/reset/confirm; compare response headers of both hosts; review of the DNS records.
tests.exp: Non-production hosts have the same controls as production or are not reachable from the internet. They hold no production data.

tests.title: Check that API documentation is limited to authorized users
tests.obj: Finds public API descriptions and explorers that expose the full attack surface.
steps: Request /openapi.json, /swagger.json, /api-docs, /doc and /swagger on every API host.
Request them without a token and with a low-privilege token.
Compare the document with the routes that really exist.
Look for internal routes and test servers in the document.
tests.ex: curl -s https://api.example/openapi.json | jq '.paths|keys'; ZAP OpenAPI add-on; nuclei -t exposures/apis.
tests.exp: API descriptions and explorers are available only to authorized users and only for the routes that the user may call.

tests.title: Compare the API description with the real behavior
tests.obj: Finds undocumented endpoints, parameters and security rules in the real API.
steps: Import the OpenAPI file into a proxy or a test tool.
Call endpoints that the file does not list and send fields that it does not define.
Build a table of the effective security rules for each operation, with overrides of the global rule.
Write down each difference between file and behavior.
tests.ex: ZAP OpenAPI add-on; Burp OpenAPI Parser; Schemathesis; jq on the security and paths keys of the file.
tests.exp: The description lists all endpoints, parameters, authentication, errors and limits that the API has. No difference remains.

tests.title: Search public sources and client code for API information
tests.obj: Finds leaked API documents, keys and hidden endpoints in public sources.
steps: Search web and code hosts for the API host name, the paths and keys.
Read the JavaScript and mobile client for API routes and secrets.
Read robots.txt and sitemap files for API paths.
Check collections shared on API directories.
tests.ex: Google dorks site:example.com inurl:/api; GitHub code search for the host; JSMiner; trufflehog github --org example.
tests.exp: No API key, internal route or private document is in public sources. Findings go to the incident process.

tests.title: Review the inventory of integrated services and sensitive data flows
tests.obj: Finds data shared with third parties without approval, inventory or detail.
steps: Read the list of third-party services that the API calls or that call the API.
For each, find the business reason, the approval and the data types shared.
Compare with real outbound traffic of a test environment.
Look for flows that are not in the list.
tests.ex: Review of the architecture document; mitmproxy capture of outbound calls; data flow diagram per service.
tests.exp: Each third-party data flow has an owner, an approval and a list of data types. No unknown flow exists.

tests.title: Check the retirement plan and the security updates for old API versions
tests.obj: Finds versions that stay open without a plan or without security patches.
steps: Read the version policy and the retirement dates.
List the versions that run and the clients that still use them.
Find security fixes of the new version and check if the old version has them.
Check that documentation is built in the pipeline and stays current.
tests.ex: Review of the changelog and the gateway analytics per version; diff of the security rules between versions.
tests.exp: Each version has a retirement date. Security fixes are moved to old versions or the old version is closed.

tests.title: Check that non-production APIs do not use production data
tests.obj: Finds test environments that hold real user data under weaker controls.
steps: List the databases and storage that the non-production APIs use.
Look for real names, emails and tokens in test data.
If production data is needed, compare the controls with production.
tests.ex: Review of data copy jobs; sample queries on the test database; scan for personal data patterns.
tests.exp: Non-production APIs use synthetic data. Any real data has the same controls as in production.

tests.title: Call back-end services directly and skip the API gateway
tests.obj: Finds services that trust the gateway and have no checks of their own.
pre: Network access to the internal segment from a test client.
steps: List the internal services and their addresses from the architecture document.
From a test client in the network, call a service directly without a gateway.
Send requests without the headers that the gateway adds.
Check the network rules that restrict direct access.
tests.ex: curl http://orders.internal:8080/v1/orders/1 from a test pod; kubectl get networkpolicy; nmap of the service ports.
tests.exp: Services accept calls only from the gateway or from authenticated services. Direct calls without checks fail.

tests.title: Test object and tenant rules at each service behind the gateway
tests.obj: Finds services that rely on the edge for object and tenant checks.
steps: Send calls to an internal service with the identity of user A and an object of user B.
Change the tenant in the call.
Check each internal hop for its own checks.
Check that denials are logged.
tests.ex: curl -H 'X-User-Id: <idA>' http://orders.internal/v1/orders/<idB> from a test pod; Postman against the service address.
tests.exp: Each service enforces object, tenant and business rules itself. Edge checks are not the only protection.

tests.title: Test identity propagation between services
tests.obj: Finds forged or reused user context headers and tokens between services.
steps: Find how the user context moves between services: header, signed token or mTLS identity.
Change the user ID or role in the context.
Send a call with a context for a user without the caller service identity.
Replay a context after the token has expired.
tests.ex: curl with a changed X-User header; jwt_tool on the internal token; Burp between two test services.
tests.exp: Services check the integrity of the user context. They authenticate the service that makes the call separately from the user.

tests.title: Check service-to-service authentication and token validation
tests.obj: Finds internal calls with no authentication, weak tokens or slow revoke.
steps: List the authentication method for each service call: mTLS or tokens.
Call a service without a client certificate or token.
Use a token meant for another service.
Revoke a token. Measure how long it still works. Check that a failed validation rejects the call.
tests.ex: openssl s_client -cert; curl with a token for another audience; introspection endpoint checks.
tests.exp: Internal calls need mTLS or a validated token. Revoke takes effect in a known time. Failed validation rejects the request.

tests.title: Review the architecture document for services, data flows and API definitions
tests.obj: Finds absent records of services, relations, data assets and API definitions.
steps: Read the list of services, stores and queues with their API definitions.
Read the list of service-to-service and service-to-store relations.
Compare with the real traffic and the cluster objects.
Mark services that have no entry or that have broad scopes.
tests.ex: kubectl get svc -A; service mesh traffic graph; comparison with the architecture document.
tests.exp: The document lists all services, relations, data assets and API definitions. Each service has least privilege scopes.

tests.title: Check the logs of a service architecture
tests.obj: Finds services that log secrets or cannot be traced across calls.
steps: Make one call that passes through several services.
Find the correlation ID in the log entries of each service.
Look for secrets and tokens in the logs.
Check that the log agent and broker use mutual authentication.
tests.ex: Search in the central log system for the request ID; review of the agent and broker configuration.
tests.exp: Each service logs a correlation ID and no secrets. Log transport is authenticated and encrypted.

tests.title: Find out what each rate limit is based on
tests.obj: Finds rate limits that one client can bypass with a new IP, key or session.
pre: Agree the request volume with the owner. Do not run on production.
steps: Send requests to an expensive endpoint until the API returns 429. Record the count and the time window.
Change the source IP header, the user agent and the client ID. Send again.
Log in as a second user and repeat. Check if the limit is per user or per key.
Check if an authenticated session removes the limit.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder; ffuf -rate; curl with X-Forwarded-For set to random values; record the 429 point and the Retry-After header.
tests.exp: Limits apply per account and per API key, not only per IP. A header change or a login does not remove the limit.

tests.title: Test the page size and the number of records per response
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that return very large result sets in one response.
steps: Find parameters such as limit, page_size, per_page and count.
Send very large, zero and negative values.
Send a request without a page size and check the default.
Compare the response size and time.
tests.ex: curl 'https://api.example/v1/items?limit=1000000'; Burp Intruder with a number list for the limit parameter.
tests.exp: The API enforces a maximum page size on the server. Invalid values give 400 or the default value.

tests.title: Test the limits for body size, string length and array size
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that accept very large payloads.
steps: Send a body that is larger than the documented maximum.
Send a string with a length far over the field limit.
Send an array with many thousands of elements.
Send deeply nested JSON.
tests.ex: curl --data-binary @big.json -H 'Content-Type: application/json' https://api.example/v1/items; python -c to build a nested JSON file; check for HTTP 413.
tests.exp: The API rejects oversize requests with 413 or 400 before it does costly work. Limits exist at the gateway and in the service.

tests.title: Test file upload size limits and the work after the upload
tests.obj: Finds upload endpoints where a large or many files use too much memory or CPU.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Find endpoints that take files or Base64 data and process them, for example thumbnails.
Send a file over the size limit.
Send many small uploads in parallel.
Watch the server time and memory in a test environment.
tests.ex: curl -F file=@big.png https://api.example/v1/avatar; Turbo Intruder with 50 parallel uploads; monitoring graphs of the test host.
tests.exp: The API checks the size before it processes the file. The number of uploads and the work per upload have limits.

tests.title: Test slow requests and operations that run too long
tests.obj: Finds absent timeouts for slow clients and for expensive queries.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Open a connection and send the request headers or the body very slowly.
Send expensive search, sort and filter requests.
Measure the time until the server stops the request.
Compare with the documented timeout.
tests.ex: slowhttptest -c 1000 -H -u https://test.api.example/ ; curl --limit-rate 10; a search request with a wildcard filter.
tests.exp: The server closes slow connections and stops long requests after a set time. Minimum data rates and absolute timeouts exist.

tests.title: Check that costly third-party calls are limited per target and per account
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that trigger paid SMS, email or other provider calls without a limit.
pre: Use a sandbox of the provider. Do not send real SMS.
steps: Find endpoints that make the back end call a paid provider, such as SMS or email.
Send many requests for the same phone number and for different numbers.
Count the provider calls in the test sandbox of the provider.
Check the cost limits and cost alerts at the provider.
tests.ex: Mock provider or sandbox account; Burp Turbo Intruder on POST /initiate_forgot_password; review of provider billing settings.
tests.exp: The API limits requests per target and per account. The provider account has a cost limit or a cost alert.

tests.title: Check the limit on single operations such as OTP check and recovery
tests.obj: Finds operations that a client can repeat without a limit, for example OTP checks.
steps: List operations that must have a low repeat count: OTP check, recovery and coupon check.
Repeat each operation many times with one account.
Note the count where the API blocks or delays.
Repeat the test with a second token of the same account.
tests.ex: Burp Turbo Intruder with a 6-digit OTP range on a test account; Postman runner with 100 iterations.
tests.exp: Each sensitive operation has its own low limit per account. A new token does not reset the count.

tests.title: Check that limits bound the work of one request
tests.obj: Finds endpoints where one request does a large amount of work.
steps: Find search, export, bulk write and report endpoints.
Send one request that asks for the maximum work, such as a full export.
Send the same request in parallel up to the rate limit.
Compare the server load with a normal request.
tests.ex: curl 'https://api.example/v1/export?format=csv&all=true'; bulk write with 10000 items; load graph in the test environment.
tests.exp: Costly operations have limits on the work per request, such as items and time, and on concurrent runs per client.

tests.title: Check CPU, memory and process limits of the API runtime
tests.obj: Finds services that can use all the memory, file descriptors or processes of the host.
steps: Read the container or serverless settings of each API service.
Look for limits on memory, CPU, restarts, file descriptors and processes.
Check the limits for open connections and simultaneous files.
Check the alerts for the limits.
tests.ex: kubectl describe pod and docker inspect for limits; ulimit -a in the container; review of the deployment files.
tests.exp: Each API service has limits for memory, CPU, file descriptors and processes. Alerts show when a limit is near.

tests.title: Build a security test matrix from the OpenAPI description
tests.obj: Finds operations whose real security rule differs from the rule in the description.
pre: The OpenAPI or Swagger file, or a request collection, from the customer.
steps: Import the OpenAPI file. Read the global security rule and each operation override.
Build a table of operation, method, required scheme and required scope or role.
Call each operation with every credential type and role in the table.
Mark each result that differs from the table.
tests.ex: Schemathesis; ZAP OpenAPI add-on; Burp OpenAPI Parser; Postman collection generated from openapi.json; Newman for the matrix.
tests.exp: The behavior of each operation matches its documented security rule. No operation allows more than the table says.

tests.title: Mutate valid requests one constraint at a time from the schema
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that fail or misbehave when a field leaves its declared type or range.
steps: Send a valid request that follows the declared types, required fields and enum values.
Change one constraint at a time: type, length, range, enum value or a required field.
Record every 5xx response, every accepted invalid value and every long delay.
Check that the server rejects the bad value with 400.
tests.ex: schemathesis run openapi.json --checks all; RESTler fuzz; ZAP OpenAPI active scan; Burp Intruder on single fields.
tests.exp: The API rejects each invalid value with 400 or 422 and a generic message. No 5xx response occurs.

tests.title: Find hidden parameters in headers, URL segments and structured values
tests.obj: Finds API inputs that the description and the user interface do not show.
steps: Record full requests with a proxy while you use all functions with accounts of each role.
Look for unusual headers and URL segments that repeat with different values.
Find structured values in JSON, XML or custom formats.
Test suspected segments with an invalid value to see if they are parameters.
tests.ex: Burp Param Miner; Arjun; ZAP spider with the AJAX spider; ffuf for parameter names.
tests.exp: All inputs are known and documented. Unknown inputs are ignored or rejected.

tests.title: Check that each endpoint allows only the documented HTTP methods
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that accept methods which the API does not need.
steps: Send OPTIONS to each endpoint of the API description and read the Allow header.
Compare the Allow header with the methods that the API description lists.
Send each other method, also HEAD, and check for 405.
Check that the caller may use each allowed method on the object.
tests.ex: curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example/v1/items; Burp Intruder with a list of HTTP methods.
tests.exp: Only documented methods work. Other methods return 405. Authorization checks also apply to each allowed method.

tests.title: Check that input is validated for type, length, range and unexpected fields
tests.obj: Finds endpoints that process unchecked input from JSON, XML or form bodies.
steps: Send wrong types, negative numbers, empty strings and values over the length limit.
Send extra fields and repeated fields.
Send injection test strings in every field.
Send XML with external entities if the endpoint accepts XML.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder with a type-confusion list; curl -d '{"qty":"abc"}'; ZAP active scan.
tests.exp: The API checks each field on the server against a schema or allowlist. Unexpected content gives 400 and a log entry.

tests.title: Check that status codes do not reveal more than needed
tests.obj: Finds APIs that use wrong status codes or show if a hidden object exists.
steps: Request objects that exist, that do not exist and that belong to others.
Compare status codes and bodies. Look for 200 with an error text in the body.
Request protected routes without a token (401) and with a weak role (403).
Check for a generic 500 body.
tests.ex: curl -i for each case; Burp Comparer; Postman tests with expected status codes.
tests.exp: The API uses 401, 403, 404, 405, 413, 415, 429 and 5xx as defined. It does not show whether an object of another user exists.

tests.title: Check the audit log of API security events
tests.obj: Finds absent or unsafe logs for authentication, token and validation failures.
steps: Make failed logins, bad tokens, denied calls and validation errors in a test environment.
Find each event in the log system.
Check the fields: who, when, where, what and a request ID.
Send log injection test strings. Check that secrets are not logged.
tests.ex: Splunk or Kibana search for the test request ID; curl with a header that holds a newline marker in a test environment.
tests.exp: Security events are logged before and after the action with a request ID. Log data is cleaned and holds no secrets.

tests.title: Check that SOAP messages are validated against the XML schema
tests.obj: Finds SOAP services that accept messages that do not match the schema.
steps: Read the XSD of the service for maximum lengths, character sets and patterns.
Send messages with wrong types, fields over the length limit and unexpected elements.
Send malformed XML.
Check that each is rejected.
tests.ex: SoapUI security tests; Burp WSDL Wizard and Scanner; ZAP WSDL import.
tests.exp: The service validates each message against the XSD. The schema sets length, character set and patterns for every field.

tests.title: Test SOAP endpoints against oversize, recursive and expanded XML
tests.obj: Finds services that use too many resources for large, deep or expanded XML.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Send a message over the size limit.
Send deeply nested elements and very long element names.
Send a message with entity expansion in a test environment.
Watch CPU, memory and response time.
tests.ex: SoapUI with a generated large message; Burp Intruder; a small billion-laughs file on a test system.
tests.exp: The parser rejects oversize, recursive messages and entity expansion. A message size limit and resource limits exist.

tests.title: Check authentication and authorization for each SOAP method
tests.obj: Finds web service methods that are open or that rely on weak authentication.
steps: Call each method without credentials.
Check whether Basic authentication works over plain HTTP.
Call administrative methods as a normal client.
Check for client certificate use for sensitive services.
tests.ex: SoapUI with and without WS-Security headers; curl --cacert --cert for mTLS; Burp Autorize.
tests.exp: TLS protects every call. Each method checks the rights of the client. Administrative methods are separate and limited.

tests.title: Check message integrity, confidentiality and attachment scans
tests.obj: Finds sensitive SOAP data without signature, message encryption or file scans.
steps: Find messages with sensitive data that are stored or forwarded after receipt.
Check for XML signatures and for encryption of sensitive elements.
Change a signed element. Check that the service rejects it.
Send a test file with the EICAR string as an attachment.
tests.ex: SoapUI WS-Security configuration; xmlsec1 to check signatures; EICAR test file.
tests.exp: Sensitive messages use signatures and element encryption beyond TLS. Attachments are scanned before they are stored.

tests.title: Find API parameters that make the server fetch a URL
tests.obj: Finds API features such as webhooks, import and preview that call client-supplied URLs.
steps: Search the API description and the client code for parameters named url, uri, callback, webhook and image_url.
Look for features that fetch files, send test requests or build link previews.
Send a URL to a server that you control. Look for a request in its log.
Write down the source IP, headers and protocol of each request.
tests.ex: Burp Collaborator or interactsh-client for an out-of-band URL; Burp Param Miner; example body: {"picture_url":"https://<collaborator>/p.jpg"}.
tests.exp: Every URL parameter is known and documented. Each one is tied to an allowlist or a controlled fetch service.

tests.title: Test URL parameters for access to internal addresses and ports
tests.obj: Finds API endpoints that call loopback, private or internal hosts for the client.
pre: Written permission to scan the internal network from the API host.
steps: Send a URL that points to the loopback address or an internal host name.
Send private network addresses and a different port for each request.
Compare the response time and the error text for open and closed ports.
Read the response body for data of the internal service.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder on the url parameter with an internal address list; compare response times in Burp Logger.
tests.exp: The API refuses internal and private targets. Errors and response time do not show which internal ports are open.

tests.title: Test webhook creation and test requests for response disclosure
tests.obj: Finds webhook features that show the response of the target to the user.
steps: Create a webhook that points to a server that you control.
Check the options that send a test request at creation time.
Create a webhook to an internal address. Read the API response and the delivery log.
Check if the full response body of the target returns to the client.
tests.ex: POST /graphql createNotificationChannel with a callback URL; interactsh for blind calls; read the delivery history endpoint.
tests.exp: The API does not send raw responses of the target back to the client. Internal targets are refused at creation and at delivery.

tests.title: Test if the fetch follows redirects to internal targets
tests.obj: Finds fetch code that follows redirects and so passes the allowlist check.
steps: Host a URL on an allowed domain that sends a redirect to an internal address.
Send this URL in the API parameter.
Look at the logs of the redirect target.
Check the option for redirects in the HTTP client.
tests.ex: python -m http.server with a 302 handler; interactsh as the redirect target; code review of the HTTP client options.
tests.exp: The fetch client does not follow redirects, or it checks each redirect target with the same rules.

tests.title: Test URL parser differences and allowlist bypass cases
tests.obj: Finds allowlists that fail because of URL parser differences or address forms.
steps: Send URLs with user info, extra dots, mixed case and alternative IP notations.
Send an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address and a name with more than one A record.
Send a name that resolves to a public address and then to a private one.
Check that the check and the request use the same parsed host.
tests.ex: Burp Intruder with a list of URL forms and address notations; a DNS test domain with short TTL.
tests.exp: The API uses one URL parser. It checks the resolved IP address, binds the request to it and normalizes addresses before it compares them.

tests.title: Check the allowed schemes, ports and media types of fetch features
tests.obj: Finds fetch features that accept protocols or content that the feature does not need.
steps: Read which schemes and ports the fetch feature must use.
Send file, ftp and other non-HTTP schemes.
Send ports that are not on the allowlist.
Send a URL that returns a type that the feature does not expect.
tests.ex: curl -X POST https://api.example/api/profile/upload_picture -d '{"picture_url":"file:///etc/hostname"}' on a test system.
tests.exp: Only the listed schemes, ports and media types work. Other values give a generic 400 error.

tests.title: Check outbound network rules and metadata service protection
tests.obj: Finds hosts that can reach internal services and cloud metadata from the API process.
steps: Read the egress firewall and network policy for the hosts that fetch URLs.
From a test host, call the cloud metadata address of the provider.
Check that the metadata service needs a session token header (IMDSv2) and that the old version is off.
Check that fetch workers run in a separate network segment.
tests.ex: aws ec2 describe-instances --query HttpTokens; kubectl get networkpolicy; curl to the metadata address from a test pod.
tests.exp: Fetch workers can reach only needed targets. The metadata service is protected and the old version is off.

tests.title: Test authorization of each WebSocket message and action
tests.obj: Finds sockets where a valid connection gives access to all actions and objects.
steps: Open a connection as a normal user with a valid token.
Send messages for admin actions and for objects of another user.
Subscribe to channels of another user.
Check the authorization again after a role change.
tests.ex: wscat -c wss://api.example/ws -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'; Burp WebSockets history and Repeater; ZAP WebSocket tab.
tests.exp: The server checks the role and the object for each message. A connection is not full access.

tests.title: Test WebSocket message validation, size and flood limits
tests.obj: Finds sockets that accept malformed, oversize or very frequent messages.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Send messages that break the JSON schema.
Send injection test strings in each field.
Send a message larger than the limit.
Send many messages in a short time.
tests.ex: wscat; Burp WebSocket Turbo Intruder; custom Python websockets script in a test environment.
tests.exp: The server checks each message against a schema, limits size to a small value and limits the message rate per client.

tests.title: Test connection limits, idle timeouts and backpressure
tests.obj: Finds sockets that let one client hold many connections or fill server memory.
pre: Test environment only.
steps: Open many connections from one user and one IP.
Leave connections idle. Measure the time until the server closes them.
Send data fast and read slowly.
Check the heartbeat frames.
tests.ex: Python script with asyncio and websockets; Artillery WebSocket engine; monitor server memory.
tests.exp: The server limits connections per user. Idle and dead connections close. Memory use stays bound under fast producers.

tests.title: Check WebSocket session end, replay protection and logs
tests.obj: Finds sockets that stay open after logout or token expiry and leave no audit trail.
steps: Open a connection. Log out or let the token expire.
Check if the connection closes and if messages still work.
Replay a captured message.
Look in the logs for connect, close, denied and flood events.
tests.ex: wscat with a recorded message; Burp WebSockets history; log search for the connection ID.
tests.exp: Connections close at logout and token expiry. Messages use nonces or timestamps. Security events are logged without secrets.

tests.title: Check that biometric authentication is bound to a key or Keychain item
tests.obj: Finds local authentication that depends only on a success callback that an attacker can bypass with hooking.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
Biometrics are set up on the test device.
steps: Android: Search for BiometricPrompt.authenticate calls and see if they pass a CryptoObject.
Android: Search for keys generated with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) that the protected operation uses.
iOS: Search for LAContext.evaluatePolicy and SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags with user presence or biometry flags.
iOS: Hook both APIs at run time and use every flow that the biometric check protects.
Hook the callback or evaluatePolicy reply to return success and try to open the protected resource.
Find sensitive resources that open after the forced success without a key operation.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "BiometricPrompt\|CryptoObject\|setUserAuthenticationRequired" src/; frida -U -f <package> -l bypass-biometric.js (objection: android ui biometrics_bypass); r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags" Payload/App.app/App; objection -g <bundle> explore -> ios ui biometrics_bypass; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -m "-[LAContext evaluatePolicy:localizedReason:reply:]" -i SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags
tests.exp: Each sensitive resource is protected by a Keystore key or Keychain item that needs authentication. A forced success callback does not open it.

tests.title: Check for fallback to device credentials on sensitive actions
tests.obj: Finds sensitive actions that accept the weaker device PIN, pattern or passcode instead of a biometric.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
steps: Android: Search for BiometricPrompt, setAllowedAuthenticators and setDeviceCredentialAllowed.
Android: Flag the DEVICE_CREDENTIAL constant, alone or combined with a biometric constant.
iOS: Search for SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags and flag kSecAccessControlUserPresence and kSecAccessControlDevicePasscode.
iOS: Hook SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags at run time and list the flags that the app uses.
Decide for each sensitive resource if a fallback fits the risk level of the app.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "DEVICE_CREDENTIAL|setDeviceCredentialAllowed|setAllowedAuthenticators" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags
tests.exp: High-risk actions need biometrics alone, without fallback to the device credential, or the team accepts and documents the risk.

tests.title: Check that biometric keys become invalid when new biometrics are enrolled
tests.obj: Finds protected keys and Keychain items that a newly enrolled fingerprint or face can unlock.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
Use a test device where you can add a new biometric.
steps: Android: Search KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder for setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment and flag the value false.
iOS: Search SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags and flag items that do not use kSecAccessControlBiometryCurrentSet.
iOS: Hook SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags at run time and list the flags.
Set up the biometric protection in the app, then enroll a new fingerprint or face on the test device.
Try to open the protected resource with the new biometric.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags (look for biometryCurrentSet)
tests.exp: The key or item becomes unusable after a new biometric enrollment. The user must authenticate again with the app credentials.

tests.title: Check that Android biometric prompts need explicit user confirmation
tests.obj: Finds sensitive actions that a passive biometric, such as face recognition, approves without a user action.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
Android only.
steps: Search the code for BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder and setConfirmationRequired.
Flag every call that sets the value to false.
Check if the call protects a sensitive action such as a payment or data access.
Run the action with face recognition and see if it completes without a tap.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "setConfirmationRequired" src/
tests.exp: Sensitive actions use setConfirmationRequired(true) or the default value, so the user confirms the action explicitly.

tests.title: Check the validity time of Android keys that biometrics unlock
tests.obj: Finds keys that stay usable for minutes or hours after one biometric authentication.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
Android only.
steps: Search for setUserAuthenticationParameters and setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds in key generation code.
Note the duration value for each key.
Flag every key for a sensitive action that has a duration above zero.
Authenticate once, then run the sensitive operation again inside the validity window.
See if the operation succeeds without a new authentication.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "setUserAuthenticationParameters|setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds" src/
tests.exp: Keys for sensitive operations need authentication for every use (duration 0), or the validity is only a few seconds and the team accepts it.

tests.title: Check that a custom app PIN or password resists guessing
tests.obj: Finds app-defined PINs and passwords that the code compares in plain text or that allow unlimited guesses.
pre: A list of the sensitive resources that local authentication protects (tokens, keys, data) is ready.
steps: Find the screens and code where the app asks for its own PIN or password.
Search the code for a plain string comparison against a stored or hardcoded value.
Enter wrong values many times and see if the app limits or delays the attempts.
Restart the app and clear its data between attempts to see if the counter resets.
Check that the app binds the secret to key material from the Keystore or Keychain.
Check that the app rejects short PINs, such as 4 digits.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "equals\(.*(pin|passcode)|compareTo" src/; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "java.lang.String!equals"; objection: android keystore list; ios keychain dump
tests.exp: The app has no plain comparison and no hardcoded PIN. It limits wrong guesses and ties the secret to hardware-backed key material.

tests.title: Check that the backend enforces authentication for app requests
tests.obj: Finds backend functions that the app can call without a valid token, which local checks cannot protect.
steps: Record the requests that the app sends for each protected function with an interception proxy.
Replay each request without the token or session cookie.
Replay each request with the token of a different user.
Hook the local authentication result to success and check what the backend still requires.
Search the app for user roles or permissions that it sends to the backend.
tests.ex: mitmproxy -s save_flows.py; burp: Repeater (delete the Authorization header, then replay); frida -U -f <package> -l bypass-local-auth.js; curl -i https://api.example.com/v1/me (no token)
tests.exp: The backend rejects requests without a valid token. A local bypass gives no access to server data, and the server decides roles and permissions.

tests.title: Check that the app uses system flows for OAuth and third-party login
tests.obj: Finds logins in embedded WebViews, OAuth without PKCE and tokens that the app accepts without checks.
steps: Find all login flows that use OAuth, OpenID Connect or a third-party identity provider.
Check if the app opens the login page in the system browser, a custom tab or ASWebAuthenticationSession.
Flag logins that load the identity provider in an embedded WebView.
Capture the authorization request and see if it carries a state value and a PKCE code challenge.
Open the app deep links with a changed authorization response and see if the app accepts it.
Check that the app validates the token signature, issuer, audience and expiry, or that the backend does.
tests.ex: mitmproxy; burp: look for code_challenge, state, redirect_uri; adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "app://callback?code=attacker" <package>; xcrun simctl openurl booted "app://callback?code=attacker"; grep -rn "ASWebAuthenticationSession\|CustomTabsIntent\|WebView" src/
tests.exp: The app signs in users with system browser flows and PKCE. It rejects forged or replayed responses and accepts only validated tokens.

tests.title: Check that login fields support password managers and one-time code fill
tests.obj: Finds login screens that block password managers and so push users to weak or reused passwords.
steps: Open the login screen and try to fill the credentials with the system password manager.
Check the autofill hints on Android and the textContentType values on iOS for the credential fields.
Check that one-time code fields support code autofill.
Check that the app is linked to its website with website association files.
Check if the app offers passkeys where the service supports them.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "autofillHints\|importantForAutofill" src/res/layout; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist | grep -i associated; grep -r "textContentType" Payload/ (storyboard or code); curl -s https://example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json
tests.exp: Credential and code fields accept autofill. The app is linked to its domain and offers passkeys where possible.

tests.title: Check that sensitive actions need step-up authentication
tests.obj: Finds high-risk actions that need no fresh authentication, or whose approval can be reused for another action.
steps: Make a list of the high-risk actions, such as payments, password changes and display of sensitive data.
Run each action in a signed-in session and see if the app asks for a new factor.
Replay the approval request with changed amount or target and see if the server accepts it.
Skip the step-up screen in the client and call the server API directly.
See if the approval is tied to the specific transaction.
tests.ex: burp: Repeater (change the amount in the approved request and replay it); frida -U -f <package> -l skip-stepup.js; mitmproxy
tests.exp: The server demands a fresh factor for each high-risk action and ties the approval to that action. The client alone cannot skip the step.

tests.title: Check that logout and timeout end the session and clear local data
tests.obj: Finds sessions that stay valid on the server, or tokens and personal data that stay on the device after logout.
steps: Sign in and note the access and refresh tokens that the app uses.
Log out in the app and replay the old tokens against the API.
Copy the app data directory and search for tokens, cached personal data and the user profile.
Wait for the inactivity timeout and see if the app asks for a new login.
Send the app to the background and bring it back after a sensitive flow. See if it asks for a new login.
tests.ex: mitmproxy; curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <old-token>" https://api.example.com/v1/me; objection -g <package> explore -> env; adb pull /data/data/<package>; grep -rniE "token|session" data/; objection: ios keychain dump
tests.exp: The server rejects old tokens after logout and timeout. The device holds no tokens or cached personal data of the ended session.

tests.title: Check that critical actions give signed proof of user approval
tests.obj: Finds critical actions that the user can later deny, or that a tampered app can show differently from what it runs.
steps: List the critical actions, such as money transfers and legal consent.
Check if the app shows a confirmation that is tied to the exact data of the action.
Check if the confirmation produces a signature from a hardware-backed, user-authenticated key.
Check that the server validates the signature and the key attestation, and keeps the signature as evidence.
Change the displayed data in a hooked app and see if the server detects the change.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "setAttestationChallenge\|Signature" src/; frida -U -f <package> -l change-amount.js; burp: Repeater
tests.exp: Each critical action carries a hardware-backed signature over the exact approved data. The server checks it and keeps it as evidence.

tests.title: Check the minimum platform version that the app supports
tests.obj: Finds apps that run on old OS versions that lack current security patches and features.
pre: Decoded APK and extracted IPA.
steps: Android: Read minSdkVersion in the AndroidManifest.xml.
iOS: Read MinimumOSVersion in the Info.plist.
Compare the value with the platform versions that still get security updates.
Android: Search the code for Build.VERSION.SDK_INT checks and the sensitive features that they protect.
Make sure the app refuses or limits sensitive features on unsupported platform versions.
tests.ex: aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep -E "sdkVersion|targetSdkVersion" ; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist | grep MinimumOSVersion ; grep -rn "Build.VERSION.SDK_INT" out/
tests.exp: The app sets a minimum platform version that still gets security updates. It limits sensitive features on older versions.

tests.title: Check that the app targets the latest platform version
tests.obj: Finds apps that miss platform protections because they target an old SDK.
pre: Decoded APK and extracted IPA.
steps: Android: Read targetSdkVersion in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: Compare it with the current Google Play target API requirement.
iOS: Find the Xcode and SDK version that built the app, and compare it with the current App Store requirement.
Look for legacy behavior that works only because of the old target, such as broad storage access.
tests.ex: aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep targetSdkVersion ; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist | grep -E "DTSDKName|DTXcode"
tests.exp: The app targets the latest platform version that the store requires. It does not depend on legacy compatibility behavior.

tests.title: Check that the app can force users to update
tests.obj: Finds apps that cannot block old, vulnerable versions after a security fix.
pre: Test build or test backend that reports a minimum version.
steps: Android: Search the code for AppUpdateManager, getAppUpdateInfo and startUpdateFlowForResult.
iOS: Search the binary for CFBundleShortVersionString, the iTunes lookup URL and a minimum version policy.
Check that the version check runs before access to protected functions and cannot be skipped.
Check that the app uses an immediate update or a screen that the user cannot dismiss.
Run the app with a version below the minimum. Capture the traffic and hook the update calls.
Make sure the app blocks use until the user updates.
tests.ex: grep -rn "AppUpdateManager\|startUpdateFlowForResult\|BuildConfig.VERSION" out/ ; frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_update.js ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; izz~itunes.apple.com/lookup ; Burp: change the version in the request or the response
tests.exp: The app checks its version at start. It blocks use of an outdated version with a non-dismissible update flow.

tests.title: Scan app dependencies for known vulnerabilities
tests.obj: Finds third-party libraries and SDKs with public vulnerabilities.
pre: Access to the project build files, or an SBOM from the developer.
steps: Android: Run a Software Composition Analysis scan on the Gradle build, or create a CycloneDX SBOM.
iOS: Collect Package.resolved, Podfile.lock and Cartfile.resolved. Scan them, or create a CycloneDX SBOM.
Upload each SBOM to a vulnerability tool such as Dependency-Track.
List dependencies with CVE identifiers. Include transitive dependencies and bundled native libraries.
Check the exploitability and the exposure of each finding in the app.
Check that a process updates or replaces vulnerable libraries.
tests.ex: ./gradlew dependencyCheckAnalyze ; cdxgen -t java -o sbom.json ; cdxgen -o sbom.json (iOS project) ; dependency-check --enableExperimental -f SARIF -s Podfile.lock ; upload sbom.json to Dependency-Track
tests.exp: The app has no dependency with a known high-impact vulnerability. A process finds and fixes new vulnerable dependencies.

tests.title: Check native binaries for compiler security features
tests.obj: Finds native code built without PIE, stack canaries or ARC, which makes memory bugs easier to use.
pre: Extracted APK and IPA.
steps: Android: Extract the native libraries from the APK.
Android: Read the canary and pic values of each library.
iOS: Extract the main binary and list the bundled libraries and frameworks.
iOS: Check the main binary and each library for pic, stack canary symbols and ARC symbols.
Flag a library that mixes Objective-C or C code with no canary symbols.
Check false positives, such as memory-safe code, with the source code and the build flags.
tests.ex: unzip -o app.apk "lib/*" -d app ; rabin2 -I app/lib/arm64-v8a/lib.so | grep -E "canary|pic" ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; i~canary,pic ; is~release,retain
tests.exp: All native libraries use position independent code and stack canaries. iOS code that is not Swift-only uses ARC.

tests.title: Check the app for deprecated APIs in security functions
tests.obj: Finds use of deprecated APIs that lack fixes or have safer replacements.
steps: Build the app with deprecation warnings on. List the warnings.
Find deprecated keystore, crypto, networking and authentication APIs in the code.
Check the release notes of each supported platform version for removed or changed features.
Check that the team tracks the move off each deprecated security API.
Run the app on all supported platform versions.
tests.ex: ./gradlew build --warning-mode all ; xcodebuild build 2>&1 | grep -i deprecated ; grep -rn "@Deprecated\|deprecated" out/ | head
tests.exp: Security-relevant code uses no deprecated APIs, and the team treats deprecation warnings as work items.

tests.title: Check that security functions use platform APIs and vetted libraries
tests.obj: Finds custom crypto, TLS, DNS or authentication code that is likely to have flaws.
steps: Search the code for custom cryptographic algorithms, custom TLS stacks and custom DNS resolvers.
Search for custom authentication flows next to the platform credential APIs.
List third-party security libraries. Check the release date and the maintenance state of each.
Compare the libraries with standards such as FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 where the app must follow them.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "implements X509TrustManager\|MessageDigest\|Cipher.getInstance\|new Socket(" out/ ; list libraries with cdxgen -t java
tests.exp: The app uses platform APIs or vetted, maintained libraries for crypto, networking, DNS and authentication. It has no home-made security code.

tests.title: Check the app supply chain for malicious or unexpected code
tests.obj: Finds trojanized SDKs, build changes or hidden features that ship in the app.
pre: Access to the build files and the release package.
steps: Compare the SBOM of the release with the declared dependencies. List components that are not declared.
Check that the build pins dependency versions with a lockfile and takes packages from a controlled repository.
Check that code review and strong sign-in protect the source repository and the build system.
Scan the release binary for unexpected code, permissions, secrets and network endpoints.
Run the release build and look for unexpected network traffic.
Check that the signing keys are protected and that releases carry a signature.
tests.ex: cdxgen -o sbom.json ; apksigner verify --print-certs app.apk ; mitmproxy to capture the first start traffic ; grep -rn "http" out/resources | sort -u
tests.exp: The release contains only reviewed and declared components. The build pins dependencies and protects signing keys, and the release shows no unexpected behavior.

tests.title: Check the app for unsafe dynamic code loading
tests.obj: Finds code that the app loads at runtime from places that attackers control.
steps: Android: Search for DexClassLoader, PathClassLoader, System.load and System.loadLibrary with a path.
iOS: Search for dlopen and downloaded scripts or plugins.
Find the folder that the loaded code comes from. Check if it is writable or on external storage.
Check that the app verifies a signature on downloaded code against a pinned key.
Check that the code arrives over a secure channel.
tests.ex: grep -rn "DexClassLoader\|PathClassLoader\|System.load" out/ ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~dlopen
tests.exp: The app loads no code from writable or external folders. Downloaded code is signed and the app checks the signature before it runs the code.

tests.title: Check input validation on all entry points of the app
tests.obj: Finds input from the UI, IPC, files or network that reaches a sensitive sink unchecked.
steps: List the entry points: UI fields, deep links, IPC, files, the clipboard and network data.
Follow the data from each entry point to its sinks, such as SQL, file paths, WebViews and parsers.
Check that the code validates type, length, range and format against an allowlist.
Check that validation runs on the server too, as client checks are easy to bypass.
Send malformed, oversized and malicious values to each entry point. Look for crashes and injection.
Check that the parsers limit size and nesting depth.
tests.ex: semgrep --config <rules> out/ ; mobsf: upload the APK or IPA for the static scan ; adb shell monkey -p <pkg> 5000 ; Burp Suite Intruder on the API calls of the app
tests.exp: The app treats all outside data as untrusted. It validates data against allowlists before use, and malformed input causes no crash or injection.

tests.title: Check that the app uses no broken symmetric encryption algorithms
tests.obj: Finds use of DES, 3DES, RC2, RC4, Blowfish and other broken ciphers in the app or its libraries.
steps: Android: Decompile the app and search for Cipher.getInstance, SecretKeyFactory.getInstance and KeyGenerator.getInstance.
iOS: Extract the binaries and search for CCCrypt and the algorithm constants kCCAlgorithmDES, 3DES, RC4, RC2, CAST and Blowfish.
Search bundled libraries such as OpenSSL, BoringSSL and libsodium for the same algorithms.
Look at the code at each hit and find the algorithm and the data that it protects.
Compare the algorithms with the current NIST and BSI guidance.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "Cipher.getInstance\(\"(DES|DESede|RC2|RC4|Blowfish|ARC4)" src/; semgrep --config p/mobsfscan src/; mobsf scan (static analyzer); unzip app.ipa; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~CCCrypt; axt sym.imp.CCCrypt" Payload/App.app/App; strings Payload/App.app/App | grep -iE "rc4|des-|blowfish"
tests.exp: The app uses no DES, 3DES, RC2, RC4 or Blowfish for sensitive data. It uses AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 instead.

tests.title: Check that the app uses no broken block modes such as ECB
tests.obj: Finds symmetric encryption in ECB mode that leaks patterns in the data.
steps: Android: Decompile the app and list all Cipher.getInstance transformation strings.
Android: Mark the strings "AES", AES/ECB/NoPadding, AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding and AES/ECB/ISO10126Padding. Ignore RSA/ECB strings.
iOS: Search the binary for CCCrypt calls and look for kCCOptionECBMode (value 2) in the options argument.
Hook Cipher.getInstance or CCCrypt at run time and use every workflow of the app with sensitive data.
Use the backtraces to see if the encrypted data is sensitive.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "Cipher.getInstance\(\"[A-Za-z0-9]+(/ECB/[A-Za-z0-9]+)?\"\)" src/; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "javax.crypto.Cipher!getInstance"; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.CCCrypt" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i CCCrypt
tests.exp: The app does not use ECB for sensitive data. It uses an authenticated mode such as GCM.

tests.title: Check that security-relevant values come from a secure random generator
tests.obj: Finds tokens, keys, IVs and nonces that come from a predictable random number generator or from the clock.
steps: Android: Search the code for java.util.Random, Math.random, SecureRandom with a fixed seed, and Date().getTime or Calendar.MILLISECOND as value sources.
iOS: Search the binary for rand, random, srand and the *rand48 functions.
Hook these APIs at run time and use every workflow of the app.
Look at the backtraces and the code to find what the value is used for.
Flag keys, IVs, nonces, tokens, session IDs, passwords and PINs.
Ignore uses that are not security-relevant, such as UI effects or game logic.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "java\.util\.Random|Math\.random|new SecureRandom\(|getTime\(\)" src/; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "java.util.Random!*"; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~rand" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i rand -i random -i arc4random
tests.exp: The app uses SecureRandom (Android) or SecRandomCopyBytes and arc4random (iOS) for all security-relevant values. Seeds are not fixed.

tests.title: Check that cryptographic keys have a sufficient size
tests.obj: Finds symmetric and asymmetric keys that are too short for current guidance.
steps: Android: Search for KeyGenerator.init, KeyPairGenerator.initialize and key sizes in KeyGenParameterSpec.
iOS: Search for CCCrypt key length arguments and for SecKeyCreateRandomKey with kSecAttrKeyType and kSecAttrKeySizeInBits.
Write down the algorithm and the key size at each location.
Compare the sizes with the current NIST guidance, for example RSA 2048 bits or more and AES 256 bits.
Flag RSA keys of 1024 bits and AES keys of 128 bits or less for the product policy.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "KeyGenerator|KeyPairGenerator|\.init\([0-9]+\)|\.initialize\([0-9]+\)" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecKeyCreateRandomKey" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i SecKeyCreateRandomKey
tests.exp: Every key meets the current size guidance for its algorithm. The app uses no RSA 1024 bit keys and no keys shorter than the policy allows.

tests.title: Check that no cryptographic keys are hardcoded in code or files
tests.obj: Finds symmetric keys, private keys and key files that ship inside the app.
steps: Android: Search the decompiled code for SecretKeySpec and other calls that take raw key bytes or strings.
iOS: Search for SecKeyCreateWithData, CCCrypt with a literal key and CryptoKit init(rawRepresentation:) calls.
Search resources and bundle files for .key, .pem, .p12, .der and .cer files and for BEGIN PRIVATE KEY markers.
Search plist and JSON files for Base64 or hex strings next to names such as key, secret or privateKey.
Look at each hit to see if it is a real key that protects data or authenticates a user.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "SecretKeySpec" src/; find out/ ipa/ -name "*.pem" -o -name "*.p12" -o -name "*.key" -o -name "*.der"; grep -rl "BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY" out/ ipa/; strings -n 16 Payload/App.app/App | grep -E "^[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{24,}$"; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecKeyCreateWithData" Payload/App.app/App; trufflehog filesystem out ipa
tests.exp: The app contains no hardcoded keys. The app creates keys on the device or gets them from a backend and stores them in the Keystore or Keychain.

tests.title: Check that keys live only in the platform keystore
tests.obj: Finds cryptographic keys that the app stores in preferences, files or code instead of the Android Keystore or iOS Keychain.
steps: List all keys, key pairs and secrets that the app creates, imports or receives.
Android: Look for KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") and for keys written to files or SharedPreferences.
iOS: Look for SecKeyCreateRandomKey with kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave and for keys in UserDefaults or files.
Compare the app data directory before and after use, and search for key material.
Check how the app imports keys and see if it wraps them before import.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "AndroidKeyStore|KeyGenParameterSpec|setIsStrongBoxBacked" src/; objection -g <package> explore -> android keystore list; objection: ios keychain dump; grep -rE "[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{32,}" data/shared_prefs/
tests.exp: The app keeps all keys in the Android Keystore or iOS Keychain. Key material never sits in preferences, plain files or code.

tests.title: Check that Android asymmetric key pairs have one purpose
tests.obj: Finds key pairs that the app uses for more than one role, such as encryption and signing.
pre: Android only. The MASTG tests have no iOS counterpart.
steps: Search the code for KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder and note the purposes argument.
Decode the purposes bitmask: 1 encrypt, 2 decrypt, 4 sign, 8 signature check, 32 wrap key.
Flag every purposes value that mixes encryption, signing and wrapping roles.
Hook Cipher.init, Signature.initSign and Signature.initVerify and use every workflow of the app.
Check that no key is used in more than one group of operations.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "KeyGenParameterSpec" src/; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "javax.crypto.Cipher!init" -j "java.security.Signature!initSign" -j "java.security.Signature!initVerify"
tests.exp: Each key pair has exactly one role: encryption, signing or key wrapping. The value 15 or any mixed value does not appear.

tests.title: Check that Android crypto calls use no explicit security provider
tests.obj: Finds getInstance calls that name a provider other than the default Conscrypt provider.
pre: Android only.
steps: Search the decompiled code for getInstance calls with a second provider argument.
Note the provider names, such as Crypto, BC or BouncyCastle.
Flag every provider except AndroidKeyStore in KeyStore.getInstance calls.
Check the targetSdkVersion, because apps for Android 9 and higher fail when they name a provider.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "getInstance\([^)]*,\s*\"(BC|Crypto|SC|SunJCE)\"" src/; grep -rn "Security.addProvider\|BouncyCastleProvider" src/; aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep targetSdkVersion
tests.exp: No getInstance call names a provider other than the default. Only KeyStore calls name AndroidKeyStore.

tests.title: Check that the app uses no broken hash functions
tests.obj: Finds MD5 and SHA-1 in security-relevant uses such as signatures, integrity checks and fingerprints.
steps: Android: Search the decompiled code for MessageDigest.getInstance with MD5, MD2, MD4 or SHA-1.
iOS: Search the binary for CC_MD2, CC_MD4, CC_MD5, CC_SHA1 and CryptoKit Insecure.MD5 and Insecure.SHA1.
Look at the code at each hit and note what the hash protects.
Check that the app does not hash passwords or passphrases with a fast hash. A password KDF is needed.
Check that digests are not truncated below the security strength that the use case needs.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "MessageDigest.getInstance\(\"(MD5|MD2|MD4|SHA-?1)\"" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~CC_MD5; afl~CC_SHA1" Payload/App.app/App; strings Payload/App.app/App | grep -E "Insecure.*(MD5|SHA1)"
tests.exp: The app uses SHA-256 or stronger for security purposes. MD5 and SHA-1 appear only in non-security uses.

tests.title: Check that the app uses MACs correctly
tests.obj: Finds missing, weak or reused message authentication codes.
steps: List the places where the app must protect the integrity of data, such as stored files, messages and tokens.
Search the code for Mac, HMAC, CCHmac, CRC32 and hash(key + message) constructions.
Flag CRC checksums, MD5 or SHA-1 based MACs and plain hash(key || message) patterns.
Check the key source, the key reuse, the tag length and the order of encryption and MAC.
Check that the app compares tags in constant time and rejects replayed messages.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "javax.crypto.Mac|HmacMD5|HmacSHA1|CRC32" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~CCHmac" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "javax.crypto.Mac!*"
tests.exp: The app uses HMAC with SHA-256 or stronger, or an AEAD mode. Keys have one purpose, tags are full length and replays fail.

tests.title: Check how the app generates cryptographic signatures
tests.obj: Finds weak signature algorithms, short signing keys and weak nonces.
steps: Search the code for Signature.getInstance, SecKeyCreateSignature and CryptoKit signing calls.
Note the signature algorithm and digest, for example SHA1withRSA.
Note the key length of each signing key.
Check that (EC)DSA nonces come from a secure random generator or use a deterministic scheme.
Check that signing keys are not used for encryption or key agreement.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "Signature.getInstance" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecKeyCreateSignature" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "java.security.Signature!getInstance"
tests.exp: The app uses ECDSA, RSA-PSS or EdDSA with approved digests and key lengths. Nonces are unpredictable and signing keys have one purpose.

tests.title: Check that the app verifies signatures and acts on the result
tests.obj: Finds signature checks that are skipped, ignored or trust keys that an attacker can replace.
steps: List the data that the app must check with signatures, such as updates, configuration, licenses and tokens.
Search the code for the Signature class, SecKeyVerifySignature and token validation calls.
Check that a failed check stops the operation and that the code does not swallow the result.
Check that the public key comes from a trusted set and not from the same download as the data.
Change signed data in transit with a proxy and make sure the app rejects it.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "\.verify(" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecKeyVerifySignature" Payload/App.app/App; frida -U -f <package> -l hook-signature-verify.js (return false and see the app behavior); mitmproxy -s tamper.py
tests.exp: The app rejects every item with a wrong, missing or foreign signature. It enforces the expected algorithm and trusted keys.

tests.title: Check that keys derived from passwords use a password KDF
tests.obj: Finds keys derived with a plain hash, a low work factor, a missing salt or a low-entropy input.
steps: Search the code for key derivation from passwords, PINs and passphrases.
Flag plain hashes such as SHA-256 of a password, used as a key.
Look for PBKDF2, scrypt or Argon2 and note the iterations, memory and parallelism values.
Check that each derivation uses a unique random salt that is not hardcoded.
Check that a short PIN is combined with a random key from the Keystore or Keychain.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "PBKDF2|SecretKeyFactory.getInstance|scrypt|Argon2" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~CCKeyDerivationPBKDF" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec!*"
tests.exp: The app derives keys from passwords only with PBKDF2, scrypt or Argon2. It uses a current work factor and a unique random salt.

tests.title: Check that the app can rotate its cryptographic keys
tests.obj: Finds keys with no cryptoperiod, no versioning and no way to replace them.
steps: Read the design documents and find how the app stores and uses long-lived keys.
Search the code for key versions, keysets and key identifiers in the stored data format.
Find the cryptoperiod that the team defined for each key type.
Replace a key in a test build. Old data must stay readable and new data must use the new key.
Make sure the app restricts old keys to decryption and then destroys them.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "keyVersion|KeysetHandle|rotate" src/; adb shell run-as <package> ls files shared_prefs (look for key version markers)
tests.exp: The data format supports key versions. The team defines cryptoperiods, and rotation works without data loss.

tests.title: Check that key use needs authentication and an unlocked device
tests.obj: Finds keys that any code in the app, or anyone with the unlocked device, can use without limits.
steps: Android: Search KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder for setUserAuthenticationRequired, setUnlockedDeviceRequired and the validity duration.
