iOS: Search SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags and the kSecAttrAccessible values of Keychain items.
Flag keys for sensitive data that need no authentication, or that work while the device is locked.
Flag iOS items with kSecAttrAccessibleAlways or without the ThisDeviceOnly suffix.
Flag keys in StrongBox or the Secure Enclave that have no use restrictions.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "setUserAuthenticationRequired|setUnlockedDeviceRequired|setUserAuthenticationParameters" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags" Payload/App.app/App; objection -g <bundle> explore -> ios keychain dump (read the Accessible column)
tests.exp: Keys for sensitive data need user authentication and an unlocked device, are bound to the device and have a short or zero validity.

tests.title: Check that the app needs a secure device lock for sensitive features
tests.obj: Finds sensitive features that work on devices with no PIN, pattern, password or biometric lock.
pre: Use a test device. Do not clear the lock of a personal device.
steps: Search the code for KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure and LAContext canEvaluatePolicy.
Search iOS Keychain items for kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly.
Remove the screen lock on a test device and start the sensitive feature.
Remove the screen lock while the app runs and use the feature again.
See if the app blocks the feature or the key access in both cases.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "isDeviceSecure\|isKeyguardSecure" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags" Payload/App.app/App; adb shell locksettings clear --old <PIN> (test device)
tests.exp: The app checks the device lock state at each use of sensitive features. It blocks the feature or the key use when no lock is set.

tests.title: Check Android activities for task affinity and task reparenting hijack
tests.obj: Find activities with a task affinity or reparenting setting that lets another app move its screen into the task of the app.
pre: The app package or its decoded AndroidManifest.xml.
For the live test, a test device and a test app that sets a taskAffinity equal to the package name of the app. Use Android 10 or lower for the live test.
steps: Decode the manifest. List all activities with the taskAffinity, allowTaskReparenting and launchMode attributes.
Find the attribute allowTaskReparenting set to true on the application or on an activity. Examine the reason.
Make sure the activities that show login or sensitive screens use the default task affinity and no custom value.
Make sure no activity uses a launch mode that places it in a task of another app without need.
Read minSdkVersion. Note if it is lower than 30. Only Android 11 and later fix version 2 of the attack.
On a test device, install the test app that sets the same taskAffinity. Start the target app and look for the screen of the test app on top.
Make sure the user does not see a foreign screen when the app opens or when a sensitive activity ends.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk -o out; grep -nE "taskAffinity|allowTaskReparenting|launchMode" out/AndroidManifest.xml; aapt dump badging app.apk | grep sdkVersion; adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -A3 "Task id"
tests.exp: No activity sets allowTaskReparenting to true or a custom taskAffinity without a reason. The target app opens its own screens only, and minSdkVersion is 30 or higher.

tests.title: Check pinning and TLS in the own network stack of cross-platform apps
tests.obj: Find cross-platform apps whose own HTTP stack ignores the platform pinning, trust and cleartext settings.
pre: A test build, a rooted or jailbroken test device and an interception proxy. Do not test other parties' servers.
A written list of first-party domains.
steps: Identify the framework from the app package. Find out if the app uses the platform HTTP stack or its own.
For Flutter, look for pinning in Dart code with SecurityContext or a badCertificateCallback. NSC and ATS pins do not apply to Dart.
Look in the Dart code for a badCertificateCallback that returns true without a check.
For React Native on iOS, check if the pins in ATS or the URLSession code cover the traffic. For Cordova, check the native pinning plugin.
Set a system proxy and start the app. A Flutter app does not use the system proxy, so route its traffic by iptables or DNS.
Look at the traffic to first-party domains with a proxy certificate that the device trusts. Make sure the connection fails.
Look for HTTP URLs and cleartext traffic that the framework allows when the platform settings forbid it.
tests.ex: reflutter app.apk (test device only); frida -U -f com.example.app -l disable-flutter-tls.js; iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to <proxy>:8080; grep -rn "badCertificateCallback\|SecurityContext" lib/
tests.exp: The app pins first-party domains in the code path that the framework uses. A trusted proxy certificate does not give access to traffic, and cleartext is not allowed.

tests.title: Check the integrity of React Native bundles and over-the-air updates
tests.obj: Find apps that run a changed or downloaded JavaScript bundle without an integrity check.
pre: A test build and the tools to unpack and repack the package on a test device.
Knowledge of the update service that the app uses, if any.
steps: Unpack the package. Find assets/index.android.bundle on Android or main.jsbundle on iOS.
Look at the bundle. Note if it is minified JavaScript or Hermes bytecode.
Change a harmless string in the bundle. Repack and re-sign the app. Install it on the test device.
Start the app. Look for an integrity check or tamper detection that stops the app.
Find the code that downloads a new bundle or update. Make sure the app checks a signature or a hash before it runs the update.
Replace the downloaded bundle in a test environment. Make sure the app rejects it.
Make sure the app does not run a bundle after a failed integrity check.
tests.ex: unzip app.apk -d out; file out/assets/index.android.bundle; hermes-dec out/assets/index.android.bundle; apktool b out; apksigner sign --ks test.jks app.apk
tests.exp: The app detects a changed bundle and refuses to run an unsigned or changed update. A failed integrity check stops the use of the resource.

tests.title: Check hybrid app WebViews, plugins and allowed origins
tests.obj: Find hybrid apps that load untrusted origins in a WebView with native bridges, or that ship vulnerable web libraries and plugins.
pre: The app package and the framework configuration files, such as config.xml or capacitor.config.
steps: List the origins that the app may load in its WebView. Read the allowed origin and navigation settings of the framework.
Make sure the list holds only the origins that the app needs and has no wildcard.
Make sure JavaScript is on only for content that the app controls.
Look at the native plugins that the page can call. Make sure untrusted content cannot reach sensitive plugins.
Try to load a page from another origin in the WebView, for example by a link or a redirect. Make sure the app blocks it.
List the plugins and the JavaScript libraries in the package. Compare their versions with known vulnerabilities.
Make sure external content opens in Custom Tabs when the app does not need a WebView for it.
tests.ex: grep -rn "loadUrl\|allow" config.xml capacitor.config.*; npm audit; retire --path www/
tests.exp: The WebView loads only listed origins. Untrusted content cannot call sensitive plugins, and plugins and web libraries have no known vulnerabilities.

tests.title: Check exported Android components for missing permissions
tests.obj: Finds activities, services and receivers that other apps can start or call without permission.
pre: Android device or emulator with the app installed.
A second test app or the shell as an untrusted caller.
steps: Android: Decode the APK and read the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: List every activity, service and receiver with android:exported and android:permission.
Android: Find components that are exported without a permission or with a normal protection level.
Android: Read the code of each exported component for sensitive data or actions.
Android: Start each exported component from the shell. Send a crafted intent to each receiver.
Android: Make sure each service checks the caller permission at runtime before it acts.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk -o out ; aapt2 d xmltree app.apk --file AndroidManifest.xml | grep -A20 -E "E: (activity|service|receiver)" ; adb shell am start -n <pkg>/<exported.Activity> ; adb shell am startservice -n <pkg>/<exported.Service> ; adb shell am broadcast -a <action> -n <pkg>/<exported.Receiver> --es key value
tests.exp: The app exports only components that must be public. Each exported component that handles sensitive data needs a signature-level permission, and no unauthenticated caller can reach it.

tests.title: Check exported content providers for missing permissions and data leaks
tests.obj: Finds content providers that give other apps read or write access to private app data.
pre: Android device with the app installed and test data entered.
steps: Android: Read the AndroidManifest.xml. List each provider with android:exported, readPermission and writePermission.
Android: Find exported providers that have no android:permission, readPermission or writePermission.
Android: Look at the protection level of each declared permission. Normal and dangerous levels do not limit access.
Android: Use the app until the database holds sensitive test data.
Android: Query each exported provider from the shell without any permission.
Android: Look at the rows that come back for sensitive data.
tests.ex: adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/<path> ; adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/<path> --where "name='Bob'" ; xmlstarlet sel -t -m "//provider" -v "@android:name" -o " exported=" -v "@android:exported" -n AndroidManifest.xml
tests.exp: No exported content provider returns or changes sensitive data for a caller without a signature-level permission. Providers for internal use are not exported.

tests.title: Check FileProvider paths for access outside the shared directory
tests.obj: Finds FileProvider path settings that let other apps open private files through content URIs.
pre: Decompiled app code.
steps: Android: Decode the APK. Find each exported FileProvider in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: Open the file paths XML resource that the provider uses.
Android: Look for root-path entries and for path values of "/", "." or an empty string.
Android: Find calls to FileProvider.getUriForFile in the code.
Android: Make sure no attacker-controlled input, such as a URI query value, reaches the file argument.
Android: Make sure the provider requires a permission with a dangerous or signature protection level.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "getUriForFile\|root-path" out/ ; cat out/resources/res/xml/file_paths.xml
tests.exp: The FileProvider shares only the intended directory. Path settings do not expose root or private storage, and attacker-controlled input never selects the file.

tests.title: Check PendingIntent objects for mutable flags and implicit base intents
tests.obj: Finds PendingIntent objects that other apps can change or redirect.
pre: Decompiled app code.
steps: Android: Search the decompiled code for PendingIntent.getActivity, getActivities, getService, getForegroundService and getBroadcast.
Android: Read the flags argument of each call for FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE.
Android: Read the minSdkVersion in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: Check if the base intent names its target with setClass, setClassName or setComponent.
Android: Find a valid use case for each mutable PendingIntent, such as an inline reply.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "PendingIntent\.\(getActivity\|getActivities\|getService\|getForegroundService\|getBroadcast\)" out/ ; grep -rn "FLAG_MUTABLE\|FLAG_IMMUTABLE" out/
tests.exp: Each PendingIntent uses FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless mutability is required and documented. Each base intent is explicit and names its target component.

tests.title: Check implicit intents used for internal communication and sensitive extras
tests.obj: Finds implicit intents that another app can intercept to read data or take over a flow.
pre: Decompiled app code.
steps: Android: Find all places where the app builds an Intent and sends it with startActivity, startService, bindService or sendBroadcast.
Android: Mark the intents that have no setPackage, setClass, setClassName or setComponent call.
Android: Check if the intent is for an internal component and not a user-selected app or chooser.
Android: Look for putExtra calls with tokens, session IDs, one-time codes or personal data.
Android: Make sure another app cannot register an intent-filter that matches the action, data and categories.
Android: Make sure each broadcast with sensitive data requires a receiver permission.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "new Intent(\"\|setAction(\|putExtra(\|sendBroadcast(" out/ ; semgrep --config <rules> out/
tests.exp: Intents for internal communication name an explicit component or package. Intents that carry sensitive extras go only to a known recipient.

tests.title: Check validation of data that other apps return to the app
tests.obj: Finds flows where data from an external intent result reaches a sensitive operation without checks.
pre: Android device with Frida server.
A test app that returns crafted results.
steps: Android: Install the app and attach a Frida hook to startActivityForResult, ActivityResultLauncher and onActivityResult.
Android: Use the app to start each flow that asks another app for a file, a document or an account.
Android: Install a test app that answers with a crafted URI scheme or a file name with path separators.
Android: Record the reads of Intent.getData, ClipData, extras and ContentResolver calls.
Android: Look at the backtraces. Find returned data that reaches file, parse, storage, network or authorization code.
Android: Make sure the app checks the data before each use.
tests.ex: frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_intent_results.js ; objection -g <pkg> explore, then android hooking watch class_method android.app.Activity.onActivityResult --dump-args --dump-backtrace
tests.exp: The app treats data returned from other apps as untrusted. It checks scheme, path, name and type before it uses the data.

tests.title: Check deep links for App Links or Universal Links verification
tests.obj: Finds deep links that another app can claim and use to capture tokens or links.
pre: Decoded APK and IPA.
steps: Android: List the intent-filters with http or https data and the VIEW and BROWSABLE entries in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: Find filters that miss android:autoVerify="true".
Android: Check on the device that each declared domain has the verified state.
Android: Look for custom URL schemes used for login, reset or payment flows.
iOS: Read the Associated Domains entitlement of the app binary.
iOS: Fetch the apple-app-site-association file of each domain and compare its paths with the app.
Make sure no deep link carries a long-lived token or other secret.
tests.ex: adb shell pm get-app-links <pkg> ; python3 deeplink_analyser.py -op verify-applinks -apk app.apk ; rabin2 -OC app_binary | grep -A3 associated-domains ; curl https://<domain>/.well-known/apple-app-site-association
tests.exp: Sensitive flows use only verified Android App Links and iOS Universal Links. Custom URL schemes do not start sensitive actions, and links carry no long-lived secrets.

tests.title: Check input validation in deep link and URL scheme handlers
tests.obj: Finds deep link handlers that use attacker-controlled parameters without checks.
pre: Know the schemes and hosts from the manifest and Info.plist.
steps: Android: Find the code for each intent-filter that has a VIEW action and a custom scheme or http scheme.
iOS: Find the code for each custom URL scheme and each Universal Link handler in the binary.
Read how the handler converts, limits and sanitizes each path and query parameter.
Look for raw strings used for amounts, file paths, SQL queries, WebView URLs or navigation.
Open the deep link on the device with a negative number, a path traversal value and a script value.
Make sure the handler rejects each value and keeps the app stable.
tests.ex: adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "myapp://open?path=../../data/x" ; adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "myapp://transfer?amount=-1" ; xcrun devicectl device process launch --device <UDID> --payload-url 'mastgtest://open?path=../../x' <bundle_id> ; xcrun simctl openurl booted "https://example.com/open?path=../../x"
tests.exp: Handlers convert each parameter to its expected type, check ranges and allowlists, and sanitize special characters before the value reaches a sink.

tests.title: Check source validation in iOS custom URL scheme handlers
tests.obj: Finds URL scheme handlers that act on sensitive requests without checking the calling app.
pre: Extracted IPA binary.
steps: iOS: Find the scene(_:openURLContexts:) method in the app binary.
iOS: Look for reads of UIOpenURLContext.options.sourceApplication.
iOS: Check if the handler compares the source with an allowlist before it acts.
iOS: Find out if the scheme starts a privileged or irreversible action.
Android: Note that Android gives no caller identity for scheme intents. Check that the handler needs a separate user approval or token for sensitive actions.
tests.ex: r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~openURLContexts ; izz~sourceApplication
tests.exp: Handlers that start security-sensitive actions read the source application and check it against an allowlist. Sensitive actions also need another check, as the source is often nil.

tests.title: Check the use of the general pasteboard and the clipboard
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data on the system clipboard that other apps or devices can read.
pre: Jailbroken iOS device with Frida, or an instrumented build.
steps: iOS: Search the binary for UIPasteboard.general and the calls addItems, setItems, string and items.
iOS: Run the app. Copy a password or personal data. Monitor the general pasteboard with Frida.
iOS: Make sure setItems uses the localOnly and expirationDate options for sensitive data.
iOS: Check that the app clears the pasteboard with items = [] when it goes to the background or ends.
Android: Search the code for ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip and ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE.
Android: Make sure sensitive fields cannot be copied, or that copied values have the sensitive flag and a short life.
Treat pasted clipboard data as untrusted input.
tests.ex: r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~UIPasteboard ; frida -U -n <app> -l monitor_pasteboard.js (poll UIPasteboard.generalPasteboard().changeCount()) ; grep -rn "setPrimaryClip\|EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE" out/
tests.exp: The app does not put secrets on the clipboard. If it must, the data is local only, expires soon, is marked sensitive and is cleared.

tests.title: Check that the app restricts custom keyboards for sensitive input
tests.obj: Finds apps that let third-party keyboards read passwords and other secrets.
pre: Extracted IPA.
steps: iOS: Look for application:shouldAllowExtensionPointIdentifier: in the app delegate of the binary.
iOS: Check that the method returns false for UIApplicationKeyboardExtensionPointIdentifier.
iOS: Check that password, PIN and OTP fields use isSecureTextEntry, so that they use the system keyboard.
iOS: Open the Info.plist of each bundled keyboard extension. Look at RequestsOpenAccess.
iOS: Find keyboard code that sends typed text off the device or writes it to a shared container.
Android: Note that this control has no MASTG test for Android. Check that sensitive fields use a non-caching text input type.
tests.ex: unzip app.ipa ; plutil -p Payload/App.app/PlugIns/*.appex/Info.plist | grep -i RequestsOpenAccess ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~shouldAllowExtensionPointIdentifier
tests.exp: The app rejects custom keyboards app-wide when it handles sensitive input. A bundled keyboard asks for Full Access only with a feature that needs it.

tests.title: Check the app for unsafe object deserialization of untrusted data
tests.obj: Finds deserialization of data from other apps or the network that can lead to code execution.
pre: Decompiled app code or extracted IPA.
steps: Android: Search for ObjectInputStream, Serializable and Parcelable reads in Intent extras, Bundles, files and network data.
iOS: Search the binary for decodeObject(forKey:), unarchiveObject(with:) and unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData.
iOS: Check that NSKeyedUnarchiver uses secure coding and a list of allowed classes.
Follow the data back to its source. Find sources that other apps or attackers control.
Make sure the app uses a data-only format such as JSON, or checks a signature, before it deserializes.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "ObjectInputStream\|readSerializable\|getSerializableExtra" out/ ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~unarchive
tests.exp: The app does not deserialize native objects from untrusted sources. If it must, it restricts the classes and checks integrity first.

tests.title: Check SQL queries built from content provider URIs for injection
tests.obj: Finds content providers that put URI or selection input into SQL text.
pre: Exported or reachable content provider.
steps: Android: Find every ContentProvider class in the decompiled code.
Android: Look at the query, update and delete methods for uses of Uri.getPathSegments and appendWhere.
Android: Find SQL text that joins strings from the URI or the selection argument.
Android: Send a quote character or an OR clause through the URI from the shell.
Android: Make sure the provider uses selection arguments or a query builder with bound parameters.
tests.ex: adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/students/1%20OR%201=1 ; adb shell content query --uri content://<authority>/students --where "name='a' OR '1'='1" ; grep -rn "appendWhere\|getPathSegments\|rawQuery" out/
tests.exp: The provider binds all input from URIs and selection arguments as parameters. No input becomes part of the SQL text.

tests.title: Check that app configuration does not allow cleartext traffic
tests.obj: Finds Android and iOS settings that let the app send HTTP traffic that anyone on the network can read.
steps: Android: Read AndroidManifest.xml and note android:usesCleartextTraffic and android:networkSecurityConfig.
Android: Read the Network Security Configuration and flag cleartextTrafficPermitted="true" in base-config or domain-config.
iOS: Read Info.plist and note the NSAppTransportSecurity dictionary.
iOS: Flag NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsForMedia, NSAllowsLocalNetworking and NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads.
Find out if each exception is needed for core app functions and has a justification.
tests.ex: apktool d -s -f app.apk -o out; grep -E "usesCleartextTraffic|networkSecurityConfig" out/AndroidManifest.xml; grep -i cleartextTrafficPermitted out/res/xml/network_security_config.xml; unzip app.ipa; plutil -convert json -o Info.json Payload/App.app/Info.plist; jq .NSAppTransportSecurity Info.json
tests.exp: The app permits no cleartext traffic. Exceptions exist only for needed domains with a documented reason.

tests.title: Check that the app sends no cleartext HTTP traffic
tests.obj: Finds hardcoded http:// URLs and real cleartext connections that carry app data.
steps: Search the unpacked app and its libraries for http:// URLs.
Follow each URL in the code and see if the app uses it to open a connection.
Set up an interception proxy or a network capture for the device.
Use every workflow of the app and look for cleartext HTTP or other cleartext protocols.
Use a capture tool when the app does not work with a proxy.
Keep only traffic that comes from the target app.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk; grep -rnoE "http://[^\" ]+" out/ src/; unzip app.ipa; strings -n 8 Payload/App.app/App | grep -E "^http://"; adb shell "tcpdump -i any -w /data/local/tmp/cap.pcap"; wireshark -r cap.pcap -Y "http || (tcp && !tls)"; rvictl -s <UDID> (iOS capture on macOS); mitmproxy --mode regular
tests.exp: The capture shows no cleartext traffic from the app. All connections use TLS.

tests.title: Check that low-level iOS networking APIs use TLS
tests.obj: Finds Network framework, CFNetwork and BSD socket connections that skip App Transport Security and send cleartext.
pre: iOS only. ATS does not cover these APIs.
steps: Extract the binaries and search for NWConnection, CFSocketStream, CFHTTPStream and the BSD socket functions.
Look at each location and see if the connection uses TLS, for example .tls in NWParameters.
Capture the traffic of the app and look for non-TLS connections.
tests.ex: unzip app.ipa; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~NWConnection; afl~CFStream; afl~connect" Payload/App.app/App; strings Payload/App.app/App | grep -E "NWParameters|NWProtocolTLS"; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i connect -i send
tests.exp: Every low-level connection uses TLS with a safe configuration. No connection sends sensitive data in cleartext.

tests.title: Check that code sets no TLS version below 1.2
tests.obj: Finds code that enables TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 on Android and iOS.
steps: Android: Search for SSLContext.getInstance("TLSv1.1") and for SSLSocket.setEnabledProtocols.
Android: Search for OkHttp ConnectionSpec.COMPATIBLE_TLS and ConnectionSpec.Builder.tlsVersions.
iOS: Search for tlsMinimumSupportedProtocolVersion and tlsMinimumSupportedProtocol in URLSessionConfiguration.
iOS: Search for sec_protocol_options_set_min_tls_protocol_version and the max version function in Network framework code.
Flag the values TLSv1.0, TLSv1.1, kTLSProtocol1 and kTLSProtocol11.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "TLSv1(\.[01])?\"|setEnabledProtocols|COMPATIBLE_TLS|tlsVersions" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~tls_protocol_version; afl~sec_protocol_options_set" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i sec_protocol_options_set_min_tls_protocol_version
tests.exp: The app enables only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. No code sets a lower minimum version or a lower maximum version.

tests.title: Check that ATS exceptions do not weaken TLS policy
tests.obj: Finds Info.plist exceptions that turn off ATS or allow TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or no forward secrecy.
pre: iOS only.
steps: Convert Info.plist to JSON and read NSAppTransportSecurity.
Flag NSAllowsArbitraryLoads set to true.
Flag any NSExceptionMinimumTLSVersion of TLSv1.0 or TLSv1.1.
Flag any NSExceptionRequiresForwardSecrecy set to false.
Look at the scope of each exception, especially with NSIncludesSubdomains.
tests.ex: unzip app.ipa; plutil -convert json -o Info.json Payload/App.app/Info.plist; jq ".NSAppTransportSecurity.NSExceptionDomains" Info.json
tests.exp: The app sets no weak TLS exceptions. Required exceptions are narrow, justified and apply only to named domains.

tests.title: Check the TLS settings of embedded and third-party network stacks
tests.obj: Finds bundled OpenSSL, BoringSSL, mbedTLS, curl or gRPC code that weakens TLS and ignores ATS.
pre: iOS only in MASTG. Use the same method for Android native libraries.
steps: List the bundled libraries and frameworks in the IPA.
Search for TLS library symbols, such as SSL_CTX_set_min_proto_version and SSL_CTX_set_verify.
Look at the code at each location and note the minimum TLS version and cipher list.
Flag disabled certificate verification and custom trust stores with no validation.
Compare the results with the settings of the platform stack.
tests.ex: unzip -o app.ipa; find Payload -type d \( -name "*.framework" -o -name "*.appex" \); r2 -qc "aaa; afl~SSL_CTX" Payload/App.app/Frameworks/<lib>.framework/<lib>; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i SSL_CTX_set_min_proto_version -i SSL_CTX_set_verify; jadx -d src app.apk (Android native libraries: strings lib/*/*.so | grep -i ssl)
tests.exp: Every embedded stack allows only TLS 1.2 and higher, uses strong cipher suites and checks certificates against a valid trust store.

tests.title: Check the TLS version in live app traffic
tests.obj: Finds connections that negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 in practice.
steps: Install the app and capture its network traffic.
Use every workflow of the app with sensitive data.
Open the capture and list the TLS version in each handshake.
Flag any connection that uses a version below TLS 1.2.
tests.ex: adb shell "tcpdump -i any -w /data/local/tmp/cap.pcap"; rvictl -s <UDID>; tshark -r cap.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.type==2" -T fields -e ip.src -e tls.handshake.version -e tls.handshake.extensions.supported_version; testssl.sh --protocols api.example.com
tests.exp: All connections use TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.

tests.title: Check that Android code checks server host names
tests.obj: Finds SSLSocket use without host name checks and HostnameVerifier code that accepts any host.
pre: Android only.
steps: Search the code for SSLSocket and SSLSocketFactory.
Check that the code calls a HostnameVerifier for each SSLSocket connection.
Search for HostnameVerifier implementations and read their host check methods.
Flag methods that return true for all hosts, use broad wildcard rules or skip some channels.
Present a valid certificate of another host with a MITM proxy and see if the app connects.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rnE "SSLSocket|HostnameVerifier|ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER|setHostnameVerifier" src/; mitmproxy --mode regular --certs *=wrong-host.pem; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "javax.net.ssl.HostnameVerifier!*"
tests.exp: The app checks the server host name against the certificate on every TLS channel, including SSLSocket. The MITM test fails to connect.

tests.title: Check that custom trust checks reject untrusted certificates
tests.obj: Finds custom TrustManager and URLSession delegate code that accepts every certificate.
steps: Android: Search for X509TrustManager and checkServerTrusted implementations.
Android: Flag empty methods, ignored exceptions, checkValidity-only checks and empty getAcceptedIssuers results.
iOS: Search for urlSession(_:didReceive:completionHandler:) and cross-references to SecTrustEvaluateWithError.
iOS: Flag code that calls completionHandler with useCredential and URLCredential(trust:) before it evaluates the trust.
Send a self-signed certificate with a MITM proxy and see if the app accepts it.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "checkServerTrusted\|X509TrustManager\|getAcceptedIssuers" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecTrustEvaluateWithError" Payload/App.app/App; strings Payload/App.app/App | grep -i "URLAuthenticationChallenge"; mitmproxy --mode regular
tests.exp: The app uses the platform trust checks. Custom code rejects bad certificates and the self-signed MITM test fails.

tests.title: Check that WebViews do not ignore TLS certificate errors
tests.obj: Finds WebView code that proceeds after a certificate error and so allows MITM attacks.
steps: Android: Search for onReceivedSslError overrides in WebViewClient classes.
Android: Flag handler.proceed() calls that do not check the error, and catch blocks that do not call cancel().
iOS: Search for WKNavigationDelegate webView(_:didReceive:completionHandler:) implementations.
iOS: Flag code that accepts the server trust credential without a successful trust evaluation.
Load a page with an invalid certificate in the WebView and see if it loads.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "onReceivedSslError\|proceed()" src/; r2 -qc "aaa; axt sym.imp.SecTrustEvaluateWithError; axt sym.imp.SecTrustEvaluateAsyncWithError" Payload/App.app/App; mitmproxy --mode regular
tests.exp: WebViews cancel loads after certificate errors. No code accepts an untrusted server trust.

tests.title: Check that Android does not trust user-installed CAs
tests.obj: Finds apps that trust CA certificates that the user or an attacker adds to the device.
pre: Android only. Debug builds may trust user CAs on purpose; test the release build.
steps: Read minSdkVersion in the manifest and flag values below 24.
Read the Network Security Configuration and look for <certificates src="user" /> in trust-anchors.
Install a proxy CA as a user certificate on a test device.
Start the app and see if it connects through the proxy.
tests.ex: apktool d -s -f app.apk -o out; grep minSdkVersion out/AndroidManifest.xml out/apktool.yml; grep -n "certificates src" out/res/xml/network_security_config.xml; adb push burp-ca.der /sdcard/Download/ (install as a user CA in Settings)
tests.exp: The app uses a minSdkVersion of 24 or higher and trusts no user CAs. The proxy cannot read the traffic.

tests.title: Check that the Android app updates the GMS security provider
tests.obj: Finds apps on Android that skip the security provider update and so keep known TLS flaws.
pre: Android only.
steps: Search the code for ProviderInstaller.installIfNeeded and installIfNeededAsync.
Check that the call runs before the first network connection.
Check that the code handles errors and does not continue silently.
tests.ex: jadx -d src app.apk; grep -rn "ProviderInstaller\|installIfNeeded" src/
tests.exp: The app calls ProviderInstaller before any network connection and handles update errors.

tests.title: Check that first-party domains use certificate pinning in app configuration
tests.obj: Finds first-party endpoints that rely only on the default CA trust and so allow MITM by a rogue CA.
steps: List the first-party domains that the app uses for core and security functions.
Android: Read the Network Security Configuration and list domain-config entries with a pin-set.
iOS: Read Info.plist and look for NSPinnedDomains in NSAppTransportSecurity.
Compare the pinned domains with the first-party list.
Check that the app connects to the unpinned domains, and look for other pinning code.
tests.ex: apktool d -s -f app.apk -o out; xmlstarlet sel -t -c "//domain-config[pin-set]" out/res/xml/network_security_config.xml; unzip app.ipa; plutil -convert json -o Info.json Payload/App.app/Info.plist; jq ".NSAppTransportSecurity.NSPinnedDomains" Info.json; strings -n 8 Payload/App.app/App | grep -E "^https://"
tests.exp: Every relevant first-party domain has a pin in the NSC or in ATS, or another documented pinning method covers it.

tests.title: Check that Android certificate pins have not expired
tests.obj: Finds NSC pins with a past expiration date that Android no longer enforces.
pre: Android only.
steps: Read the Network Security Configuration and list each pin-set with its expiration attribute.
Compare each date with the current date.
Compare the domains with the list of first-party domains that the app uses.
Check that the app still connects to those domains.
tests.ex: apktool d -s -f app.apk -o out; grep -n "pin-set\|expiration" out/res/xml/network_security_config.xml; date +%F
tests.exp: No pin-set for a first-party domain has an expiration date in the past.

tests.title: Check that a MITM proxy cannot read first-party HTTPS traffic
tests.obj: Finds first-party endpoints with no effective pinning, whatever the implementation is.
steps: Install the app on a test device and set up an interception proxy with its CA trusted by the system.
Use every workflow of the app.
Look at the proxy log for first-party domains whose HTTPS traffic it decrypted.
Watch the device log for pin check failures when pinning is active.
Ignore unrelated third-party domains.
tests.ex: burp / mitmproxy --mode regular; adb shell settings put global http_proxy <host>:8080; adb logcat | grep -i "Pin verification failed"; iOS: iproxy 2222 22; ssh -R 8080:localhost:8080 mobile@localhost -p 2222; do not disable pinning in this test
tests.exp: The proxy cannot decrypt traffic to first-party domains. The app refuses the connection with an untrusted CA.

tests.title: Check Android permissions for minimal, justified and revocable access
tests.obj: Finds permissions that the app does not need or does not explain to the user.
pre: APK and a test device.
steps: Android: Read the AndroidManifest.xml and list all declared permissions.
Android: Compare the list with the Android list of dangerous permissions.
Android: Match each dangerous permission to a visible app feature.
Android: Look for permissions that have a less intrusive option, such as coarse location or a picker.
Android: Start the app. Check that it asks for each permission at the time of use and shows a rationale.
Android: Check that the app drops permissions it no longer needs.
tests.ex: aapt2 d permissions app.apk ; aapt d permissions app.apk ; adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> | grep -A30 "requested permissions" ; adb shell pm revoke <pkg> <permission>
tests.exp: The app declares only permissions that its features need. It asks for each one when needed, explains why, and lets the user revoke it.

tests.title: Check iOS purpose strings against the protected resources that the app uses
tests.obj: Finds access to protected resources without a clear and accurate purpose string.
pre: Extracted IPA and a test device.
steps: iOS: Read the Info.plist and list all UsageDescription keys with their strings.
iOS: Search the binary for the APIs that request or use each protected resource.
iOS: Flag an API with no matching key, and a string that is vague or wrong.
iOS: Hook the protected resource APIs at runtime. Use all app flows.
iOS: Check that each system prompt shows a purpose string that matches the visible feature.
tests.ex: plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist | grep UsageDescription ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~requestAuthorization ; frida -U -f <bundle_id> -l hook_protected_apis.js
tests.exp: Each protected resource has a specific and true purpose string. The app asks only when a visible feature needs the resource.

tests.title: Check iOS entitlements for capabilities that the app does not need
tests.obj: Finds signed capabilities that widen data access without a user-visible reason.
pre: Extracted IPA and a test device.
steps: iOS: Extract the entitlements of the main binary and of each app extension.
iOS: Search the binary for APIs, shared containers and identifiers that relate to each entitlement.
iOS: Hook entitlement-backed APIs at runtime. Use all app flows.
iOS: Match each entitlement to a visible app feature.
iOS: Flag entitlements for health, shared storage, iCloud or associated domains with no use.
tests.ex: rabin2 -OC App ; codesign -d --entitlements :- App.app ; frida -U -f <bundle_id> -l hook_entitlement_apis.js
tests.exp: Each signed entitlement links to a visible feature. The app signs no entitlement that widens data access without need.

tests.title: Check network traffic for personal data that the app does not declare
tests.obj: Finds personal data that leaves the device but is missing from the privacy declarations.
pre: Test device with a trusted proxy certificate.
Store privacy declarations of the app.
steps: Write down the sensitive and personal test data that you enter into the app.
Capture and decrypt the HTTPS traffic of the app while you use all workflows.
Search the traffic for the test data, also in background requests.
Compare the found data with the Data Safety section, the Privacy Nutrition Label and the privacy policy.
Find the code that sends each undeclared item.
tests.ex: mitmproxy -s mitm_sensitive_logger.py ; Burp Suite: filter on the test data ; adb shell settings put global http_proxy <host>:8080
tests.exp: All personal data in the traffic matches the store declarations and the privacy policy. The app sends nothing undeclared, also in the background.

tests.title: Check third-party SDKs for sensitive data sharing and consent
tests.obj: Finds SDKs that receive personal data, or start to collect before the user consents.
pre: Fresh install with no consent given.
steps: Android: List the SDKs in the app. Find the APIs that send user data, such as analytics events and user properties.
Android: Hook these API calls at runtime. Record the arguments and backtraces.
Start the app for the first time. Capture the traffic before you answer any consent prompt.
Look for SDK requests that carry identifiers or personal data before consent.
Check that each SDK follows the consent signal and the data that the app declares.
tests.ex: jadx -d out app.apk ; grep -rn "logEvent\|setUserProperty\|setUserId" out/ ; frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_sdk_calls.js ; Burp Suite: capture first-start traffic
tests.exp: SDKs receive only declared data, and only after consent. No SDK collects data before the user decides.

tests.title: Check that iOS tracking domains appear in the privacy manifests
tests.obj: Finds tracking domains that the app contacts but does not declare.
pre: Extracted IPA and a test device.
steps: iOS: Extract every PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file of the app, also those from SDKs and frameworks.
iOS: Read NSPrivacyTrackingDomains in each file.
iOS: Search the binary for strings of known tracking domains.
iOS: Capture the traffic during use. List all contacted domains.
iOS: Compare the domains found with a list of known trackers and with the declared domains.
tests.ex: find . -name PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy ; plutil -convert json -o PrivacyInfo.json PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy ; jq .NSPrivacyTrackingDomains PrivacyInfo.json ; strings -a App | grep -i -E "doubleclick|facebook|adjust"
tests.exp: The privacy manifests declare every tracking domain that the code contains or that the app contacts at runtime.

tests.title: Check use of identifiers for user tracking
tests.obj: Finds persistent identifiers that let parties follow users across apps and services.
steps: Search the code and SDKs for the Advertising ID, ANDROID_ID, serial numbers, MAC addresses and identifierForVendor.
Look for non-resettable identifiers and for identifiers that join data from different services.
Check that the app asks for tracking consent where the platform needs it, and respects an opt-out.
Reset the identifier in the device settings. Check that the app does not link the new value to the old one.
Check if privacy-preserving APIs, such as Play Integrity or DeviceCheck, can replace an identifier.
tests.ex: grep -rn "AdvertisingIdClient\|ANDROID_ID\|getSerial\|identifierForVendor\|ASIdentifierManager" out/ ; Burp Suite: look for identifiers in the requests
tests.exp: The app uses resettable or app-scoped identifiers only with consent. It does not link identifiers across services.

tests.title: Check that the app anonymizes personal data before sharing it
tests.obj: Finds personal data that the app sends in a form that identifies the user.
steps: Capture the data that the app sends to its server, to SDKs and to AI services.
Look for user IDs, names, e-mail addresses, precise location and metadata such as Exif.
Check that hashes of identifiers use a secret key and are not plain stable hashes.
Check that the app does not store the key with the pseudonymized data.
Check that the app redacts sensitive fields before it sends data to AI services.
tests.ex: Burp Suite: inspect request bodies ; exiftool uploaded_image.jpg ; sha256sum <identifier> and compare with the sent value
tests.exp: The app removes or transforms identifiers before it collects or shares data. Pseudonyms are keyed, and AI services get redacted data.

tests.title: Check for privacy-preserving platform alternatives
tests.obj: Finds features that expose more user data than a platform alternative would.
steps: Look for login flows in embedded WebViews. Check if the app uses ASWebAuthenticationSession or Custom Tabs.
Look for broad photo, camera or file permissions where a system picker would work.
Look for user data that goes to a remote AI service when on-device processing is possible.
Check that the app asks for broad access only when the feature needs it.
tests.ex: grep -rn "ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT\|PickVisualMedia\|PHPickerViewController\|ASWebAuthenticationSession\|CustomTabsIntent" out/
tests.exp: The app uses system pickers, system authentication sessions and on-device processing where they can support the feature.

tests.title: Check that privacy-relevant actions show scope and consequences
tests.obj: Finds actions that share data without a clear view of what, with whom and for how long.
steps: List actions that share or publish user data, such as share, export, post and invite.
Open each action. Look for the affected data, metadata, destination and audience.
Check that the user can review and confirm the action before it completes.
Check that the app shows the resulting privacy state afterward and allows reversal.
tests.ex: Manual review with screenshots of each sharing flow
tests.exp: Each privacy-relevant action shows the data, the audience and the effect before it completes, and the user can review and undo it.

tests.title: Check that default settings expose the least data
tests.obj: Finds defaults that share more data or reach a wider audience than needed.
steps: Install the app fresh. Complete the first run without a change to any setting.
List the defaults for audience, visibility, retention, analytics and recipients.
Compare each default with the narrowest option that still gives the feature.
Check that the app asks the user before it widens an audience or shares more data.
tests.ex: Manual review of the first-run flow and the privacy settings screen
tests.exp: Defaults use the narrowest audience, the least data and the shortest retention that the feature allows.

tests.title: Check the privacy policy and the privacy labels against app behavior
tests.obj: Finds apps with a missing, unclear or wrong privacy policy.
steps: Find the privacy policy in the app and in the store listing. Check that it is easy to reach.
Check that it covers the data practices of this app and not only the company in general.
Compare it with the Data Safety section and the Privacy Nutrition Label.
Compare all three with the traffic and permissions that you saw in other tests.
tests.ex: Manual review ; compare the store listing with Burp Suite traffic logs
tests.exp: The privacy policy is easy to reach and clear. It matches the store declarations and the real behavior of the app.

tests.title: Check that the build is reproducible
tests.obj: Finds apps whose published binary cannot be matched to the claimed source code.
pre: Source code and build environment of the app.
steps: Find the source, the build scripts and the pinned toolchain versions for the release.
Build the app twice in the same environment. Compare the two outputs.
Look for timestamps, absolute paths and unstable ordering in the artifacts.
Look for published provenance for the release, such as a SLSA statement.
Check if the obfuscation settings give the same result on each build.
tests.ex: sha256sum build1.apk build2.apk ; diffoscope build1.apk build2.apk
tests.exp: Builds of the same source in the same environment give identical binaries. The release has provenance that others can check.

tests.title: Check that users can delete, export and change their data
tests.obj: Finds apps that give users no way to manage their personal data.
pre: Test account.
steps: Open the account and privacy settings. Look for delete, export, change and opt-out options.
Delete the account and the data of a test user. Check the backend for remaining data.
Export the data of the test user. Check that the export is complete.
Check that granular opt-outs for data collection and sharing exist.
Check that the app removes data automatically when the retention period ends.
tests.ex: Manual test with a test account ; compare backend records before and after the deletion
tests.exp: Users can delete, export and change their data and opt out of collection from inside the app. The deletion reaches the backend.

tests.title: Check privacy settings for control over data visibility
tests.obj: Finds apps that offer no fine control over who sees user data.
pre: Two test accounts.
steps: Open the privacy settings. List the controls for location, contacts and profile data.
Check that each data category has its own control.
Change each control. Check with a second test account that the change takes effect.
Check that help text explains each option.
tests.ex: Manual test with two test accounts
tests.exp: Users control each data category on its own, and a change takes effect for other users and for sharing partners.

tests.title: Check that consent is explicit, informed and renewed on change
tests.obj: Finds apps that process personal data without clear prior consent.
pre: Two app versions where the later one collects more data.
steps: Start a fresh install. Look at each consent prompt before any data collection.
Check that consent is not bundled into the terms of service and is not implied.
Check that the text names the data, the purpose and the effect.
Withdraw consent in the settings. Check that collection stops in the traffic.
Install an update that collects more data. Check that the app asks for consent again.
tests.ex: Burp Suite: capture traffic before and after consent and after withdrawal ; compare two app versions
tests.exp: The app asks for explicit, specific consent before it collects data. Withdrawal stops collection, and new data collection needs new consent.

tests.title: Check root and jailbreak detection
tests.obj: Finds apps that run with sensitive functions on a rooted or jailbroken device.
pre: Rooted or jailbroken test device with Frida.
steps: Android: Search the code for root checks, such as su paths, test-keys, root packages and system property reads.
iOS: Search the binary for jailbreak checks, such as Cydia paths, writable system folders and URL scheme tests.
Hook the file, property and system calls at runtime and record the checks that run.
Run the app on a rooted or jailbroken test device. Check how the app reacts.
Try an automated bypass tool. Note which checks it must bypass.
Make sure the app restricts sensitive functions or warns the backend when it detects the change.
tests.ex: frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_root_checks.js ; objection -g <pkg> explore, then android root disable ; objection -g <bundle_id> explore, then ios jailbreak disable ; frida-trace -U -f <pkg> -i "access" -i "fopen"
tests.exp: The app detects a rooted or jailbroken device with several checks. It limits sensitive functions or informs the backend when it finds one.

tests.title: Check emulator and virtual device detection
tests.obj: Finds apps that run sensitive functions in an emulator where attackers have full control.
pre: Emulator or virtual device with Frida.
steps: Android: Search the code for checks of Build properties, QEMU files and emulator sensors.
iOS: Look for hooks on the checks that find a simulator or virtual device.
Run the app in an emulator or virtual device. Hook the checks and trace the system calls.
Record which checks run and how the app reacts.
Make sure the app limits sensitive functions when it detects the virtual device.
tests.ex: frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_build_props.js ; frida-trace -U -f <pkg> -i "__system_property_get" ; run the app in an Android Virtual Device or an iOS simulator
tests.exp: The app detects emulators and virtual devices with several checks. It limits sensitive functions when it detects one.

tests.title: Check detection of app cloning and virtual app environments
tests.obj: Finds apps that run inside a virtual container where another app can read and change them.
pre: A virtualization or dual-app tool on the test device.
steps: Android: Run the app inside a known app-virtualization or dual-app tool.
Android: Look at the process path, data folder and package structure that the app reads at runtime.
Check if the app compares these values with the expected ones.
Check if the app restricts sensitive functions, informs the backend or ends when it finds a container.
tests.ex: adb shell pm list packages | grep <container> ; adb shell ps -A | grep <pkg> ; frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_process_path.js
tests.exp: The app finds that it runs in a virtual container, and it limits sensitive functions or informs the backend.

tests.title: Check device attestation in the backend
tests.obj: Finds backends that cannot tell real devices from rooted, emulated or automated ones.
pre: Test backend that you may send replayed tokens to.
steps: Find the code that asks the platform for a device attestation, such as Play Integrity or hardware key attestation.
iOS: Find the use of DeviceCheck and App Attest.
Capture the request that carries the attestation. Look for a server-issued nonce.
Replay an old attestation and send a changed one. Check that the backend rejects both.
Check that the backend checks the verdict itself and gates sensitive operations on it.
tests.ex: Burp Suite: capture and replay the attestation request ; grep -rn "IntegrityManager\|requestIntegrityToken\|DCAppAttestService" out/
tests.exp: The backend checks device attestation evidence with a fresh nonce. It blocks sensitive operations when the evidence is missing or bad.

tests.title: Check that the app detects a device without a secure screen lock
tests.obj: Finds apps that keep sensitive data and keys on devices that have no passcode.
pre: Test device where you can remove the lock.
steps: Android: Search the code for KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure and BiometricManager.canAuthenticate.
iOS: Search the binary for LAContext canEvaluatePolicy with deviceOwnerAuthentication.
iOS: Check the Keychain items for kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly.
Hook these calls at runtime. Remove the device lock and use the app.
Check that the app checks the lock again before it enables sensitive functions.
tests.ex: frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_keyguard.js ; objection -g <pkg> explore, then android hooking watch class_method android.app.KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure --dump-return
tests.exp: The app checks that a secure screen lock exists before it enables sensitive functions. Keys bind to the device lock.

tests.title: Check the app signature scheme, key size and code signature format
tests.obj: Finds weak or old signatures that attackers can abuse to repackage the app.
pre: APK or IPA of the release build.
steps: Android: Read minSdkVersion in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: List the signature schemes of the APK. Flag a v1-only signature when minSdkVersion is 24 or higher.
Android: Read the key size of each signer. Flag RSA keys below 2048 bits.
iOS: Extract the binary and read the CodeDirectory version of the code signature.
iOS: Compare it with the latest code signature format that Apple recommends.
tests.ex: apksigner verify --verbose --print-certs app.apk ; apksigner verify -v app.apk | grep -i "scheme" ; codesign -dv --verbose=4 App.app | grep -E "CodeDirectory|Format"
tests.exp: The APK uses v2 or newer signatures with strong keys. The iOS app uses the current code signature format.

tests.title: Check app attestation in the backend
tests.obj: Finds backends that accept requests from modified or repackaged copies of the app.
pre: Test backend. Do not run on production.
steps: Find the code that checks the signing identity, the package identity and the packaged files at runtime.
Find the use of App Attest or the Play Integrity app verdict.
Repackage the app with a test change. Send its requests to a test backend.
Check that the backend rejects requests from the changed app.
Check how the app reacts when its own checks fail.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk ; apktool b -o repack.apk ; apksigner sign --ks test.jks repack.apk ; adb install repack.apk
tests.exp: The backend checks an app integrity signal and rejects modified or repackaged clients. The app reacts to failed checks.

tests.title: Check integrity checks on data that the app stores locally
tests.obj: Finds apps that trust local data for security decisions without an integrity check.
pre: Rooted or jailbroken test device.
steps: Find data in SharedPreferences, UserDefaults, files and databases that drives a security decision.
Examples are login state, feature access, limits and server settings.
Search the code for HMAC, Signature and digest APIs around the reads of that data.
Change the stored value on a rooted or jailbroken device. Start the app.
Check that the app finds the change and reacts.
tests.ex: grep -rn "javax.crypto.Mac\|SharedPreferences" out/ ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; afl~CCHmac ; adb shell run-as <pkg> cat shared_prefs/<file>.xml
tests.exp: The app signs or authenticates data that drives a security decision, checks it on each read and reacts to a change.

tests.title: Check detection of hooking tools and code changes at runtime
tests.obj: Finds apps that let attackers hook sensitive APIs and read secrets without any reaction.
pre: Test device with Frida server.
steps: Install the app and attach Frida to it.
Hook sensitive APIs, such as AccountManager, KeyStore, SecItemCopyMatching and SecKey functions.
Record whether the hook runs and returns data, or whether the app ends or blocks it.
Look in the code for checks of loaded libraries, named pipes, ports and function prologues.
Check that the app reacts, for example by ending the session or warning the backend.
tests.ex: frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_keystore_getkey.js ; frida -U -f <bundle_id> -l hook_secitemcopymatching.js ; objection -g <pkg> explore
tests.exp: The hook fails or the app reacts. The app detects hooking tools and changed code with several checks.

tests.title: Check detection of malware and risky apps on the device
tests.obj: Finds apps that handle high-risk flows without any check for a hostile environment.
pre: Test app with accessibility rights.
steps: Find uses of platform threat signals, such as Play Protect status or Play Integrity verdicts.
Check if the app considers apps with accessibility or overlay rights in risk decisions.
Install a test app with accessibility rights. Start a sensitive flow.
Check if the app warns the user, asks for more checks or restricts the flow.
Check if the backend restricts the account and not only the local client.
tests.ex: adb shell settings get secure enabled_accessibility_services ; adb shell dumpsys window | grep -i overlay
tests.exp: For high-risk flows, the app uses threat signals and reacts in proportion. Restrictions apply to the account and not only to the device.

tests.title: Check code obfuscation of security-relevant logic
tests.obj: Finds readable security logic that helps attackers to find and remove checks.
steps: Android: Decompile the DEX code. Look for readable class and method names in security logic.
Android: Extract the native libraries. Look for readable strings, symbols and constants.
iOS: Extract the main binary and bundled Mach-O files. Read the symbols and strings, and demangle Swift names.
Find root checks, attestation, integrity checks and key handling.
Check that an attacker cannot find and understand these parts with reasonable effort.
tests.ex: jadx-gui app.apk ; strings -a lib/arm64-v8a/lib.so | head -100 ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; izz ; xcrun swift-demangle <symbol>
tests.exp: Security-relevant code is obfuscated in the Java, Kotlin and native layers. An attacker needs much effort to find and understand it.

tests.title: Check obfuscation of resources and identifiers
tests.obj: Finds readable resources and strings that show how the app works.
steps: Unpack the APK or IPA. List strings, layouts, configuration files and bundled data.
Look for descriptive resource and string names that map to security features.
Look for sensitive strings and settings in clear form.
Check if integrity checks protect the obfuscated resources from replacement.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk -o out ; cat out/res/values/strings.xml ; unzip app.ipa ; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist
tests.exp: Resources that reveal security behavior are obfuscated or encrypted. Their identifiers carry no meaning in release builds.

tests.title: Check native binaries for debug symbols
tests.obj: Finds binaries with symbols that show names and structure of the code.
pre: Extracted release package.
steps: Android: Extract the native libraries and read their symbol and line number information.
Android: Flag libraries that are not stripped or that have line numbers.
iOS: Extract the binaries. List the symbols of each executable and library.
iOS: Flag symbols that are marked as debug symbols.
Check that release builds keep dSYM files out of the app package.
tests.ex: r2 -A lib.so ; i~stripped,linenum,lsyms ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; is~debug ; nm -a lib.so | head
tests.exp: Release binaries are stripped. They hold no debug symbols or line numbers.

tests.title: Check release builds for debug logging and StrictMode
tests.obj: Finds logs that show implementation details to attackers.
pre: Release build of the app.
steps: Android: Search the code for StrictMode setVmPolicy and setThreadPolicy.
Android: Run the release build and read the logcat output for StrictMode messages.
iOS: Search the binary for NSLog, print, dump, debugPrint and os_log calls and their strings.
Run the release build and trigger errors, such as network failures and invalid input.
Read the device logs for stack traces, endpoints, internal paths and verbose messages.
tests.ex: adb logcat | grep -i StrictMode ; adb logcat --pid=$(adb shell pidof <pkg>) ; xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream --style compact --level debug --predicate 'process CONTAINS[c] "App"'
tests.exp: Release builds do not use StrictMode. Logs show no implementation details, debug messages or detailed errors.

tests.title: Check that release builds are not debuggable
tests.obj: Finds builds that let an attacker attach a debugger and read app memory and data.
pre: Release build of the app.
steps: Android: Read the android:debuggable attribute in the AndroidManifest.xml.
Android: Flag the value true.
iOS: Extract the entitlements of the main binary and look for get-task-allow.
iOS: Flag the value true.
Try to attach a debugger to the release build.
tests.ex: aapt2 d badging app.apk | grep -i debuggable ; apktool d app.apk ; grep debuggable out/AndroidManifest.xml ; rabin2 -OC App | grep -A1 get-task-allow ; adb jdwp
tests.exp: The release build is not debuggable. The debuggable flag and the get-task-allow entitlement are false or missing.

tests.title: Check that WebView debugging is off in release builds
tests.obj: Finds WebViews that let attackers inspect and change web content with remote tools.
pre: Release build on a device with USB debugging.
steps: Android: Search the code for WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled.
Android: Flag calls with true that do not check ApplicationInfo.FLAG_DEBUGGABLE.
Android: Open chrome://inspect with the release build running. Look for WebViews to inspect.
tests.ex: grep -rn "setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled" out/ ; open chrome://inspect on the host with the device connected by USB
tests.exp: The app calls setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled with true only when FLAG_DEBUGGABLE is set. The release build offers no WebView to inspect.

tests.title: Check detection of attached debuggers
tests.obj: Finds apps that keep running while a debugger controls them.
pre: Release build and a test device.
steps: Android: Search for Debug.isDebuggerConnected, ptrace, TracerPid reads and JDWP checks.
iOS: Search the binary for ptrace with PT_DENY_ATTACH, sysctl P_TRACED, getppid and exception port checks.
Hook the detection calls at runtime. Record return values and backtraces.
Attach a debugger to the running app.
Check that the app ends, limits functions or informs the backend.
tests.ex: adb jdwp ; adb forward tcp:7777 jdwp:<pid> ; jdb -attach localhost:7777 ; grep -rn "isDebuggerConnected\|TracerPid" out/ ; frida -U -f <pkg> -l hook_debug_detect.js
tests.exp: The app detects an attached debugger in the Java, Kotlin, native and iOS code. It reacts when it finds one.

tests.title: Check application-level encryption of API payloads
tests.obj: Finds apps whose API payloads show in clear text once an attacker defeats TLS pinning.
pre: Test device with an intercepting proxy.
steps: Defeat certificate pinning on a test device. Capture the app traffic.
Read the request and response bodies of security-relevant calls.
Check if the app encrypts or signs the payloads in a second layer.
Check that the keys come from the platform keystore.
Change a captured request and replay it. Check that the server rejects it.
tests.ex: objection -g <pkg> explore, then android sslpinning disable ; Burp Suite: capture, edit and replay requests
tests.exp: Security-relevant payloads have a second layer of encryption or signature on top of TLS. The server rejects changed requests.

tests.title: Check that Android private storage holds no plaintext sensitive data
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data that the app writes unencrypted to its Android private data directory or to SharedPreferences.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
Run only on test devices. Use test accounts.
steps: Install the app and make a first copy of its private data directory.
Hook the SharedPreferences write methods and the Cipher classes with Frida.
Use every workflow of the app and enter sensitive data wherever possible.
Make a second copy of the private data directory and find the files that are new or changed.
Search the new files and the hook output for the sensitive values.
Decode base64, hex, URL-encoded and compressed content, because these methods hide data but do not protect it.
Look at the hook trace to see if each write of a sensitive value follows a Cipher operation.
tests.ex: adb install app.apk; objection -g <package> explore -> env (shows data paths); adb shell run-as <package> tar cf - . > data1.tar (debuggable builds) or adb pull /data/data/<package>; diff -r data1 data2; grep -rniE "token|passw|secret" data2/shared_prefs data2/databases; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "android.content.SharedPreferences$Editor!putString" -j "javax.crypto.Cipher!*"; trufflehog filesystem data2/
tests.exp: The app stores no sensitive data in plaintext or in trivially encoded form. Sensitive values are encrypted with keys that the Android Keystore protects.

tests.title: Check that iOS private storage and Keychain hold no plaintext secrets
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data that the app writes unencrypted to the iOS sandbox, UserDefaults or the Keychain with weak settings.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
A jailbroken device or a simulator gives access to the sandbox. Use test accounts.
steps: Extract the app binaries from the IPA and search them for file, UserDefaults, Core Data, SQLite and Keychain APIs.
List the Keychain calls with their access control and accessibility attributes.
Install the app, list the files in the sandbox and take a first snapshot of the Keychain.
Hook the file and Keychain APIs with Frida and use every workflow of the app with sensitive data.
List the files and the Keychain again and compare both snapshots.
Search new and changed files for sensitive values in plaintext, base64, hex and binary plist forms.
Make sure each secret is in the Keychain or encrypted with a Keychain key before the app writes it.
tests.ex: unzip app.ipa; r2 -qc "aaa; afl~SecItem" Payload/App.app/App; objection -g <bundle> explore -> env; ios keychain dump; ios plist cat Library/Preferences/<bundle>.plist; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -m "-[NSUserDefaults setObject:forKey:]" -m "-[NSFileManager createFileAtPath:*]" -i SecItemAdd -i SecItemUpdate; diff -r sandbox1 sandbox2
tests.exp: The app stores no sensitive data in plaintext in the sandbox. Secrets are in the Keychain or encrypted with keys from the Keychain.

tests.title: Check the data protection class of iOS files with sensitive data
tests.obj: Finds files with sensitive data that have the data protection class NSFileProtectionNone.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
steps: Start the test from a clean install and use every workflow of the app with sensitive data.
List the files in the app sandbox with their data protection classes.
List the files in the App Group shared containers that the app and its extensions use, with their classes.
Mark the files that hold sensitive data.
Find the marked files that have the class NSFileProtectionNone.
tests.ex: objection -g <bundle> explore -> env (shows the data and App Group paths); cd <path>; ls (the NSFileProtection column shows the class of each file); look for NSFileProtectionNone
tests.exp: Files with sensitive data use a protection class that locks them when the device is locked. No such file has the class NSFileProtectionNone.

tests.title: Check that iOS App Group containers hold no unprotected secrets
tests.obj: Finds secrets in shared UserDefaults or shared files that the app and all its extensions can read.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
steps: Extract the main binary and every extension binary in PlugIns/*.appex.
Search them for UserDefaults(suiteName:), containerURL(forSecurityApplicationGroupIdentifier:) and shared Core Data stores.
Look at the code at each location and find the values that the app writes to the shared container.
Mark the values that are credentials, tokens or keys.
Make sure the app keeps each secret in a shared Keychain and does not write it to the container.
Look at the entitlements for keychain-access-groups and the protection class of the shared files.
tests.ex: unzip app.ipa; find Payload -name "*.appex"; r2 -qc "aaa; iz~suiteName" Payload/App.app/PlugIns/X.appex/X; codesign -d --entitlements :- Payload/App.app; grep -a "group\." on the entitlements output
tests.exp: The shared container holds no secrets in plaintext. Secrets are in a shared Keychain or are encrypted and protected with a strong protection class.

tests.title: Check that sensitive data is not written to shared storage
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data that the app writes unencrypted to Android external storage or to iOS folders that the user can reach.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
steps: Android: List the files in external storage before and after you use the app.
Android: Hook the external storage APIs and FileOutputStream with Frida and use every workflow of the app.
Android: Reverse engineer the app and look for these APIs and for the WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE and MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permissions.
iOS: Read Info.plist and look at UIFileSharingEnabled and LSSupportsOpeningDocumentsInPlace.
iOS: Search the binary for writes to the Documents directory and look at the data that the code writes.
Look at each new file or code location to see if it holds sensitive data without encryption.
tests.ex: adb shell ls -R /sdcard/Android/data/<package> /sdcard/Download > before.txt (repeat after use, then diff); frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "android.os.Environment!getExternalStorageDirectory" -j "android.content.Context!getExternalFilesDir"; apktool d app.apk; grep -R "getExternalStorage\|MediaStore" smali*/; aapt d permissions app.apk; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Info.plist | grep -E "UIFileSharing|LSSupportsOpening"
tests.exp: The app writes no sensitive data unencrypted to shared storage. The iOS app does not expose a Documents folder that holds sensitive data.

tests.title: Check that the app does not write sensitive data to logs
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data in Android logcat output or in iOS device logs.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
steps: Reverse engineer the app and list the uses of logging APIs.
Android: Look for Log, Logger, System.out.print, System.err.print and printStackTrace.
iOS: Look for NSLog, NSAssert, NSCAssert, print and printf in the binary.
Monitor the device log while you use every workflow of the app with sensitive data.
Close the app and search the log for the sensitive values.
Look at the code of each match to find which log call writes the data.
tests.ex: adb logcat --pid=$(adb shell pidof -s <package>) > app.log; grep -iE "token|passw|secret|card" app.log; frida-trace -U -f <package> -j "android.util.Log!*"; apktool d app.apk; grep -R "Landroid/util/Log;" smali*/; xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream --style compact --predicate 'process CONTAINS[c] "App"'; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -i NSLog
tests.exp: Logs contain no passwords, tokens, personal data or other sensitive values. Release builds remove or disable such log calls.

tests.title: Check that sensitive files are excluded from backups
tests.obj: Finds sensitive data that the system copies to a cloud backup, a device transfer or a local backup.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
Android: A rooted or debuggable test device is needed for the backup step.
steps: Android: Read AndroidManifest.xml and note the values of allowBackup, fullBackupContent and dataExtractionRules.
Android: Read backup_rules.xml or data_extraction_rules.xml and see if all sensitive files are excluded.
Android: Use the app with sensitive data, then back up and restore its data with the backup daemon.
Android: Reinstall the app, restore the data and list the restored files.
iOS: Search the binary for isExcludedFromBackup and list the files that the code marks.
iOS: Hook the file APIs and list the files that the app creates outside tmp and Library/Caches.
Find the sensitive files in these lists.
tests.ex: apktool d -s -f app.apk; grep -E "allowBackup|fullBackupContent|dataExtractionRules" AndroidManifest.xml; cat res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml; adb root; adb shell bmgr backupnow <package>; adb pull /data/data/com.android.localtransport/files/1/_full/<package> app.ab; tar xvf app.ab; r2 -qc "aaa; iz~isExcludedFromBackup" Payload/App.app/App; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -m "-[NSFileManager createFileAtPath:*]"
tests.exp: Sensitive files are not in the backup or the restored set. iOS files that need exclusion are also encrypted, because isExcludedFromBackup gives no guarantee.

tests.title: Check that iOS text fields with sensitive input disable keyboard caching
tests.obj: Finds iOS input fields that let the keyboard cache or suggest sensitive text.
pre: A list of the sensitive data the app handles is ready (tokens, passwords, personal data, keys). The app is installed on a test device or emulator.
steps: Search the binary for UITextField, UITextView and UISearchBar and the input trait settings.
Look at isSecureTextEntry, autocorrectionType and spellCheckingType at each location, and in storyboards.
Hook the text field classes with Frida and use every input screen with sensitive data.
Note the trait values and the entered value of each field.
Find the fields with sensitive data where isSecureTextEntry is off or autocorrection or spell checking is on or default.
tests.ex: r2 -qc "aaa; iz~autocorrectionType" Payload/App.app/App; plutil -p Payload/App.app/Base.lproj/*.storyboardc/*.nib; frida-trace -U -f <bundle> -m "-[UITextField setSecureTextEntry:]" -m "-[UITextField setAutocorrectionType:]" -m "-[UITextField setSpellCheckingType:]"
tests.exp: Each field for sensitive input has isSecureTextEntry on, or autocorrection and spell checking off. The keyboard does not cache the entered text.

tests.title: Check that the app package holds no hardcoded secrets
tests.obj: Finds API keys, passwords, tokens and private keys that ship inside the APK or IPA.
steps: Unpack the APK or IPA and decompile the code.
Search code, resources, plists, JSON files, native libraries and bundled frameworks for secrets.
Run a secret scanner over the unpacked package.
Look at each hit to see if it is a live API key, credential or private key.
Check the scope and the permissions of each secret that you find.
Make sure the app gets static secrets from a backend at run time or uses scoped tokens that expire.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk -o out; jadx -d src app.apk; unzip app.ipa -d ipa; strings -n 8 ipa/Payload/App.app/App | grep -iE "api[_-]?key|secret|passw|BEGIN (RSA|EC|PRIVATE)"; grep -riE "api[_-]?key|secret|token" out/res src/; gitleaks detect --no-git -s out; trufflehog filesystem out ipa
tests.exp: The package holds no live secrets, credentials or private keys. Unavoidable static keys have the least permissions and can be rotated.

tests.title: Check that sensitive screens stay out of screenshots and the app switcher
tests.obj: Finds screens that leak sensitive data through task snapshots, screenshots or screen recordings.
pre: Rooted Android device or emulator, and a jailbroken iOS device, to read snapshot files.
steps: List the screens that show sensitive data, such as login, payment, health and personal data.
Android: Search the code for FLAG_SECURE, setRecentsScreenshotEnabled, setSecure on SurfaceView and SecureOn in Compose dialogs.
Android: Open each sensitive screen. Press Home. Pull the system task snapshot files from the device.
Android: Try a screenshot and a screen recording on each sensitive screen.
iOS: Open each sensitive screen. Press Home. Pull the snapshot files from the SplashBoard folder of the app.
Look at each snapshot image for passwords, tokens, personal data or other secrets.
tests.ex: adb shell ls /data/system_ce/0/snapshots (root) ; adb pull /data/system_ce/0/snapshots ; adb exec-out screencap -p > shot.png ; grep -rn "FLAG_SECURE\|setRecentsScreenshotEnabled" out/ ; iOS: scp the Library/SplashBoard/Snapshots folder of the app container
tests.exp: No snapshot, screenshot or recording shows sensitive data. The app hides or protects sensitive screens when it moves to the background.

tests.title: Check that Android keyboards do not cache sensitive input
tests.obj: Finds input fields that let the keyboard learn and suggest sensitive text.
pre: Decoded APK.
steps: Android: Extract the layout files from the app package.
Android: List every android:inputType attribute and every setInputType call.
Android: Find fields for passwords, PINs, card data and other secrets.
Android: Check that these fields use a non-caching type such as textPassword or textNoSuggestions.
tests.ex: apktool d app.apk -o out ; grep -rn "android:inputType" out/res/layout ; grep -rn "setInputType" out/
tests.exp: Every field that takes sensitive data uses an input type that stops keyboard caching and suggestions.

tests.title: Check that password, PIN and code fields hide the typed text
tests.obj: Finds secret input fields that show characters to bystanders and screen recordings.
pre: Decompiled app code or extracted IPA.
steps: Android: Find text fields for passwords, PINs and one-time codes in XML and in Compose code.
Android: Flag a plain TextField, and flag a SecureTextField that uses TextObfuscationMode.Visible.
iOS: Check that each UITextField for a secret sets isSecureTextEntry to true.
iOS: Check that SwiftUI code uses SecureField and not TextField for secrets.
Type test secrets into each field at runtime. Look at the screen for visible characters.
tests.ex: grep -rn "textPassword\|TextObfuscationMode\|SecureTextField" out/ ; r2 -A <app_binary> ; izz~isSecureTextEntry ; frida -U -f <bundle_id> -l hook_uitextfield.js
tests.exp: Every field for a password, PIN or code masks the typed characters. Full values show only after a user action and for a short time.

tests.title: Check that notifications hold no sensitive data
tests.obj: Finds notifications that show secrets or personal data on the lock screen or to other apps.
pre: Android device. Test data that triggers each notification.
