tests.ex: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep kubernetes_feature_enabled | grep " 1$"; kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep feature-gates
tests.exp: No unused alpha or beta feature is on. Each enabled one has an owner and a written risk decision.

tests.title: Review the rights that third-party integrations request
tests.obj: Finds add-ons with cluster-wide rights that are wider than their job needs.
steps: List the add-ons and operators that run in the cluster.
Read the ClusterRoles and bindings of each add-on.
Find add-ons that read all secrets or create pods in system namespaces.
Check if each add-on can work in one namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o wide; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>
tests.exp: Each add-on has only the rights for its job. No untrusted component creates pods in kube- namespaces or in namespaces that allow privileged pods.

tests.title: Check removal of unused components and periodic scans
tests.obj: Finds old components that stay in the cluster and are not scanned.
steps: List the components of the cluster, the pipeline and the nodes.
Find components with no owner or no use.
Check the plan to remove them.
Check the date of the last vulnerability scan and the last penetration test.
Make sure the findings have owners and due dates.
tests.ex: kube-bench run; kubescape scan framework nsa; trivy k8s --report summary cluster
tests.exp: Unused components are removed. Scans and penetration tests run on a fixed schedule and the findings are fixed in time.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Upgrading and application security practices

tests.title: Check that worker nodes have no public IP addresses
tests.obj: Finds nodes that the Internet can reach directly.
steps: List the nodes with their external IP addresses.
Check the subnet and route table of each node pool.
Scan the external addresses of nodes from an outside network.
Check that nodes use a NAT gateway for outbound traffic.
tests.ex: kubectl get nodes -o wide; nmap -Pn <node-external-ip>
tests.exp: Nodes have only private addresses. Services reach the Internet through load balancers or a NAT gateway.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Worker node segmentation

tests.title: Check firewall and network policy limits around the control plane
tests.obj: Finds control plane ports that untrusted networks can reach.
steps: Read the firewall rules for port 6443 and the other control plane ports.
Read the network policies of the kube-system namespace.
From a user network and from a worker node, try to reach each control plane port.
Make sure the rules allow the control plane to talk to the worker nodes.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -p 6443,2379,2380,10250,10257,10259 <control-plane-ip>; kubectl -n kube-system get netpol
tests.exp: Only trusted networks reach the API server. Network rules around kube-system block Internet access and still allow control plane traffic.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Control plane hardening

tests.title: Check image pull policy, digest pins and deprecated registry paths
tests.obj: Finds workloads that can run an old or swapped image behind a mutable tag.
steps: List images that use a mutable tag and their pull policy.
Make sure the pull policy is Always where a mutable tag is in use.
List images that are not pinned to a sha256 digest.
List images from the deprecated k8s.gcr.io registry.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath="{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}" | grep -v "@sha256"; kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -c "k8s.gcr.io"
tests.exp: Production images use a digest. Mutable tags use the pull policy Always. No component pulls from the deprecated registry path.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Upgrading and application security practices

tests.title: Check that image signature checks fail closed and block bad images
tests.obj: Finds clusters where an unsigned, tampered or bypassed image can still start.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Read the signature policy or the ImagePolicyWebhook configuration and the trusted keys.
In a test namespace, start an unsigned image and a tampered image.
Stop the verification service in a test cluster and start a pod.
Check that the policy engine runs a fixed version without known signature bypass flaws.
tests.ex: kubectl run unsigned --image=<registry>/unsigned:1 -n test; cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image>
tests.exp: The cluster rejects unsigned and tampered images and rejects pods when the verifier is down. The policy engine has no known bypass flaw.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Kubernetes Pod security, Building secure container images

tests.title: Check the image scan gate at admission
tests.obj: Finds clusters that deploy images that failed the scan policy.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find the admission webhook or policy that checks scan results.
Read the rules for severity levels and false-positive handling.
In a test namespace, deploy an image that has a known critical flaw.
Check that rejected deployments appear in the audit log.
tests.ex: kubectl run vuln --image=<known-vulnerable-image> -n test; trivy image --severity CRITICAL <image>
tests.exp: A webhook or policy blocks images that break the scan policy. Waivers for false positives have an owner and an end date.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Kubernetes Pod security, Building secure container images

tests.title: Find workloads that mount cloud credential files from the node
tests.obj: Finds pods that can read cloud credentials stored on the node.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List hostPath volumes that point to cloud credential folders or files.
Check the node for credential files of the cloud provider.
From a test pod, try to read those paths.
Replace the mounts with workload identity.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.hostPath.path | tostring | test("azure|aws|gcloud|cloud")) | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: No pod mounts cloud credential paths from the node. Workloads get short-lived credentials through workload identity.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Protecting sensitive cloud infrastructure

tests.title: Check audit log retention, rotation and access on the API server
tests.obj: Finds audit logs that expire too fast or that many users can read.
steps: Read the audit log path, maximum age, maximum backups and maximum size flags.
Compare the retention to the policy and to the time needed for investigations.
Read the mode and owner of the audit log files and of the audit policy.
Check if audit events also go to a webhook backend or to a remote store.
tests.ex: kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep audit; ls -l /var/log/kubernetes/audit
tests.exp: Audit logs are kept for at least 30 days or the policy time. Rotation is set, and only administrators and the log agent can read the files.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Kubernetes native audit logging configuration

tests.title: Check that logs cover all layers of the environment
tests.obj: Finds layers with no logs, so that incident responders cannot follow an attack.
steps: List the log sources: hosts, applications, containers, container engine, registry, API server and cloud.
Find sources that do not send logs to the central service.
Check that the node agent runs on each node, for example as a DaemonSet.
Check that kubelet and runtime logs go to journald or syslog and then to the central store.
tests.ex: kubectl get ds -A | grep -Ei "fluent|vector|promtail|filebeat"; journalctl -u kubelet --since "1 hour ago" | head
tests.exp: Every layer sends logs to one central service. The logging agent runs on every node.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Logging
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Worker node and container logging
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Syslog

tests.title: Check alerts for anonymous requests, new mounts, root pods and new CronJobs
tests.obj: Finds attack steps that no alert rule detects.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Read the alert rules of the monitoring system.
Make an anonymous request to the API in a test cluster.
Create a test pod that runs as root with a hostPath mount and create a test CronJob.
Check that each action creates an alert and that the alert reaches an owner.
Check for alerts on low disk space and on a log service that is down.
tests.ex: kubectl --as=system:anonymous get pods -n default; kubectl apply -f root-hostpath-pod.yaml
tests.exp: Anonymous requests, risky volume mounts, root pods and new CronJobs raise alerts. Alerts also cover low disk space and log service failure.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Threat Detection
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Alerting

tests.title: Check automatic response and intrusion detection for compromised pods
tests.obj: Finds clusters that detect an attack but do not limit it.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Find the intrusion detection or runtime tool and the response rules.
Check the rule for a pod IP listed as the source of a pod creation request.
In a test namespace, trigger a rule and watch the response, such as eviction of the pod.
Check that a clean pod starts from the original image after the response.
Check who reviews each automatic response.
tests.ex: falco -r rules.yaml; kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=Evicted
tests.exp: Rules for suspect pods exist and work. The response limits the damage, a clean pod replaces the old one, and logs stay available for review.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Threat Detection
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Tools

tests.title: Check TLS on Ingress routes and HTTPS load balancers
tests.obj: Finds public routes that send traffic in clear text or with a weak certificate setup.
steps: List all Ingress objects and check for a tls section.
List the Services of type LoadBalancer and their listeners.
Request each public route with HTTP and check for a redirect to HTTPS.
Scan each public listener with a TLS scanner.
tests.ex: kubectl get ingress -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.spec.tls==null) | .metadata.name"; testssl.sh https://<host>
tests.exp: Each Ingress and load balancer listener uses TLS 1.2 or 1.3 with valid certificates. HTTP requests are redirected or refused.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Network policies

tests.title: Check network zones for nodes, control plane and sensitive services
tests.obj: Finds flat networks where a compromised node can reach databases and the control plane.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Draw the network zones of the control plane, worker nodes, databases and internal services.
Read the firewall and security group rules between the zones.
From a worker node, try to connect to a database and to an internal service in another zone.
Make sure only needed ports are open between the zones.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -p 22,2379,6443,10250,3306,5432 <target-range> from a worker node
tests.exp: Worker nodes, the control plane and sensitive services are in separate zones. Firewalls allow only the listed flows.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Worker node segmentation
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Network policies

tests.title: Check network policy selectors for tenant isolation
tests.obj: Finds network policies that open traffic between tenants through wide selectors.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List network policies that use an empty namespaceSelector or podSelector.
Check that each tenant namespace has a default deny policy plus an allow rule for DNS.
Check that namespace labels used in selectors cannot be set by tenants.
From a pod in one tenant namespace, try to reach a pod in another tenant namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get netpol -A -o yaml | grep -B3 -A3 "namespaceSelector: {}"; kubectl exec -n tenant-a <pod> -- wget -qO- -T3 http://<svc>.tenant-b
tests.exp: Tenant namespaces cannot reach each other. Selectors name specific namespaces, and tenants cannot change the labels that policies use.

tests.title: Find workloads exposed through Gateway API or mesh gateways
tests.obj: Finds routes that make workloads reachable from the Internet outside the Ingress list.
steps: List Gateway, HTTPRoute, TCPRoute and UDPRoute objects.
List mesh gateway objects such as Istio Gateway.
Map each route to the workload and the owner.
From an outside network, request each listener address.
Ask the owner to justify each public route.
tests.ex: kubectl get gateways,httproutes,tcproutes,udproutes -A; kubectl get gateways.networking.istio.io -A
tests.exp: Each public route has an owner and a reason. Internal workloads have no public route, and listeners need TLS.

tests.title: Check namespaces as boundaries and workloads in default or system namespaces
tests.obj: Finds workloads that share a namespace with other teams or with cluster services.
steps: List the namespaces and the teams or tenants that own them.
List pods in the default, kube-system and kube-public namespaces.
Find user workloads in these namespaces.
Check that RBAC, quotas and network policies exist for each application namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -n default; kubectl get pods -n kube-public; kubectl get ns --show-labels
tests.exp: Each application has its own namespace with its own RBAC, quota and network policy. The default, kube-system and kube-public namespaces hold no user workloads.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Namespaces

tests.title: Review Pod Security admission exemptions and cluster defaults
tests.obj: Finds users, runtime classes and namespaces that skip pod security checks.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Read the admission configuration of the API server for the PodSecurity plugin.
List exempt usernames, runtime class names and namespaces.
Make sure ordinary users and service accounts that create workloads are not exempt.
Read the default enforce level of the cluster.
Create a violating pod in an exempt namespace in a test cluster.
tests.ex: kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep admission-control-config-file; cat <admission-config.yaml>
tests.exp: Exemptions are few and have an owner. No user who creates workloads is exempt, and the default level is baseline or restricted.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Kubernetes Pod security, Pod security enforcement

tests.title: Check control plane and storage isolation between tenants
tests.obj: Finds shared resources through which one tenant can reach or harm another.
steps: List the tenants and the namespaces or virtual control planes of each.
Check that RBAC limits each tenant to its own namespaces and that quotas bound object counts.
Check the StorageClass of each tenant and the reclaim policy of shared classes.
Check shared services such as DNS, logging and the kubelet for tenant access.
Decide if the tenants are trusted or hostile and check that the isolation level fits.
tests.ex: kubectl get sc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RECLAIM:.reclaimPolicy; kubectl get resourcequota -A
tests.exp: Tenants have separate namespaces, rights and quotas. Shared storage classes use the Delete reclaim policy, and hostile tenants have sandboxes or separate clusters.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Kubernetes Pod security, Hardening container environments

tests.title: Find subjects that can exec, attach or port-forward into pods
tests.obj: Finds users and service accounts that can run commands in containers or open tunnels to pods.
steps: List roles with create on pods/exec, pods/attach and pods/portforward.
List the subjects bound to these roles.
Check that day-to-day accounts do not hold these rights in production namespaces.
Check that each use of exec appears in the audit log.
Ask the owner to justify each subject.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=<user> -n <ns>; kubectl get clusterrole,role -A -o json | jq ".. | select(.resources?) | select(.resources[]|test("pods/(exec|attach|portforward)"))"
tests.exp: In production only a small, named group has exec and port-forward rights. These actions are logged and alerts exist for them.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Alerting

tests.title: Find subjects that can create workloads and the limits on them
tests.obj: Finds users who can create pods and so can reach secrets, service accounts and nodes.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List subjects with create, update or patch on pods, deployments, jobs, cronjobs and daemonsets.
List the service accounts in each namespace where these subjects can create workloads.
Make sure Pod Security admission enforces the baseline or restricted level there.
Create a privileged pod in a test namespace as one of these subjects.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=<user> -n <ns>; kubectl get clusterrolebinding,rolebinding -A -o wide
tests.exp: Workload creation rights are rare and limited by namespace. The enforced pod security level blocks privileged pods for these subjects.

tests.title: Find subjects that can delete resources or Kubernetes events
tests.obj: Finds accounts that can destroy workloads and data or erase traces of their actions.
steps: List roles with the delete or deletecollection verb on workloads, volumes, namespaces and nodes.
List roles with delete on events.
List the subjects bound to these roles.
Check that daily-use accounts do not hold these rights.
Check that events also go to a store outside the cluster.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i delete events -A --as=<user>; kubectl get clusterrole -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.rules[]?.verbs[]? | test("delete"))" | head
tests.exp: Delete rights are limited to a named group. Only controllers can delete events, and events are copied to a separate log store.

tests.title: Find subjects that can create volumes, approve CSRs or mint tokens
tests.obj: Finds rights that let a user escalate to node or cluster control.
steps: List subjects that can create PersistentVolumes.
List subjects with update on certificatesigningrequests/approval and the sign verb.
List subjects that can create serviceaccounts/token.
List subjects that can create, change or delete webhook configurations.
Ask the owner to justify each subject.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i create persistentvolumes --as=<user>; kubectl auth can-i update certificatesigningrequests/approval --as=<user>; kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts/token -n <ns> --as=<user>
tests.exp: Only cluster administrators and control plane controllers hold these rights. Other subjects do not hold them.

tests.title: Check that nobody uses the system:masters group after bootstrap
tests.obj: Finds users and components that hold unlimited rights through a group that RBAC cannot restrict.
steps: List client certificates and kubeconfig entries with the organization system:masters.
List the bindings and OIDC group mappings that give the group to a user or service account.
Check that the controller manager does not run as system:masters.
Check that the CertificateSubjectRestriction plugin is on.
Check the break-glass process for this group.
tests.ex: kubectl get csr -o json | jq ".items[].spec.request" ; openssl x509 -in client.crt -noout -subject; grep -r "system:masters" ~/.kube
tests.exp: No user or component uses system:masters in daily work. It is a break-glass credential with a record of each use.

tests.title: Find workloads whose service accounts hold admin or takeover rights
tests.obj: Finds pods that give an attacker cluster control after an application flaw.
steps: List workloads and their service accounts.
List the roles of each service account, including aggregated roles.
Find service accounts with cluster-admin, secret read, or workload create and update rights.
Rank the findings by exposure of the workload to the Internet.
Replace broad roles with narrow roles.
tests.ex: kubescape scan control C-0267,C-0272,C-0053; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>
tests.exp: No workload service account holds admin rights or rights to read secrets or create workloads across the cluster without a written reason.

tests.title: Find subjects that can change the CoreDNS configuration
tests.obj: Finds accounts that can poison cluster DNS and take over service names.
steps: Find the CoreDNS ConfigMap in kube-system.
List subjects with update or patch on that ConfigMap.
List subjects with update or patch on the CoreDNS deployment.
Make sure changes to the ConfigMap raise an alert.
tests.ex: kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml; kubectl auth can-i update configmaps/coredns -n kube-system --as=<user>
tests.exp: Only cluster administrators can change the CoreDNS ConfigMap and deployment. Each change creates an alert.

tests.title: Check periodic access reviews, CA protection and certificate lifetimes
tests.obj: Finds clusters where old access stays and certificates live too long.
steps: Find the access review records and the date of the last review.
Check that the interval between reviews is not more than 24 months.
Read the validity period of intermediate and leaf certificates.
Check how the root CA key is stored and who can use it.
tests.ex: openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates; kubeadm certs check-expiration
tests.exp: Reviews take place at least every 24 months. Certificates expire within 3 years. The root CA is offline or online with strict access.

tests.title: Check etcd disposal, swap use and secret scope in pods
tests.obj: Finds places where secret data stays on disk or reaches containers that do not need it.
steps: Check if old etcd storage is wiped or shredded when it is no longer in use.
Check the swap setting of each node and the encryption of swap space.
List pods with several containers and check which containers mount each secret.
Check that secret manifests are not in source repositories.
tests.ex: swapon --show; kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.spec.containers|length>1) | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: Old etcd storage is wiped. Swap is off or encrypted, and each secret is mounted only in the containers that need it.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Secrets

tests.title: Check the KMS provider setup for the Secret encryption key
tests.obj: Finds clusters where the key for Secret encryption sits on the same node as the data.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Read the encryption configuration file and find the provider type for secrets.
Check if a KMS provider holds the key, so the raw key is not on the local disk.
Check the access policy and the audit log of the KMS key.
Check the process to rotate the key and to rewrite all Secrets.
tests.ex: cat /etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml; kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
tests.exp: A KMS provider holds the key outside the node. Key use is logged and the key is rotated. Secrets are rewritten after each key change.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Network separation and hardening, Secrets

tests.title: Check hostPath volumes for read-only use, narrow paths and admission blocks
tests.obj: Finds pods that can read or write host files through hostPath mounts.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List all pods with hostPath volumes and the host path of each.
Find mounts that are writable or that mount a parent directory such as / or /var.
Find subPath mounts on affected Kubernetes versions.
Check that an admission rule blocks hostPath outside an approved list.
Try to create a pod with a hostPath mount in a test namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.hostPath) | .metadata.namespace+"/"+.metadata.name"; kubescape scan control C-0045,C-0203
tests.exp: Only approved system pods use hostPath, with narrow paths and read-only mounts. Admission rules reject all other hostPath volumes.

tests.title: Find pods that use hostPort or Windows HostProcess containers
tests.obj: Finds pods that open node ports or run as processes on the Windows host.
steps: List containers that set hostPort.
List pods that set hostProcess in the Windows security context.
Ask the owner to justify each case.
Check that admission rules reject both settings outside system namespaces.
Replace hostPort with a Service of type ClusterIP or NodePort.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.spec.containers[].ports[]?.hostPort) | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: No application pod uses hostPort or hostProcess. Admission rules block both settings.

tests.title: Find SSH servers and sudo in container images and commands
tests.obj: Finds containers that give remote shell access or raise privileges at start.
steps: List containers that expose port 22 or 2222.
Search the entry point and command of each container for sudo.
Search the image file systems for an sshd binary.
Remove SSH and sudo from the images and use kubectl debug for support work.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.spec.containers[].ports[]?.containerPort | IN(22,2222)) | .metadata.name"; kubescape scan control C-0042,C-0062
tests.exp: No container runs an SSH server or uses sudo in its start command. Support access uses audited Kubernetes access.

tests.title: Check noexec, nosuid and nodev options on writable mounts
tests.obj: Finds writable volumes from which an attacker can start dropped binaries.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List writable volume mounts of each container, including emptyDir and hostPath.
Read the mount options of each mount.
In a test pod, write a script to a writable mount and set it executable.
Try to run the script from the mount.
tests.ex: kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c "cp /bin/true /tmp/t && /tmp/t"; kubectl exec <pod> -- mount | grep -E "noexec|nosuid"
tests.exp: Writable mounts use the options noexec, nosuid and nodev where the application allows it. The test script does not run.

tests.title: Check CPU and memory requests and the QoS class of workloads
tests.obj: Finds pods that can starve others or get evicted first because they set no requests.
steps: List CPU and memory requests for each container.
Find pods with the QoS class BestEffort.
Check that the memory limit is not lower than the memory request.
Check that critical workloads have the Guaranteed or Burstable class with fitting values.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.status.qosClass=="BestEffort") | .metadata.namespace+"/"+.metadata.name"
tests.exp: Each container sets CPU and memory requests. No application pod is BestEffort, and memory limits fit the requests.

tests.title: Check controllers, probes, update strategy and labels of workloads
tests.obj: Finds pods and deployments that drift from the code, stay unhealthy or lack an owner.
steps: List pods that have no owner controller.
List containers without readiness and liveness probes.
List deployments that use a non-rolling update strategy.
List workloads without the common app and owner labels.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.metadata.ownerReferences==null) | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: Each pod belongs to a controller with probes and a rolling update. Labels name the app and the owner.

tests.title: Review CronJobs and Jobs for unknown scheduled workloads
tests.obj: Finds scheduled jobs that an attacker may use for persistence or execution.
steps: List all CronJobs and Jobs in all namespaces.
Read the image, command and service account of each CronJob.
Compare the list to the change records.
Check who can create CronJobs.
tests.ex: kubectl get cronjob,job -A -o wide; kubectl get cronjob -A -o json | jq ".items[].spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers[].image"
tests.exp: Each CronJob is known and approved. The image is trusted and the service account has only the needed rights.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Logging

tests.title: Check volume encryption and workload access to volumes, secrets and ConfigMaps
tests.obj: Finds data volumes without encryption and workloads with more storage access than needed.
steps: List StorageClasses and PersistentVolumes with their encryption settings.
Find volumes without encryption.
List workloads that mount PVCs, secrets or ConfigMaps.
Remove mounts that the workload does not need.
tests.ex: kubectl get sc,pv -o wide; kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.persistentVolumeClaim) | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: All PersistentVolumes use encrypted storage. Each workload mounts only the volumes, secrets and ConfigMaps that it needs.

tests.title: Find dangling and mismatched objects that hide broken controls
tests.obj: Finds policies and routes that target nothing and so give false safety.
steps: List NetworkPolicies whose pod selector matches no pod.
List Services, Ingresses, Gateway routes and autoscalers that point to missing targets.
List workloads where the selector does not match the pod labels.
List pods with duplicate environment variables, missing or deprecated service account fields.
tests.ex: kubescape scan control C-0299,C-0293,C-0296,C-0295,C-0294,C-0307; kubectl get netpol,svc,ing -A
tests.exp: Each policy selects at least one workload. Services, routes and autoscalers have valid targets. Selectors, environment variables and service accounts are correct.

tests.title: Check hardening of Agent Sandbox workloads
tests.obj: Finds sandbox templates for AI agents that lack isolation, limits or egress control.
pre: The cluster uses the Agent Sandbox resources.
steps: List Sandbox and SandboxTemplate resources.
Check that each uses an approved hardened runtime class.
Check CPU and memory limits, image registry and image digest for each container.
Check the egress policy mode and that claims cannot override template settings.
Check that service account tokens are not mounted.
tests.ex: kubectl get sandboxtemplates,sandboxes -A -o yaml; kubescape scan control C-0297,C-0301,C-0303,C-0309,C-0314,C-0316
tests.exp: Sandboxes use a hardened runtime, set resource limits and pin images from approved registries. Egress is limited, tokens are off, and claims cannot override the template.

tests.title: Check pod placement by sensitivity tier and node isolation
tests.obj: Finds sensitive pods that share nodes with less trusted workloads.
steps: List the sensitivity tiers of the workloads and the node pools.
Read nodeSelector and tolerations of sensitive workloads.
Check that PodNodeSelector or PodTolerationRestriction limits placement by namespace.
Check that users cannot remove the taints or labels that separate the pools.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o wide; kubectl get nodes --show-labels; kubectl describe node <node> | grep Taints
tests.exp: Sensitive workloads run on separate nodes or in sandboxed runtimes. Admission rules enforce the placement and users cannot bypass it.

tests.title: Check custom seccomp profiles and audit mode for baselines
tests.obj: Finds workloads without a tailored syscall filter and without syscall baselines.
steps: List workloads that use a Localhost seccomp profile.
Read the profile directory of the kubelet on a sample node.
Check if audit mode profiles record the syscalls of a new workload.
Use the recorded syscalls to build a tighter profile.
tests.ex: ls /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/; kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[].spec.securityContext.seccompProfile"
tests.exp: Sensitive workloads use a custom profile that allows only needed syscalls. Audit profiles help build the baseline before enforcement.

other: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Audit Logging and Threat Detection, Seccomp: audit mode
NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance 1.2, section Kubernetes Pod security, Hardening container environments

tests.title: Check that the cluster admits only approved and signed images
tests.obj: Finds clusters that run images from unknown registries or with no proof of origin.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List all images in the cluster with their registries.
Find images from public or unknown registries.
Check the admission rule that limits registries and checks signatures.
Try to start a pod from an unapproved registry in a test namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath="{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}" | sort -u; kubectl run t --image=docker.io/library/nginx -n <test-ns>; cosign verify <image> --key <pub> (if signing is used)
tests.exp: Only images from approved registries, with a valid signature or known digest, start in the cluster. The unapproved test pod is rejected.

tests.title: Check image tags, digests and use of stale images
tests.obj: Finds workloads that use mutable tags or old images that miss fixes.
steps: List images that use the latest tag or no tag.
Compare running image digests to the registry.
Check the build date of each image.
Check the policy for maximum image age.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ".items[].spec.containers[].image" | sort -u | grep -E ":latest$|^[^:]+$"; docker inspect <image> --format "{{.Created}}"
tests.exp: Images use fixed tags or digests. No image is older than the policy age, and base images are rebuilt on a set schedule.

tests.title: Scan running images for known vulnerabilities
tests.obj: Finds deployed images that contain components with known vulnerabilities, including new ones found after the build.
steps: List all images that run in the cluster.
Scan each image for vulnerabilities with a scanner.
Check if the cluster is scanned on a schedule, not only at build.
Rank the findings by severity and by exposure of the workload.
tests.ex: trivy image <image>; trivy k8s --report summary cluster; grype <image>
tests.exp: Running images have no unfixed critical or high vulnerabilities without a written exception. The cluster is scanned on a set schedule.

tests.title: Check that images are minimal and hold no shells or package tools
tests.obj: Finds images with extra tools that help an attacker after a breach.
steps: List the base image of each workload.
Check for a shell, package manager and compilers in the image.
Try to start a shell in a test pod.
Check for distroless or minimal base images.
tests.ex: kubectl exec <pod> -- sh; docker run --rm --entrypoint sh <image> -c "which apt apk curl"; trivy image --list-all-pkgs <image>
tests.exp: Production images use minimal or distroless bases. They hold no shell, package manager or network tools without need.

tests.title: Check registry access control and the transport to registries
tests.obj: Finds registries that allow anonymous push, wide pull rights or plain HTTP.
steps: List the registries that the cluster uses.
Check who can push and pull for each repository.
Check that every pull uses TLS.
Check the image pull secrets in each namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson; curl -sI http://<registry>/v2/; check the registry access policy in the provider
tests.exp: Registries need authentication for push and pull. Only build systems can push. All transfers use TLS and pull secrets are limited per namespace.

tests.title: Check an SBOM and provenance for each deployed image
tests.obj: Finds images that cannot be traced to a source, a build and a list of components.
steps: Pick three running images.
Find the SBOM and provenance record of each.
Check that the SBOM matches the image digest.
Make sure the admission policy uses the provenance.
tests.ex: cosign verify-attestation <image> --type slsaprovenance --key <pub>; trivy sbom <file>; syft <image>
tests.exp: Each image links to an SBOM and provenance that match its digest. The cluster rejects images without them.

tests.title: Check the cloud permissions of node roles
tests.obj: Finds node identities with wide cloud rights that every pod on the node can use.
steps: Find the cloud identity attached to each node pool.
List the policies of each node identity.
Find rights to storage, databases, IAM and compute creation.
Compare them to the minimum that a node needs.
tests.ex:
aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name ; az aks show -n -g --query identityProfile; gcloud container node-pools describe

--cluster --format="value(config.serviceAccount)"
tests.exp: Node identities hold only the rights that the node agent needs. Application rights come from workload identities.

tests.title: Check that pods use workload identity and not the node identity
tests.obj: Finds pods that inherit the node role when a per-service-account cloud role is available.
steps: List service accounts with cloud role annotations or identity bindings.
Find workloads that call cloud APIs without a workload identity.
From a test pod, request cloud credentials and note whose identity returns.
Check the scope of each workload role.
tests.ex: kubectl get sa -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.metadata.annotations) | {n:.metadata.name, a:.metadata.annotations}"; kubectl exec <pod> -- aws sts get-caller-identity
tests.exp: Each workload gets a scoped, short-lived cloud role through EKS Pod Identity, IRSA, GKE Workload Identity or AKS Workload Identity. The returned identity is not the node role.

tests.title: Check that pods cannot reach the instance metadata service
tests.obj: Finds pods that can steal node credentials from the metadata address.
steps: From a test pod, request the metadata address 169.254.169.254.
Check the NetworkPolicy that blocks egress to this address.
Check the metadata settings of the node: token required and hop limit.
Check other provider metadata addresses.
tests.ex: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/; aws ec2 describe-instances --query "Reservations[].Instances[].MetadataOptions"
tests.exp: The request from the pod fails. The node requires session tokens for metadata (IMDSv2) and a network policy blocks the address.

tests.title: Find static cloud credentials in the cluster
tests.obj: Finds long-lived cloud keys in Secrets, ConfigMaps, env variables and images.
steps: Search Secrets, ConfigMaps and pod specs for cloud access key patterns.
Scan images for cloud key files.
Check the age and last use of each key found.
Replace each key with workload identity.
tests.ex: trivy image --scanners secret <image>; kubectl get secrets,cm -A -o yaml | grep -E "AKIA|aws_access_key|client_secret|private_key"; gitleaks detect
tests.exp: The cluster holds no static cloud keys. Any key found is revoked and replaced with a short-lived identity.

tests.title: Check runtime detection of tools and shells in containers
tests.obj: Finds clusters that do not alert on shells, discovery tools or cloud CLIs that start inside a container.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Check that a runtime security tool runs on all nodes.
In a test pod, start a shell and run curl and a cloud CLI.
Check for an alert for each action.
Check who receives the alerts.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A | grep -iE "falco|tetragon"; kubectl exec -it <test-pod> -- sh -c "curl -m 3 https://example.com; which aws"
tests.exp: The tool raises an alert for each unexpected shell and tool. The alerts reach the response team.

tests.title: Check that Kubernetes API audit logging is on
tests.obj: Finds clusters that keep no record of API requests.
steps: Read the audit policy and audit log flags of the API server or the managed service setting.
Make a test change in a test namespace.
Find the event in the audit log.
Check that the event has user, verb, object and time.
tests.ex: kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep audit; kubectl create ns audit-test; grep audit-test /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | head -1
tests.exp: The API server writes audit events for all requests that the policy requires. The test change appears with user, verb, object and time.

tests.title: Check the audit policy covers credentials and sensitive actions
tests.obj: Finds policies that miss the creation of tokens and certificates, which the cluster does not store.
steps: Read the audit policy file rule by rule.
Check rules for serviceaccounts/token, certificatesigningrequests, RBAC objects and pods/exec.
Create a test token and a test CSR.
Find both events in the audit log.
tests.ex: kubectl create token <sa> -n <test-ns>; kubectl get csr; grep -E "serviceaccounts/token|certificatesigningrequests" /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | head
tests.exp: The audit log shows who made each token and certificate request. Secrets and configmaps use the Metadata level only.

tests.title: Check that logs go to protected storage outside the cluster
tests.obj: Finds logs that an attacker with node or cluster access can edit or delete.
steps: Find where audit, node and workload logs go.
Check that an agent ships logs from every node.
Check that the log store is append-only and outside the cluster.
Check who can delete or edit logs.
tests.ex: kubectl get ds -A | grep -iE "fluent|filebeat|vector"; kubectl logs <pod>; check the retention and write controls of the log store
tests.exp: Logs leave the node in near real time to a store outside the cluster. Only a small group can read them, and none can edit them.

tests.title: Check log buffering and delivery during outages
tests.obj: Finds log pipelines that drop records when the central store is down.
pre: Use a test setup only.
steps: Find the buffer type and size at each node agent.
Stop the log destination in a test setup for a short time.
Restore the destination.
Count the records that arrive after recovery.
tests.ex: Read the agent configuration (Fluent Bit or Fluentd); compare event counts before and after the outage
tests.exp: The agent buffers records on disk and delivers them after recovery. A message broker decouples ingestion from storage. Lost records are reported.

tests.title: Check alerts on API failures and risky cluster actions
tests.obj: Finds clusters where authorization failures and risky actions raise no alert.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Send requests that return 403 from a test account.
Run kubectl exec into a test pod and create a privileged pod in a test namespace.
Look for alerts in the monitoring system.
Check the alert route and the response time.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=<test-user>; kubectl exec <test-pod> -- id; query the log platform for responseStatus.code 403
tests.exp: Spikes of 403 responses, exec into pods and privileged pod creation raise alerts that reach the response team in the agreed time.

tests.title: Check monitoring of container activity and network flows
tests.obj: Finds clusters with no view of process, file and network behavior of containers.
steps: Find the tools that record process, file and network events of containers.
Start a test pod that makes an outbound connection.
Find the event in the tool.
Compare the replicas of one deployment for odd behavior.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A | grep -iE "falco|tetragon|cilium"; kubectl exec <test-pod> -- curl -m 3 https://example.com
tests.exp: The tools record unexpected process starts, sensitive file reads and outbound connections. A replica that differs from its peers is flagged.

tests.title: Check monitoring of cluster resource use and configuration changes
tests.obj: Finds clusters that miss resource exhaustion and unplanned changes to cluster configuration.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Check that CPU, memory and storage use of nodes and pods is monitored with alerts.
Check that Kubernetes events go to the central log.
Make a test change to a ConfigMap.
Find an alert or record of the change.
tests.ex: kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail; kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods -A
tests.exp: Resource alerts exist for node and pod limits. Events and configuration changes appear in the central log before they expire.

tests.title: Check that the CNI plugin enforces network policies
tests.obj: Finds clusters where network policies exist but the network plugin ignores them.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Identify the CNI plugin in use.
Check the vendor documentation for NetworkPolicy support.
Create a deny policy in a test namespace.
Test that traffic to the pod is blocked.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -iE "calico|cilium|flannel|weave"; kubectl run -n <test-ns> curl --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -m 3 <pod-ip>
tests.exp: The CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy. The test deny policy blocks the traffic.

tests.title: Check default deny network policies in every namespace
tests.obj: Finds namespaces where all pods can talk to all other pods.
steps: List NetworkPolicy objects for each namespace.
Find namespaces without a default deny policy for ingress and egress.
From a test pod, connect to a pod in another namespace.
Check that allow rules exist only for needed flows.
tests.ex: kubectl get networkpolicy -A; kubectl get ns -o name | while read n; do kubectl get networkpolicy -n ${n#namespace/} -o name | wc -l; done
tests.exp: Each namespace has default deny for ingress and egress. Allow rules cover only documented flows, and the cross-namespace test connection fails.

tests.title: Check egress rules to the Internet and to the control plane
tests.obj: Finds pods that can send data out of the cluster or reach node and control plane services.
steps: From a test pod, connect to an external host.
From the pod, connect to the API server and to node ports.
Review the egress rules for the namespace.
Check that DNS is the only egress allowed by default.
tests.ex: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -m 3 https://example.com; kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -k -m 3 https://kubernetes.default.svc/version
tests.exp: Egress is limited to named destinations. Pods without need cannot reach the Internet, the node ports or the API server.

tests.title: Find pods that use host networking
tests.obj: Finds pods that bypass network policy and reach services bound to the node loopback.
steps: List pods with hostNetwork set to true.
Ask the owner to justify each case.
Check that these pods are limited to system components such as the CNI.
From such a pod, try a connection to localhost services of the node.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.spec.hostNetwork==true) | .metadata.namespace+\"/\"+.metadata.name"
tests.exp: Only system components such as the CNI use host networking. Application pods use the pod network.

tests.title: Check encryption and mutual authentication between services
tests.obj: Finds service traffic in plaintext or with no caller identity inside the cluster.
steps: List the services and their ports.
Capture traffic between two test pods.
Check if a service mesh or application TLS gives mutual authentication.
Send a request to a service without a valid client identity.
tests.ex: istioctl x describe pod <pod> (if Istio); kubectl exec <pod> -- tcpdump -i any -A port <port>; curl -v http://<service>:<port>
tests.exp: Service-to-service traffic uses TLS with mutual authentication. A request with no valid identity is rejected.

tests.title: Check that internal services have no public route
tests.obj: Finds internal microservices that the ingress or a load balancer exposes by mistake.
steps: List all Ingress rules and public Services.
Map each route to a service and its owner.
From an outside network, request the paths of internal services.
Check that internal-only services use ClusterIP.
tests.ex: kubectl get ingress -A -o wide; kubectl get svc -A | grep LoadBalancer; curl -sI https://<public-host>/<internal-path>
tests.exp: Only intended services have public routes. Requests for internal paths fail from outside.

tests.title: Check Pod Security Admission labels on every namespace
tests.obj: Finds namespaces with no enforced pod security level.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List the pod-security labels of every namespace.
Find namespaces with no enforce label or with the privileged level.
Check that the audit and warn labels are set.
In a test namespace, create a pod that breaks the enforced level.
tests.ex: kubectl get ns --show-labels | grep -v pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce; kubectl run test --image=nginx --privileged -n <test-ns>
tests.exp: Each application namespace enforces the baseline level or better, and restricted where possible. The pod that breaks the level is rejected.

tests.title: Check that a policy engine enforces cluster rules beyond Pod Security
tests.obj: Finds clusters that depend on manual review for rules such as registries, labels and ingress settings.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List validating admission policies and admission webhooks.
Find the policy engine in use, such as Gatekeeper, Kyverno or Kubewarden.
Read the policy list and the mode of each policy.
Create a test object that breaks one policy.
tests.ex: kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy,validatingadmissionpolicybinding,validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations; kubectl get constrainttemplates; kubectl get clusterpolicies
tests.exp: Policies for privileged settings, allowed registries and required labels are active and set to deny. The test object is rejected.

tests.title: Check failure mode and scope of admission webhooks
tests.obj: Finds webhooks that fail open, skip namespaces, or let a user bypass policy.
steps: List each webhook with its failurePolicy, namespaceSelector and objectSelector.
Find webhooks with failurePolicy set to Ignore after the rollout phase.
Check which namespaces and objects the selectors exclude.
Check that users cannot add labels that exclude their pods.
tests.ex: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o yaml | grep -E "failurePolicy|namespaceSelector|objectSelector"
tests.exp: Production webhooks fail closed. Selectors exclude only system namespaces, and users cannot change labels to skip a policy.

tests.title: Check that new policies start in audit mode and move to enforce
tests.obj: Finds policies that stay in audit or warn mode and so block nothing.
steps: List the policies and the mode of each one.
Find policies in audit or warn mode longer than the rollout plan allows.
Review the audit results for current violations.
Check the plan and date to move to enforce.
tests.ex: kubectl get ns -o json | jq ".items[] | {n:.metadata.name, l:.metadata.labels}"; kubectl get constraints; kubectl get policyreport -A
tests.exp: Each policy has an owner and a date to move to deny. Open violations are fixed or have an exception on record.

tests.title: Check that admission decisions go to a central log
tests.obj: Finds policy denials and exceptions that no one sees.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: Create a denied object in a test namespace.
Look for the denial in the audit log and in the policy engine log.
Check that the central log system receives both.
Check that an alert exists for repeated denials.
tests.ex: kubectl logs -n <policy-ns> deploy/<policy-engine> | grep -i deny; query the central log platform for the denied request
tests.exp: Denials and policy changes appear in the central log with the user, object and rule. Repeated denials raise an alert.

tests.title: Check that RBAC is on and no other authorizer widens access
tests.obj: Finds clusters where the authorization mode is not RBAC or where a second authorizer adds hidden rights.
steps: Read the authorization-mode flag of the API server or the managed service setting.
List all configured authorizers, including webhook authorizers.
Make sure AlwaysAllow is not in the list.
Review the rights that each non-RBAC authorizer grants.
tests.ex: kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep authorization-mode; kube-bench run --targets master
tests.exp: The API server uses RBAC, and Node if needed. AlwaysAllow is off. Rights from each other authorizer are listed and reviewed.

tests.title: Find unneeded cluster-admin bindings
tests.obj: Finds users and service accounts with unlimited cluster rights.
steps: List all ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings that grant cluster-admin.
List the subjects of each binding.
Find service accounts and groups such as system:authenticated in these bindings.
Ask the owner to justify each subject.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.roleRef.name==\"cluster-admin\") | .subjects"
tests.exp: Only a few named break-glass or admin subjects hold cluster-admin. No service account or broad group has it.

tests.title: Find wildcard rules and wide built-in roles
tests.obj: Finds roles with verb or resource wildcards and use of the broad view and edit roles.
steps: List all Roles and ClusterRoles that use * in verbs, resources or apiGroups.
List the bindings to the built-in roles admin, edit and view.
Compare the granted rights to the needs of each subject.
Replace wide roles with narrow custom roles.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterroles,roles -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.rules[]? | (.verbs[]==\"*\") or (.resources[]?==\"*\")) | .metadata.name"; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user>
tests.exp: No custom role uses wildcards without a written reason. Built-in broad roles are bound only where the full rights are needed.

tests.title: Check who can read secrets through get, list or watch
tests.obj: Finds subjects that can read secret values, including by the list and watch verbs.
steps: List all roles with get, list or watch on secrets.
Find roles that give secrets access cluster-wide.
Check that the rights of each subject are scoped to named secrets where possible.
Test list on secrets with a low-rights account.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=<subject>; kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.rules[]? | .resources[]?==\"secrets\") | .metadata.name"
tests.exp: Only a few named subjects can get, list or watch secrets. Access is limited to the namespace and the secret names that the workload needs.

tests.title: Find escalate, bind, impersonate and node proxy rights
tests.obj: Finds rights that let a subject skip privilege checks, impersonate users, or reach the Kubelet API.
steps: List roles with the verbs escalate, bind or impersonate.
List roles with access to nodes/proxy.
List roles that can create pods in kube-system or create rolebindings.
Check that impersonation is limited to named resources.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.rules[]? | .verbs[]? | IN(\"escalate\",\"bind\",\"impersonate\")) | .metadata.name"; kubectl auth can-i get nodes/proxy --as=<subject>
tests.exp: Few trusted subjects hold escalate, bind, impersonate or nodes/proxy. Impersonation is limited to named users or groups.

tests.title: Check who can patch namespaces and change policy labels
tests.obj: Finds subjects that can edit namespace labels and so weaken Pod Security Admission or network policies.
pre: Do not run on production.
steps: List subjects with patch or update rights on namespaces.
In a test namespace, change the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label with a low-rights account.
Try to add a label that a NetworkPolicy selector uses.
Revert the labels.
tests.ex: kubectl auth can-i patch namespaces --as=<subject>; kubectl label ns <test-ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged --overwrite --as=<subject>
tests.exp: Only cluster administrators can change namespace labels. A policy rule blocks label changes that lower the Pod Security level.

tests.title: Review rights from Helm charts, operators and role aggregation
tests.obj: Finds third-party packages that install wide roles or extend built-in roles without notice.
steps: List ClusterRoles and ClusterRoleBindings created by Helm charts and operators.
Find roles with wildcard verbs or resources from these packages.
Check ClusterRoles that carry aggregation labels for admin, edit or view.
Compare the rights to the documented needs of the package.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterroles -l rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin=true; helm template <chart> | grep -B2 -A8 "kind: ClusterRole"
tests.exp: Each third-party role has only the rights its function needs. No package adds rights to admin, edit or view without review.

tests.title: Check that the default service account has no extra rights
tests.obj: Finds workloads that inherit API rights through the default service account of a namespace.
steps: List RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings for the default service account in each namespace.
Check the rights of the default service account.
Check that each workload uses its own service account.
Test a request from a pod with the default token.
tests.ex: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .name==\"default\" and .kind==\"ServiceAccount\")"; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default
tests.exp: The default service account has no bindings. Each workload that needs API access uses a dedicated service account with minimal rights.

tests.title: Check that elevated access is temporary and recorded
tests.obj: Finds standing admin access with no approval, expiry or record.
pre: Interview the cluster owner.
steps: Find the process to request elevated access for debug or one-off changes.
Check that grants expire without manual removal.
Check that each grant has a record of the approver and reason.
Make sure the API audit log shows the grant and use.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq ".items[] | {n:.metadata.name, c:.metadata.creationTimestamp}"; kubectl --as=<user> --as-group=<group> get pods
tests.exp: Admin access is time-bound, approved and logged. Day-to-day accounts have low rights and use impersonation or short-lived grants for admin work.

tests.title: Find secrets in ConfigMaps, manifests and pod specs
tests.obj: Finds credentials stored in objects with weaker access control than Secrets.
steps: Dump all ConfigMaps and pod specs.
Scan the output for passwords, tokens, keys and connection strings.
Scan the manifest and Helm repositories for the same values.
List each hit with its owner and the credential type.
tests.ex: kubectl get configmaps -A -o yaml | gitleaks detect --no-git --source - (or trufflehog); kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep -iE "password|token|secret|key"
tests.exp: ConfigMaps and pod specs hold no credentials. All credentials are in a secret store and are not in manifests or repositories.

tests.title: Check that secrets reach containers as files and not as env variables
tests.obj: Finds secrets exposed as environment variables, where debug output and crash dumps can leak them.
steps: List all env entries that use secretKeyRef or envFrom with a secretRef.
Check that each secret is mounted as a read-only volume instead.
Look at the process list and the debug endpoints of a sample pod for the env values.
Check the mount mode of secret volumes.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.spec.containers[].env[]?.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or .spec.containers[].envFrom[]?.secretRef) | .metadata.name"; kubectl exec <pod> -- env
tests.exp: Workloads read secrets from read-only mounted files or from an in-memory fetch. Secrets are not set in env variables or image layers.

tests.title: Check that Secrets are encrypted at rest in etcd
tests.obj: Finds clusters that store Secret objects in etcd in plaintext.
pre: Read access to etcd or the managed cluster settings.
steps: Read the encryption provider configuration of the API server or the managed service setting.
Check that a non-identity provider is first for secrets.
Read a test secret directly from etcd.
Check that existing secrets were rewritten after the change.
tests.ex: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/<ns>/<name> | hexdump -C | head; kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - (rewrite after change)
tests.exp: The etcd value of a test secret starts with the encryption provider prefix and shows no plaintext. Existing secrets are rewritten. Backups are encrypted.

tests.title: Check use of an external secret store and workload identity
tests.obj: Finds clusters that keep long-lived static credentials in Secret objects when a short-lived option exists.
steps: List the Secret objects of type Opaque and kubernetes.io/service-account-token.
Find static cloud or database credentials among them.
Check if workloads use an external secret operator or workload identity federation.
Check the age and rotation date of each credential.
tests.ex: kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=Opaque; kubectl get externalsecrets -A (if External Secrets Operator is in use); kubectl get secrets -A -o json | jq ".items[] | {n:.metadata.name, c:.metadata.creationTimestamp}"
tests.exp: Workloads get short-lived credentials from a managed vault or workload identity. Few static secrets remain and each has an owner and rotation date.

tests.title: Check rotation and lifetime of cluster and service account credentials
tests.obj: Finds long-lived tokens and certificates that stay valid after a leak.
steps: List secrets of type service-account-token and check their age.
Check that pods use projected tokens from the TokenRequest API with an expiry.
Check the validity period of client and serving certificates.
Check the rotation process and owner for each credential type.
tests.ex: kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token; kubectl create token <sa> --duration 10m; kubeadm certs check-expiration (self-managed)
tests.exp: Pods use short-lived projected tokens. No long-lived service account token Secrets exist without a written reason. Certificates rotate on a set schedule.

tests.title: Check that secret values do not reach logs or audit records
tests.obj: Finds secrets written to pod logs, central log platforms or API audit logs.
steps: Search pod logs and the central log platform for known test secret values.
Read the audit policy for rules on secrets and configmaps.
Check that these resources use the Metadata level only.
Check who can read pods/log and the log platform.
tests.ex: kubectl logs <pod> | grep -i "<test-secret>"; grep -B2 -A6 secrets /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
tests.exp: Secret values never appear in logs. The audit policy records secrets and configmaps at the Metadata level only.

tests.title: Scan container filesystems and images for stored secrets
tests.obj: Finds tokens, keys and passwords embedded in running containers or in the images that start them.
steps: List the images that run in the cluster.
Scan each image for secrets.
Scan the file system of a running container for keys and token files.
Check that found credentials were revoked.
tests.ex: trivy image --scanners secret <image>; trivy fs --scanners secret <path>; gitleaks detect --source <repo>
tests.exp: Images and running containers hold no embedded secrets. Any secret found is revoked and rotated.

tests.title: Check access paths and audit of the secret store itself
tests.obj: Finds secret managers with broad access and no record of who read which secret.
steps: List the principals that can read secrets in the external store.
Check that each workload can read only its own secrets.
Check that reads create audit records with the identity and source.
Make sure alerts fire for reads from an unexpected source.
tests.ex: Check the provider audit log for secret read events; vault audit list (HashiCorp Vault); aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetSecretValue
tests.exp: Each workload reads only its own secrets. Every read is recorded with identity and source, and unusual reads raise an alert.

tests.title: Check that containers run as a non-root user
tests.obj: Finds workloads that run as UID 0 and make a container breakout easier.
steps: List all pods with their runAsUser, runAsNonRoot and hostUsers settings.
Find containers that run as UID 0 or set no user.
Open a shell in a sample pod and run id.
Check if the image Dockerfile sets a USER instruction.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | {n:.metadata.name, sc:.spec.securityContext, c:[.spec.containers[].securityContext]}"; kubeaudit nonroot; trivy config .
tests.exp: All containers run as a non-root UID. The pod sets runAsNonRoot or runAsUser above 0, or uses user namespaces with hostUsers set to false.

tests.title: Check that containers drop all Linux capabilities
tests.obj: Finds containers that keep default or extra capabilities that help an attacker escape.
steps: List the capabilities added and dropped for each container.
Find containers that do not drop ALL.
Find containers that add capabilities such as SYS_ADMIN or NET_ADMIN.
Ask the owner to justify each added capability.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath="{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].securityContext.capabilities}{"\n"}{end}"; kubeaudit capabilities; docker run --cap-drop all --cap-add CHOWN alpine (local test)
tests.exp: Each container drops ALL capabilities. Added capabilities are few, documented, and limited to values the application needs.

tests.title: Check that privilege escalation is blocked in containers
tests.obj: Finds containers where setuid binaries can raise the process privileges.
steps: List allowPrivilegeEscalation for each container.
Find containers where the value is true or not set.
In a test pod, look for setuid binaries in the image.
Try to run a setuid binary to change the user.
tests.ex: kubeaudit privesc; kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation"; docker run --security-opt=no-new-privileges (local test)
tests.exp: Every container sets allowPrivilegeEscalation to false. The no_new_privs flag is active and setuid binaries do not raise privileges.

tests.title: Find privileged containers and host namespace use
tests.obj: Finds containers that break the isolation between the workload and the node.
steps: List containers with privileged set to true.
List pods that set hostPID, hostIPC or hostNetwork.
List hostPath volumes and mounts of the container runtime socket.
Ask the owner to justify each case.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | select(.spec.hostPID==true or .spec.hostIPC==true or .spec.hostNetwork==true)"; kubeaudit privileged
tests.exp: No application workload runs privileged, uses host namespaces, or mounts the runtime socket. Exceptions are system workloads with a written reason.

tests.title: Check that seccomp and a Linux security module are active
tests.obj: Finds workloads that run without the runtime syscall filter or mandatory access control.
steps: List the seccompProfile type for each pod and container.
Find workloads that use Unconfined or set no profile.
Check for AppArmor or SELinux settings on the workloads.
Check that the node enables the profile.
tests.ex: kubeaudit seccomp; kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[].spec.securityContext.seccompProfile"; docker info --format "{{.SecurityOptions}}"
tests.exp: Every workload sets seccompProfile to RuntimeDefault or Localhost. AppArmor or SELinux profiles are active where the node supports them.

tests.title: Check that the container root filesystem is read-only
tests.obj: Finds containers that let an attacker write tools or persistence files into the image layer.
steps: List readOnlyRootFilesystem for each container.
Find containers where the value is not true.
In a test pod, try to write a file to /bin and /tmp.
Check that writable paths use emptyDir volumes.
tests.ex: kubeaudit rootfs; kubectl exec <pod> -- touch /bin/test; docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp alpine (local test)
tests.exp: Containers set readOnlyRootFilesystem to true. Writes go only to named emptyDir or tmpfs volumes. A write to /bin fails.

tests.title: Check that pods mount service account tokens only when needed
tests.obj: Finds pods that hold an API token without need and so give an attacker API access.
steps: List pods that mount a service account token.
Find pods that use the default service account.
Check that pods without API use set automountServiceAccountToken to false.
From a test pod, send a request to the API with the token.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[] | {n:.metadata.name, a:.spec.automountServiceAccountToken, sa:.spec.serviceAccountName}"; kubeaudit sa; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>
tests.exp: Pods that do not call the Kubernetes API set automountServiceAccountToken to false. Each workload that needs the API has its own service account.

tests.title: Check that containers have CPU and memory limits
tests.obj: Finds workloads that can use all node resources and cause denial of service.
pre: Do not run the stress pod on production.
steps: List requests and limits for CPU and memory for each container.
Find containers with no limits.
Check for a LimitRange that sets defaults in each namespace.
In a test namespace, run a memory stress pod and watch the node.
tests.ex: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq ".items[].spec.containers[] | {n:.name, r:.resources}"; kubeaudit limits; kubectl get limitrange -A
tests.exp: Every container has CPU and memory limits. Each namespace has a LimitRange. A stress pod is stopped at its limit and does not harm other pods.

tests.title: Check namespace quotas on compute and object counts
tests.obj: Finds namespaces without aggregate limits that let one tenant exhaust the cluster.
pre: Do not run the over-quota request on production.
steps: List ResourceQuota objects for each namespace.
Find namespaces with no quota for CPU, memory and pod count.
Check that quotas also limit the number of services and PVCs.
Try to create pods above the quota in a test namespace.
tests.ex: kubectl get resourcequota -A; kubectl describe quota -n <ns>; kubectl create -f compute-resources.yaml --namespace=<test-ns>
tests.exp: Each tenant namespace has a ResourceQuota. A request above the quota is rejected by the API server.

tests.title: Check sandboxed runtimes for untrusted or multi-tenant workloads
tests.obj: Finds untrusted workloads that share the host kernel with no extra isolation.
steps: Identify workloads from different trust levels or tenants on the same nodes.
List the RuntimeClass objects in the cluster.
Check that untrusted workloads use a sandbox runtime such as gVisor or Kata Containers.
Check that the node pool of those workloads is separate.
tests.ex: kubectl get runtimeclass; kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath="{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.runtimeClassName}{"\n"}{end}"
tests.exp: Untrusted and multi-tenant workloads run in a sandbox runtime on separate nodes from high-value workloads.

tests.title: Check that nodes block unused kernel modules
tests.obj: Finds nodes where a container process can auto-load network protocol kernel modules.
steps: Read the modprobe configuration on a sample node.
Check that unused modules such as dccp and sctp are blocked.
Check if the node loads any of the blocked modules.
Repeat on each node pool.
tests.ex: cat /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf; lsmod | grep -E "dccp|sctp"
tests.exp: Unused protocol modules are blocked in the modprobe configuration and are not loaded on any node.

tests.title: Make sure remote administration uses a managed access point with MFA
tests.obj: Finds administration paths that are open to the internet or that need only a password.
pre: Written approval for scans and logins on the hosts in scope.
steps: Make a list of all remote administration methods, such as SSH, RDP, web consoles and VPN.
Scan the public ranges and the user networks for the ports of these methods.
Read the rules and the documentation of each method and its rationale.
Try to log in with a password only, with no second factor.
Make sure the administration traffic goes through a dedicated, managed interface.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV -p 22,23,80,443,3389,5985,5986,8443,8080 <range> ; ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no <user>@<host>
tests.exp: Remote administration is not reachable from the internet. Each method goes through a managed access point and needs multi-factor authentication.

tests.title: Check that all non-console administration uses strong cryptography
tests.obj: Finds Telnet, HTTP and other clear-text administration paths on servers and devices.
pre: Written approval for scans and traffic capture in scope.
steps: Scan the devices for administration ports and list the protocol of each.
Log in as an administrator and capture the traffic.
Look for passwords and commands in clear text in the capture.
Scan the encrypted administration services for protocol versions and algorithms.
Compare the result with the cryptography standard of the organization.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV -p 22,23,80,443,8443 --script ssh2-enum-algos,ssl-enum-ciphers <host> ; ssh-audit <host> ; tshark -i eth0 -Y "telnet || http.authorization"
tests.exp: All non-console administration uses encrypted protocols with strong algorithms. No clear-text administration port answers.

tests.title: Check SSH keys, host keys and key storage on managed systems
tests.obj: Finds shared, unprotected or never-changed SSH keys that give access to many systems.
pre: Read access to the systems in scope.
steps: List the authorized keys on a sample of servers and devices.
Match each key to an owner and a current need.
Look for private keys in home folders, scripts, repositories and backups.
Look at the permissions of the private key files.
Make sure keys of former staff and old systems are removed.
tests.ex: find / -name authorized_keys 2>/dev/null ; find / -name "id_*" -not -name "*.pub" 2>/dev/null ; ls -l ~/.ssh ; ssh-keygen -lf <key.pub>
tests.exp: Each authorized key has a current owner and need. No private key is in scripts, repositories or backups, and key files are not readable by other users.

tests.title: Review the VPN gateway for strong authentication and limited network access
tests.obj: Finds VPN services that give too much network access or accept weak login.
pre: Written approval for tests of the VPN gateway in scope.
steps: Scan the VPN gateway for open ports and look at the product and version.
Scan the gateway for protocol versions and algorithms.
Log in with a test account without the second factor.
Connect with a test account and scan the internal ranges.
Compare the reachable ranges with the access rights of that account.
tests.ex: nmap -sU -sT -p 500,4500,443,1194 -sV <vpn-ip> ; ike-scan <vpn-ip> ; testssl.sh <vpn-ip>:443 ; nmap -Pn -p- <internal-range> from the VPN client
tests.exp: The VPN uses current software and strong cryptography. It needs multi-factor authentication, and a user can reach only the ranges that the rights allow.

other: NIST SP 800-115 appendix lists IKE-Scan for remote access testing

tests.title: Check session timeout and the way to disable remote access fast
tests.obj: Finds administration sessions that stay open and remote access that cannot be stopped fast in an incident.
steps: Open an administration session and leave it idle.
Measure the time until the system ends the session.
Read the procedure to disable remote access for an account or a method.
Test the procedure on a test account and measure the time.
tests.ex: show line | include timeout ; grep -E "ClientAliveInterval|TMOUT" /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/profile ; time <disable-account-command>
tests.exp: Idle sessions end after the set time. The team can disable remote access within the time that the policy sets.

tests.title: Review the management plane of network devices for exposure and role limits
tests.obj: Finds routers, switches and appliances whose management interface is open to user networks.
pre: Written approval for scans of the devices in scope.
steps: Find the management addresses of routers, switches, firewalls and load balancers.
Scan those addresses from the user network, the server network and the internet.
Read the access lists on the management interfaces.
Look at the roles and accounts on each device.
Make sure each administrator has only the rights that the role needs.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV -p 22,23,80,443,161,830,8443 <mgmt-range> ; show running-config | section line|aaa|snmp|http ; show users
tests.exp: The management interfaces answer only from a dedicated management network. Each account has only the rights that its role needs.

tests.title: Check that network configurations are controlled, backed up and checked for change
tests.obj: Finds device and infrastructure configurations that change without approval or record.
steps: Get the stored configuration of a sample of devices.
Compare it with the running configuration.
Look for the change tickets of the differences.
Make sure the infrastructure code or the configuration store has access control and version history.
Make sure secrets are not stored in the infrastructure code.
tests.ex: diff <(ssh <device> show running-config) stored/<device>.cfg ; git log --stat -- network/ ; tfsec . or checkov -d .
tests.exp: Running configurations match the stored and approved ones. Each change has a ticket and a version record, and the code holds no secrets.

tests.title: Look for backups, dumps and state files on exposed hosts and shares
tests.obj: Finds backup archives, database dumps and configuration copies that anyone on the network can read.
pre: Written approval for logins and file listing on the hosts in scope.
steps: List the file shares, FTP and TFTP services, and storage services found by the port scan.
List the files that anonymous or low-rights users can read.
Look for archives, database dumps, configuration backups, state files and environment files.
Open a small sample of the files and look for secrets and personal data.
Write down each file, its location and the data that it holds.
tests.ex: smbmap -H <host> -u guest ; ftp -n <host> (anonymous) ; nmap --script ftp-anon,nfs-ls -p 21,2049 <host> ; find /srv /mnt \( -name "*.bak" -o -name "*.sql" -o -name "*.tar.gz" -o -name "*.tfstate" -o -name ".env" \) -perm -o+r
tests.exp: Low-rights users and outside users cannot read backups, dumps, state files or configuration copies. No such file sits on a public or shared location.

tests.title: Check that backups are encrypted, kept apart and reachable by few
tests.obj: Finds backups that an attacker on the production network can read or delete.
steps: Find the storage systems and the network paths that carry backups.
Make sure the backup data is encrypted in transit and at rest.
Make sure a copy is in a separate facility that is not with the operational system.
Look at which hosts and accounts can reach the backup storage on the network.
Try to read a backup from a normal server account.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV -p- <backup-server> ; showmount -e <backup-server> ; smbclient -L //<backup-server> -U <server-account> ; check rules for the backup zone
