tests.exp: Backups are encrypted and a copy is stored in a separate place. Only the backup system and backup admins can reach the backup storage.

tests.title: Check who can read the configuration backups of network devices
tests.obj: Finds configuration copies with passwords and community strings that many hosts can read.
steps: Find the systems that store configuration backups of routers, switches and firewalls.
Look at the protocol the devices use to send their backups.
Look at the permissions of the backup folder and the network services that serve it.
Search the backup files for clear-text secrets.
tests.ex: nmap -sU -p 69 --script tftp-enum <host> ; ls -l /srv/tftp /var/backups/network ; grep -rniE "password|secret|community" /srv/tftp
tests.exp: Device backups are stored on a protected system and sent over an encrypted channel. Only network administrators can read them and they hold no clear-text secrets.

tests.title: Look for vendor default accounts on network services and devices
tests.obj: Finds routers, switches, databases and services that still use vendor default passwords.
pre: Written approval to try logins on the services in scope.
Do not run on production without approval. Use the vendor list with a low rate to avoid lockouts.
steps: Use the service and version results to list devices and products with a login.
Get the default accounts for each product from the vendor documentation.
Try each default account on the login of the service, within the agreed rate.
Look at the system accounts of each product that the admins did not change.
Write down each default account that is active.
tests.ex: nmap -sV --script default-http-login-hunter,ftp-anon,mysql-empty-password -p <ports> <host> ; hydra -C defaults.txt <host> ssh
tests.exp: No vendor default account works. Default accounts are removed or disabled, or they have a unique strong password.

tests.title: Check the password policy settings on network systems and directories
tests.obj: Finds systems that accept short, common or breached passwords.
steps: Export the password policy of the directory and of each network device or service with local accounts.
Make sure the minimum length is 12 characters, or the maximum the system supports.
Make sure the system checks new passwords against a list of common and breached passwords.
Make sure the lockout limit is not more than 10 failed attempts, for at least 30 minutes.
Compare the policy with the written password policy.
tests.ex: Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy ; net accounts ; chage -l <user> ; grep -E "PASS_MIN_LEN|minlen" /etc/login.defs /etc/security/pwquality.conf
tests.exp: Passwords have at least 12 characters and are checked against a list of common and breached passwords. Failed logins lock the account after at most 10 tries.

tests.title: Test online password guessing and lockout on remote services
tests.obj: Finds remote services that let an attacker try many passwords with no limit.
pre: Written approval to try logins on the services in scope, with a test account.
Do not run on production. Lockout of real accounts can stop users from work.
steps: Pick remote services with a login, such as SSH, RDP, VPN and management interfaces.
Send repeated failed logins with a test account until the lockout limit.
Try one common password against many test accounts at a slow rate.
Make sure the service locks the account or slows the logins.
Make sure the service logs the failed logins.
tests.ex: hydra -l testuser -P short-list.txt -t 2 ssh://<host> ; medusa -h <host> -u testuser -P short-list.txt -M ssh
tests.exp: The service blocks or slows repeated failed logins from one source or against one account. Failed logins appear in the logs.

tests.title: Crack password hashes offline to find weak passwords
tests.obj: Finds accounts with passwords that an attacker can recover from hashes.
pre: The assessment plan says how the hashes are collected and who stores them.
Do not run on production. Crack the hashes offline on a protected system.
steps: Get the password hashes from the system or from a capture, as the plan says.
Set up the cracker with the rules of the password policy.
Run a dictionary attack, then a hybrid attack, then a limited brute force attack.
Count the accounts that the cracker recovers and the time it needed.
Report the accounts to the owner without the plain passwords. Delete the hashes and results at the end.
tests.ex: hashcat -m <mode> hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r rules/best64.rule ; john --wordlist=wordlist.txt hashes.txt
tests.exp: The cracker recovers no password in the agreed time. The hashes use a salted hash with a high work factor, such as Argon2id.

tests.title: Look for hard-coded passwords in device configurations and scripts
tests.obj: Finds passwords in clear text in configuration files, scripts and backups.
pre: Read access to the configurations and scripts in scope.
steps: Export the running and saved configurations of routers, switches and firewalls.
Collect the scripts and configuration files of servers and automation tools.
Search the files for passwords, community strings, keys and tokens.
Check that password fields hold hashes or encrypted values.
Write down each clear-text secret and where it is stored.
tests.ex: grep -rniE "password|passwd|secret|community|key" /etc /opt/scripts ; show running-config | include password|secret ; trufflehog filesystem <dir>
tests.exp: No file holds a clear-text secret. Secrets come from a secrets store, and stored passwords are hashed or encrypted.

tests.title: Find live hosts in scope and compare them with the inventory
tests.obj: Finds hosts that are on the network but not in the inventory.
pre: Written approval for scans of the address ranges in scope.
Do not run on production without a scan window and the approval of the network owner.
steps: Get the list of address ranges in scope and the asset inventory.
Run a host discovery scan from the external viewpoint.
Run a host discovery scan from the internal viewpoint.
Compare the live hosts with the inventory.
Write down each live host that has no owner or is not in the inventory.
tests.ex: nmap -sn -PE -PS22,80,443 -PA3389 -oA disc-ext <range> ; masscan <range> -p80,443,22 --rate 1000 -oL masscan.txt
tests.exp: Every live host is in the inventory and has an owner. No unknown host answers in the ranges in scope.

tests.title: Use passive discovery to find hosts, protocols and traffic relations
tests.obj: Finds hosts and flows that active scans miss, such as hosts that are off or filtered.
pre: Written approval for traffic capture on the segment.
steps: Connect the sniffer to a tap or a mirror port on the segment.
Capture traffic for a full business cycle.
List the IP and MAC addresses, the protocols and the talk pairs in the capture.
Compare the list with the inventory and the active scan results.
Write down each host, protocol or flow that is not in the inventory or the diagram.
tests.ex: tshark -i eth1 -a duration:3600 -w seg.pcap ; tshark -r seg.pcap -q -z conv,ip ; Wireshark: Statistics > Conversations
tests.exp: Every host, protocol and flow in the capture is in the inventory and the data-flow diagram. No unapproved protocol is in use.

tests.title: Detect rogue wired devices and trace them to the switch port
tests.obj: Finds unauthorized devices that connect to the wired network.
pre: Written approval from the network owner.
steps: Get the list of approved devices, vendors and operating systems.
Scan the network and list the MAC address vendor and the operating system of each host.
Mark each host that does not match the approved list.
Find the switch and the port of each marked host in the switch MAC table.
Make sure the network has a control that alerts on new devices.
tests.ex: nmap -O -sV --osscan-guess <range> -oX os.xml ; show mac address-table | include <mac> (on the switch)
tests.exp: Only approved devices are on the network. The network raises an alert when an unknown device connects.

tests.title: Scan all TCP ports and compare open ports with the approved list
tests.obj: Finds open ports that are not approved or that have no business need.
pre: Written approval for port scans of the hosts in scope.
Do not run on production without a scan window. Use a slow scan rate on old systems.
steps: Get the list of approved services, protocols and ports for each host.
Run a TCP scan of all 65535 ports from the external viewpoint.
Run the same scan from the internal viewpoint.
Compare the open ports with the approved list.
Write down each open port that is not approved.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sS -p- --min-rate 500 -T3 -oA tcp-all <host> ; masscan <range> -p0-65535 --rate 1000 -oL masscan.txt
tests.exp: Only approved ports are open. Each open port has a business reason, an owner and an approval.

other: NIST SP 800-115 section 4.2 (port and service identification)

tests.title: Scan UDP ports and look for unapproved UDP services
tests.obj: Finds UDP services, such as SNMP, TFTP and NTP, that are open without approval.
pre: Written approval for port scans of the hosts in scope.
Do not run on production without a scan window. UDP scans are slow and can load old devices.
steps: Run a UDP scan of the common service ports on each host in scope.
Run a version scan on the open and open-filtered ports.
Compare the result with the approved list of services.
Write down each UDP service that is not approved.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 200 -sV --version-intensity 0 -oA udp-top <host>
tests.exp: Only approved UDP services answer. Services that need no external access do not answer from untrusted networks.

other: NIST SP 800-115 section 4.2 (port and service identification)

tests.title: Identify services and versions and compare them with the approved list
tests.obj: Finds services that run another product or version than the inventory lists.
pre: Written approval for scans of the hosts in scope.
steps: Run a service and version scan on each open port.
Look at the banner of each service.
Compare the product and version with the inventory.
Do not trust the port number. Confirm the real service on each port.
Write down each service that is unknown, old or not supported.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p <ports> -oX svc.xml <host> ; nc -nv <host> <port> (banner grab)
tests.exp: Each port runs the approved service and a supported version. Banners do not give more detail than needed.

other: NIST SP 800-115 section 4.2 (service identification and banner grabbing)

tests.title: Compare the scan result with the firewall ruleset
tests.obj: Finds rules that do not work as the ruleset says, and paths that go around the firewall.
pre: Written approval for scans from the viewpoint of an untrusted network.
Do not run on production without a scan window.
steps: Get the firewall rules that apply to the hosts in scope.
Scan the hosts from an untrusted network with the normal scan type.
Scan again with other scan types, for example ACK, FIN and Xmas scans.
Compare the result with the rules.
Write down each port that answers and is not allowed by a rule.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -sS -sA -p- <host> ; nmap -Pn -sF -sX -p 1-1024 <host> ; Wireshark capture behind the firewall
tests.exp: The scan shows only the ports that the ruleset allows. Other scan types do not find more open ports.

other: NIST SP 800-115 sections 3.3 and 4.2 (ruleset review and alternate scan types)

tests.title: Make sure no insecure or clear-text service listens on the network
tests.obj: Finds Telnet, FTP, TFTP and similar services that send data or passwords in clear text.
pre: Written approval for scans of the hosts in scope.
steps: Use the open-port results of the TCP and UDP scans.
Look for Telnet, FTP, TFTP, rlogin, rsh and other clear-text services.
Look for clear-text management ports on routers, switches and servers.
Check if each insecure service has a documented business reason and extra controls.
tests.ex: nmap -Pn -p 21,23,69,79,512-514,5900 -sV <range> ; nmap -sU -p 69 --script tftp-enum <host>
tests.exp: No insecure service listens. A service that must stay has a written reason and extra controls, and it is not reachable from untrusted networks.

other: NIST SP 800-115 section 4.2 (insecure protocols such as TFTP and telnet)

tests.title: Make sure the origin server is not reachable without the CDN
tests.obj: Finds origin servers that accept traffic from the internet and not only from the CDN.
pre: Written approval for tests on the origin address.
steps: Find origin IP addresses from DNS history, certificate transparency logs and leaked headers.
Send a request directly to each origin IP address.
Send the request with the Host header of the public site.
Read the rules that restrict the origin to the CDN or load balancer.
tests.ex: curl -sk --resolve www.example.com:443:<origin-ip> https://www.example.com/ -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
tests.exp: The origin does not answer to the internet. It answers only to the CDN or load balancer address ranges.

other: WSTG-CONF-01 table row on load balancer and CDN configuration

tests.title: Check that discovery scans run on a schedule and find new devices
tests.obj: Finds networks where new devices and services appear and nobody sees them.
steps: Look at the schedule of discovery and port scans.
Make sure the scan covers all address ranges, including new ranges.
Add a test host and a test listener in a scan window.
Make sure the scan or the monitoring tool reports the new host and the new service.
tests.ex: cron: nmap -sS -p- -oX scan-$(date +%F).xml <range> ; ndiff scan-old.xml scan-new.xml
tests.exp: Scans run on a fixed schedule. New hosts and new open ports create an alert and a ticket.

tests.title: Search internet scan databases for exposed assets of the organization
tests.obj: Finds services, devices and certificates that outsiders can already see.
steps: List the domains, address ranges and organization names in scope.
Search internet scan databases for these names and ranges.
Compare the hosts and open services found with the inventory and the approved port list.
Write down each host or service that is not in the inventory.
tests.ex: shodan search net:<range> ; shodan host <ip> ; censys search "ip: <range>" ; compare with nmap -sV results
tests.exp: The databases show only approved hosts and services. Each exposed service is in the inventory and has an owner.

tests.title: Make sure name servers refuse DNS zone transfers from unknown hosts
tests.obj: Finds name servers that give the full list of hosts in a zone to anyone.
pre: Written approval for queries to the name servers in scope.
steps: List the name servers of each domain in scope.
Request a zone transfer from each name server.
Request a zone transfer again from a host that is not on the transfer allow list.
Write down each name server that returns zone data.
tests.ex: dig NS example.com +short ; dig AXFR example.com @ns1.example.com ; host -l example.com ns1.example.com ; dnsrecon -d example.com -t axfr
tests.exp: Each name server refuses zone transfers from unknown hosts. Only listed secondary servers can get a transfer.

tests.title: Check the DNS record inventory and the order of service decommissioning
tests.obj: Finds DNS records with no owner and processes that leave records for removed services.
steps: Get the DNS inventory that links each record to a resource and an owner.
Export all records of the zone and compare them with the inventory.
Look for CNAME, NS and MX records that point to removed or third-party services.
Read the decommission procedure. Make sure it removes the DNS record before the resource.
Make sure a scheduled scan checks that each record target still exists.
tests.ex: dig AXFR example.com @ns1 (if allowed) ; dnsrecon -d example.com -t std ; for h in $(cat cnames.txt); do dig +short $h; done
tests.exp: Every record has an owner and a live target. The procedure removes the DNS record first, and a scan finds dangling records at least weekly.

tests.title: Check CAA records and Certificate Transparency monitoring for the domains
tests.obj: Finds domains where any certificate authority can issue certificates and nobody sees new ones.
steps: Query the CAA records of each domain and subdomain.
Compare the listed certificate authorities with the ones the organization uses.
Search the Certificate Transparency logs for certificates of the domain.
Look for certificates that nobody in the organization asked for.
Make sure an alert exists for new certificates.
tests.ex: dig CAA example.com +short ; curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" | jq -r ".[].name_value" | sort -u
tests.exp: CAA records list only approved certificate authorities. Each logged certificate is known, and new certificates raise an alert.

tests.title: Make sure recursive resolvers do not answer queries from the internet
tests.obj: Finds open resolvers that attackers use for amplification and for cache attacks.
pre: Written approval for queries to the resolvers in scope.
Do not run on production with large query volumes.
steps: Find the hosts that answer on UDP and TCP port 53.
From an external host, send a query for a name that the server does not host.
Look at the response flags to see if the server resolves the name for you.
Make sure authoritative and recursive roles run on separate servers.
tests.ex: nmap -sU -sT -p 53 --script dns-recursion <range> ; dig @<ns-ip> www.example.net A +norecurse ; dig @<ns-ip> www.example.net A
tests.exp: Authoritative servers do not resolve names for outside hosts. Recursive resolvers answer only internal clients.

tests.title: Check DNSSEC signing of zones and validation on resolvers
tests.obj: Finds zones and resolvers with no data origin authentication of DNS answers.
pre: Written approval for queries to the name servers in scope.
steps: Query the DNSKEY and DS records of each public zone.
Check that answers from the authoritative servers carry signatures.
Send a query for a name with a bad signature to the internal resolver.
Look at the answer to see if the resolver rejects it.
tests.ex: dig DNSKEY example.com +dnssec +multi ; dig DS example.com +trace ; dig @<resolver> dnssec-failed.org A (expect SERVFAIL)
tests.exp: Public zones are signed and the chain of trust is complete. Resolvers check signatures and reject answers that fail.

tests.title: Look for internal host names and addresses in public DNS data
tests.obj: Finds public DNS data that shows the internal layout of the network.
steps: Query the public zone for all common record types.
Run reverse queries on the public address ranges.
Search passive DNS and certificate logs for the domain.
Look for internal host names, private addresses and test systems in the results.
tests.ex: dnsrecon -d example.com -t std,brt,rvl -r <range>/24 ; dig -x <ip> +short ; dig example.com ANY
tests.exp: Public DNS data holds no internal host names and no private addresses. Reverse records exist only for hosts that need them.

tests.title: Review the DoS inventory for single points of failure and scaling options
tests.obj: Finds components whose failure or overload stops the service, with no redundancy.
steps: Get the list of network and service components and their capacity.
Mark each component that has no second instance or no fail-over.
Look for the scaling options of each marked component.
Look for a plan for graceful degradation if a part fails.
Write down each single point of failure that has no plan.
tests.ex: Review of the architecture diagram and the load balancer and firewall fail-over configuration: show failover ; haproxy -c -f haproxy.cfg
tests.exp: No single point of failure stops the service without a plan. Each critical component has a fail-over or a scaling option.

tests.title: Test slow connection attacks against network edge services
tests.obj: Finds servers and load balancers that hold connections open for slow clients until they run out of slots.
pre: Written approval and a test window. Use a test system with the same settings.
Do not run on production.
steps: Read the minimum data rate, read timeout and connection timeout settings of the service.
Open many connections and send the request very slowly.
Look at the number of connections that the server keeps open.
Send a normal request from another host and look at the answer time.
tests.ex: slowhttptest -c 1000 -H -g -o slow -i 10 -r 200 -t GET -u https://<test-host>/ ; nmap --script http-slowloris-check <test-host>
tests.exp: The server closes slow connections after the set timeout. Normal requests still get an answer during the test.

tests.title: Check rate limits, connection limits and timeouts on edge devices
tests.obj: Finds edge devices that accept unlimited traffic, connections or sessions from one source.
steps: Read the configuration of firewalls, load balancers and proxies.
Look for a minimum ingress data rate with a read timeout.
Look for an absolute connection timeout and a maximum data rate.
Look for a total bandwidth limit and a load limit per resource.
Look at the session timeout for inactive sessions.
tests.ex: show running-config | include rate|limit|timeout ; nginx -T | grep -E "limit_req|limit_conn|timeout" ; httpd -M | grep reqtimeout
tests.exp: The edge devices set a minimum data rate, connection timeouts, rate limits and a load limit. Inactive sessions end after a set time.

tests.title: Test the connection limits of edge devices with a low-rate flood
tests.obj: Finds devices that fail when many half-open or new connections arrive.
pre: Written approval and a test window with the network owner and the ISP, if needed.
Use a test target behind the same device type and a rate that stays far below the link capacity.
Do not run on production.
steps: Read the connection table limit and the flood protection settings of the device.
Send TCP SYN packets to the test target at a low, agreed rate.
Raise the rate in small steps and stop at the agreed limit.
Look at the connection table, the CPU of the device and the answer time of normal requests.
tests.ex: hping3 -S -p 443 -i u1000 <test-target> ; show conn count ; Wireshark and the device monitoring
tests.exp: The device uses flood protection and keeps its connection table below the limit. Normal requests still work at the agreed test rate.

tests.title: Check the ISP and DDoS filtering service for coverage and capacity
tests.obj: Finds services that depend on one link and have no plan against volumetric attacks.
steps: Get the contract or service description of the ISP and of the DDoS filtering provider.
Look for more than one internet access point and for the bandwidth of each.
Look at the mitigation capacity and the layers that the provider covers.
Look at the contact and the escalation process for an attack.
Look at where the provider routes and inspects the traffic, and compare it with the privacy rules.
tests.ex: Review of contracts and runbooks. Check routes with: traceroute -n <service-ip> ; dig +short <service-name> to see if DNS points to the filter
tests.exp: The service has more than one access point and enough capacity. A filtering service covers the large attacks, and the escalation process is known.

tests.title: Check that DoS indicators are monitored and create alerts
tests.obj: Finds networks where a flood or resource drain goes unseen until the service fails.
pre: Written approval and a test window.
Do not run on production at high rates.
steps: Look at the monitoring of bandwidth, connection counts, CPU and memory on edge systems.
Look at the alert thresholds and the persons who get the alerts.
Send a small, safe burst of test traffic that crosses a threshold.
Look at the alert and the time until a responder sees it.
tests.ex: iperf3 -c <test-host> -t 30 -P 8 (test link only) ; check the monitoring dashboard and the alert mail
tests.exp: The monitoring shows the flood or drain and raises an alert to the responders in the agreed time.

tests.title: Check that auditd is installed, enabled and active from boot
tests.obj: Finds hosts where audit events are lost because the daemon or the early boot audit is missing.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the audit and audit plugin packages.
Look at the auditd service state.
Look at the kernel command line for audit=1 and the audit_backlog_limit value.
Read auditctl -s and look at the enabled flag and the lost counter.
tests.ex: rpm -q audit audispd-plugins || dpkg -l auditd ; systemctl is-enabled auditd ; systemctl is-active auditd ; cat /proc/cmdline ; auditctl -s
tests.exp: The audit packages are installed. The auditd service is enabled and active. The kernel starts auditing at boot with a backlog limit that meets the standard.

tests.title: Check auditd log size, disk-full actions and flush settings
tests.obj: Finds hosts that lose audit records or keep running with no audit when the disk is full.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/audit/auditd.conf.
Look at max_log_file, max_log_file_action, num_logs and space_left.
Look at space_left_action, admin_space_left_action, disk_full_action and disk_error_action.
Look at flush, freq, overflow_action, log_format, name_format and local_events.
Look at the size of the partition that holds /var/log/audit.
tests.ex: grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/audit/auditd.conf ; df -h /var/log/audit ; grep -E "active|direction|path|type" /etc/audit/plugins.d/*.conf
tests.exp: Audit logs have enough space and rotate by the standard. A full disk sends an alert and halts or changes to single user mode. The daemon writes to disk at the set rate.

tests.title: Check the owner and mode of audit logs, rules and tools
tests.obj: Finds audit logs, rule files or audit binaries that other users can read or change.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the files in /var/log/audit and the directory itself.
List /etc/audit/auditd.conf, /etc/audit/audit.rules and /etc/audit/rules.d.
List the audit binaries auditctl, auditd, ausearch, aureport, autrace and augenrules.
Make sure root owns each item and the modes are as strict as the standard sets.
tests.ex: stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /var/log/audit /var/log/audit/* /etc/audit/auditd.conf /etc/audit/rules.d/* /sbin/auditctl /sbin/auditd /sbin/ausearch /sbin/aureport /sbin/augenrules
tests.exp: Root owns audit logs, configuration and tools. Logs have a mode of 0600 or 0640, the log directory 0700 or 0750, and the binaries 0755 or stricter.

tests.title: Check the base audit rules, immutable mode and OSPP rule set
tests.obj: Finds hosts where an attacker can switch off or change audit rules after a login.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the rule files in /etc/audit/rules.d.
Look for the first rule that clears old rules and for the backlog and failure mode settings.
Look for the immutable flag -e 2 as the last rule.
Look for the rules that watch module loading and login UIDs.
Run auditctl -s and look at the enabled value.
tests.ex: cat /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules ; auditctl -s | grep enabled ; auditctl -l | head -20 ; grep -rn "loginuid_immutable\|^-e " /etc/audit/rules.d/
tests.exp: The rules start from a clean state, set a backlog limit and log failures to the system log. The configuration is immutable and the login UID cannot change.

tests.title: Check audit rules for identity files, logins, sudoers and cron
tests.obj: Finds hosts that do not record changes to accounts, logins, privilege rules and scheduled jobs.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run auditctl -l and compare the output with the rules in /etc/audit/rules.d.
Look for watches on /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/gshadow.
Look for watches on /etc/sudoers, /etc/sudoers.d, /etc/cron.d and /var/spool/cron.
Look for watches on login, session and failure logs such as faillock, lastlog, wtmp, btmp and utmp.
Change a test account and make sure ausearch shows the event.
tests.ex: auditctl -l | grep -E "passwd|shadow|group|gshadow|sudoers|cron|faillock|lastlog|wtmp|btmp|utmp|setuid" ; ausearch -k identity -ts recent ; augenrules --check
tests.exp: Each identity, login, sudoers and cron file has an audit watch with a key. A change to a watched file creates an audit record.

tests.title: Check audit rules for privileged commands and security tools
tests.obj: Finds hosts that do not record the use of setuid programs and of tools that change access rules.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Find the setuid and setgid programs on the local file systems.
Run auditctl -l and look for a rule for each program, with the auid filter and a key.
Look for rules on chacl, setfacl, chcon, restorecon, semanage and setsebool.
Look for rules on shutdown, reboot, poweroff and init.
Run one program and look for the record with ausearch.
tests.ex: find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) 2>/dev/null ; auditctl -l | grep -E "privileged|perm=x" ; ausearch -k privileged -ts recent
tests.exp: Each setuid and setgid program has an audit rule for user executions. The rules for access-change tools and for shutdown commands exist.

tests.title: Check audit rules for permission, owner and extended attribute changes
tests.obj: Finds hosts that do not record changes of file modes, owners and extended attributes.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run auditctl -l and compare the output with the rules in /etc/audit/rules.d.
Look for rules on chmod, fchmod, fchmodat, chown, fchown, fchownat and lchown.
Look for rules on setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr, removexattr and the related calls.
Look for the b32 and b64 variants and the auid filter.
Run chmod on a test file and look for the record with ausearch.
tests.ex: auditctl -l | grep -E "chmod|chown|setxattr|removexattr" ; touch /tmp/t && chmod 600 /tmp/t && ausearch -k perm_mod -ts recent
tests.exp: Rules exist for each permission, owner and attribute system call, for both 32-bit and 64-bit calls. A mode change creates an audit record.

tests.title: Check audit rules for failed access, file creation, change and deletion
tests.obj: Finds hosts that do not record denied access or the deletion and change of files by users.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run auditctl -l and compare the output with the rules in /etc/audit/rules.d.
Look for rules on open, openat, truncate and creat that log EACCES and EPERM results.
Look for rules on unlink, unlinkat, rename, renameat and rmdir.
Look for rules on file creation and change with success results.
Try to open a protected file as a test user and look for the record with ausearch.
tests.ex: auditctl -l | grep -E "EACCES|EPERM|unlink|rename|rmdir|creat|truncate" ; ausearch -k access -ts recent ; ausearch -k delete -ts recent
tests.exp: Failed access and file delete or change calls have audit rules. A denied access try creates an audit record with the user ID.

tests.title: Check audit rules for kernel modules, time, network and MAC changes
tests.obj: Finds hosts that do not record module loads, clock changes, network setting changes and policy changes.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for rules on init_module, finit_module and delete_module.
Look for rules on adjtimex, settimeofday, clock_settime and /etc/localtime.
Look for rules on sethostname, setdomainname and the network configuration files.
Look for watches on the SELinux or AppArmor policy directories.
Look for the audit rules for system shutdown, media export and journal files.
tests.ex: auditctl -l | grep -E "module|adjtimex|settimeofday|clock_settime|localtime|sethostname|/etc/hosts|selinux|apparmor|mount" ; ausearch -k modules -ts recent
tests.exp: Rules exist for module loads, clock changes, network identity changes and mandatory access control policy files. Each rule has a key.

tests.title: Check rsyslog and syslog-ng files, remote input and logging services
tests.obj: Finds log services that accept remote messages without a need or create log files that others can read.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the state of the rsyslog or syslog-ng service and make sure only one log service is active.
Read the rsyslog configuration for the FileCreateMode and the owner of the files.
Look for imtcp, imudp and the listen options. Make sure they are off unless the host is a log server.
Look for rules that log cron, authentication and kernel messages.
Look at the logwatch settings on a log server.
tests.ex: systemctl is-active rsyslog syslog-ng journald ; grep -rnE "FileCreateMode|imtcp|imudp|InputTCPServerRun|\$ModLoad" /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/ ; ss -ulnp | grep :514 ; grep -E "cron|authpriv" /etc/rsyslog.conf
tests.exp: One log service runs and logs the standard facilities. New log files have a mode of 0640 or stricter. Remote input is off, except on a named log server.

tests.title: Check journald storage, forwarding and journal file permissions
tests.obj: Finds hosts where the system journal is lost at restart or can be read by other users.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/systemd/journald.conf and the files under journald.conf.d.
Look at Storage, Compress and ForwardToSyslog.
List /var/log/journal and the journal files with their owner and mode.
Look at the owner and mode of the journalctl program.
Look for the journal-remote socket and make sure it is off unless the host receives logs.
tests.ex: systemd-analyze cat-config systemd/journald.conf ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /var/log/journal /var/log/journal/* /usr/bin/journalctl ; systemctl is-enabled systemd-journal-remote.socket
tests.exp: Storage is persistent. Journal files and the journal directory are owned by root and the systemd-journal group with restricted modes. The remote receive socket is off.

tests.title: Check /var/log file permissions and the log rotation setup
tests.obj: Finds log files that all users can read or change and logs that grow with no rotation.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the files and directories under /var/log with their owner, group and mode.
Look for log files with a mode wider than 0640 and for files with the wrong group.
Look at the package and the timer or cron job for logrotate.
Read /etc/logrotate.conf and look at the rotation count and the size limits.
tests.ex: find /var/log -type f \( -perm -0004 -o -perm -0020 \) -ls ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /var/log/messages /var/log/secure /var/log/syslog /var/log/auth.log /var/log/wtmp /var/log/btmp ; systemctl is-enabled logrotate.timer ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/logrotate.conf
tests.exp: Log files are not readable or changeable by other users. Root owns them and the modes follow the standard. Logrotate runs on a schedule.

tests.title: Check that firewalld runs with a default deny zone
tests.obj: Finds hosts where firewalld is off or the default zone accepts traffic that no rule allows.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the firewalld package and service state. Make sure only one firewall service is active.
Run firewall-cmd --get-default-zone and --list-all.
Look at the target of the zone. Make sure it is DROP or REJECT (default).
Look at the loopback rules and at the rate limit settings.
Look at the backend setting in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf.
tests.ex: systemctl is-active firewalld ; firewall-cmd --get-default-zone ; firewall-cmd --list-all ; firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --get-target ; grep FirewallBackend /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf
tests.exp: firewalld is active and enabled. The default zone target is DROP or REJECT. Loopback traffic is allowed only on the loopback interface.

tests.title: Check iptables and ip6tables default policies and rule persistence
tests.obj: Finds hosts where the INPUT, FORWARD or OUTPUT policy is ACCEPT and rules are lost after a restart.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run iptables -S and ip6tables -S.
Look at the default policy of INPUT and FORWARD. Look at the OUTPUT rules for new and established connections.
Look at the rules for the loopback interface and for loopback spoofing.
Look at the persistence service and the owner and mode of /etc/iptables.
Make sure the saved rules match the live rules.
tests.ex: iptables -S ; ip6tables -S ; iptables -L -v -n ; systemctl is-enabled iptables ip6tables netfilter-persistent ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/iptables /etc/sysconfig/iptables
tests.exp: The INPUT and FORWARD policies are DROP. Only the needed outbound and established traffic is allowed. Rules for both IPv4 and IPv6 persist after a restart.

tests.title: Check nftables tables, base chains and default deny policy
tests.obj: Finds hosts where nftables has no base chains or accepts traffic by default.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run nft list ruleset.
Look for a table and base chains for input, forward and output.
Look at the policy of each base chain. Look for the loopback and established rules.
Read the saved ruleset in /etc/nftables and make sure the service loads it at boot.
Look at the owner and mode of /etc/nftables.
tests.ex: nft list ruleset ; systemctl is-enabled nftables ; grep -rn "include" /etc/nftables.conf ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/nftables /etc/nftables.conf
tests.exp: Base chains for input, forward and output exist. The input and forward policy is drop. The ruleset loads at boot and only root can change the files.

tests.title: Check UFW and SuSEfirewall2 state and default policy
tests.obj: Finds hosts where the front-end firewall is installed but not active, or allows traffic by default.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run ufw status verbose.
Look at the default incoming, outgoing and routed policies.
Look for the loopback rules and the rate limit rule for SSH.
On SUSE hosts, look at the SuSEfirewall2 package, service and DoS protection settings.
Make sure no second firewall service is active.
tests.ex: ufw status verbose ; grep -E "^DEFAULT" /etc/default/ufw ; systemctl is-enabled ufw SuSEfirewall2 ; grep FW_PROTECT_FROM_INT /etc/sysconfig/SuSEfirewall2
tests.exp: The firewall service is active. Incoming and routed policy is deny. Outgoing policy follows the standard. Loopback rules exist.

tests.title: Check IPsec packages, tunnels and configuration file permissions
tests.obj: Finds IPsec tunnels that no one approved or secret files that other users can read.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the libreswan or strongswan package.
List the active tunnels with ipsec status.
Compare each tunnel with the approved tunnel list.
List /etc/ipsec.conf, /etc/ipsec.secrets and /etc/ipsec.d with owner and mode.
tests.ex: rpm -q libreswan strongswan ; ipsec status ; ipsec trafficstatus ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/ipsec.conf /etc/ipsec.secrets /etc/ipsec.d
tests.exp: Every tunnel is on the approved list. Root owns the IPsec files and the secrets file has a mode of 0600.

tests.title: Check host network settings: DHCP, DDNS, zeroconf, sniffing and DNS mode
tests.obj: Finds hosts with automatic network features that an attacker on the LAN can use.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the interfaces and look for the promiscuous flag.
Look at DHCP client options in /etc/dhcp/dhclient.conf and at the use of static addresses.
Look for zeroconf, DDNS updates and wireless or Bluetooth interfaces that the role does not need.
Read the name resolution and NetworkManager DNS mode settings.
Look at the permissions to change network settings with nmcli.
tests.ex: ip -d link | grep -i promisc ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/dhcp/dhclient.conf ; grep -r NOZEROCONF /etc/sysconfig/network ; nmcli radio ; grep dns /etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf ; nmcli general permissions
tests.exp: No interface is in promiscuous mode. Zeroconf and DDNS are off. Unused wireless and Bluetooth interfaces are off. Only approved users can change network settings.

tests.title: Check the IPv4 sysctl settings for routing, redirects and spoofing
tests.obj: Finds hosts that act as routers, accept redirects or source routes, or skip reverse path checks.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the live values with sysctl for net.ipv4.conf.all, net.ipv4.conf.default and net.ipv4.
Look at ip_forward, accept_redirects, send_redirects, secure_redirects and accept_source_route.
Look at rp_filter, log_martians, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts and tcp_syncookies.
Look at the files under /etc/sysctl.d and /etc/sysctl.conf. Make sure the values stay after a restart.
tests.ex: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts ; sysctl --system | grep -i ipv4
tests.exp: Forwarding, redirects and source routing are off unless the host is a router. Reverse path filtering, martian logging, SYN cookies and the broadcast ping filter are on. The values persist.

tests.title: Check the IPv6 sysctl settings and the IPv6 interface plan
tests.obj: Finds hosts that accept router advertisements, redirects or source routes, or that run IPv6 with no plan.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the live values of net.ipv6.conf.all and net.ipv6.conf.default with sysctl.
Look at accept_ra, accept_redirects, accept_source_route, forwarding, autoconf and max_addresses.
Look at disable_ipv6 and compare it with the plan: IPv6 in use or IPv6 off.
Look at the address, gateway and privacy extension settings of the network manager.
tests.ex: sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -E "net.ipv6.conf.(all|default).(accept_ra|accept_redirects|accept_source_route|forwarding|autoconf|disable_ipv6|max_addresses)" ; ip -6 addr ; nmcli -f ipv6 connection show <name>
tests.exp: Router advertisements, redirects and source routes are off unless the host needs them. If the network does not use IPv6, IPv6 is off. Values persist after a restart.

tests.title: Check kernel and filesystem sysctl hardening values
tests.obj: Finds hosts that leak kernel addresses, allow unsafe debug features or lack link and file protections.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the values with sysctl: kernel.kptr_restrict, kernel.dmesg_restrict, kernel.randomize_va_space and kernel.yama.ptrace_scope.
Read kernel.kexec_load_disabled, kernel.sysrq, kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled and net.core.bpf_jit_harden.
Read kernel.perf_event_paranoid, user.max_user_namespaces and vm.mmap_min_addr.
Read fs.protected_symlinks, fs.protected_hardlinks, fs.protected_fifos, fs.protected_regular and fs.suid_dumpable.
Look at the owner and mode of /etc/sysctl.d and make sure the values persist.
tests.ex: sysctl kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.dmesg_restrict kernel.randomize_va_space kernel.yama.ptrace_scope kernel.kexec_load_disabled kernel.sysrq kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled net.core.bpf_jit_harden kernel.perf_event_paranoid vm.mmap_min_addr fs.protected_symlinks fs.suid_dumpable ; stat -c "%U:%G %a" /etc/sysctl.d
tests.exp: Values are at least as strict as the rule values: for example kptr_restrict 1, randomize_va_space 2, suid_dumpable 0, protected_symlinks 1 and sysrq 0. Root owns /etc/sysctl.d.

tests.title: Check core dump storage and execution protection settings
tests.obj: Finds hosts that write process memory to disk, where it can expose keys and passwords.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/security/limits.conf and limits.d for the core limit of users.
Read /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and look at Storage and ProcessSizeMax.
Look at the state of systemd-coredump and at kernel.core_pattern.
Look at the daemon umask and at the BIOS or CPU no-execute setting.
tests.ex: grep -rE "^\*.*core" /etc/security/limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/ ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/systemd/coredump.conf ; sysctl kernel.core_pattern fs.suid_dumpable ; systemctl is-enabled systemd-coredump.socket ; grep umask /etc/sysconfig/init
tests.exp: Core dumps are off for users or are not stored. The core pattern does not write files. The no-execute feature is on.

tests.title: Check that unneeded kernel modules cannot load
tests.obj: Finds hosts that can load rare network, wireless, file system and media modules that add attack surface.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Find the modprobe files that set install lines or blacklist entries.
Look for the modules atm, can, dccp, firewire-core, rds, sctp and tipc.
Look for the file system modules cramfs, freevxfs, hfs, hfsplus, jffs2, squashfs, udf, vfat and usb-storage.
Look for the wireless, bluetooth and uvcvideo modules on servers.
Run lsmod. Try modprobe for one module and make sure it does not load.
tests.ex: grep -rE "install .* /bin/(true|false)|blacklist" /etc/modprobe.d/ ; for m in dccp sctp rds tipc cramfs squashfs udf usb-storage; do modprobe -n -v $m; done ; lsmod | grep -E "dccp|sctp|rds|tipc|cramfs|squashfs|udf|usb_storage"
tests.exp: The modules that the host role does not need cannot load. Each one is blacklisted or has an install line that runs /bin/false. lsmod does not list them.

tests.title: Check the kernel command line for mitigation and memory hardening options
tests.obj: Finds hosts that boot without CPU flaw mitigations or kernel memory protections.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /proc/cmdline and the default kernel arguments in /etc/default/grub.
Look for pti, spectre_v2, spec_store_bypass_disable, l1tf, mds, mitigations and nosmep or nosmap (must be absent).
Look for slab_nomerge, init_on_alloc, init_on_free, page_alloc.shuffle and vsyscall.
Look for audit=1 and the debug-shell argument (must be absent).
Read the mitigation status files under /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities.
tests.ex: cat /proc/cmdline ; grep GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX /etc/default/grub ; grep -r . /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/ ; grubby --info=ALL | grep args
tests.exp: The command line has the mitigation and memory options that the standard lists and none of the options that switch protections off. The CPU status files show mitigations.

tests.title: Check the kernel build options for hardening
tests.obj: Finds kernels that were built without memory protection, module signing and attack surface reduction.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Find the kernel config file for the running kernel.
Look for CONFIG_MODULE_SIG, CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE, CONFIG_STRICT_KERNEL_RWX and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY.
Look for CONFIG_STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG, CONFIG_FORTIFY_SOURCE, CONFIG_RANDOMIZE_BASE and CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED.
Look for CONFIG_DEBUG_FS, CONFIG_DEVKMEM, CONFIG_ACPI_CUSTOM_METHOD and CONFIG_IA32_EMULATION (should be off where not needed).
Compare the result with the build standard of the organization.
tests.ex: zcat /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null || cat /boot/config-$(uname -r) | grep -E "CONFIG_(MODULE_SIG|STRICT_KERNEL_RWX|HARDENED_USERCOPY|STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG|FORTIFY_SOURCE|RANDOMIZE_BASE|DEBUG_FS|DEVKMEM|SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED)="
tests.exp: The kernel config enables the memory protections, signing and randomization options of the standard. Debug and legacy options are off.

tests.title: Check the owner and mode of account files and their backups
tests.obj: Finds password and group files that other users can read or change.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, /etc/gshadow and /etc/shells.
List the backup files with a dash suffix, such as /etc/shadow-.
List /etc/security/opasswd and opasswd.old.
Make sure root owns the files and the modes are as strict as the standard sets.
tests.ex: stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/group /etc/gshadow /etc/shells /etc/passwd- /etc/shadow- /etc/group- /etc/gshadow- /etc/security/opasswd
tests.exp: Root owns all account files. /etc/passwd and /etc/group have a mode of 0644 or stricter. Shadow files and password history have a mode of 0000 or 0640 at most.

tests.title: Find world-writable, unowned and unauthorized setuid files
tests.obj: Finds files that any user can change, files without an owner and setuid programs that are not approved.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Find world-writable files on the local file systems.
Find world-writable directories without the sticky bit.
Find files and directories with no owner or no group.
Find setuid and setgid files and compare them with the approved list.
tests.ex: find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -ls ; find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 -ls ; find / -xdev \( -nouser -o -nogroup \) -ls ; find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -ls
tests.exp: No file is world-writable. Each world-writable directory has the sticky bit. No file lacks an owner or a group. Only approved programs have setuid or setgid.

tests.title: Check ownership and mode of system binaries, libraries and boot map files
tests.obj: Finds system programs and libraries that non-root users can replace.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the files in /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/local/bin and /usr/local/sbin with their owner and mode.
List the files in /lib, /lib64, /usr/lib and /usr/lib64.
Find files with a group-write or world-write bit and files not owned by root.
List System.map, /etc/crypttab and the sysconfig files for sshd.
tests.ex: find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin /lib /lib64 /usr/lib /usr/lib64 \( -perm /022 -o ! -user root \) -ls ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /boot/System.map-* /etc/crypttab
tests.exp: Root owns all system programs and libraries. None has a group-write or world-write bit. System.map and crypttab have a mode of 0600 or 0644 and are owned by root.

tests.title: Check mount options nodev, nosuid and noexec on partitions
tests.obj: Finds partitions where users can run programs, create devices or use setuid files.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/fstab and the live mounts with findmnt.
Look at /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /home, /boot, /var and /var/log and /var/log/audit.
Make sure each one has nodev, nosuid and noexec where the role allows.
Look at the mount options of removable media and of remote file systems (NFS, SMB).
Look at hidepid on /proc and at the quota options on /home.
tests.ex: findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm /home /boot /var /var/log /var/log/audit /proc ; grep -vE "^#" /etc/fstab ; mount | grep -E "nfs|cifs"
tests.exp: Each partition has the options that the standard lists, at least nodev and nosuid, and noexec on /tmp, /var/tmp and /dev/shm. Remote and removable file systems use nosuid, nodev and noexec.

tests.title: Check separate partitions and disk encryption for data and logs
tests.obj: Finds hosts where a full or abused directory can stop the system, or where data on disk is not encrypted.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the mounts with lsblk and findmnt.
Look for separate partitions for /boot, /home, /tmp, /var, /var/tmp, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /srv, /opt, /usr and /dev/shm.
Check if /tmp is a systemd tmp.mount unit or a partition.
Look for encrypted volumes with cryptsetup.
tests.ex: lsblk -f ; findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE /boot /home /tmp /var /var/tmp /var/log /var/log/audit /srv /opt ; systemctl is-enabled tmp.mount ; cryptsetup status <name>
tests.exp: The directories that the standard names are on separate partitions. Data volumes are encrypted at rest.

tests.title: Check that USB storage, automount and BIOS boot options are limited
tests.obj: Finds hosts that mount removable media on their own or boot from an unapproved device.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the autofs package and service.
Look at the usb-storage module and the nousb kernel argument.
Look at the udisks and desktop automount settings.
Read the firmware settings for boot devices and the firmware password.
tests.ex: systemctl is-enabled autofs ; modprobe -n -v usb-storage ; grep -o "nousb" /proc/cmdline ; lsmod | grep usb_storage
tests.exp: Automount is off. USB storage is blocked on hosts that do not need it. Boot from removable media is off and the firmware has a password.

tests.title: Check bootloader password, file permissions and recovery options
tests.obj: Finds hosts where a person with console access can change boot options or start a root shell.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /boot/grub2/grub.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/<vendor>/grub.cfg and the user.cfg file.
Look for the superuser line and the password hash. Make sure the hash is PBKDF2.
List the owner and mode of grub.cfg and user.cfg.
Look for the recovery menu entries and for the removable media boot option.
Look at the zipl bootmap on s390 systems if they are in scope.
tests.ex: grep -E "set superusers|password_pbkdf2" /boot/grub2/grub.cfg /boot/grub2/user.cfg /boot/efi/EFI/*/user.cfg ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /boot/grub2/grub.cfg /boot/grub2/user.cfg /boot/efi/EFI/*/grub.cfg ; grep -c "recovery" /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
tests.exp: The bootloader needs a superuser and a hashed password to edit boot entries. Root owns the grub files and the mode is 0600 or 0700 as the standard says. Recovery entries are off.

tests.title: Check that UEFI Secure Boot is on
tests.obj: Finds hosts that start unsigned boot components.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run mokutil --sb-state or read the firmware setting.
Look at the kernel messages for the Secure Boot line.
Look at the list of enrolled keys.
tests.ex: mokutil --sb-state ; dmesg | grep -i "secure boot" ; bootctl status | grep -i secure
tests.exp: Secure Boot is enabled and the host starts only signed boot components.

tests.title: Check that SELinux is enforcing with the targeted policy
tests.obj: Finds hosts where mandatory access control is off or lets daemons run unconfined.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run getenforce and sestatus.
Read /etc/selinux/config for SELINUX and SELINUXTYPE.
Look at the kernel command line for selinux=0 or enforcing=0.
List unconfined processes and unlabeled device files.
Look at the SELinux user mappings for logins.
tests.ex: getenforce ; sestatus ; grep -E "^SELINUX" /etc/selinux/config ; grep -E "selinux=0|enforcing=0" /proc/cmdline ; ps -eZ | grep unconfined_service_t ; semanage login -l
tests.exp: SELinux runs in enforcing mode with the targeted policy. No daemon runs unconfined and no device file is unlabeled. The SELinux packages are installed and troubleshooting tools are removed.

tests.title: Check that risky SELinux booleans are off
tests.obj: Finds SELinux booleans that give daemons more rights than the default policy.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List all booleans with getsebool -a.
Compare the on booleans with the list of rules in the tool check references.
Find each boolean that is on and is not in the approved list.
Check the need and the owner of each exception.
tests.ex: getsebool -a | grep -- "--> on" ; semanage boolean -l -C
tests.exp: The booleans that the standard names as risky are off. Each boolean that is on has a written need.

tests.title: Check that AppArmor is loaded and its profiles are enforced
tests.obj: Finds hosts where profiles are missing or are only in complain mode.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run aa-status.
Look at the number of profiles in enforce, complain and unconfined mode.
Look for the AppArmor kernel argument and packages.
Look at the pam_apparmor module.
tests.ex: aa-status ; cat /sys/module/apparmor/parameters/enabled ; grep apparmor /proc/cmdline ; dpkg -l apparmor apparmor-utils libpam-apparmor
tests.exp: AppArmor is on. All profiles are in enforce mode. The packages are installed.

tests.title: Check desktop login, screen lock and remote access settings
tests.obj: Finds desktop hosts that allow guest login, automatic login, unlocked screens or open remote desktops.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/gdm/custom.conf and /etc/dconf/db for the lock, idle and login settings.
Look at AutomaticLogin, TimedLogin, guest login and XDMCP.
Look at the idle delay, the lock delay and the settings locks.
Look at automount, autorun, remote access encryption and the user list.
Look for X server packages on hosts that do not need a desktop.
tests.ex: grep -rE "AutomaticLogin|TimedLogin|Enable=" /etc/gdm/custom.conf ; dconf dump /org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/ ; gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay ; systemctl get-default ; rpm -q gdm xorg-x11-server-common
tests.exp: Automatic login, guest login and XDMCP are off. The screen locks after idle time and users cannot change the lock settings. Servers have no desktop.

tests.title: Check that PAM locks accounts after repeated failed logins
tests.obj: Finds hosts where online password guessing is not slowed or stopped by an account lockout.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Open the PAM files /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth, or the files that the distribution uses.
Look for the pam_faillock module in the auth section, before and after pam_unix.
Read /etc/security/faillock.conf for the deny, fail_interval and unlock_time values.
Look at the lockout of the root account and at the directory that stores the failure records.
Try wrong passwords on a test account until the limit. Make sure the account locks and the lockout is logged.
tests.ex: grep -rE "pam_faillock|pam_tally2|pam_faildelay" /etc/pam.d/ ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/security/faillock.conf ; faillock --user testuser ; grep FAIL_DELAY /etc/login.defs
tests.exp: The pam_faillock module is active in auth. The deny, interval and unlock values meet the organization standard. Lockouts are logged and persist after a restart.

tests.title: Check that PAM enforces password complexity rules
tests.obj: Finds hosts that accept short, simple or dictionary passwords.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Make sure the pam_pwquality package is installed and the module is in the password stack.
Read /etc/security/pwquality.conf and the options in /etc/pam.d/system-auth and password-auth.
Look at minlen, minclass, the credit values, difok, maxrepeat, maxsequence and dictcheck.
Look for enforce_for_root and the retry limit.
Try to set a short or common password on a test account. Make sure the system refuses it.
tests.ex: rpm -q libpwquality || dpkg -l libpam-pwquality ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/security/pwquality.conf ; grep -r pwquality /etc/pam.d/ ; grep PASS_MIN_LEN /etc/login.defs
tests.exp: pam_pwquality is active for all password changes. Minimum length, character classes and dictionary checks meet the organization standard. The rules also apply to root.

tests.title: Check password hashing, password history and PAM module order
tests.obj: Finds weak stored hashes, password reuse and PAM stacks that skip the required modules.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the password lines in the PAM files and look for pam_unix options such as sha512, yescrypt, rounds and use_authtok.
Look at ENCRYPT_METHOD and the rounds or cost values in /etc/login.defs and /etc/libuser.conf.
Look for pam_pwhistory with the remember option, and for the same setting for root.
Look at the authselect profile or the PAM files for pam_wheel on su and for pam_namespace.
Make sure all password hashes in /etc/shadow use the approved algorithm.
tests.ex: grep -rE "pam_unix|pam_pwhistory|pam_wheel|pam_namespace" /etc/pam.d/ ; grep -E "ENCRYPT_METHOD|SHA_CRYPT|YESCRYPT" /etc/login.defs ; authselect current ; awk -F: '$2 ~ /^\$/ {print $1, substr($2,1,3)}' /etc/shadow
tests.exp: Passwords use the approved hash with enough rounds. The history keeps the number of old passwords that the standard sets, also for root. su is limited to a wheel group.

tests.title: Check password aging and account expiration settings
tests.obj: Finds accounts with passwords that never expire, never warn or stay active after long inactivity.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS and PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs.
Read the default inactivity period with useradd -D.
List the aging values of the existing accounts with chage.
Look at emergency and temporary accounts for an expiration date.
Find accounts with a last change date in the future.
tests.ex: grep -E "^PASS_(MAX|MIN|WARN)" /etc/login.defs ; useradd -D | grep INACTIVE ; chage -l <user> ; awk -F: '{print $1,$3,$4,$5,$7}' /etc/shadow
tests.exp: New and existing accounts follow the aging limits of the organization standard. Temporary accounts have an end date. No last change date is in the future.

tests.title: Check local accounts for duplicates, empty passwords and root misuse
tests.obj: Finds shared identifiers, empty passwords, extra UID 0 accounts and weak root controls.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List accounts with an empty password field in /etc/shadow.
List accounts with UID 0 and groups with GID 0. Only root may appear.
Look for duplicate user names, group names, UIDs and GIDs.
Look for legacy "+" NIS entries in passwd, group and shadow.
Look for .rhosts, .netrc and .forward files and for system accounts with a shell or an unlocked password.
tests.ex: awk -F: '($2==""){print $1}' /etc/shadow ; awk -F: '($3==0){print $1}' /etc/passwd ; getent passwd | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -d ; grep "^+" /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/shadow ; find /home /root -name ".rhosts" -o -name ".netrc" -o -name ".forward"
tests.exp: No account has an empty password. Only root has UID 0 and GID 0. All names and IDs are unique. System accounts are locked and have no login shell.

tests.title: Check user session limits, umask, home directories and root PATH
tests.obj: Finds loose default file modes, open home directories, unsafe root paths and sessions that never end.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the umask value in /etc/login.defs, /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc and the PAM umask setting.
Read the TMOUT value and the limits for concurrent logins in /etc/security/limits.conf.
Look at the owner and mode of each interactive home directory and of the files in it.
Look at the initialization files and the shell history for wrong owners and wide modes.
Print the PATH of root. Look for a dot, an empty entry or a writable directory.
tests.ex: grep -rn umask /etc/login.defs /etc/profile /etc/profile.d /etc/bashrc ; grep -rn TMOUT /etc/profile.d /etc/profile ; grep maxlogins /etc/security/limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/ ; stat -c "%U %a %n" /home/* ; sudo -i sh -c 'echo $PATH'
tests.exp: The umask blocks access by other users. Idle sessions end after the set time. Home directories have a mode of 0750 or stricter and the right owner. Root PATH has only safe directories.

tests.title: Check the login warning banners and the files that hold them
tests.obj: Finds hosts that show no legal notice or let ordinary users change the banner text.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/issue, /etc/issue.net and /etc/motd.
Compare the text with the banner text of the organization.
Look at the owner, group and mode of the three files.
Make sure the SSH daemon and the graphical login show the same banner.
tests.ex: cat /etc/issue /etc/issue.net /etc/motd ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/issue /etc/issue.net /etc/motd ; sshd -T | grep -i banner ; dconf read /org/gnome/login-screen/banner-message-text
tests.exp: The banner files hold the approved text. Root owns the files and the mode is 0644 or stricter. Each remote and local login path shows the banner.

tests.title: Check console access controls, Ctrl-Alt-Del and session lock tools
tests.obj: Finds hosts where a person at the console can reboot, skip authentication or avoid the screen lock.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the systemd target for Ctrl-Alt-Del and its burst action.
Read the rescue and emergency service files and make sure they need a password.
Look for the debug-shell service and for interactive boot options.
Look for tmux, screen or vlock settings that lock the session after inactivity.
Read the idle session settings of logind.
tests.ex: systemctl status ctrl-alt-del.target ; grep -E "ExecStart" /usr/lib/systemd/system/rescue.service /usr/lib/systemd/system/emergency.service ; systemctl is-enabled debug-shell.service ; grep -r "lock-" /etc/tmux.conf ; grep StopIdleSessionSec /etc/systemd/logind.conf
tests.exp: Ctrl-Alt-Del does not reboot the host. Single user and emergency modes need a password. The debug shell is off and idle sessions lock or end.

tests.title: Check smart card login settings for PAM and SSSD
tests.obj: Finds hosts that claim multifactor login but do not check the card certificate chain or revocation status.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the opensc, pcsc-lite and pcscd packages and services.
Read the PAM files and look for the smart card option in the auth stack.
Read the card driver and CA settings of opensc and the NSS database.
Look at the certificate status check and the CRL cache settings.
Try a login with a card from an unknown CA. Make sure the login fails.
tests.ex: rpm -q opensc pcsc-lite ; systemctl is-enabled pcscd.socket ; grep -rE "pam_pkcs11|pam_sss.*cert|try_cert_auth|use_mappers" /etc/pam.d/ ; grep -E "card_drivers|cert_policy" /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf
tests.exp: Smart card login is on where the policy needs it. The login checks the CA chain and the revocation status, and unknown cards are refused.

tests.title: Check central authentication clients: SSSD, LDAP, Kerberos and authselect
tests.obj: Finds central login clients that use clear-text binds, skip certificate checks or let PAM files drift.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the authselect profile or the PAM files and make sure they are not changed by hand.
Read /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and look at the ldap_id_use_start_tls, ldap_tls_reqcert and CA settings.
Read /etc/openldap/ldap.conf and the nss_ldap settings for TLS.
Look at the offline credential and cache expiration values.
Look for unused LDAP, Kerberos and 389-ds server packages.
tests.ex: authselect current ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/sssd/sssd.conf ; grep -E "TLS|URI" /etc/openldap/ldap.conf ; ls -l /etc/krb5.keytab ; rpm -q openldap-servers krb5-server 389-ds-base
tests.exp: Directory binds use TLS with a full certificate check. The SSSD service runs as the sssd user. Credential caches expire. Unneeded directory servers are not installed.

tests.title: Check sudo configuration, file permissions and privilege rules
tests.obj: Finds sudo rules that give passwordless root, keep unsafe environments or allow users to avoid the log.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/sudoers and all files under /etc/sudoers.d.
Look for NOPASSWD, !authenticate and negated commands. Look for rules that target ALL or the root user.
Look for the Defaults use_pty, env_reset, logfile, passwd_timeout and timestamp settings.
Look at the owner and mode of the sudo binary, /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d.
Make sure the include directory is only the default one and that visudo accepts the files.
tests.ex: grep -rnE "NOPASSWD|!authenticate|^Defaults" /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ ; visudo -c ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d /usr/bin/sudo ; sudo -l -U <user>
tests.exp: Sudo needs a password and a real terminal. The environment is reset. Rules name exact commands. Only root owns the sudo files and the log file records each command.

tests.title: Check the system crypto policy and its use by services
tests.obj: Finds hosts that use the LEGACY policy or have local overrides that bring back weak algorithms.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Run update-crypto-policies --show.
Make sure the policy is not LEGACY and that no module in /etc/crypto-policies/policies/modules weakens it.
Look at the symlinks in /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends. Make sure they point to the generated files.
Look at the OpenSSL, GnuTLS, BIND, Kerberos, SSH and Libreswan settings and make sure they follow the policy.
Look at the random number source for OpenSSL.
tests.ex: update-crypto-policies --show ; update-crypto-policies --check ; ls -l /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ ; grep -r "crypto-policies" /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d ; openssl list -cipher-algorithms | head
tests.exp: The policy is DEFAULT or stricter, not LEGACY. No local file overrides the back-end files. The services use the system policy.

tests.title: Check FIPS mode, boot setup and certified OS status
tests.obj: Finds hosts that must use validated cryptography but run with FIPS mode off.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled.
Run fips-mode-setup --check.
Look at the kernel command line for fips=1 and the dracut fips module.
Look at the crypto policy and sub-policy names.
Compare the result with the compliance requirement of the host.
tests.ex: cat /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled ; fips-mode-setup --check ; grep -o "fips=1" /proc/cmdline ; lsinitrd | grep fips ; update-crypto-policies --show
tests.exp: On hosts that need FIPS, FIPS mode is on at boot and the crypto policy is FIPS. The OS build is a certified build.

tests.title: Check endpoint protection, HIDS and user data backup tools
tests.obj: Finds hosts with no malware scanner, no host intrusion detection or no backup of user data.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the endpoint protection or antivirus agent and its service state.
Look at the date of the last signature update.
Look for a host intrusion detection tool, or for a written reason why audit and SELinux are enough.
Look for the backup job for user data and find the last good run.
tests.ex: systemctl status nails mfetpd 2>/dev/null ; rpm -qa | grep -iE "mcafee|MFE|clamav|aide|ossec|wazuh" ; ls -l /var/log/backup* ; crontab -l
tests.exp: An approved endpoint protection agent runs with current signatures. A host intrusion detection tool or an approved alternative exists. User data backups run on schedule.

tests.title: Check package signature checks, repositories and automatic updates
tests.obj: Finds hosts that install unsigned packages or take packages from unapproved repositories.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the gpgcheck, localpkg_gpgcheck and repo_gpgcheck values in /etc/dnf/dnf.conf or /etc/yum.conf.
Read each file in /etc/yum.repos.d and look for gpgcheck=0.
List the repositories. Compare them with the approved list. Look for EPEL.
Run rpm -qa gpg-pubkey and compare the keys with the vendor keys.
Look at dnf-automatic and its timer, the upgrade type and the weak dependency setting.
tests.ex: grep -rE "gpgcheck" /etc/dnf/dnf.conf /etc/yum.conf /etc/yum.repos.d/ ; dnf repolist ; rpm -qa gpg-pubkey ; systemctl is-enabled dnf-automatic.timer ; grep -E "upgrade_type|apply_updates" /etc/dnf/automatic.conf
tests.exp: Package, local package and repository metadata signature checks are on for all repositories. Only approved repositories are enabled. The vendor keys match.

tests.title: Check APT sources, keys, authentication and file permissions
tests.obj: Finds hosts that accept unauthenticated packages or allow others to change the package sources.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d. Compare the sources with the official list.
Search /etc/apt/apt.conf.d for AllowUnauthenticated.
Look at APT::Install-Recommends, APT::Install-Suggests and the weak dependency setting.
List the owner and mode of the source, key and auth.conf.d directories and files.
tests.ex: grep -rn "AllowUnauthenticated\|Install-Recommends\|Install-Suggests" /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/ ; cat /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/* ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/apt/sources.list.d /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d /etc/apt/auth.conf.d /usr/share/keyrings
tests.exp: APT does not allow unauthenticated packages. The sources are official and signed. Root owns the APT files and no other user can write to them.

tests.title: Check installed and removed system tool packages against the standard
tests.obj: Finds hosts that miss required security tools or keep crash reporters and extra tools that leak data.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the installed packages with rpm -qa or dpkg -l.
Look for the required tools: cryptsetup, openscap-scanner, scap-security-guide, rng-tools, nss-tools, gnutls-utils, tar and vim.
Look for the packages that the standard removes: abrt and its plug-ins, libreport plug-ins, tuned, pigz, geolite2 and gssproxy.
Look at the OS word size and the entropy settings.
tests.ex: rpm -q cryptsetup openscap-scanner scap-security-guide rng-tools nss-tools gnutls-utils ; rpm -qa | grep -E "^(abrt|libreport|tuned|pigz|geolite2|gssproxy)" ; uname -m
tests.exp: The required tools are installed. The removed packages are not installed. Any deviation has an approval.

tests.title: Check that the SSH daemon blocks root login and weak authentication
tests.obj: Finds SSH settings that allow direct root login, empty passwords or trust based on host names.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Print the effective SSH daemon configuration with sshd -T.
Look at PermitRootLogin, PermitEmptyPasswords, HostbasedAuthentication and IgnoreRhosts.
Look at PubkeyAuthentication, GSSAPIAuthentication, KerberosAuthentication and UsePAM.
Look at PermitUserEnvironment, StrictModes and IgnoreUserKnownHosts.
Try to log in as root and with an empty password. Make sure both fail.
tests.ex: sshd -T | grep -iE "permitrootlogin|permitemptypasswords|hostbasedauthentication|ignorerhosts|pubkeyauthentication|gssapiauthentication|kerberosauthentication|usepam|permituserenvironment|strictmodes|ignoreuserknownhosts" ; ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password root@<host>
tests.exp: Root cannot log in over SSH with a password. Empty passwords and host-based trust are off. Only the needed authentication methods are on.

tests.title: Check the ciphers, MACs and key exchange of the SSH daemon
tests.obj: Finds SSH services that accept weak ciphers, weak MACs, weak key exchange or compression before login.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Print the Ciphers, MACs, KexAlgorithms and Compression values with sshd -T.
Compare the lists with the approved algorithms of the organization.
Look for the include line of the system crypto policy in sshd_config.
Look at the RekeyLimit value and the SSH_USE_STRONG_RNG setting.
Scan the port with a tool that lists the offered algorithms.
tests.ex: sshd -T | grep -iE "^(ciphers|macs|kexalgorithms|compression|rekeylimit)" ; grep -rn "crypto-policies" /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ ; nmap -p22 --script ssh2-enum-algos <host> ; ssh-audit <host>
tests.exp: The daemon offers only the approved strong ciphers, MACs and key exchange algorithms. Compression is off or delayed. Session keys renew at the set limit.

tests.title: Check SSH forwarding, X11 and warning banner settings
tests.obj: Finds SSH settings that let users tunnel traffic past the firewall or log in with no legal notice.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Print the effective SSH daemon configuration with sshd -T.
Look at DisableForwarding, AllowTcpForwarding, X11Forwarding and X11UseLocalhost.
Look at the Banner path and read the file.
Try to open a port forward with ssh -L from a test account. Make sure it fails.
