tests.ex: sshd -T | grep -iE "disableforwarding|allowtcpforwarding|x11forwarding|x11uselocalhost|banner" ; ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:80 testuser@<host>
tests.exp: Forwarding is off unless a written need exists. X11 forwarding is off or bound to the loopback address. The banner file shows the approved notice.

tests.title: Check SSH session limits, logging and privilege separation
tests.obj: Finds SSH services that allow unlimited guessing, keep idle sessions or log too little.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Print the effective SSH daemon configuration with sshd -T.
Look at MaxAuthTries, LoginGraceTime, MaxSessions and MaxStartups.
Look at ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax.
Look at LogLevel and PrintLastLog.
Make sure privilege separation is on and the AllowGroups or AllowUsers rule limits access.
tests.ex: sshd -T | grep -iE "maxauthtries|logingracetime|maxsessions|maxstartups|clientalive|loglevel|printlastlog|useprivilegeseparation|allowgroups|allowusers"
tests.exp: Authentication tries, grace time and open sessions have limits that meet the standard. Idle sessions end. LogLevel is INFO or VERBOSE. Only approved groups can log in.

tests.title: Check the owner and mode of SSH daemon files and host keys
tests.obj: Finds SSH configuration files and host private keys that other users can read or change.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List /etc/ssh/sshd_config, /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d and the vendor drop-in files.
List the host private keys /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.
List the host public keys /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.pub.
Make sure root owns each file and the modes are not wider than the standard allows.
tests.ex: stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/* /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.pub
tests.exp: Root owns all SSH daemon files. Configuration files have a mode of 0600 or 0644, private keys 0600 or 0640, and public keys 0644 or stricter.

tests.title: Check the SSH package, service and firewall state against the host role
tests.obj: Finds hosts where the SSH server is on without a need, or is needed but blocked.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the OpenSSH server and client packages.
Look at the sshd service state.
Look at the firewall rule for the SSH service.
Compare the result with the role of the host.
tests.ex: rpm -q openssh-server openssh-clients || dpkg -l openssh-server ; systemctl is-enabled sshd ; firewall-cmd --list-services ; ss -tlnp | grep :22
tests.exp: The SSH server is on only where the host role needs it. The firewall allows the port only from approved sources.

tests.title: Check SSH client settings for ciphers, MACs and entropy
tests.obj: Finds SSH clients that connect with weak algorithms or weak random number sources.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Print the effective client configuration with ssh -G.
Look at the Ciphers, MACs and RekeyLimit values.
Compare the lists with the approved algorithms.
Look at the SSH_USE_STRONG_RNG variable in the shell profile files.
tests.ex: ssh -G <host> | grep -iE "^(ciphers|macs|rekeylimit)" ; grep -rn SSH_USE_STRONG_RNG /etc/profile.d/ /etc/profile /etc/csh.cshrc
tests.exp: The client offers only approved ciphers and MACs. The client uses a strong random source for the seed.

tests.title: Check time synchronization client settings: chrony, ntpd and timesyncd
tests.obj: Finds hosts with no time source, one weak time source or a time service that runs as root.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at which time service is active. Make sure only one is active.
Read /etc/chrony.conf, /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf.
Look for at least two remote servers or a pool, and for NTS if the server supports it.
Look at the maxpoll value and the user that runs the daemon.
Run chronyc tracking or timedatectl and look at the offset and the synchronized flag.
tests.ex: systemctl is-active chronyd ntpd systemd-timesyncd ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/chrony.conf ; chronyc tracking ; chronyc sources -v ; timedatectl status ; stat -c "%U:%G %a" /etc/chrony.keys
tests.exp: One time service runs with at least two remote sources. The clock is synchronized with a small offset. The daemon runs as an unprivileged user and key files are root-only.

tests.title: Check cron and at: service state, user lists and file permissions
tests.obj: Finds hosts where any user can schedule jobs or where job files can be changed by others.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the cron and atd service state.
List /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, /etc/cron.monthly and /etc/cron.yearly with owner and mode.
Look for /etc/cron.allow and /etc/at.allow. Make sure cron.deny and at.deny do not exist.
List the owner and mode of the allow files.
Look at anacron if the host is not always on.
tests.ex: systemctl is-enabled crond cron atd ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/crontab /etc/cron.* /etc/at.allow ; ls -l /etc/cron.deny /etc/at.deny
tests.exp: Root owns all cron files and none is writable by group or others. Only listed users can use cron and at. The at service is off if no one needs it.

tests.title: Check for obsolete clear-text services: telnet, rsh, tftp, NIS, talk, rsync, xinetd
tests.obj: Finds old remote access and file transfer services that send passwords in clear text or trust host names.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the packages telnet, rsh, rlogin, rexec, talk, tftp, ypbind, ypserv, rsync and xinetd.
Look at the state of the matching services and sockets.
Look for .rhosts, hosts.equiv and other host trust files.
Look at nsswitch.conf for NIS entries.
Read /etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny where TCP wrappers are in use.
tests.ex: rpm -qa | grep -E "telnet|rsh|talk|tftp|ypbind|ypserv|xinetd|rsync" ; systemctl list-unit-files | grep -E "telnet|rsh|rlogin|rexec|tftp|rsyncd|xinetd|ypbind" ; find / -name ".rhosts" -o -name hosts.equiv 2>/dev/null ; grep nis /etc/nsswitch.conf
tests.exp: None of the obsolete packages or services is present. No host trust file exists. If TFTP must stay, it runs in secure mode.

tests.title: Check NFS and RPC services, exports and client mounts
tests.obj: Finds NFS servers that export to all hosts or trust remote root, and hosts that run RPC with no need.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the NFS, rpcbind and rpc services and the packages.
Read /etc/exports.
Look for no_root_squash, all_squash, insecure_locks, wildcard clients and missing Kerberos security flavors.
Look at the fixed ports of lockd, mountd and statd.
Look at the client mount options for sec=krb5, nosuid, nodev and noexec.
tests.ex: systemctl is-enabled nfs-server rpcbind ; cat /etc/exports ; exportfs -v ; rpcinfo -p ; findmnt -t nfs,nfs4
tests.exp: The NFS and RPC services run only on hosts that serve or use NFS. Exports name hosts, use root squash and Kerberos, and clients mount with nosuid, nodev and noexec.

tests.title: Check Samba and FTP services for signing, uploads and anonymous access
tests.obj: Finds file transfer services that allow anonymous login, uploads or unsigned SMB sessions.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the samba and vsftpd packages and services.
Read /etc/samba/smb.conf and look at client signing, server signing and root login.
Read /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf and look at anonymous_enable, write_enable, xferlog_enable and banner settings.
Look at the firewall rule for FTP and at the file system of the FTP home.
tests.ex: rpm -q samba vsftpd ; testparm -s | grep -iE "signing|root|guest" ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf ; systemctl is-enabled smb vsftpd
tests.exp: Samba and FTP are off unless the host role needs them. Where in use, SMB signing is required, anonymous login is off, uploads are off and transfers are logged.

tests.title: Check DHCP, DNS, proxy, RADIUS and routing daemons on the host
tests.obj: Finds servers with network infrastructure daemons that the host role does not need or that are not hardened.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the packages and services dhcpd, kea, named, dnsmasq, unbound, squid, freeradius and quagga.
For each one found, compare it with the role of the host.
For a DHCP server, read dhcpd.conf for logging, bootp and DDNS settings.
For a DNS server, look at dynamic updates in named.conf.
tests.ex: rpm -qa | grep -E "dhcp|kea|bind|dnsmasq|unbound|squid|freeradius|quagga" ; systemctl is-enabled dhcpd named dnsmasq squid zebra ; grep -E "ddns-update-style|deny bootp|log-facility" /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf ; grep allow-update /etc/named.conf
tests.exp: No unneeded daemon is installed or enabled. A server that must run has logging on, bootp and dynamic updates off, and serves only the data that it needs.

tests.title: Check Postfix and Dovecot: network listening, relay and TLS
tests.obj: Finds mail services that relay for anyone, listen on all interfaces or accept clear-text passwords.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at which MTA is installed. Make sure sendmail is not.
Read /etc/postfix/main.cf and look at inet_interfaces, smtpd_banner and the relay restrictions.
Look at the relayhost and the root and postmaster aliases.
Read the Dovecot settings for ssl, ssl_cert, ssl_key and disable_plaintext_auth.
Try an open relay test from another host.
tests.ex: postconf -n | grep -E "inet_interfaces|smtpd_banner|smtpd_relay_restrictions|mynetworks|relayhost" ; doveconf -n | grep -E "^ssl|disable_plaintext_auth" ; ss -tlnp | grep -E ":25|:143|:993"
tests.exp: A local-only MTA listens on the loopback address. A mail server relays only for approved networks. IMAP and POP need TLS and refuse clear-text passwords.

tests.title: Check the SNMP agent: installation, service state and protocol version
tests.obj: Finds hosts with an SNMP agent that is not needed or that uses SNMP version 1 or 2c.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look for the net-snmp package and the snmpd service.
Read /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf and look at the version, the users and the access control entries.
Make sure SNMP version 3 with authentication and privacy is in use.
tests.ex: rpm -q net-snmp ; systemctl is-enabled snmpd ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf ; ss -ulnp | grep :161
tests.exp: The SNMP agent is removed if not needed. Where in use, only SNMP version 3 with authentication and encryption is on.

tests.title: Check that unneeded services and daemons are off
tests.obj: Finds services that add attack surface or leak information and that the host role does not need.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the enabled unit files and the listening sockets.
Look for avahi, cups, abrt, apport, cockpit, kdump, netconsole, rdisc, saslauthd, sysstat and rhnsd.
Look for the services acpid, certmonger, oddjobd, portreserve, qpidd and quota_nld.
Look at the list of masked units. Compare the rest with the role of the host.
Look at the avahi and cups settings if they must stay.
tests.ex: systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled ; ss -tulnp ; systemctl is-enabled avahi-daemon cups abrtd apport cockpit.socket kdump rdisc ; grep -vE "^#|^$" /etc/avahi/avahi-daemon.conf
tests.exp: Only the services that the host role needs are enabled. Print, discovery, crash report and remote management services are off.

tests.title: Check USBGuard and fapolicyd allow-list controls
tests.obj: Finds hosts that accept any USB device or run any program without a policy.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the usbguard and fapolicyd packages and services.
Run usbguard list-rules and look at the HID, hub and default policy.
Read the usbguard audit backend setting.
Read the fapolicyd rules and look for a final deny rule and the home folder rule.
Try to run a program from a home folder or plug a test device.
tests.ex: systemctl is-active usbguard fapolicyd ; usbguard list-rules ; grep -E "AuditBackend|ImplicitPolicyTarget" /etc/usbguard/usbguard-daemon.conf ; fapolicyd-cli --list | tail -5
tests.exp: USBGuard blocks devices that no rule allows and logs its decisions. fapolicyd uses a deny-all policy with exceptions for approved software.

tests.title: Check Apache httpd TLS, authentication and banner settings
tests.obj: Finds web servers that offer old TLS versions, accept clear-text logins or show internal notices.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/ssl.conf and the ssl.conf in /etc/httpd/conf.d.
Look at the SSLProtocol, SSLCipherSuite and certificate settings.
Look at the authentication method for protected paths: digest, LDAP or client certificate.
Look for the use of TLS for logins, sessions and uploads.
Scan the TLS port to list the protocols.
tests.ex: grep -rnE "SSLProtocol|SSLCipherSuite|SSLCertificateFile|SSLVerifyClient|AuthType" /etc/httpd/ ; httpd -M | grep -E "ssl|auth" ; nmap -p443 --script ssl-enum-ciphers <host>
tests.exp: Only TLS 1.2 and newer are on, with a valid server certificate. Logins, sessions and uploads use TLS. Protected paths need strong authentication.

tests.title: Check Apache httpd directory access, methods and file permissions
tests.obj: Finds web servers that allow overrides, symlinks, dangerous methods or loose rights on content and logs.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the Directory blocks for the root, the document root and the critical directories.
Look at AllowOverride, Options (FollowSymLinks, Indexes) and the LimitExcept rules.
List the owner and mode of the configuration, module and log directories.
Look for backup files, sample CGI scripts and anonymous content in the document root.
Look at the partition of the web content.
tests.ex: grep -rnE "AllowOverride|Options|LimitExcept|TraceEnable" /etc/httpd/ ; stat -c "%U:%G %a %n" /etc/httpd/conf /etc/httpd/conf.d /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d /var/log/httpd ; find /var/www -name "*.bak" -o -name "*~" ; findmnt /var/www
tests.exp: The root directory denies access by default. Overrides and symlinks are off. Only needed methods are allowed. Only root can change the configuration and logs.

tests.title: Check Apache httpd and nginx modules, logging, tokens and role
tests.obj: Finds web servers with unneeded modules, little logging, version leaks or a wrong placement.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the httpd and nginx packages and services. Compare them with the role of the host.
List the loaded modules with httpd -M. Look for status, info, proxy, cache, webdav, rewrite, include and cgi.
Look at ServerTokens, ServerSignature, LogLevel, LogFormat and KeepAliveRequests.
Look for mod_security and for compilers and sample files on the host.
Look at the firewall rule and the network zone of the server.
tests.ex: httpd -M ; grep -rnE "ServerTokens|ServerSignature|LogLevel|LogFormat|MaxKeepAliveRequests|ErrorLog|CustomLog" /etc/httpd/ ; rpm -q mod_security gcc ; curl -sI http://<host> | grep -i server
tests.exp: Only needed modules load. ServerTokens is Prod and ServerSignature is Off. Errors and access are logged. The web server is off when the host does not serve web content.

tests.title: Check Docker host settings: storage driver, SELinux and daemon state
tests.obj: Finds container hosts that use loopback storage or run containers without SELinux support.
pre: Root or sudo read access to the host in scope.
Do not change settings on a production host without a change window.
steps: Look at the docker package and service.
Run docker info and look at the storage driver and the SELinux flag.
Read /etc/docker/daemon.json for storage-opts and selinux-enabled.
tests.ex: docker info | grep -iE "storage driver|security options|selinux" ; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json ; systemctl is-enabled docker
tests.exp: Docker uses a supported production storage driver, not loopback devices. SELinux support is on in the daemon where the host uses SELinux.

tests.title: Review membership of privileged and operator groups in Active Directory
tests.obj: Finds accounts, service accounts and nested groups that hold domain-wide admin or operator rights without need.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: List the members of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins and Administrators. Include nested groups.
List the members of Server Operators, Backup Operators, Print Operators and Account Operators.
Note each service account and each stale account (no logon for 90 days) in these groups.
Ask the owner of each account for a written reason.
Make sure each privileged person uses a separate admin account.
tests.ex: Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Select SamAccountName,objectClass ; Get-ADGroupMember "Backup Operators" -Recursive ; Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like "*"} -Properties MemberOf,LastLogonDate
tests.exp: Privileged groups hold only named admin accounts with a recorded reason. Operator groups are empty or hold documented members. No service account or stale account is a member.

other: MDI assessments: service accounts in privileged groups, operator groups

tests.title: Check that admin accounts belong to Protected Users and tier limits
tests.obj: Finds admin accounts that can leave NTLM, RC4 or unlimited-lifetime tickets on member hosts.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: List the members of the Protected Users group.
Compare the list with the members of the privileged groups.
Make sure no service account or computer account is in Protected Users.
Make sure the domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 or higher.
Look at authentication policies and silos in Active Directory Administrative Center. Note the TGT lifetime and the allowed devices for admin accounts.
Note that the built-in Administrator (RID 500) is exempt from authentication policies.
tests.ex: Get-ADGroupMember "Protected Users" ; (Get-ADDomain).DomainMode ; Get-ADAuthenticationPolicy -Filter * ; Get-ADAuthenticationPolicySilo -Filter *
tests.exp: Interactive admin accounts are in Protected Users, or an authentication policy limits where they sign in. Service and computer accounts are not members.

tests.title: Check that privileged accounts have the sensitive-and-cannot-be-delegated flag
tests.obj: Finds privileged accounts that a service can impersonate through Kerberos delegation.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: List all members of the privileged groups.
Read the UserAccountControl value of each account.
Look for the NOT_DELEGATED flag (0x100000).
Do the same for privileged computer accounts.
tests.ex: Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties AccountNotDelegated,MemberOf | Where {$_.AccountNotDelegated -eq $false} ; Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Get-ADUser -Properties AccountNotDelegated
tests.exp: Every Domain Admin, Enterprise Admin and privileged service account has "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated" set, or is in Protected Users.

tests.title: Find unconstrained, constrained and resource-based delegation on non-DC objects
tests.obj: Finds servers and accounts that can act for any user, including a domain admin, towards other services.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Search for computers and users with the TrustedForDelegation flag. Ignore domain controllers.
Search for objects that have a value in msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo.
Look for the protocol transition flag (TrustedToAuthForDelegation) on these objects.
Search for objects that have a value in msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity.
Note any entry that points to a sensitive service, such as a domain controller.
Make sure each remaining entry has a business owner.
tests.ex: Get-ADComputer -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} ; Get-ADUser -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} ; Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter "(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)" -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo ; Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount
tests.exp: Only domain controllers use unconstrained delegation. Each constrained or resource-based entry has an owner and does not point to a sensitive service or user.

tests.title: Check service accounts with SPNs for gMSA use and password age
tests.obj: Finds user accounts with an SPN whose weak or old password an attacker can crack offline.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: List all user accounts that have a ServicePrincipalName.
Note the password last set date and the password policy of each account.
Note the accounts that are not gMSA, sMSA or dMSA.
Look for privileged accounts in this list.
Look at the supported Kerberos encryption types of each account.
Ask the owner whether the service can use a managed service account.
tests.ex: Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like "*"} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet,msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes,MemberOf ; Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * ; Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy
tests.exp: Services use managed service accounts. Each remaining SPN account has a long random password, no privileged group membership and AES encryption types.

tests.title: Find account attributes that weaken Kerberos or password protection
tests.obj: Finds accounts with no pre-authentication, DES, reversible encryption or no password requirement.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Search for accounts with the flag Do not require Kerberos preauthentication.
Search for accounts with Use Kerberos DES encryption types.
Search for accounts with Store password using reversible encryption.
Search for accounts with Password not required.
Search for user accounts that have no AES encryption type set.
Note the accounts that fail and the privilege of each.
tests.ex: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true} ; Get-ADUser -Filter {UseDESKeyOnly -eq $true} ; Get-ADUser -Filter {AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption -eq $true} ; Get-ADUser -Filter {PasswordNotRequired -eq $true}
tests.exp: No account has these attributes. Every account that uses Kerberos has AES enabled.

tests.title: Check the krbtgt and built-in Administrator password age
tests.obj: Finds a krbtgt key that is old enough for an attacker to reuse stolen keys to forge tickets.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Read the PasswordLastSet value of the krbtgt account in each domain.
Compare it to the limit of 180 days.
Read the PasswordLastSet value of the built-in Administrator account.
Ask the owner for the date of the last double reset of krbtgt.
tests.ex: Get-ADUser krbtgt -Properties PasswordLastSet ; Get-ADUser -Filter {SamAccountName -eq "Administrator"} -Properties PasswordLastSet
tests.exp: The krbtgt password changed in the last 180 days, with two resets at least 10 hours apart. The built-in Administrator password is current.

tests.title: Check that Windows LAPS manages local administrator passwords on all hosts
tests.obj: Finds hosts that share one local administrator password, which allows lateral movement.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: List the computer objects in the domain. Read the Windows LAPS attributes for each.
Note the hosts with no LAPS password or with a password older than the policy age.
Read the LAPS policy: account name, password age, length and complexity.
Make sure domain controllers back up the DSRM password.
Look for the legacy LAPS client extension on hosts that use native Windows LAPS.
tests.ex: Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime,ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime | Where {-not $_."msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime" -and -not $_."ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime"} ; Get-LapsADPassword -Identity <host> (read only for the test host) ; gpresult /h gp.html
tests.exp: Every managed host has a unique password with a future expiry. The policy sets a length and a rotation age. Domain controllers back up the DSRM password.

tests.title: Review who can read or reset Windows LAPS passwords
tests.obj: Finds accounts that can read local administrator passwords and so become local admins everywhere.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Read the ACL on each OU that holds managed computers. Find the extended right to read the LAPS password attributes.
List the principals that hold this right.
Make sure password encryption is on in the LAPS policy and that only named groups can decrypt.
Look for the event log entries that record password reads.
tests.ex: Find-LapsADExtendedRights -Identity "OU=Servers,DC=corp,DC=example" ; Get-LapsAADPassword is for Entra ID ; Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-LAPS/Operational"
tests.exp: Only named admin groups can read or reset LAPS passwords. Password encryption is on. Reads leave an audit event.

tests.title: Find non-admin accounts that hold directory replication rights
tests.obj: Finds accounts that can copy password hashes from a domain controller (DCSync).
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Read the ACL on the domain root object.
Find the rights Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All.
List each principal that holds both rights.
Note each principal that is not a domain controller, Domain Admin or Enterprise Admin.
Note service accounts, such as sync accounts, and the owner of each.
tests.ex: (Get-Acl "AD:DC=corp,DC=example").Access | Where {$_.ObjectType -in "1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2","1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2"} | Select IdentityReference,ObjectType
tests.exp: Only domain controllers and a short list of documented admin groups hold the two replication rights.

tests.title: Find non-admin write rights on sensitive groups and AdminSDHolder
tests.obj: Finds identities that can change membership or ACLs of privileged groups.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Read the ACL of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins and Administrators.
Look for WriteDACL, WriteOwner, GenericAll and member write rights held by non-admin identities.
Read the ACL of the AdminSDHolder object in the System container.
Note any non-sensitive account on this ACL.
Look for the event that records a change to AdminSDHolder.
tests.ex: (Get-Acl "AD:CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=example").Access ; (Get-Acl "AD:CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=example").Access | Where {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match "WriteDacl|WriteOwner|GenericAll|WriteProperty"}
tests.exp: Only privileged groups and system principals hold write rights on sensitive groups and on AdminSDHolder.

tests.title: Review admin sign-in restrictions: log on rights and authentication policy silos
tests.obj: Finds admin accounts that can sign in to low-trust hosts and leave credentials there.
pre: Read access to Active Directory (a standard domain user is enough for most steps).
Read-only review. Do not reset passwords or change group membership on production.
steps: Read the user rights "Deny log on locally" and "Deny access to this computer from the network".
Note whether the privileged groups are in these deny lists for hosts of a lower tier.
Read the authentication policies and silos for admin accounts.
Read the Log On To restriction of privileged service accounts.
tests.ex: gpresult /h gp.html ; secedit /export /cfg sec.inf (read SeDenyInteractiveLogonRight and SeDenyNetworkLogonRight) ; Get-ADAuthenticationPolicy -Filter * | fl
tests.exp: Domain admin accounts cannot sign in to workstations or member servers outside their tier. Authentication policies or deny rights enforce this.

tests.title: Find certificate templates that let the requester supply the SAN
tests.obj: Finds templates that allow any enrolled user to request a certificate for another account (ESC1).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: List all certificate templates that a CA publishes.
Look at the Subject Name tab. Note each template with Supply in the request turned on.
Look at the EKUs. Note each template with Client Authentication, Smartcard Logon, PKINIT Client Authentication or Any Purpose.
Look at the enrollment ACL. Note each template that Authenticated Users, Domain Users or Everyone can enroll.
Look for Manager approval or required authorized signatures on each template you noted.
tests.ex: certutil -v -template > templates.txt ; Get-ADObject -SearchBase "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example" -Filter * -Properties msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag,pKIExtendedKeyUsage,nTSecurityDescriptor ; msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag bit ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT (1)
tests.exp: No authentication template has Supply in the request on while an unprivileged group can enroll without Manager approval or authorized signatures.

tests.title: Find templates with Any Purpose EKU, no EKU or arbitrary Application Policies
tests.obj: Finds templates that let an unprivileged user get a broadly trusted certificate (ESC2, ESC15).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: List the published templates and their EKUs.
Note each template with the Any Purpose EKU or with no EKU.
Note each template that an unprivileged group can enroll.
Note each schema version 1 template with Supply in the request turned on.
Look for the patch for CVE-2024-49019 on each CA server.
Look for Manager approval and signing requirements on the templates you noted.
tests.ex: certutil -v -template ; Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter "(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)" -SearchBase "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example" -Properties pKIExtendedKeyUsage,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version ; Get-HotFix on each CA
tests.exp: No published template has Any Purpose or no EKU with open enrollment. Supply in the request is off on version 1 templates. Each CA has the CVE-2024-49019 patch.

tests.title: Review enrollment agent certificate templates and agent restrictions
tests.obj: Finds enrollment agent templates that let a user request certificates for any other user (ESC3).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: Find each template that has the Certificate Request Agent EKU.
Look at the enrollment ACL. Note each template that an unprivileged group can enroll.
Look for Manager approval on the template and on the CA.
Open the CA properties. Look at the Enrollment Agents tab for restrictions on agents, templates and subjects.
Make sure the enrollment agents are not also certificate managers.
tests.ex: certutil -v -template | findstr /i "1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1" ; certsrv.msc > CA Properties > Enrollment Agents ; certutil -CAInfo role
tests.exp: Only a named agent group can enroll the agent template. The CA limits each agent to listed templates and subjects. Agents cannot approve their own requests.

tests.title: Review the owner and ACL of certificate template objects
tests.obj: Finds templates that unprivileged groups can change or own (ESC4).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: List the ACL of each template object in the Certificate Templates container.
Note any Full Control, Write DACL, Write Owner or Write property right for Authenticated Users, Domain Users or Everyone.
Look at the owner of each template. Make sure a privileged and monitored account owns it.
List the templates that no CA publishes. Make a note to remove them.
tests.ex: (Get-Acl "AD:CN=<template>,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=example").Access ; (Get-Acl ...).Owner
tests.exp: Only PKI administrators can write to template objects and own them. No unprivileged built-in group holds a write right. Templates that nobody needs are not published.

tests.title: Make sure the CA does not let requesters set the SAN
tests.obj: Finds a CA where EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 lets every requester name the SAN on any template (ESC6).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: Read the CA policy EditFlags value on each CA.
Look for the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag in the value.
Ask why the flag is on, if you find it.
tests.ex: certutil -getreg policy\EditFlags ; reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration\<CA name>\PolicyModules\CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy /v EditFlags
tests.exp: The EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag is off on every CA.

tests.title: Review CA permissions and the split between CA roles
tests.obj: Finds unprivileged users that hold Manage CA or Manage Certificates rights on a CA (ESC7).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: Open the CA properties. Look at the Security tab.
Note each unprivileged group with Manage CA or Manage Certificates.
Compare the members of CA administrator, certificate manager, enrollment agent and auditor groups. Look for overlap.
Read the CA role information and look at whether role separation is on.
Look for CA events 4882 and 4890 in the Security log for permission changes.
tests.ex: certsrv.msc > CA Properties > Security ; certutil -CAInfo role ; Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security";Id=4882,4890}
tests.exp: Only named PKI groups hold Manage CA or Manage Certificates. The role groups do not overlap. Each change to CA permissions leaves an event.

tests.title: Check AD CS web enrollment endpoints for NTLM relay protection
tests.obj: Finds HTTP enrollment endpoints that accept NTLM without HTTPS or Extended Protection for Authentication (ESC8).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: List the servers that run the Certificate Authority Web Enrollment or Certificate Enrollment Web Service role.
Look at the IIS bindings for the certsrv and CES sites. Make sure HTTPS is the only binding.
Look at the Windows Authentication settings. Make sure Extended Protection is set to Required.
Look at whether NTLM is off for these sites, if Kerberos works.
tests.ex: Import-Module WebAdministration; Get-WebBinding -Name "Default Web Site" ; Get-WebConfigurationProperty -Filter system.webServer/security/authentication/windowsAuthentication/extendedProtection -Name tokenChecking -PSPath IIS:\ -Location "Default Web Site/CertSrv"
tests.exp: The enrollment endpoints use HTTPS only. Extended Protection for Authentication is Required, or NTLM is off.

tests.title: Check that the CA RPC enrollment interface needs encryption
tests.obj: Finds a CA that accepts unencrypted RPC certificate requests that an attacker can relay (ESC11).
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: Read the CA InterfaceFlags value on each CA.
Look for the IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST flag.
Find clients that need the flag to be off. Plan an upgrade for them.
tests.ex: certutil -getreg CA\InterfaceFlags
tests.exp: The IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST flag is on, so the RPC interface needs packet privacy.

tests.title: Check CA audit filter and the Audit Certification Services policy
tests.obj: Finds a CA that does not log requests, issuance and permission changes.
pre: Read access to the AD CS enterprise CA and to the certificate template objects in Active Directory.
Read-only review. Do not change templates or CA settings on production.
steps: Read the CA AuditFilter value. Compare it to the full filter value 127.
Read the effective audit policy for the Audit Certification Services subcategory. Look for Success and Failure.
Find events 4886, 4887, 4888, 4882, 4885 and 4890 in the Security log.
Make sure the CA forwards these events to a collector and that the log is large enough.
tests.ex: certutil -getreg CA\AuditFilter ; auditpol /get /subcategory:"Certification Services" ; Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security";Id=4886,4887,4888}
tests.exp: The AuditFilter is 127 or an approved baseline. Success and Failure are on. The CA events arrive at a central collector.

other: Microsoft ESC id: AD CS auditing

tests.title: Find Java debug (JDWP) and JMX/RMI ports open to the network
tests.obj: Finds Java processes that give code execution to any host that can reach a debug or management port.
pre: Written permission for the hosts in scope. Do not run on production.
Only identify the service. Do not run commands on the target.
steps: Scan the hosts in scope for TCP ports 5005, 8000, 1098, 1099 and 9010. Use service detection.
Send the JDWP handshake string to each open port. Look for the same string in the reply.
Ask the RMI registry for its bound names. Look for JMX connectors.
Make sure no JDWP port answers from any host except the developer workstation.
Make sure each JMX port needs authentication and TLS, or listens only on localhost.
tests.ex: nmap -sV -p5005,8000,1098,1099,9010 host ; nmap -p1099 --script rmi-dumpregistry host ; printf "JDWP-Handshake" | nc host 5005
tests.exp: No JDWP port answers from the network. JMX and RMI ports are not reachable, or need authentication and TLS.

tests.title: Find distcc and X11 services that accept connections from the network
tests.obj: Finds build and display services that run commands or show screens without a login.
pre: Written permission for the hosts in scope. Do not run on production.
Only identify the service. Do not run commands on the target.
steps: Scan the hosts in scope for TCP port 3632 and for the TCP ports 6000 to 6009.
Run the nmap distcc script against each open port 3632. Do not run a command.
Run xdpyinfo against each open X11 port. Look for a reply without credentials.
Make sure X11 listens only on a Unix socket, and distcc has an allow list of build hosts.
Make sure the host firewall blocks both ports from other networks.
tests.ex: nmap -sV -p3632,6000-6009 host ; nmap -p3632 --script distcc-cve2004-2687 --script-args="distcc-cve2004-2687.cmd=id" host (only with a written approval) ; xdpyinfo -display host:0
tests.exp: Ports 3632 and 6000 to 6009 are closed to the network. Distcc accepts only listed build hosts. X11 accepts no TCP connection.

tests.title: Find AJP and FastCGI ports open outside the web tier
tests.obj: Finds back-end web protocols that trust the front end and give file read or code execution to other hosts.
pre: Written permission for the hosts in scope. Do not run on production.
Only identify the service. Do not run commands on the target.
steps: Scan the web servers for the TCP ports 8009 and 9000, and for other ports found by service detection.
Run the AJP check with nmap against each open port 8009. Look for a reply to a forwarded request.
Run a FastCGI check against each open port 9000. Look for a reply to a begin-request record.
Make sure the AJP connector has a secret set, or is off, and listens only on localhost.
Make sure PHP-FPM and other FastCGI services use a Unix socket or an allow list.
tests.ex: nmap -sV -p8009,9000 host ; nmap -p8009 --script ajp-headers,ajp-methods host ; cgi-fcgi -bind -connect host:9000 (only with a written approval)
tests.exp: AJP and FastCGI ports are closed to every host except the front-end web server. AJP needs a secret.

tests.title: Test that access ports cannot form trunks or reach other VLANs
tests.obj: Finds access ports that form a trunk with an attacker and allow VLAN hopping.
pre: Written permission and a lab or test port. Do not run on production.
Test host with a tool for 802.1Q frames (scapy or yersinia).
steps: List the switch ports that connect to users and printers. Look at the configured mode of each port.
Make sure each access port is fixed as access mode and has trunk negotiation off.
From a test host on one access port, try to form a trunk with a negotiation frame.
Send a frame with a second VLAN tag to a host in another VLAN. Look for a reply.
Make sure no trunk comes up and no frame reaches the other VLAN.
tests.ex: show interfaces trunk ; show run interface Gi1/0/1 (switchport mode access, switchport nonegotiate) ; scapy: Dot1Q(vlan=1)/Dot1Q(vlan=20)/IP(dst=target)/ICMP()
tests.exp: Every access port is a fixed access port with negotiation off. The test host cannot form a trunk or reach another VLAN.

tests.title: Check that unused switch ports are off and in a dead-end VLAN
tests.obj: Finds open wall and rack ports where an attacker can plug in and join the network.
pre: Access to the switch configuration in read-only mode.
steps: Get the list of all ports and their state from each access switch.
Compare the list with the port inventory and the patch panel records.
Make sure each unused port is in the shutdown state.
Make sure each unused port is in a VLAN that has no route and no gateway.
Plug a test laptop into one unused port. Make sure it gets no address.
tests.ex: show interfaces status ; show vlan brief ; show run | section interface
tests.exp: All unused ports are shut down and in a dead-end VLAN. A device on an unused port gets no network access.

tests.title: Check that the native VLAN is not used for users or management
tests.obj: Finds trunks where untagged frames land in a user or management VLAN.
steps: List all trunk ports and the native VLAN of each trunk.
Make sure both ends of each trunk use the same native VLAN.
Make sure the native VLAN is an unused VLAN. No user port and no management interface may be in it.
Make sure each trunk allows only the VLANs it needs.
Make sure VLAN 1 has no user port and no management address.
tests.ex: show interfaces trunk ; show vlan id 1 ; show run interface Po1 (switchport trunk native vlan 999, switchport trunk allowed vlan ...)
tests.exp: Each trunk uses an unused native VLAN. The allowed VLAN list is limited. No user or management interface is in the native VLAN or VLAN 1.

tests.title: Test that wired ports need 802.1X or MAB before they give access
tests.obj: Finds wired ports where an unknown device gets full access without authentication.
pre: Written permission. Do not run on production.
Test laptop that the NAC team knows about.
steps: Find out which ports are in scope for port-based access control. Get the policy from the NAC team.
Connect an unknown test laptop to a user port. Look at the VLAN and address it gets.
Make sure the laptop gets no access, or only a restricted guest VLAN, before it authenticates.
Connect a laptop with a valid certificate or account. Make sure it gets the right VLAN.
Look at the MAB list. Make sure it holds only approved MAC addresses and the devices are in a limited VLAN.
tests.ex: show authentication sessions ; show dot1x all ; wpa_supplicant / ip addr on the test laptop
tests.exp: An unknown device gets no access or only guest access. An authenticated device gets the correct VLAN. MAB is limited to listed devices.

tests.title: Check that BGP sessions are protected: ACL, TTL security and TCP-AO
tests.obj: Finds BGP speakers that accept session packets from unknown or spoofed sources.
pre: Read access to the router configuration. Do not run on production without a change window.
steps: List the BGP neighbors from the router configuration.
Make sure an ACL on the control plane allows TCP port 179 only from the listed neighbors.
Make sure each directly connected peering uses TTL security (GTSM). Make sure the TTL check value is set on both ends.
Make sure each peering has TCP-AO, or at least an MD5 key that is not a default value.
Send a TCP SYN to port 179 from an unlisted address. Make sure the router does not answer.
tests.ex: show ip bgp neighbors | include TTL|MD5|TCP-AO ; show ip access-lists (permit tcp host <peer> any eq 179) ; nmap -Pn -p179 router
tests.exp: Only listed neighbors reach port 179. Direct peerings use GTSM. Each session has TCP-AO or a strong MD5 key.

tests.title: Check BGP prefix filters and the maximum prefix limit on each peering
tests.obj: Finds peerings that accept wrong, bogon or too many routes, which allows route leaks and hijacks.
steps: List the inbound and outbound route policies of each peer.
Make sure customer peers can announce only their own prefixes and AS paths.
Make sure bogon, special-purpose and too-specific prefixes are rejected.
Make sure each peer has a maximum prefix limit with a warning threshold.
Make sure the router does not announce routes learned from one upstream to another upstream.
tests.ex: show ip bgp neighbors <peer> policy ; show ip prefix-list ; show route-map ; show ip bgp neighbors | include maximum-prefix
tests.exp: Inbound and outbound filters limit each peer to approved prefixes. A maximum prefix limit exists on every peering.

tests.title: Check that OSPF uses cryptographic authentication and passive interfaces
tests.obj: Finds routing domains where an attacker on a user network can inject routes.
pre: Do not run on production. Use a lab for the adjacency test.
steps: List the OSPF interfaces on each router.
Make sure user-facing interfaces are passive, so that they send no hello packets.
Make sure each other interface uses cryptographic authentication with HMAC-SHA. Plain text and null authentication are not allowed.
Make sure keys are not the same on all routers and have a rollover plan.
Connect a test router to a user port. Make sure it does not form an adjacency.
tests.ex: show ip ospf interface | include Passive|auth ; show ip ospf neighbor ; show run | section router ospf
tests.exp: User-facing interfaces are passive. All adjacencies use HMAC-SHA authentication. A test router forms no adjacency.

tests.title: Check that MTA-STS is published and enforced for each mail domain
tests.obj: Finds mail domains where a downgrade or MX spoof lets an attacker read mail in transit.
steps: Get the TXT record at _mta-sts.<domain>. Make sure one record starts with v=STSv1 and has an id.
Get the policy file from https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt.
Make sure the HTTPS certificate is valid for the mta-sts host name.
Make sure the policy has mode enforce and a max_age of at least one week.
Compare the mx lines of the policy with the real MX records of the domain.
tests.ex: dig +short TXT _mta-sts.example.com ; curl -sv https://mta-sts.example.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt ; dig +short MX example.com
tests.exp: The TXT record and the policy file exist. The certificate is valid. The mode is enforce. The mx lines match the MX records. The max_age is long.

tests.title: Check that a TLS-RPT record is published and the report address works
tests.obj: Finds mail domains that cannot see STARTTLS or MTA-STS failures that other senders report.
steps: Get the TXT record at _smtp._tls.<domain>.
Make sure exactly one record starts with v=TLSRPTv1;.
Make sure the rua value is a mailto: or https: address under the control of the domain owner.
Ask the mail team for a TLS-RPT report that arrived in the last 30 days.
Make sure someone reads the reports and acts on policy failures.
tests.ex: dig +short TXT _smtp._tls.example.com
tests.exp: One valid TLS-RPT record exists. The rua address belongs to the domain owner. Reports arrive and the team reviews them.

tests.title: Check DANE TLSA records for the MX hosts of DNSSEC-signed domains
tests.obj: Finds MX hosts where a TLSA record is missing, not signed or does not match the certificate.
steps: Find out if the zone and the MX host zone have DNSSEC. Skip the test if they do not.
Get the TLSA record at _25._tcp.<mx-host> with DNSSEC validation. Make sure the answer is secure.
Make sure the record uses usage 3 or 2. Prefer 3 1 1.
Connect with STARTTLS. Make sure the server certificate matches the TLSA data.
Make sure the TLSA record is updated before each certificate key change.
tests.ex: dig +dnssec TLSA _25._tcp.mx.example.com ; openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect mx.example.com:25 -dane -verify 3 -verify_return_error
tests.exp: Each MX host has a DNSSEC-validated TLSA record that matches its certificate. Usage 3 or 2 is in use.

tests.title: Test that the mail server does not relay outside-to-outside mail
tests.obj: Finds open relays that spammers use to hide the origin of mail.
pre: Written permission for the mail server in scope.
Use only mailboxes that you own as the target recipients.
steps: Connect from an outside address to port 25 of the mail server.
Send MAIL FROM and RCPT TO with two external domains that you control.
Make sure the server rejects the RCPT command with a 5yz code.
Try a source-routed forward-path and a RCPT TO with a percent sign in the local part.
Try the same checks on port 587 without authentication.
tests.ex: nmap -p25 --script smtp-open-relay mail.example.com ; swaks --to a@external-test.example --from b@external-test2.example --server mail.example.com
tests.exp: The server rejects every outside-to-outside recipient. No message is queued. Port 587 needs authentication.

tests.title: Check that VRFY and EXPN do not reveal valid addresses to outsiders
tests.obj: Finds mail servers that let outsiders list valid users or members of a mailing list.
steps: Connect to port 25 from an outside address and send EHLO.
Look at the EHLO reply. Make sure EXPN is not listed as an extension.
Send VRFY with a valid local user and with an unknown user.
Send EXPN with a mailing list name.
Compare the replies.
tests.ex:
nmap -p25 --script smtp-commands,smtp-enum-users --script-args smtp-enum-users.methods={VRFY,EXPN} mail.example.com ; printf "VRFY root
EXPN staff
QUIT
" | nc mail.example.com 25
tests.exp: VRFY gives the same 252 reply for valid and unknown users, or needs authentication. EXPN is off for outsiders.

tests.title: Test that the mail server accepts only CRLF.CRLF as end of data
tests.obj: Finds mail servers that treat a bare line feed as end of data, which allows SMTP smuggling.
pre: Use only mailboxes that you own. Do not run on production.
steps: Send DATA to the mail server from a test client that you control.
Send a message that has the line <LF>.<LF> inside the body, followed by a second MAIL FROM command.
Make sure the server does not end the message at the bare <LF>.<LF>.
Send the same test with <CR>.<CR>.
Look at the delivered mail. Make sure it is one message and not two.
tests.ex: Use a raw socket script (python3 socket) that sends "\n.\n" inside DATA, then "MAIL FROM:<x@test>" ; read the delivered messages in the test mailbox
tests.exp: The server ends data only at <CRLF>.<CRLF>. A bare line feed or carriage return does not start a new mail transaction.

tests.title: Test that RA Guard blocks rogue router advertisements, also with extension headers
tests.obj: Finds access networks where a rogue router advertisement lets an attacker become the default gateway.
pre: Written permission and an isolated test VLAN. Do not run on production.
Test hosts with scapy or the THC-IPv6 tools.
steps: List the access ports. Make sure RA Guard is on for the host-facing ports.
From a test host, send a router advertisement with a different prefix. Do not set a valid router role.
On a second host, look at the routes and the addresses. Make sure the rogue prefix is not there.
Repeat the test with a Destination Options extension header before the ICMPv6 header.
Repeat the test with the packet split into fragments. Make sure the switch logs each drop.
tests.ex: show ipv6 nd raguard policy ; scapy: Ether()/IPv6(src=fe80::bad)/IPv6ExtHdrDestOpt()/ICMPv6ND_RA()/ICMPv6NDOptPrefixInfo(prefix="2001:db8:bad::",prefixlen=64) ; ip -6 route on the victim
tests.exp: The switch drops the rogue router advertisements in all three forms. Hosts show no rogue prefix or router. The drops are logged.

tests.title: Test that DHCPv6 Shield blocks rogue DHCPv6 servers on access ports
tests.obj: Finds access networks where a rogue DHCPv6 server can set DNS servers or addresses for hosts.
pre: Written permission and an isolated test VLAN. Do not run on production.
steps: Look at the switch configuration. Make sure DHCPv6 server messages are allowed only on trusted ports.
Start a test DHCPv6 server on an access port. Give it a different DNS server address.
Ask for a DHCPv6 lease from a second test host.
Make sure the host does not get an answer from the rogue server.
Look at the switch log. Make sure it shows the dropped server messages.
tests.ex: show ipv6 dhcp guard policy ; dnsmasq --dhcp-range=::100,::200,constructor:eth0,ra-stateless (lab only) ; dhclient -6 -v eth0
tests.exp: DHCPv6 server messages from access ports are dropped. Hosts use only the approved server. The switch logs the drops.

tests.title: Check that IPv6 firewall rules match the IPv4 policy
tests.obj: Finds networks where IPv6 gives access that the IPv4 firewall blocks.
steps: Find all hosts and edge devices that have IPv6 enabled. Get the IPv4 and IPv6 rulesets.
Compare each IPv4 allow rule with its IPv6 rule. Make sure the IPv6 rules are not wider.
Scan the same hosts from outside over IPv4 and over IPv6. Compare the open ports.
Send IPv6 first fragments that do not hold the full header chain. Make sure the firewall drops them.
Make sure the host firewalls also have IPv6 rules.
tests.ex: nmap -6 -Pn -p- host6 ; nmap -4 -Pn -p- host4 ; ip6tables -S ; nft list ruleset ; show ipv6 access-list
tests.exp: IPv6 rules are as strict as IPv4 rules. Open ports are the same on both. The firewall drops incomplete first fragments.

tests.title: Check that external SIP signalling uses TLS and not plain text
tests.obj: Finds SIP servers that send registrations, passwords and call data in clear text.
pre: Written permission for the SIP servers in scope.
steps: Scan the SIP servers for UDP and TCP port 5060 and TCP port 5061.
Make sure external users and trunks use TLS on port 5061, or an IPsec tunnel.
Run a TLS scan on port 5061. Make sure the protocol and cipher list is strong.
Make sure the server certificate is valid and names the SIP domain.
Make sure plain port 5060 is closed to outside networks, or only trusted carriers can reach it.
tests.ex: nmap -sUV -sT -p5060,5061 sip.example.com ; nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p5061 sip.example.com ; openssl s_client -connect sip.example.com:5061 -verify_return_error
tests.exp: External SIP traffic uses TLS with a valid certificate and strong settings. Plain port 5060 is not open to untrusted networks.

tests.title: Test that SIP registration needs authentication and limits failed attempts
tests.obj: Finds SIP registrars where an attacker can hijack an extension or guess passwords without limit.
pre: Use a test extension. Do not run on production without a change window.
steps: Send a REGISTER request for a test extension without credentials. Look for a 401 or 407 reply.
Send a REGISTER request with a wrong digest. Make sure the server rejects it.
Send 50 wrong attempts from one address. Look for a block or a delay.
Make sure all extensions use long random passwords and not the extension number.
Make sure the server gives the same error for a known extension and an unknown extension.
tests.ex: sipvicious: svmap sip.example.com ; svwar -m REGISTER -e 100-110 sip.example.com ; nmap -sU -p5060 --script sip-methods,sip-enum-users sip.example.com
tests.exp: The registrar rejects unauthenticated and wrong REGISTER requests. Repeated failures cause a block or a delay. Error replies do not reveal valid extensions.

tests.title: Check that voice media uses SRTP with message authentication
tests.obj: Finds voice calls that an attacker can hear, change or fill with bogus media packets.
pre: Written permission to capture traffic on the voice VLAN.
steps: Make a test call between two phones in scope. Capture the media packets on the network.
Look at the capture. Make sure the media uses SRTP and not plain RTP.
Look at the SDP in the signalling. Make sure the crypto line or DTLS setup shows an authentication tag.
Make sure the NULL cipher and the NULL authentication tag are not offered.
Make sure keys are exchanged over the TLS signalling channel or with DTLS-SRTP.
tests.ex: tshark -i eth0 -Y "rtp || srtp || sip" ; tshark -Y sdp -T fields -e sdp.media -e sdp.crypto.tag ; Wireshark: Telephony > RTP > RTP Streams
tests.exp: All test calls use SRTP with an authentication tag. No plain RTP and no NULL cipher is offered. Keys do not travel in clear text.

tests.title: Make sure SMB signing is required on clients and servers
tests.obj: Finds Windows hosts that accept unsigned SMB sessions, which an attacker can relay or change in transit.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the SMB server setting RequireSecuritySignature on the host.
Read the SMB client setting RequireSecuritySignature on the host.
Read the policies "Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)".
Look for third-party SMB servers that need signing off. Note each one.
Look at the OS version. Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 have different defaults.
tests.ex: Get-SmbServerConfiguration | fl RequireSecuritySignature,EnableSecuritySignature ; Get-SmbClientConfiguration | fl RequireSecuritySignature ; reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters /v RequireSecuritySignature
tests.exp: RequireSecuritySignature is True on the SMB client and server. The two "always" policies equal 1. No exception exists for guest access.

tests.title: Make sure domain controllers need LDAP signing and refuse clear-text binds
tests.obj: Finds domain controllers that accept unsigned SASL binds or simple binds without TLS.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
Enable the LDAP diagnostic log level only for a short time. It has a performance cost.
steps: Read the policy "Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements" on the domain controllers.
Read the policy "Network security: LDAP client signing requirements" on member hosts.
Look for Directory Service events 2886, 2887, 2888 and 2889.
If event 2887 shows unsigned binds, set LDAP Interface Events to level 2. Read event 2889 for the client list.
Try a simple bind on port 389 with ldp.exe. Do not use a privileged account.
Look at the channel binding setting and events 3039 to 3041 for TLS connections.
tests.ex: gpresult /h gp.html ; Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Directory Service";Id=2886,2887,2888,2889} ; ldp.exe > Connection > Connect (port 389) > Bind > Simple bind ; expected error: Strong Authentication Required
tests.exp: The signing policy is Require signing. Event 2888 appears and 2887 does not. A simple bind on port 389 fails with Strong Authentication Required.

tests.title: Check that NTLMv1 and LM are off and NTLMv2 is the minimum
tests.obj: Finds hosts that still send or accept LM or NTLMv1 responses that an attacker can crack or relay.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the policy "Network security: LAN Manager authentication level".
Read the policy "Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change".
Read the NTLM SSP minimum session security for clients and servers.
Read "Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos".
Look for NTLM audit or restriction policies and for NTLM events on the domain controllers.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LmCompatibilityLevel ; reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v NoLMHash ; reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 /v NtlmMinClientSec /v NtlmMinServerSec
tests.exp: LmCompatibilityLevel is 5 (NTLMv2 only, refuse LM and NTLM). NoLMHash is 1. NTLM minimum session security is 537395200 for clients and servers.

other: Related: EPA on HTTP endpoints, see NET-ADCS-007

tests.title: Check that LSA protection runs LSASS as a protected process
tests.obj: Finds hosts where a tool can inject code into LSASS to read credentials.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the RunAsPPL value in the Lsa registry key.
Look at the CodeIntegrity operational log for events 3033, 3063, 3065 and 3066.
Note each LSA plug-in or driver that fails to load as a protected process.
Look at the AuditLevel value under the LSASS.exe image options key, if LSA protection is not yet on.
Make sure Smart App Control does not hide the audit events.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL ; reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\LSASS.exe" /v AuditLevel ; Get-WinEvent -LogName Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational
tests.exp: RunAsPPL is set (1 or 2) and the host runs LSASS as a protected process. No unsigned plug-in is in the failure events.

tests.title: Check that Credential Guard is running
tests.obj: Finds hosts that keep NTLM hashes and Kerberos secrets in LSASS memory.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Open System Information. Look at Virtualization-based Security Services Running.
Read SecurityServicesRunning from Win32_DeviceGuard.
Read the registry values EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity and LsaCfgFlags.
Look at the group policy "Turn On Virtualization Based Security" and the Credential Guard option.
Note hosts where hardware or a legacy application blocks Credential Guard.
tests.ex: msinfo32.exe ; (Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesRunning ; reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LsaCfgFlags
tests.exp: SecurityServicesRunning includes the value 1. LsaCfgFlags is 1 or 2. The host shows Credential Guard as running.

tests.title: Check that WDigest does not keep clear-text passwords
tests.obj: Finds hosts where WDigest stores clear-text credentials in memory.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the UseLogonCredential value under the WDigest key.
Read the policy "WDigest Authentication" in the security baseline.
Look at the OS version and the KB2871997 update level on older hosts.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest /v UseLogonCredential
tests.exp: WDigest Authentication is disabled (UseLogonCredential is 0 or missing on a patched host).

tests.title: Check the number of cached domain logons
tests.obj: Finds hosts that keep many cached domain logon verifiers that an attacker can crack offline.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the policy "Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache".
Compare the value with 1 to 4.
Set a lower value for servers that always reach a domain controller.
tests.ex: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v CachedLogonsCount
tests.exp: The cached logon count is in the range 1 to 4 on laptops. It is 0 on servers that always reach a domain controller.

tests.title: Check that App Control or AppLocker enforces rules on servers
tests.obj: Finds hosts where any program or script can run, so malware runs without a block.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the active App Control policies and AppLocker rule collections on the host.
Look at the policy mode. Note any policy in audit mode.
Look for rules that allow user-writable paths.
Look for App Control events 8028 and 8029 for audited and blocked scripts.
Look at the process that updates the list of authorized software.
tests.ex: Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard | fl CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus,UsermodeCodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus ; Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml ; Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script"
tests.exp: An allow-by-exception policy runs in enforce mode on servers and admin hosts. No rule allows a user-writable path.

tests.title: Check PowerShell logging and language mode on servers and admin hosts
tests.obj: Finds hosts where PowerShell runs in full language mode without script logs.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the policy "Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging".
Look at the policy "Turn on PowerShell Transcription" and note its state.
Open a PowerShell session as a normal user. Read the language mode.
Look at the PowerShell event log for script block events.
Look at whether the App Control policy puts untrusted scripts in ConstrainedLanguage mode.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging /v EnableScriptBlockLogging ; $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode ; Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational";Id=4104} -MaxEvents 5
tests.exp: Script block logging is on. A normal user session runs in ConstrainedLanguage mode on hosts under an enforced App Control policy.

tests.title: Check that AlwaysInstallElevated is off in both registry hives
tests.obj: Finds hosts where a standard user can install any MSI package with SYSTEM rights.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read AlwaysInstallElevated under HKLM Software Policies Microsoft Windows Installer.
Read the same value under HKCU for a standard user.
Note that the value 1 in both hives gives SYSTEM rights to every MSI.
Read the policy "Always install with elevated privileges" in the computer and user policy.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated ; reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
tests.exp: AlwaysInstallElevated does not exist or equals 0 in both hives.

tests.title: Look for writable service binaries, service keys and unquoted service paths
tests.obj: Finds services that a standard user can change to run code as SYSTEM.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the services with their binary path and run-as account.
Note each path that has spaces and no quotation marks.
Read the ACL of each service binary and its folder. Look for write rights for Users or Everyone.
Read the ACL of each service registry key. Look for write rights for non-admin groups.
Note the services that run as LocalSystem.
tests.ex: Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select Name,StartName,PathName ; icacls "<service binary path>" ; (Get-Acl "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>").Access
tests.exp: No service binary, its folder or its registry key allows write access to non-admin users. All paths with spaces use quotation marks.

other: CWE-732, CWE-276, CWE-428 definitions in sources/cwe/cwec_latest.xml.zip. Thin source: no Microsoft page for service ACL checks.

tests.title: Look for writable autorun and scheduled task targets
tests.obj: Finds startup items and tasks that run as a privileged user from a folder that standard users can write to.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: List the Run and RunOnce keys for the machine and the startup folder for all users.
List the scheduled tasks that run as SYSTEM or an admin.
Read the ACL of each target file and folder.
Note any target that standard users can write to or replace.
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run ; Get-ScheduledTask | % { $_.Actions.Execute } ; icacls "<target path>"
tests.exp: Every autorun and scheduled task target is in a folder that only administrators and SYSTEM can write to.

other: CWE-732 and CWE-276 in sources/cwe/cwec_latest.xml.zip. Thin source.

tests.title: Check sensitive user rights: debug, impersonate and log on
tests.obj: Finds accounts that hold rights that allow token theft or privilege escalation.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the user right "Debug programs".
Read the user right "Impersonate a client after authentication".
Read "Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller" and "Allow log on locally".
List the services that run as an account with the impersonate right and that a user can reach.
tests.ex: secedit /export /cfg sec.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS ; findstr "SeDebugPrivilege SeImpersonatePrivilege SeTrustedCredManAccessPrivilege SeInteractiveLogonRight" sec.inf
tests.exp: Debug programs is limited to Administrators. Impersonate is limited to Administrators, Service, Local Service and Network Service. Credential Manager trust is held by no one.

tests.title: Check that User Account Control uses Admin Approval Mode for admins
tests.obj: Finds hosts where admin tokens run without a prompt or on a non-secure desktop.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read "Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode".
Read "Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account".
Read the elevation prompt behavior for administrators and standard users.
Read "Switch to the secure desktop when prompting for elevation".
Read "Only elevate UIAccess applications that are installed in secure locations".
tests.ex: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA /v FilterAdministratorToken /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin /v ConsentPromptBehaviorUser /v PromptOnSecureDesktop
tests.exp: Admin Approval Mode is on for all admins. The prompt for administrators is 2 and the prompt for standard users is 0. The secure desktop is on.

tests.title: Check WinRM for Basic authentication, clear-text traffic and stored credentials
tests.obj: Finds WinRM settings that allow weak or clear-text authentication.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the WinRM client and service setting "Allow Basic authentication".
Read the setting "Allow unencrypted traffic" for the client and the service.
Read the setting "Disallow Digest authentication".
Read the setting "Disallow WinRM from storing RunAs credentials".
List the WinRM listeners. Make sure each listener uses HTTPS or an encrypted transport.
tests.ex: winrm get winrm/config ; winrm enumerate winrm/config/listener ; reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM\Service /v AllowBasic /v AllowUnencryptedTraffic
tests.exp: Basic authentication is off, unencrypted traffic is off, Digest is off and RunAs credentials are not stored. No listener sends clear text.

tests.title: Check RDP settings: NLA, encryption level, saved passwords, log on rights
tests.obj: Finds RDP hosts that skip Network Level Authentication or allow broad access.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the setting "Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication".
Read "Set client connection encryption level" and "Always prompt for password upon connection".
Read "Do not allow passwords to be saved" and "Do not allow drive redirection".
Read the user right "Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services". List the members.
Look for the policy "Remote host allows delegation of non-exportable credentials" for Remote Credential Guard.
tests.ex: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication /v MinEncryptionLevel ; reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services"
tests.exp: NLA is on. The encryption level is High. A password prompt is required. Only Administrators and Remote Desktop Users can log on. Passwords are not saved.

tests.title: Check that local and guest accounts cannot log on from the network
tests.obj: Finds hosts where guest and local accounts can sign in over SMB or RPC.
pre: Local administrator read access to the Windows host in scope.
Read-only review. Do not change policy on a production host without a change window.
steps: Read the user right "Deny access to this computer from the network".
Make sure the right includes Guests. Note any other denied group.
Read the user rights "Deny log on as a batch job", "as a service" and "locally".
Read the setting "Sharing and security model for local accounts".
Read "Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only".
tests.ex: secedit /export /cfg sec.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS ; findstr "SeDenyNetworkLogonRight SeDenyBatchLogonRight SeDenyServiceLogonRight SeDenyInteractiveLogonRight" sec.inf
tests.exp: The deny network logon right includes Guests. The sharing model for local accounts is Classic. Blank passwords work at the console only.

other: Remote UAC token filtering is not in the sources read. See notes-gap3B.md.

tests.title: Review firewall, router and IDS logs for blocked and unusual traffic
tests.obj: Finds attacks, misconfigurations and compromised hosts that the logs show but nobody acts on.
steps: Get the logs of firewalls, routers, IDS or IPS and authentication servers for a set period.
Look for unauthorized connection attempts and traffic that the rules should block.
Look for outbound connections from internal hosts to unknown destinations.
Look for repeated failed logins and for account changes.
Write down each event that nobody investigated.
tests.ex: grep -E "DENY|DROP|REJECT" /var/log/firewall.log | awk "{print \$<src-col>}" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head ; zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h < conn.log
tests.exp: The logs show the events that the logging policy requires. Each unusual event has an investigation record, and no log shows traffic that the rules should block.

tests.title: Check that devices send logs securely to a central server
tests.obj: Finds devices whose logs stay on the device, where an attacker can delete them.
steps: List all firewalls, routers, switches, IDS and servers in scope.
Read the log destination on each device.
Make sure the destination is a separate central log server.
Make sure the transport is secure, for example syslog over TLS.
Generate a test event on a device and find it on the log server.
tests.ex: show logging | include host ; logger -p auth.notice "net-log-test" ; grep net-log-test /var/log/central/*.log
tests.exp: Every device sends its logs promptly to a central log server on a separate system, over a secure channel. The test event arrives on the server.

tests.title: Check that devices share one time source and keep logs long enough
tests.obj: Finds logs that cannot be matched across devices, or that are gone when needed.
steps: Compare the clocks of a sample of devices and servers with the time source.
Look at the time zone and the time format in the log entries.
Read the retention settings of the log server.
Make sure logs of the last 12 months exist.
Make sure logs of the last three months are ready for analysis.
tests.ex: chronyc tracking ; ntpq -p ; show clock detail ; ls -l /var/log/central/ | head
tests.exp: All devices follow one time source and log in a common time format. Logs are kept for at least 12 months, with the last three months ready for analysis.

tests.title: Check that a port scan and failed logins create logs and alerts
tests.obj: Finds monitoring that does not see common attack steps on the network.
pre: Written approval and notice to the security operations team, as the plan says.
Do not run on production without a test window.
steps: Tell the contact in the plan about the source address of the test.
Run a port scan from an external test host.
Send a small number of failed logins to a test account on a remote service.
