tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/members --paginate --jq '.[].login' | xargs -I{} gh api users/{} --jq '.email'; glab api application/settings | jq .domain_allowlist
tests.exp: Only addresses from domains that the organization manages can hold accounts. Exceptions are documented and reviewed.

tests.title: Review external collaborators and their access expiry
tests.obj: Finds external collaborators with permanent or excessive access to repositories and pipelines.
pre: Admin read access to the SCM, CI and artifact registry.
steps: List external collaborators and outside contractors on all CI/CD systems.
Look at the permission level and the repositories of each one.
Make sure each access has an expiry date and an internal sponsor.
Make sure access ends when the work is done.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/outside_collaborators --paginate; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/invitations
tests.exp: External collaborators have least privilege on named repositories only. Each access has an expiry date and an internal owner.

tests.title: Check for shared accounts and shared service credentials
tests.obj: Finds accounts or credentials that several people or systems share.
pre: Admin read access to the SCM, CI and artifact registry.
steps: List service accounts and the systems that use each one.
Find accounts that more than one person or more than one pipeline uses.
Look at the audit log for one account that logs in from several locations.
Make sure each context has its own account with its own permissions.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/audit-log --jq '.[]|select(.actor=="SERVICE_ACCOUNT")|.actor_ip' | sort -u
tests.exp: Each person and each pipeline context has its own identity. No credential is shared between people, between systems, or between people and systems.

tests.title: Check package publishing accounts for 2FA and trusted publishing
tests.obj: Finds package publishing accounts and tokens that an attacker can use to push malicious versions.
pre: Account access to the package registry.
steps: List the accounts and tokens that can publish packages for your organization.
Make sure 2FA is on for each publisher account.
Make sure CI publishing uses trusted publishing with OIDC where the registry supports it.
Make sure remaining tokens are granular, short-lived and not committed.
tests.ex: npm token list; npm profile get; npm access list collaborators PACKAGE
tests.exp: Publishing needs 2FA or trusted publishing. Tokens are granular, scoped to named packages and expire soon.

tests.title: Build an inventory of all CI/CD systems and instances
tests.obj: Finds CI/CD systems that nobody monitors, such as self-managed servers run by one team.
pre: Get approval before network scans.
steps: List the SCM, CI, registry, package manager, CD and orchestration systems.
Search the network and cloud for additional instances of each.
Record the owner and the log status of each instance.
Add unknown instances to the inventory.
tests.ex: nmap -p 8080,443 -sV --script http-title CIDR; aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:role,Values=ci; shodan-style search of own domains
tests.exp: The inventory covers every CI/CD instance. Each has an owner and a log status.

tests.title: Check that audit logs are on for human and programmatic access
tests.obj: Finds systems that do not log logins, permission changes and token use.
pre: Admin read access. Use a harmless test change.
steps: For each CI/CD system, read the audit log settings.
Make sure logs cover user creation, login, permission changes and token creation.
Make sure logs cover access by apps, service accounts and tokens.
Run a test change and look for it in the log.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/audit-log?per_page=5; curl -s https://JENKINS/manage/log/; glab api audit_events
tests.exp: Audit logging is on in each system. A test change appears in the log with the actor, time and source.

tests.title: Check that pipeline events go to a central log system
tests.obj: Finds push, build and upload events that stay in local systems where an attacker can erase them.
pre: Read access to the SIEM.
steps: List the events that matter: pushes, builds, artifact uploads, deployments.
Find the log forwarder or export setting for each system.
Search the SIEM for a test push, build and upload.
Make sure events from different systems can be matched.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/audit-log/streams; logger -p auth.info 'cicd-test'; SIEM search: source=ci AND repo=TEST
tests.exp: Audit and application events of all CI/CD systems arrive in the central log system within the set delay.

tests.title: Test alerts for attacks on the CI/CD pipeline
tests.obj: Finds attacks on the pipeline that raise no alert.
pre: Use a test repository only. Do not run on production.
steps: List the alert rules for CI/CD, such as branch protection changes, new tokens and workflow file changes.
On a test repository, change a branch protection rule and create a test token.
Wait for the alert time and look for the alerts.
Add rules for the events that raised no alert.
tests.ex: gh api -X DELETE repos/ORG/TEST/branches/main/protection  # test repository only; SIEM search for action:protected_branch.destroy
tests.exp: Alerts exist for changes to protection rules, new tokens, new workflows, odd secret reads and odd outbound traffic. A test change raises an alert.

tests.title: Check log content, format and retention
tests.obj: Finds logs that hold secrets, cannot be parsed or are kept too short for an investigation.
pre: Handle exported logs as sensitive data.
steps: Read the log policy for CI/CD systems.
Make sure logs use a parsable format such as JSON or syslog.
Search logs for secrets and personal data.
Make sure the retention period fits investigation and legal needs.
tests.ex: gitleaks detect --no-git -s exported-audit-log.json; jq . exported-audit-log.json | head
tests.exp: Logs are parsable, hold no secrets and are kept for the set period. Audit logs cannot be changed by pipeline users.

tests.title: Check that secret manager requests trace back to the pipeline run
tests.obj: Finds secret reads that cannot be tied to the user, commit or job that caused them.
pre: Use a test secret.
steps: Run a test pipeline that reads one test secret.
Find the read event in the secret manager log.
Make sure the event holds the workflow identity, repository, branch or run.
Make sure unusual reads raise an alert.
tests.ex: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetSecretValue; vault audit list
tests.exp: Each secret read shows which pipeline run, commit or user caused it. Unusual reads raise an alert.

tests.title: Check tamper evidence of build records
tests.obj: Finds build logs and records that an attacker with build access could change without trace.
pre: Use a test record.
steps: Find where build logs and records are stored.
List the accounts that can change or delete them.
Make sure a copy goes to write-once or separate storage.
Try to change a test record and look for the change event.
tests.ex: aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket LOGS; aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket LOGS
tests.exp: Build logs are tamper-evident. Pipeline users cannot change or delete them. Changes raise an event.

tests.title: Check that secrets are scoped to the pipeline, step and environment
tests.obj: Finds secrets that every pipeline or every branch can read.
pre: Admin read access to the CI settings.
steps: List the secrets at organization, repository and environment level.
Find secrets that all repositories or all branches can read.
Compare each secret with the pipelines that use it.
Make sure production secrets are only in protected environments.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/actions/secrets --jq '.secrets[]|{name,visibility}'; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/environments --jq '.environments[].name'; glab api projects/ID/variables
tests.exp: Each secret is available only to the pipelines and steps that need it. Production secrets need a protected branch or environment.

tests.title: Check the default permissions of the job token
tests.obj: Finds pipeline tokens that have write access to code or packages by default.
pre: Read access to the repository settings.
steps: Read the default token permission of the organization and the repository.
Make sure the default is read-only.
Look at each workflow for a permissions block.
Make sure each write permission is granted only to the job that needs it.
tests.ex: gh api repos/ORG/REPO/actions/permissions/workflow; zizmor .github/workflows/ ; grep -rn 'permissions:' -A4 .github/workflows
tests.exp: The default token is read-only. Each job lists the exact permissions it needs. Write access is granted per job.

tests.title: Check runner isolation and clean state after each job
tests.obj: Finds shared build nodes that keep files, caches or credentials between jobs.
pre: Use a test runner. Do not run on production runners.
steps: List the runners and the pipelines that use each one.
Make sure pipelines with different sensitivity do not share a node.
Make sure each job runs on an ephemeral node or a clean container.
Run two jobs one after the other on a test runner and look for left-over files.
tests.ex: gh api repos/ORG/REPO/actions/runners --jq '.runners[]|{name,labels}'; ls -la "$RUNNER_TEMP" ~/.cache  # in a test job
tests.exp: Nodes are ephemeral or reset after each job. Pipelines with different sensitivity never share a node, cache or workspace.

tests.title: Check the OS rights of the job and the container
tests.obj: Finds jobs that run as root, in privileged containers or with access to the Docker socket.
pre: Read access to a test runner and its configuration.
steps: Read the runner service account and its OS permissions.
Look for the privileged flag, host mounts and added capabilities in job containers.
Look for a mount of the Docker socket in the job.
Make sure jobs run as a non-root user.
tests.ex: ps -o user= -C Runner.Listener; grep -rnE 'privileged|docker.sock|cap_add|--cap-add' .github/ docker-compose*.yml; docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' CONTAINER
tests.exp: Jobs run as an unprivileged user. Job containers are not privileged and have no Docker socket or broad host mount.

tests.title: Test outbound network access from build nodes
tests.obj: Finds build nodes that can send data to any host on the internet.
pre: Use a test job without secrets.
steps: Read the egress rules for the build network.
Start a test job that connects to a harmless external host that is not on the allowlist.
Look at the result of the connection.
Make sure the allowlist holds only the registries and services that the build needs.
tests.ex: curl -sS -m 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.org  # in a test job
tests.exp: Build nodes can reach only allowlisted hosts. The test connection to an unlisted host fails and the event is logged.

tests.title: Check network segmentation and metadata service access from jobs
tests.obj: Finds jobs that can reach internal systems or the cloud instance identity service.
pre: Use a test job. Do not run on production runners.
steps: List the internal networks and services that the runner network can reach.
Compare the list with the resources the pipelines need.
From a test job, try to reach the cloud metadata address and an unrelated internal host.
Make sure the instance metadata service needs a session token or is blocked.
tests.ex: curl -sS -m 3 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/  # in a test job; nmap -Pn -p 22,443 INTERNAL_HOST
tests.exp: Runners reach only the systems that the pipelines need. Jobs cannot read the metadata service without a protected session token.

tests.title: Check what controller access pipeline jobs have
tests.obj: Finds jobs that can read other jobs, run on the CI controller or change CI settings.
pre: Use a test job.
steps: Make sure no job runs on the CI controller node.
Read the permissions of the job identity on the CI platform.
From a test job, try to list other projects, credentials and nodes.
Make sure the request fails.
tests.ex: curl -s -u JOBTOKEN: https://JENKINS/api/json?tree=jobs[name]; gh api repos/OTHER_ORG/OTHER_REPO/actions/secrets  # with the job token
tests.exp: Jobs run on separate nodes. The job identity cannot list other projects, read stored credentials or change CI settings.

tests.title: Check that third-party build steps run in a scoped context
tests.obj: Finds third-party actions, plugins and scripts that run with the full rights of the job.
pre: Use a test branch.
steps: List the third-party actions, plugins, orbs and downloaded scripts that jobs use.
Find the jobs where they run together with secrets or write tokens.
Move the step to a job without secrets on a test branch.
Make sure the step still works with its limited rights.
tests.ex: grep -rnE 'uses: [^./]' .github/workflows | grep -v '@[0-9a-f]\{40\}'; zizmor .github/workflows/
tests.exp: Third-party steps run in jobs with minimal secrets, a read-only token and limited egress. They do not share a job with deploy credentials.

tests.title: Test direct poisoned pipeline execution from an unreviewed branch
tests.obj: Finds pipelines where a changed CI file on an unreviewed branch runs with secrets.
pre: Do not run on production. Use a test repository or a test branch with no real secrets.
steps: List the events that start each pipeline, such as push and pull request.
Make sure the pipeline for a push to an unprotected branch has no secrets and no deploy rights.
Push a harmless change to a CI file on a test branch that prints a marker text.
Look at the run and make sure no secret or protected environment was available.
tests.ex: zizmor .github/workflows/; actionlint; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/actions/secrets; echo CANARY-OK in a test workflow
tests.exp: A changed CI file on an unreviewed branch or pull request runs without secrets, without deploy rights and without protected environments.

tests.title: Check that CI configuration files need review before they run
tests.obj: Finds CI definitions that a user can change without a second person reviewing them.
pre: Read access to the repository settings.
steps: Find where the CI configuration file is stored.
Make sure a named owner must review changes to it, or that it comes from a protected source.
Read the CODEOWNERS file for the workflow and pipeline paths.
Make sure branch protection requires the code owner review.
tests.ex: cat .github/CODEOWNERS | grep -E 'workflows|Jenkinsfile|\.gitlab-ci'; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/branches/main/protection --jq .required_pull_request_reviews.require_code_owner_reviews
tests.exp: CI configuration changes need code owner review. Or the pipeline reads its definition from a protected branch or a separate protected repository.

tests.title: Test indirect poisoned pipeline execution through referenced files
tests.obj: Finds jobs that run repository files, such as Makefile, scripts and test code, with secrets.
pre: Do not run on production. Use a test branch with no real secrets.
steps: List the files that the pipeline runs, such as Makefile, scripts, test code and linter configuration.
Find the jobs that run these files together with secrets.
Change a referenced script on a test branch to print a marker text.
Make sure the changed file runs without secrets until a reviewer approves it.
tests.ex: grep -rnE 'make |bash |sh |python |npm run' .github/workflows Jenkinsfile; grep -rn 'secrets\.' .github/workflows
tests.exp: Jobs with secrets run only reviewed files. Unreviewed files run in a job without secrets, or the secret step does not run repository scripts.

tests.title: Test public poisoned pipeline execution from forks
tests.obj: Finds public repositories that run code from anonymous contributors with secrets or write tokens.
pre: Read access to the repository settings.
steps: List the workflows that run on pull requests from forks.
Make sure forks do not receive secrets and get a read-only token.
Look for pull_request_target or similar triggers that check out and run fork code.
Make sure first-time contributors need manual approval before a run.
tests.ex: zizmor --pedantic .github/workflows/; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/actions/permissions/fork-pr-contributor-approval; grep -rn 'pull_request_target' .github/workflows
tests.exp: Fork pull requests run without secrets and with a read-only token. Triggers with write rights never run fork code. Outside contributors need approval.

tests.title: Check that public repository pipelines do not share runners with private ones
tests.obj: Finds public project builds that run on the same CI instance or runner as private projects.
pre: Admin read access to the CI settings.
steps: List the runners and the CI instances for public and private repositories.
Find runners that serve both.
Look for shared caches, volumes and credentials between them.
Make sure public builds use separate ephemeral runners.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/actions/runner-groups --jq '.runner_groups[]|{name,visibility,allows_public_repositories}'
tests.exp: Public and private pipelines use separate runners, caches and credentials. Runners for public builds are ephemeral.

tests.title: Test CI steps for injection from untrusted context values
tests.obj: Finds steps that put names of branches, pull request titles or commit messages into shell commands.
pre: Use a test repository. Use only a harmless marker text.
steps: Search the pipeline files for context values that enter run steps, such as titles, branch names and issue text.
Make sure the values pass through environment variables, not direct text insertion.
Open a test pull request with a title that holds a harmless command substitution marker.
Look at the run log and make sure the marker is printed as plain text.
tests.ex: zizmor --format plain .github/workflows/ | grep -i injection; actionlint -shellcheck=; grep -rn '\${{ github.event' .github/workflows
tests.exp: Untrusted values never go into shell code. The marker text appears in the log as plain text.

tests.title: Check user-controlled build parameters
tests.obj: Finds build parameters that let a user change how the build runs, for example scripts or URLs.
pre: Read access to the pipeline configuration.
steps: List the manual triggers and the input parameters of each pipeline.
Find parameters that set commands, URLs, branches or script paths.
Make sure only authorized users can start these triggers.
Remove the parameters that are not needed.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'workflow_dispatch\|parameters {' -A8 .github/workflows Jenkinsfile
tests.exp: Build parameters are few. They accept only validated values and do not set commands or script locations. Only authorized users can start the build.

tests.title: Make sure pipeline definitions and build scripts are in version control
tests.obj: Finds pipeline settings that exist only in the CI user interface with no history or review.
pre: Read access to the CI system.
steps: List the pipelines and jobs in the CI system.
Find jobs whose definition is only in the CI user interface.
Make sure each pipeline definition and build script is in a repository.
Make sure the audit log shows who changed a job setting.
tests.ex: curl -s https://JENKINS/api/json?tree=jobs[name,_class]; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/contents/.github/workflows
tests.exp: Every pipeline definition and build script is in version control with review and history. No job exists only in the user interface.

tests.title: List all third-party integrations in the SCM and CI
tests.obj: Finds integrations that nobody approved, such as apps, OAuth apps, tokens, SSH keys and webhooks.
pre: Admin read access to the SCM organization.
steps: List GitHub or GitLab apps, OAuth apps, personal tokens, deploy keys and webhooks.
Record the owner, the method and the permission level of each.
Find integrations without an approval record.
Check that webhook targets belong to known vendors and use a secret.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/installations; gh api orgs/ORG/hooks; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/keys; gh api repos/ORG/REPO/hooks
tests.exp: Every integration has an approval record, an owner and a known permission level. No unknown app, key or webhook exists.

tests.title: Compare granted and used permissions of third-party integrations
tests.obj: Finds integrations with more access than they use.
pre: Admin read access to the SCM organization.
steps: For each integration, read the permissions it holds and the repositories it can reach.
Look at the audit log for the permissions it used in the last 90 days.
Mark unused and excess permissions.
Reduce the access to the used set.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/installations --jq '.installations[]|{app_slug,permissions,repository_selection}'
tests.exp: Each integration holds only the permissions it uses, on the repositories it needs. Excess permissions are removed.

tests.title: Check that third-party actions and plugins are approved and pinned
tests.obj: Finds build steps that load unreviewed third-party code that can change without notice.
pre: Read access to the pipeline files.
steps: Read the allowed actions policy of the organization.
List each action, plugin or orb in the pipelines.
Make sure each is on an approved list.
Make sure each is pinned to a full commit hash or a fixed version.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/actions/permissions --jq .allowed_actions; zizmor --pedantic .github/workflows/; pinact run --check
tests.exp: Only approved third-party steps are allowed. Each one is pinned to a commit hash or a fixed version, and the pin changes only through review.

tests.title: Check who can install plugins and add integrations
tests.obj: Finds users who can extend the CI/CD platform without vetting.
pre: Admin read access to the CI platform.
steps: List the roles that can install plugins, apps and integrations.
Make sure the group is small.
Read the vetting steps for a new plugin: vendor history, upkeep and needed settings.
Look at the last three additions and find their approval record.
tests.ex: curl -s https://JENKINS/role-strategy/strategy/getAllRoles; gh api orgs/ORG --jq .members_can_install_apps
tests.exp: Only a small group can add plugins and integrations. Each addition has a vetting record and enters configuration management.

tests.title: Check assessment of third-party suppliers and components
tests.obj: Finds suppliers and open-source components that entered the chain without a risk review.
pre: Access to the supplier review records.
steps: Pick five recent new suppliers or components.
Look for a record of security history, upkeep and vulnerability handling.
Make sure the review matches the criticality of the component.
Make sure the process names who approves.
tests.ex: scorecard --repo=github.com/OWNER/PROJECT; osv-scanner --lockfile=package-lock.json
tests.exp: Each supplier and component has a review record. High-risk items get a deeper review and a named approver.

tests.title: Review removal of unused integrations
tests.obj: Finds integrations, apps and webhooks that stay active after the need ended.
pre: Admin read access to the SCM organization.
steps: List integrations and their last activity date.
Find integrations with no activity in the policy period.
Make sure there is a periodic review with named owners.
Remove one unused test integration and check the process.
tests.ex: gh api orgs/ORG/installations --jq '.installations[]|{app_slug,updated_at}'; gh api orgs/ORG/audit-log?phrase=action:integration_installation
tests.exp: A scheduled review removes unused integrations. No integration is idle longer than the policy period.

tests.title: Check the dependency vulnerability scan gate in the pipeline
tests.obj: Finds pipelines that build and ship components with known vulnerabilities without a gate.
pre: Use a test branch.
steps: Find the SCA or vulnerability scan step in the pipeline.
Make sure it scans direct and transitive dependencies.
Make sure the step fails the build above the defined severity.
Add a known vulnerable test dependency on a test branch and run the pipeline.
tests.ex: trivy fs --scanners vuln --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .; grype dir:. --fail-on high; osv-scanner -r .
tests.exp: The pipeline scans all dependencies on every build. The build fails when a finding exceeds the allowed severity.

tests.title: Check scanning of the final build output and container images
tests.obj: Finds images and binaries that contain vulnerable or unauthorized components after the build.
pre: Read access to the artifact registry.
steps: Find the image or binary that the pipeline publishes.
Scan the final output, not only the source.
Make sure the scan covers OS packages and bundled libraries.
Lint the Dockerfile for a USER directive and pinned base images.
tests.ex: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL IMAGE@sha256:DIGEST; grype IMAGE@sha256:DIGEST; hadolint Dockerfile
tests.exp: The pipeline scans the final image or binary before release. Findings above the limit block the release.

tests.title: Check ongoing monitoring of deployed releases for new advisories
tests.obj: Finds released software that nobody re-checks when a new advisory appears.
pre: Read access to the SBOM store.
steps: Find where the release SBOMs are stored and how they map to deployed systems.
Make sure a job scans these SBOMs again on a schedule.
Look for alert subscriptions to advisory sources for the components in use.
Check that a new finding creates a ticket with an owner.
tests.ex: grype sbom:sbom.cdx.json --fail-on high; osv-scanner --sbom=sbom.cdx.json; dependency-track API: GET /api/v1/finding/project/UUID
tests.exp: Deployed releases are re-checked against advisories on a schedule. New findings create a ticket with an owner and a due date.

tests.title: Review temporary mitigations and virtual patches for vulnerable components
tests.obj: Finds vulnerabilities that stay open behind a mitigation that nobody tests or removes.
pre: Do not run bypass tests on production.
steps: List the vulnerable components that have a temporary mitigation, wrapper or virtual patch.
Make sure each one links to a CVE, an owner and an end date.
Test the mitigation with alternate inputs on a test system.
Make sure the scanner suppression covers only that CVE.
tests.ex: grep -rn 'ignore\|suppress' .trivyignore .grype.yaml dependency-check-suppressions.xml; git log --since=180.days -- .trivyignore
tests.exp: Each mitigation has a CVE, an owner and an end date. Tests show it blocks alternate inputs. A suppression covers only its CVE.

tests.title: Check that the pipeline scans infrastructure as code
tests.obj: Finds infrastructure code that reaches production without a misconfiguration scan.
pre: Read access to the IaC repository.
steps: Find the IaC repositories and the pipeline steps that apply them.
Make sure a static IaC scan runs on each pull request.
Make sure the scan fails the change above the defined severity.
Make sure IaC changes follow the same review rules as application code.
tests.ex: trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .; checkov -d . --quiet; tflint
tests.exp: A static IaC scan runs on every change and blocks serious findings. IaC changes need pull request review.

tests.title: Check static code analysis and secret scan steps in the pipeline
tests.obj: Finds pipelines that build custom code without any automated code analysis.
pre: Read access to the repository.
steps: Find the SAST and secret scan steps in the pipeline.
Make sure they run on every pull request and on the default branch.
Make sure the findings block the merge above the defined severity.
Make sure the rules and tools are updated on a schedule.
tests.ex: semgrep scan --config auto --error --severity ERROR .; gitleaks detect --redact
tests.exp: Static analysis and secret scan run on each pull request. Serious findings block the merge. Rules are kept current.

tests.title: Check that privileges are approved by authorized personnel
tests.obj: Find access rights that no authorized person approved.
pre: Access to access request records
steps: Pick ten users with access to systems or data in scope, including three privileged users.
Find the access request and the approval for each user.
Make sure the approver is authorized and is not the requester.
Compare the approved privileges with the privileges that are set on the system.
Look for privileges that were not approved.
tests.ex: Compare identity governance requests with the group memberships in the directory
tests.exp: Each user privilege has an approval from an authorized person. The privileges on the system match the approval.

tests.title: Check the six-month review of user accounts and access rights
tests.obj: Find accounts and rights that stay after the role changed or the person left.
pre: Access to review records and directory exports
steps: Ask for the account review procedure.
Find the records of the last two reviews. Make sure they are less than six months apart.
Make sure the review covers all user accounts, third-party and vendor accounts and their rights.
Make sure management confirmed that access is still right and removed access is closed.
Compare a sample of accounts with the HR and contract records.
tests.ex: User access review reports; directory export compared to the HR list
tests.exp: A review of all user accounts and rights runs at least every six months. Management confirms access and inappropriate access is removed.

tests.title: Check the periodic review of application and system account access
tests.obj: Find application and system accounts with rights that no one reviews.
pre: Access to review records
steps: Ask for the review process for application and system accounts.
Make sure the review frequency comes from the targeted risk analysis.
Find the records of the last review.
Make sure the rights follow least privilege.
Make sure management confirmed the access and that removed rights are closed.
tests.ex: Service account lists; database grants; cloud role assignments; review records
tests.exp: Application and system accounts are reviewed at a risk-based frequency. Rights follow least privilege and management confirms them.

tests.title: Check that users query cardholder data only through controlled applications
tests.obj: Find direct access to data stores with cardholder data that bypasses application controls.
pre: Test user account without administrator rights
steps: List the repositories of stored cardholder data, such as databases and files.
List the users and groups with direct query access.
Make sure only the responsible administrators can query the repository directly.
Make sure all other access goes through applications with role-based, least-privilege actions.
Try a direct database login with an ordinary user account.
tests.ex: SELECT grantee, privilege_type FROM information_schema.table_privileges; psql -h db -U appuser
tests.exp: Only the responsible administrators can query repositories directly. Other users reach cardholder data through applications with role limits.

tests.title: Check that every user has a unique ID before access is allowed
tests.obj: Find users who share an ID or whose actions cannot be linked to one person.
pre: Access to user lists and audit logs
steps: Export the user list of each system and application in scope.
Look for IDs that two or more people use, such as admin, root or team names.
Interview two users of each system. Ask whether they use their own ID.
Pick five events in the audit logs. Link each one to one named person.
Look for access that needs no ID.
tests.ex: getent passwd; SELECT username FROM users; compare with the HR list; follow five log entries to a person
tests.exp: Each user has a unique ID before access is allowed. Every logged action can be linked to one person.

tests.title: Check that shared and generic IDs are rare and controlled
tests.obj: Find group, shared or generic IDs that are used without a need or without individual accountability.
pre: Access to the account lists and the vault
steps: List all group, shared and generic IDs and shared credentials, including service and vendor IDs.
Make sure each has a written business reason and management approval.
Make sure use is blocked by default and open only for the time of the exception.
Make sure the system confirms the identity of the person before the use of the account.
Pick one recent use. Make sure the log links each action to one person.
tests.ex: Privileged access management check-out log; vault session records; sudo log
tests.exp: Shared and generic IDs are used only by exception, with approval, a time limit, identity confirmation and individual accountability.

tests.title: Check that remote access factors are unique for each customer
tests.obj: Find service providers that reuse one credential for remote access to several customers.
pre: Service provider scope
steps: Ask for the list of customers that the provider can reach with remote access.
Examine the authentication factors that are used for each customer environment.
Look for factors that two or more customer environments share.
Make sure the remote access tool stores the factors per customer.
Make sure a leak of one factor opens only one customer environment.
tests.ex: Remote support tool configuration; vault entries per customer
tests.exp: Each customer premises has its own authentication factors. No factor works on more than one customer environment.

tests.title: Check that access of terminated users is revoked at once
tests.obj: Find accounts of former staff and contractors that still work.
pre: Access to the leaver list and directories
steps: Get the list of users who left in the last 90 days.
Look for each user in the local, remote, VPN, application and database accounts.
Compare the leave date with the date the access ended.
Make sure the access ended at once, in the same working day.
Try to log in with one disabled account on a test system.
tests.ex: Compare the HR leaver list with: ldapsearch, lastlog, aws iam list-users, VPN user list
tests.exp: Every account of a terminated user is removed or disabled at once on every system, for local and remote access.

tests.title: Check that inactive accounts are removed or disabled within 90 days
tests.obj: Find user accounts that stay active after 90 days with no use.
pre: Access to last-login data
steps: Export last-login dates for all user accounts of each system in scope.
Find accounts with no use for more than 90 days.
Make sure each such account is removed or disabled.
Make sure an automatic job or a documented process does this.
Make sure the reason is on file for any exception.
tests.ex: lastlog; SELECT last_login FROM users; aws iam generate-credential-report; Get-ADUser -Filter {LastLogonDate -lt $d}
tests.exp: No user account is active after 90 days of inactivity. A process removes or disables inactive accounts.

tests.title: Check that third-party remote access accounts are limited and monitored
tests.obj: Find vendor accounts that stay enabled all the time or run with no monitoring.
pre: Access to vendor account records
steps: List all accounts that third parties use for remote access.
Make sure each account is disabled when not in use.
Make sure the account is open only for the time needed, with approval.
Look at the logs of the last vendor session. Make sure it was monitored for unexpected activity.
Try to log in with a vendor account outside an approved period.
tests.ex: VPN account list; vendor access schedule; session recording of the last vendor session
tests.exp: Third-party remote accounts are enabled only for the needed period and disabled otherwise. Their use is monitored.

tests.title: Check that sessions need new authentication after 15 minutes of idle time
tests.obj: Find terminals and sessions that stay open for more than 15 minutes with no activity.
pre: Test account on each system
steps: Find the idle timeout settings for each application, operating system and remote access tool in scope.
Make sure each value is 15 minutes or less.
Log in to a test system and stay idle for 16 minutes.
Try to use the session. Make sure the system asks for authentication again.
Try the same on a session that the user locked, and on a remote desktop session.
tests.ex: Application session timeout setting; Windows screen lock policy; sshd ClientAliveInterval; TMOUT
tests.exp: A session that is idle for more than 15 minutes needs authentication again. All in-scope systems have a timeout of 15 minutes or less.

tests.title: Check the lockout limit and duration for invalid logins
tests.obj: Find login functions that allow more than 10 invalid attempts or unlock too early.
pre: Test account that can be locked
steps: Find the lockout settings for each login function in scope.
Make sure the lockout starts after no more than 10 invalid attempts.
Send 10 wrong passwords to a test account. Then send the correct password.
Make sure the account stays locked for at least 30 minutes or until an administrator confirms the user.
Try the same on the API and on remote access.
tests.ex: Active Directory account lockout policy; application lockout setting; hydra against a test account
tests.exp: An account locks after no more than 10 invalid attempts. It stays locked for at least 30 minutes or until the identity is confirmed.

tests.title: Check the password length and character type rules against PCI DSS
tests.obj: Find password settings that allow fewer than 12 characters or no mix of numbers and letters.
pre: Test account
steps: Find the password settings for each system and application that uses passwords as a factor.
Make sure the minimum length is 12 characters, or 8 where the system cannot support 12.
Try to set a password of 11 characters. Make sure the system refuses it.
Try to set a password of only letters and one of only digits. Make sure the system refuses both.
Make sure the rule is enforced on the server.
tests.ex: Active Directory password policy; /etc/security/pwquality.conf; the application password rule
tests.exp: Passwords need at least 12 characters, or 8 where 12 is not supported, and contain both numbers and letters.

tests.title: Check that a new password differs from the last four passwords
tests.obj: Find systems that allow users to reuse a recent password.
pre: Test account
steps: Find the password history setting for each system in scope.
Make sure the history size is at least four.
Change the password of a test account five times.
Try to set the second password again. Make sure the system refuses it.
Try to set the first password. Make sure the system accepts it only after four changes.
tests.ex: net accounts; /etc/pam.d/common-password remember=4; application password history table
tests.exp: A user cannot set a new password that matches any of the last four passwords.

tests.title: Check that single-factor passwords change every 90 days or get dynamic analysis
tests.obj: Find accounts that use a password as the only factor and keep it more than 90 days with no risk analysis.
pre: Access to authentication configuration
steps: List the systems where a password is the only authentication factor.
Find the password age rule of each. Make sure it is 90 days or less.
If the system uses dynamic analysis, examine how it decides on access in real time.
Examine the posture signals that the analysis uses.
Look for accounts with a password older than 90 days and no dynamic analysis.
tests.ex: Active Directory maxPwdAge; account password last set date; risk-based access policy export
tests.exp: Single-factor passwords change at least every 90 days, or the posture of the account is analyzed and access is set in real time.

tests.title: Check that a service provider guides customers on single-factor passwords
tests.obj: Find customer password guidance that omits change timing and the conditions for a change.
pre: Service provider scope
steps: Find out if customer users can reach cardholder data with a password as the only factor.
Ask for the guidance that the provider gives to these users.
Make sure the guidance tells users when and how often to change the password.
Make sure it states the conditions for a password change.
Or make sure the provider uses dynamic analysis of the account posture instead (see 8.3.10.1).
tests.ex: Customer onboarding documents; portal help pages; password policy of the customer portal
tests.exp: The provider gives customer users guidance on password change timing and conditions. Passwords change every 90 days or accounts are analyzed dynamically.

tests.title: Check that tokens, smart cards and certificates belong to one user
tests.obj: Find authentication tokens that several people share or that others can use.
pre: Access to token and certificate records
steps: List the physical and logical tokens, smart cards and certificates in use.
Compare each with the user it is assigned to.
Look for tokens or certificates that more than one person uses.
Make sure a PIN, a biometric or another control stops others from using the factor.
Look for client certificates and keys saved in shared folders.
tests.ex: Token inventory; certificate subject check; PIN policy; keystore file search
tests.exp: Each token, smart card or certificate is assigned to one user. Controls stop other persons from using the factor.

tests.title: Check that interactive use of application and system accounts is limited
tests.obj: Find service accounts that people use to log in with no need, approval or attribution.
pre: Access to account lists and logs
steps: List application and system accounts that can log in interactively.
Make sure interactive login is blocked unless an exceptional circumstance needs it.
Make sure each exception has a business reason and management approval.
Make sure use is limited in time and the identity of the person is confirmed before access.
Pick one recent use. Make sure the log links each action to one person.
tests.ex: grep -v nologin /etc/passwd; service account shell and logon type audit; vault check-out log
tests.exp: Interactive use of application and system accounts is blocked by default. Exceptions are approved, time limited and attributable to a person.

tests.title: Check that each server has one primary function or isolated security levels
tests.obj: Find systems that run functions with different security needs without separation.
pre: Access to system inventory and configuration
steps: List the primary function of each system in scope, such as web server, database server and DNS server.
Find systems that run more than one primary function.
For each, make sure the functions are isolated in virtual machines, containers or separate processes with different privileges.
Make sure the functions on one system need the same security level.
Try to reach the data of the more sensitive function from the less sensitive one.
tests.ex: docker ps; systemctl list-units --type=service; hypervisor VM list; compare with the configuration standard
tests.exp: Each system has one primary function, or functions with different security needs are isolated from each other.

tests.title: Check that production changes follow the change control procedure
tests.obj: Find changes to production systems that skip reason, security impact, approval, testing or a back-out plan.
pre: Access to the change records
steps: Ask for the change control procedure.
Pick ten recent changes to production systems and software.
Make sure each change has a reason, a description, a security impact record and an approval by authorized parties.
Make sure each change has a test record that shows no negative security impact. For bespoke software, make sure the tests cover 6.2.4.
Make sure each change has a procedure to return to a secure state.
tests.ex: Change tickets; pipeline approval records; test reports; roll-back plans
tests.exp: Every change has a reason, a security impact record, an authorized approval, a test result and a way to return to a secure state.

tests.title: Check that PCI DSS controls are confirmed after significant changes
tests.obj: Find new or changed systems that go live with no check of the PCI DSS controls.
pre: Access to the change records
steps: Ask for the definition of a significant change.
Pick two significant changes from the last 12 months.
Find the record that confirms that the applicable PCI DSS requirements are in place on the new or changed systems.
Make sure the scope, the network and data flow diagrams and the inventories were updated.
Make sure the change closed only after the confirmation.
tests.ex: Post-change review checklist; updated data flow diagram; scan and test results after the change
tests.exp: After each significant change, the applicable requirements are confirmed in place and the documentation is updated.

tests.title: Check that access control enforces the split of pre-production and production
tests.obj: Find pre-production systems that reach or share accounts with production.
pre: Test account in pre-production
steps: List the pre-production and production environments.
Examine the network rules between them. Make sure they allow only approved flows.
Make sure the accounts, keys and secrets of the two environments are different.
Log in with a pre-production account. Try to reach a production system and its data.
Examine the access control lists of each environment.
tests.ex: Network and cloud account review; try an SSH or API call from a staging host to production
tests.exp: Access controls enforce the split. Pre-production accounts and credentials cannot reach production.

tests.title: Check that live PANs are not in pre-production environments
tests.obj: Find real card numbers in test and development data.
pre: Read access to pre-production data
steps: Ask whether any pre-production environment is part of the cardholder data environment.
If not, search the test databases, files, logs and backups for PAN values that pass a Luhn check.
Check each hit against known test card ranges.
Ask how the test data is made. Make sure no live data is copied from production.
Make sure a process removes found live PANs.
tests.ex: PAN discovery tool run on the staging database; compare BIN ranges with the test card list
tests.exp: No live PAN exists in pre-production unless that environment is in the cardholder data environment and fully protected.

tests.title: Check that test data and test accounts are removed before go-live
tests.obj: Find test accounts, test data and test code that stay in production.
pre: Access to the production listings
steps: Ask for the process that removes test data and test accounts before a system goes live.
List all accounts on a new production system. Find test, demo and vendor accounts.
Search the production database for test records and test card numbers.
Look at the last release record for a clean-up step.
Try to log in with known test credentials on a test copy of the release.
tests.ex: SELECT user FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'test%'; check for demo and qa accounts in the identity provider
tests.exp: No test account, test data or test card number exists on a production system. A release step removes them.

tests.title: Check that stored account data is limited by retention and disposal rules
tests.obj: Find account data that is kept longer than the business need or the documented retention period.
pre: Read access to the data stores in scope
List of all places where account data is stored
steps: Ask for the data retention and disposal policy for account data.
Make sure the policy sets a retention period and a business reason for each data store.
Search each data store for account data that is older than the retention period.
Make sure a job or process removes or overwrites expired data on a schedule.
Make sure the quarterly process finds stored account data that is not in the policy.
tests.ex: SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE created_at < now() - interval '13 months'; scan file shares with a PAN discovery tool
tests.exp: Account data is kept only for the documented period and need. Expired data is removed in a secure way, and a quarterly process finds unknown copies.

tests.title: Check that sensitive authentication data is unrecoverable after authorization
tests.obj: Find sensitive authentication data that stays on a system after the authorization process ends.
pre: Test card data from the acquirer
Test system, not production
steps: Ask which systems receive sensitive authentication data and how long it stays on them.
Examine the documented process that removes this data after authorization.
Make an authorized test transaction with a test card on the test system.
Search databases, files, logs, queues, caches and memory dumps for the test values after authorization.
Make sure the secure deletion method makes the data unrecoverable.
tests.ex: grep -r <test track or CVV value> /var/log /data; strings core.dump | grep <test PAN>
tests.exp: No sensitive authentication data remains after authorization, even in encrypted form. The deletion method makes the data unrecoverable.

tests.title: Check that full track data is not stored after authorization
tests.obj: Find full magnetic-stripe or chip track data that is kept after the authorization process ends.
pre: Test card data
Test system, not production
steps: Make a test transaction with a test card on the test system.
Look at the payment application files, databases and logs for the track 1 and track 2 format.
Search for the sentinel patterns of track data, for example a leading % or ; and an = separator.
Look at debug output, crash dumps, backups and error reports for the same patterns.
Examine the capture code or configuration for fields that keep track data.
tests.exp: No data store, log, backup or dump holds the full contents of any track after authorization is complete.

tests.title: Check that the card verification code is not stored after authorization
tests.obj: Find CVV, CVC or similar card verification values that stay after the authorization process ends.
pre: Test card data
Test system, not production
steps: Make a test transaction with a known test card verification code.
Search database columns, files, logs and message queues for the test code.
Look at the request logs, the proxy logs and the browser or app crash reports for the code.
Examine the application code and the log filters for fields called cvv, cvc, cid or security code.
Look at backups and replicas of the data stores.
tests.ex: grep -rn -i -E 'cvv|cvc|cid|security_code' /data /var/log; search for the test value in database dumps
tests.exp: No data store, log, backup or report holds the card verification code after authorization is complete.

tests.title: Check that PIN and PIN block data is not kept after authorization
tests.obj: Find PIN or PIN block data that stays after the authorization process ends.
pre: Test PIN data
Test system, not production
steps: Ask whether the system receives PIN or PIN block data.
Make a test PIN transaction on the test system if the system supports it.
Search databases, files, logs, queues and dumps for the encrypted PIN block and for PIN fields.
Examine the application code and the log filters for fields called pin or pinblock.
Look at backups and replicas of the data stores.
tests.ex: grep -rn -i -E 'pin_?block|pinblock|\bpin\b' /data /var/log; search database dumps for the test PIN block
tests.exp: No data store, log, backup or report holds a PIN or a PIN block after authorization is complete.

tests.title: Check that sensitive authentication data is encrypted before authorization ends
tests.obj: Find sensitive authentication data that waits in clear text on a system before the authorization is complete.
pre: Test card data
Test system, not production
steps: Ask where sensitive authentication data is stored before authorization is complete.
Make a test transaction and stop it before the authorization response.
Look at the data stores, queues, files and swap space for the test values in clear text.
Examine the encryption algorithm and key length against current industry guidance.
Make sure the stored data is deleted when the authorization is complete.
tests.ex: Pause the test transaction at the gateway; inspect the queue and database; run strings on the swap file
tests.exp: All sensitive authentication data that is stored before authorization is complete is encrypted with strong cryptography.

tests.title: Check that displayed PANs show only the BIN and last four digits
tests.obj: Find screens, reports, exports and receipts that show more PAN digits than the business need allows.
pre: Test accounts for each role
Test PANs
steps: Ask for the list of roles that need to see more than the BIN and the last four digits.
Make sure each role on the list has a documented business need.
Log in as a role that is not on the list. Open each screen, report and export that shows a PAN.
Count the visible digits. Make sure only the BIN and the last four digits show.
Look at the API responses and the page source for the full PAN.
Log in as a listed role and make sure the full PAN shows only where the business need exists.
tests.ex: Compare the API response to the screen; curl -s /api/orders/123 | grep -E '[0-9]{13,19}'
tests.exp: Roles with no documented need see at most the BIN and the last four digits. The full PAN is not in any response sent to those roles.

tests.title: Check that remote access tools block copy and move of the PAN
tests.obj: Find remote sessions that allow a user to copy or move PAN data to a local device.
pre: Test PAN in a test system
Test accounts with and without authorization
steps: List the remote-access technologies that reach systems with account data.
Ask for the list of users with documented authorization to copy or move PAN.
Open a remote session as a user who is not on the list.
Try to copy PAN text, drag a file out, map a local drive and use the clipboard and print functions.
Make sure the technical controls block each action and log the try.
tests.ex: RDP: check drive, clipboard and printer redirection policy; Citrix: check client drive mapping and clipboard policy
tests.exp: Technical controls block copy and move of PAN in remote sessions. Only users with documented authorization and a defined business need can do it.

tests.title: Check that the PAN is unreadable in every place it is stored
tests.obj: Find stored PAN in clear text in databases, files, logs, backups, caches and temporary files.
pre: Test PANs
Test system, not production
steps: Ask for the documentation of the method that makes the PAN unreadable.
Make sure the method is a keyed hash, truncation, an index token or strong cryptography with key management.
Insert a test PAN. Search databases, files, logs, queues, caches and backups for the test value.
Search the payment application logs and the debug output for PAN patterns that pass a Luhn check.
Make sure the algorithm and key length meet current industry guidance.
tests.ex: grep -rE '\b[3-6][0-9]{12,18}\b' /data /var/log then run a Luhn check; use a data discovery tool such as a PAN scanner
tests.exp: The PAN is unreadable everywhere it is stored, including logs, backups and temporary files. The method is hash, truncation, token or strong cryptography.

tests.title: Check that hashed and truncated copies of one PAN cannot be correlated
tests.obj: Find environments where a hash and a truncated value of the same PAN let a person rebuild the PAN.
pre: Test PANs
Access to the data stores
steps: Find out if the same PAN is stored in both a hashed form and a truncated form.
Ask for the controls that stop the correlation of these two forms.
Try to join the hashed records and the truncated records to rebuild the PAN.
Make sure the access rights to the two data sets are separate.
Make sure the hash does not replace the truncated part of the PAN.
tests.ex: Join test records on the last four digits and the BIN; try a brute force of the missing digits against the hash
tests.exp: No user or process can rebuild the original PAN from the hashed and truncated copies. Access to the two forms is separate.

tests.title: Check that PAN hashes are keyed cryptographic hashes of the whole PAN
tests.obj: Find PAN hashes that use no key, a weak hash function or only part of the PAN.
pre: Test PANs
Source code or configuration access
steps: Find the code or the database function that hashes the PAN.
Make sure the hash is a keyed hash such as HMAC-SHA-256 and covers the entire PAN.
Make sure the key is not in the code or in the same data store as the hashes.
Compute a plain SHA-256 of a test PAN. Make sure it does not match the stored hash.
Examine the key management process for the hash key.
tests.ex: echo -n <test PAN> | sha256sum; compare to the stored value; search the source for the HMAC key
tests.exp: PAN hashes are keyed hashes of the entire PAN. The key is managed under the key management rules and a plain hash does not match.

tests.title: Check that disk or partition encryption alone does not protect stored PAN
tests.obj: Find non-removable storage where only disk-level or partition-level encryption protects the PAN.
pre: Access to the host and storage configuration
steps: List the storage that holds PAN and the encryption method on each volume.
Find volumes that use only disk-level or partition-level encryption.
Make sure these volumes are removable media.
For non-removable volumes, make sure file-level, column-level or field-level encryption also protects the PAN.
Mount a volume on a running system and read a PAN file as a normal user.
tests.ex: lsblk -f; cryptsetup status <volume>; SELECT column-level encryption settings in the database
tests.exp: Disk-level or partition-level encryption is used alone only on removable media. Other storage also has file, column or field-level protection.

tests.title: Check the management of disk and partition encryption for PAN
tests.obj: Find disk encryption where the operating system login or a user account unlocks the data.
pre: Access to the host and encryption configuration
steps: Find the access control for the disk encryption product.
Make sure logical access is managed apart from the operating system login and access control.
Make sure the decryption keys are not tied to user accounts.
Find where the unlock passphrase or key is stored. Make sure the storage is secure.
Log in as an operating system administrator. Try to read the data without the separate unlock factor.
tests.ex: cryptsetup luksDump <device>; check the key slots; check the TPM and key escrow settings
tests.exp: Access to the decryption is separate from the operating system accounts. Keys are not tied to user accounts and unlock factors are stored securely.

tests.title: Check that keys for stored account data resist disclosure and misuse
tests.obj: Find keys that protect stored account data and that people or processes can read or use without a need.
pre: Access to the key management system
steps: Ask for the procedures that protect the keys used to encrypt stored account data.
List all data-encrypting keys and key-encrypting keys with their owners and uses.
Examine who and what can read each key and who and what can call it for decrypt operations.
Make sure each key has one purpose and the application can use it only through its own identity.
Look at the key use logs for calls from unknown identities.
tests.ex: aws kms get-key-policy; vault policy read; openssl list key stores; review HSM partition roles
tests.exp: The procedures protect the keys against disclosure and misuse. Only named identities with a need can use or read each key.

tests.title: Check the cryptographic architecture document of the service provider
tests.obj: Find service providers with no current description of the cryptography that protects account data.
pre: Service provider scope
steps: Ask for the cryptographic architecture document.
Make sure it lists the algorithms, protocols, key strengths and the key expiry date.
Make sure it names each key with its purpose and where it is used.
Make sure it lists each hardware security module and other secure cryptographic device.
Compare five entries with the real systems.
tests.ex: Document review; compare with the cryptographic inventory and the key store export
tests.exp: A current document describes the algorithms, protocols, key strengths, key uses, expiry dates and secure devices. The document matches the real systems.

tests.title: Check that secret and private keys are stored only in approved forms
tests.obj: Find data-encrypting keys that are stored in clear text next to the data they protect.
pre: Access to the hosts and the key store
steps: List where each secret and private key for account data is stored.
Make sure each key has a key-encrypting key, a secure cryptographic device or split key components.
Make sure the key-encrypting key is at least as strong as the key it protects.
Make sure the key-encrypting key is stored apart from the data-encrypting key.
Search configuration files, code and environment variables for a clear-text key.
tests.ex: grep -rE 'BEGIN (RSA |EC )?PRIVATE KEY' /app /etc; check the HSM or KMS key wrapping settings
tests.exp: Every secret and private key exists only as an encrypted key, in a secure cryptographic device, or as split components. The key-encrypting key is separate.

tests.title: Check that few custodians can access clear-text key components
tests.obj: Find clear-text key components that too many people can reach.
pre: Access to key management records
steps: Ask for the list of key custodians and the key components each person holds.
Compare the list with the key ceremony records and the access list of the key store.
Make sure no person has access to a full clear-text key unless the process needs it.
Make sure each custodian has a documented role and a business need.
Look for custodians who changed role or left the company.
tests.ex: Review the key custodian list, the HSM smart card holders and the key ceremony logs
tests.exp: Only the fewest necessary custodians can access clear-text key components. Each custodian has a documented need and the list is current.

tests.title: Check that keys exist in the fewest possible places
tests.obj: Find copies of cryptographic keys in extra places such as backups, build servers and developer systems.
pre: Access to the hosts and repositories
steps: Ask for the list of approved key storage locations.
Search the production hosts, the backup media, the code repositories and the build servers for key files.
Search developer systems and shared drives for exported keys.
Compare the result with the approved list.
Make sure each extra copy has a documented reason.
tests.ex: find / -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.p12' -o -name '*.jks' 2>/dev/null; gitleaks detect
tests.exp: Keys exist only in the approved locations. No unneeded copy exists in backups, code repositories or on developer systems.

tests.title: Check that strong keys are generated for account data protection
tests.obj: Find keys that are weak, predictable or made with a poor random source.
pre: Access to the key generation system
steps: Ask for the key generation procedure.
Make sure the keys come from a validated random number generator in a hardware module or a vetted library.
Make sure the key length meets current industry guidance for the algorithm.
Generate a test key by the procedure and examine the algorithm and length.
Search for keys that came from a password or a fixed seed.
tests.ex: openssl rand -hex 32; aws kms describe-key; pkcs11-tool --list-mechanisms
tests.exp: Keys are made with a validated random source in a secure device or vetted library. Key lengths meet current industry guidance.

tests.title: Check that keys are distributed in a secure way
tests.obj: Find key distribution that sends keys in clear text or over open channels.
pre: Access to the key management records
steps: Ask for the key distribution procedure.
Follow one key from the generation point to the system that uses it.
Look at each hop. Make sure the key is wrapped or split during transfer.
Search e-mail, chat, tickets and shared drives for clear-text keys.
Make sure only the intended recipient can unwrap the key.
tests.ex: Trace a key import into the HSM; capture the transfer; search the ticket system for 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY'
tests.exp: Keys move only in encrypted or split form between authorized systems and custodians. No key travels in clear text.

tests.title: Check that keys change at the end of their cryptoperiod
tests.obj: Find keys that stay in use after the end of the defined cryptoperiod.
pre: Access to the key store and the key policy
steps: Ask for the cryptoperiod of each key type and the reason for its length.
Look at the creation date and last rotation date of each key.
Find keys that are older than their cryptoperiod.
Make sure the process also changes a key when a compromise is suspected.
Do a test rotation. Make sure the application still reads the old data.
tests.ex: aws kms list-keys --query ... ; vault read transit/keys/<name>; compare the creation date to the policy
tests.exp: Each key changes at the end of its defined cryptoperiod or at a suspected compromise. No key is older than its cryptoperiod.

tests.title: Check that retired keys are destroyed or archived under protection
tests.obj: Find old keys that stay active, readable or unprotected after they are retired.
pre: Access to the key store and the key log
steps: Ask for the procedure to retire, replace or destroy keys.
Pick five retired keys from the key log.
Make sure each key is destroyed, or kept only for decryption of old data in a protected archive.
Make sure keys with known or suspected weakness are replaced.
Make sure a retired key cannot encrypt new data.
tests.ex: Check the key state in the KMS (disabled, pending deletion); search backups for the retired key files
tests.exp: Retired and replaced keys are destroyed or archived under protection. A retired key cannot protect new data.

tests.title: Check split knowledge and dual control for manual clear-text key operations
tests.obj: Find manual key operations that one person can do alone.
pre: Manual key operations exist in scope
steps: Find all manual operations on clear-text keys, such as load, export and import.
Ask for the procedure for each operation.
Make sure the procedure uses split knowledge and dual control.
Look at the records of the last two key ceremonies for two named custodians.
Make sure one custodian alone cannot complete the operation.
tests.ex: Review the HSM quorum settings (M of N); review the key ceremony records
tests.exp: Each manual clear-text key operation needs split knowledge and dual control. One person cannot complete it alone.

tests.title: Check that nobody can replace a key without approval
tests.obj: Find ways to put an unauthorized key in place of a valid key.
pre: Test key and test account in the key store
steps: Ask for the controls that prevent unauthorized key substitution.
Examine who can import, replace or alias a key in the key store.
Try to replace a test key as a user without the key administrator role.
Make sure the key store logs each import, replace and alias change.
Make sure a person other than the requester must approve the change.
tests.ex: aws kms update-alias test; vault write transit/keys/test/import; check the audit log for the event
tests.exp: Only authorized key administrators can replace a key. Each change needs approval and creates a log entry.

tests.title: Check that a service provider documents key sharing with its customers
tests.obj: Find service providers that share keys with customers without guidance on how to handle the keys.
pre: Service provider scope
steps: Find out if the provider shares keys with customers for transmission or storage of account data.
Ask for the key management guidance that the provider gives to the customers.
Make sure the guidance covers secure transmission, storage and update of the shared keys.
Make sure it follows the key management rules for generation, distribution, storage, change and retirement.
Compare the guidance with how the provider shares a real key.
tests.ex: Document review of the customer onboarding and key exchange procedure
tests.exp: The provider gives customers guidance on how to handle shared keys. The guidance covers the full key lifecycle.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record all individual access to cardholder data
tests.obj: Find reads and changes of cardholder data that leave no audit record.
pre: Test user account
Test cardholder record
steps: List the applications and data stores that hold cardholder data.
Log in as a test user. View, export, change and delete a test cardholder record.
Look at the audit log for one entry for each action.
Make sure each entry names the user and the record.
Do the same through the API and by a direct database query.
tests.ex: Application audit trail query; database audit log (pgaudit, Oracle audit, SQL Server audit); API gateway logs
tests.exp: Each individual access to cardholder data creates an audit log entry that names the user, action and record.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record all actions of administrative users
tests.obj: Find administrative actions, including interactive use of service accounts, that leave no record.
pre: Test administrative account
steps: List the administrative roles and the accounts with administrative access.
Log in as an administrator on a test system. Change a setting, add a user and run a privileged command.
Do the same with a service account if interactive use is possible.
Look at the logs for one entry for each action.
Make sure the entry shows the person behind a shared or service account.
tests.ex: sudo log; auditd rules for execve by uid 0; cloud audit trail; database admin audit
tests.exp: Every action of an administrative user is logged, including interactive use of application and system accounts.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record all access to the audit logs
tests.obj: Find reads and changes of the audit logs that leave no record.
pre: Test account with log access
steps: Find where the audit logs are stored and who can reach them.
As a test user with log access, open a log file or query the log platform.
Try to change a setting of the log platform.
Look at the audit trail of the log system for one entry for each action.
Make sure the entry names the user.
tests.ex: Log platform audit trail; file access auditing on the log directory; object store access logs
tests.exp: All access to the audit logs creates an entry that names the user and the action.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record changes to credentials and authentication factors
tests.obj: Find changes to identities, factors and privileges that leave no record.
pre: Test account and test administrator
steps: Use a test account to create an ID, change a password and enrol a factor. Remove a factor and change a privilege.
Look at the audit log for one entry for each action.
Make sure the entry names the person who made the change and the affected account.
Make sure the entry never holds the password or the secret.
Include elevation of privilege and add or change of administrator rights.
tests.ex: Directory service event IDs 4720, 4723, 4724, 4728; application audit trail; identity provider event log
tests.exp: Each addition, change or deletion of an identity or an authentication factor and each privilege elevation is logged without secrets.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record the start, stop and pause of logging
tests.obj: Find ways to stop or pause logging without a record.
pre: Test system. Do not run on production.
steps: Find the logging agents and log services on a test system.
Stop the logging service, then start it again.
Pause or change the audit configuration if the system allows it.
Look in the central log system for an entry for each of these events.
Make sure a new log file or new log source also creates an entry.
tests.ex: systemctl stop auditd; auditctl -e 0; Windows event 1100 and 1102; check the central log
tests.exp: Every start, stop, pause and initialization of an audit log creates a log entry that is stored in a protected place.

tests.title: Check that audit logs record creation and deletion of system-level objects
tests.obj: Find system-level objects that appear or vanish with no record.
pre: Test system
steps: List the system-level objects of the platform, such as database tables, stored procedures, scheduled jobs and services.
On a test system, create a scheduled job, a database object and a service. Then delete them.
Look at the audit log for one entry for each action.
Make sure the entry names the user and the object.
Include object creation by a cloud API.
tests.ex: auditd watch rules; SQL DDL audit; Windows event 4698 and 7045; cloud audit trail for resource creation
tests.exp: The creation and deletion of each system-level object creates an audit log entry with the user and the object name.

tests.title: Check that file integrity or change detection alerts on audit log changes
tests.obj: Find audit log changes that raise no alert.
pre: Test system. Do not run on production.
steps: Find the file integrity monitoring or change-detection tool that covers the audit logs.
Make sure it covers all log locations, including the central log store.
On a test system, change an old entry in a log file. Delete a log file.
Make sure the tool raises an alert in the agreed time.
Make sure normal appends of new entries do not raise an alert.
tests.ex: AIDE or Tripwire configuration; OSSEC syscheck; object lock plus hash chain; echo test >> old.log
tests.exp: A tool alerts personnel when existing log data is changed or deleted. Normal additions do not raise an alert.

tests.title: Check the daily review of security and cardholder data system logs
tests.obj: Find security event logs and critical system logs that no one reviews every day.
pre: Access to review records
steps: Ask for the list of logs that need a daily review and the review procedure.
Make sure it covers security events, systems that handle cardholder data, critical systems and security functions.
Pick seven days in the last 30 days. Find the review record for each day.
Make sure the record shows who reviewed the logs.
Make sure the review covers each log on the list.
tests.ex: SIEM dashboard review records; ticket log; shift handover notes
tests.exp: All security events and logs of in-scope and critical systems are reviewed at least once a day, with a record.

tests.title: Check that automated mechanisms do the log review
tests.obj: Find log review that depends on manual work only.
pre: Access to the log review system
steps: Find the automated mechanisms that review logs, such as a SIEM or log analysis tool.
Make sure the mechanisms cover the logs that need a daily review.
Send a test event that should match a rule.
Make sure the mechanism raises an alert or a finding.
Examine the rules and the update dates.
tests.ex: SIEM correlation rules; alert history; use case list
tests.exp: Automated mechanisms review the required logs. They raise findings for test events and the rules are current.

tests.title: Check the periodic review of other system component logs
tests.obj: Find logs of other components that no one reviews, or a review frequency with no risk analysis.
pre: Access to review records
steps: Ask for the list of the other system components that are not in the daily review.
Find the targeted risk analysis that sets the review frequency.
Make sure the frequency in the procedure matches the analysis.
Find the review records for the last period.
Make sure all components on the list have records.
tests.ex: Targeted risk analysis document; review schedule; review tickets
tests.exp: The logs of other components are reviewed at the frequency in the targeted risk analysis. Records exist for each component.

tests.title: Check that exceptions found in log reviews are addressed
tests.obj: Find anomalies from log reviews that nobody handles.
pre: Access to tickets
steps: Pick five anomalies or exceptions that log reviews found in the last 90 days.
Find the ticket or incident for each one.
Make sure each was investigated and resolved or accepted by an authorized person.
Compare the time to resolve with the procedure.
Look for reviews that found nothing for a long time and ask why.
tests.ex: Ticket system; incident log; SIEM case history
tests.exp: Each exception and anomaly from a log review is investigated and closed or accepted, with a record.

tests.title: Check that audit logs are kept 12 months, with 3 months online
tests.obj: Find audit logs that are kept too short or that need a long restore to read.
pre: Access to the log platform
steps: Ask for the log retention policy.
Make sure it states at least 12 months of history.
Look at the oldest log record in the log store. Make sure it is at least 12 months old.
Run a search for the last three months. Make sure the result comes back at once.
Restore a record from an older period and make sure it is complete.
tests.ex: SIEM retention setting; S3 lifecycle rule; log index list; query the date range
tests.exp: Audit log history for at least 12 months exists. The most recent three months are immediately available for analysis.

tests.title: Check that systems use trusted time sources and the same time
tests.obj: Find systems that take time from an untrusted source or drift apart.
pre: Access to system time settings
steps: Find the time sources of each class of system in scope.
Make sure systems use designated central time servers, and those servers use industry-accepted time sources.
Make sure the time servers accept time only from the approved sources.
Compare the clock offset of ten systems.
Make sure systems peer with each other only through the designated time servers.
tests.ex: chronyc sources -v; ntpq -p; w32tm /query /status; compare date -u across hosts
tests.exp: Systems get time from designated central servers with industry-accepted sources. The clocks on all systems are consistent.

tests.title: Check that time settings and time data are protected
tests.obj: Find time settings that unauthorized persons can read or change.
pre: Test system. Do not run on production.
steps: List who can read and change the time settings and the time data on critical systems.
Make sure access is limited to personnel with a business need.
On a test system, change the time as an ordinary user. Make sure it fails.
Change a time setting as an administrator. Make sure it creates a log entry.
Make sure the log entry is monitored and reviewed.
tests.ex: chrony.conf permissions; Windows event 4616; auditd rule for settimeofday and clock_settime
tests.exp: Only personnel with a business need can reach time data. Changes to time settings on critical systems are logged, monitored and reviewed.

tests.title: Check that failures of critical security controls raise alerts
tests.obj: Find control failures that no one notices.
pre: Test system. Do not run on production.
steps: List the critical security control systems: network controls, IDS or IPS, change detection, anti-malware, access control and audit logging.
Include audit log review tools, segmentation controls and automated security test tools if used.
On a test system, stop one control. Make sure an alert reaches the response team in the agreed time.
Repeat for each type of control on the list.
Look at the last alert history for real failures.
tests.ex: Stop the agent or service on a test system; check the monitoring alert; heartbeat monitor configuration
tests.exp: A failure of each critical security control creates an alert that reaches personnel promptly.

tests.title: Check the response to failures of critical security controls
tests.obj: Find control failures that stay open or have no cause analysis.
pre: Access to incident records
