steps: Pick three real failures of critical security controls from the last 12 months.
Make sure each control was restored.
Make sure the record shows the cause, the duration and the security gap during the failure.
Make sure the record shows that the team looked for new risks and fixed the cause.
Make sure the monitoring resumed and the failure was recorded.
tests.ex: Incident tickets; post-incident reviews; control uptime reports
tests.exp: Each failure is answered with a restore of the control, a root cause record, a check for security issues and a fix.

tests.title: Check the targeted risk analysis behind flexible requirement frequencies
tests.obj: Find requirements with a risk-based frequency that has no documented analysis.
pre: Access to risk analysis records
steps: List the requirements where the entity sets its own frequency, such as log review and password change.
Ask for the targeted risk analysis document for each one.
Make sure each document names the assets, the threats, the likelihood and the review date.
Make sure each document sets the frequency and the reason.
Make sure a person reviewed the analysis in the last 12 months.
tests.ex: Targeted risk analysis records; compare the frequency in the procedure with the analysis
tests.exp: A current targeted risk analysis supports every risk-based frequency. Each analysis states the threats, the reason for the frequency and the review date.

tests.title: Check scans after a significant change and rescans of fixed findings
tests.obj: Find significant changes that go live with no vulnerability scan.
pre: Access to scan reports
steps: Ask for the definition of a significant change.
Pick two significant changes from the last 12 months.
Find an internal and an external vulnerability scan after each change.
Make sure high-risk and critical findings were fixed and rescanned.
Make sure the scan was done by qualified persons who are independent of the change.
tests.ex: Change record; scan report dates; rescan reports
tests.exp: Internal and external scans run after each significant change. High-risk and critical findings are fixed and rescanned.

tests.title: Check that approved scanning vendor scans pass every quarter
tests.obj: Find external scans that are missing, not from an approved vendor, or not passing.
pre: Access to ASV reports
steps: Ask for the ASV scan reports of the last 12 months.
Make sure at least one scan exists for each three-month period.
Make sure each scan came from a PCI SSC approved scanning vendor.
Make sure the scan has a passing status or the failed findings were fixed and rescanned.
Compare the scanned addresses with the list of public addresses in scope.
tests.ex: ASV attestation of scan compliance; scan scope list compared to the external address inventory
tests.exp: An approved scanning vendor scanned every in-scope public address once every three months. The latest scans pass.

tests.title: Check that bespoke software follows a secure development process
tests.obj: Find development processes that ignore industry standards, PCI DSS needs or security in the life cycle phases.
pre: Access to development records
steps: Ask for the secure development procedures for bespoke and custom software.
Make sure they follow an industry standard or best practice for secure development.
Make sure they cover PCI DSS needs such as secure authentication and logging.
Make sure each phase of the life cycle has a security task.
Pick one recent release and find the records of each security task.
tests.ex: Compare the procedure with OWASP SAMM or NIST SSDF; examine tickets, design reviews and test reports of one release
tests.exp: The procedures follow an industry standard and PCI DSS. Each life cycle phase has a security task and the last release has the records.

tests.title: Check that code is reviewed before release and findings are fixed
tests.obj: Find releases of bespoke software that reach production without a code review for vulnerabilities.
pre: Access to the code review records
steps: Ask for the code review procedure for bespoke and custom software.
Make sure it requires review against secure coding guidelines before each release.
Make sure the review looks for both existing and new types of software vulnerabilities.
Pick five recent releases. Find the review record for each one.
Make sure each finding was corrected before the release.
tests.ex: Pull request history; SAST reports; ticket links between the findings and the fix commits
tests.exp: Every release has a completed code review against the secure coding guidelines. Findings are corrected before release.

tests.title: Check that manual code reviews use independent reviewers and approval
tests.obj: Find manual code reviews done by the author or released without management approval.
pre: Access to the repository settings
steps: Ask who does manual code reviews and what skills they have.
Pick five reviews. Make sure the reviewer is not the author.
Make sure the reviewers know code review methods and secure coding practices.
Make sure management reviewed and approved the results before release.
Try to merge a change with no approval on a test copy.
tests.ex: Branch protection settings; pull request approval rules; review checklist
tests.exp: Reviewers know the methods, are not the author, and management approves the results before each release.

tests.title: Check the documented methods that prevent each common software attack
tests.obj: Find attack classes that have no defined technique for prevention in the development procedure.
pre: Access to development procedures and developers
steps: Ask for the documented techniques for bespoke software developers.
Make sure they cover injection attacks, attacks on data and data structures, and attacks on cryptography use.
Make sure they cover attacks on business logic, attacks on access control and other high-risk vulnerabilities.
Interview two developers. Ask how they prevent an injection attack and a broken access control.
Run the existing tests for each attack class and record the result.
tests.ex: Compare the procedure to the sheet tests WEB-INJ, WEB-XSS, WEB-CRYPTO, WEB-BIZ and WEB-AUTHZ
tests.exp: Defined methods cover each attack class. Developers can name and use them, and the test results show they work.

tests.title: Check that security vulnerabilities are found and ranked by risk
tests.obj: Find missing sources of vulnerability data or missing risk ranking for high-risk vulnerabilities.
pre: Access to vulnerability management records
steps: Ask for the process that finds new security vulnerabilities.
Make sure it uses industry-recognized sources, including alerts from national and international CERTs.
Make sure each vulnerability gets a risk rank by industry practice and potential impact.
Make sure the ranks identify at least all high-risk and critical vulnerabilities.
Make sure the process covers bespoke software and third-party software such as operating systems and databases.
tests.ex: Examine the vulnerability tracker; look at the CVSS and local risk fields; examine the subscription list of advisory feeds
tests.exp: New vulnerabilities come from recognized sources. Each one gets a risk rank, and high-risk and critical items are identified for bespoke and third-party software.

tests.title: Check the inventory of bespoke software and third-party components
tests.obj: Find software and components that are not in the inventory, so no one patches them.
pre: Access to the build files of two applications
steps: Ask for the inventory of bespoke and custom software and the third-party components in it.
Compare the inventory with the build files, lock files and deployed packages of two applications.
Make sure each entry shows version and owner.
Pick one recent advisory. Find the affected component in the inventory within one hour.
Make sure the inventory is updated when components change.
tests.ex: SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format; npm ls, pip freeze, mvn dependency:tree compared to the inventory
tests.exp: A current inventory lists all bespoke software and third-party components with versions. The team uses it to find and fix vulnerabilities.

tests.title: Check the method that addresses new threats on public web applications
tests.obj: Find public web applications with no ongoing review for new threats and vulnerabilities.
pre: List of public web applications
steps: List the public-facing web applications.
Find out which method is used: a vulnerability assessment or an automated technical solution.
For an assessment, make sure it runs at least every 12 months and after significant changes.
Make sure the assessment uses tools or manual methods that find the current attacks, and that fixes are made.
For an automated solution, make sure the test of the web application firewall settings is on file.
tests.ex: Application assessment reports and dates; DAST scan schedule; manual penetration test report
tests.exp: Every public web application has a defined method for new threats. Assessments are recent, cover current attacks and lead to fixes.

tests.title: Check that an automated solution detects and blocks web attacks
tests.obj: Find public web applications with no web application firewall or one that is in log-only mode with no review.
pre: Test window agreed with the owner
steps: List the public-facing web applications and the web attack solution in front of each.
Make sure the solution is in front of the application and in block mode, or alerts are reviewed at once.
Make sure the rule sets and signatures are up to date.
Send a test SQL injection and a test XSS string. Make sure the solution blocks or alerts.
Make sure the solution writes audit logs and personnel review the alerts.
tests.ex: curl 'https://app.example/?q=<script>alert(1)</script>' ; curl "https://app.example/?id=1' OR '1'='1" ; review WAF logs
tests.exp: A maintained solution sits in front of each public web application and writes audit logs. It blocks attacks, or an alert is investigated at once.

tests.title: Check that payment page scripts are authorized and protected from tampering
tests.obj: Find scripts on the payment page that are not authorized, not checked for integrity or not in the inventory.
pre: Test copy of the payment page
Access to the script inventory
steps: Open the payment page in a browser. List all scripts that load, including third-party and fourth-party scripts.
Compare the list with the inventory of payment page scripts.
Make sure each script has a written business or technical reason and an authorization record.
Make sure each script has an integrity control such as Subresource Integrity or a Content-Security-Policy with hashes or nonces.
Change a script on a test copy. Make sure the page blocks or reports the change.
tests.ex: Browser developer tools network tab; Content-Security-Policy header review; integrity attribute check; compare the script list with the inventory
tests.exp: Every payment page script is in the inventory with a reason and an authorization. An integrity control blocks or reports a changed script.

tests.title: Check that tamper detection watches payment page headers and scripts
tests.obj: Find payment pages where a change to the HTTP headers or scripts raises no alert.
pre: Test copy of the payment page
steps: Find the change- and tamper-detection mechanism for the payment pages.
Make sure it evaluates the headers and the scripts as the consumer browser receives them.
Make sure it runs at least weekly, or at the frequency in the targeted risk analysis.
Change a security header and a script on a test copy. Make sure the mechanism alerts personnel.
Look at the alert record. Make sure personnel investigated the alert.
tests.ex: Monitor that fetches the page with a headless browser and compares header and script hashes; review the alert log
tests.exp: A mechanism checks the received headers and scripts at least weekly. It alerts personnel to unauthorized changes, additions and deletions.

tests.title: Check the inventory of trusted keys and certificates for PAN transmission
tests.obj: Find certificates and keys that protect PAN in transit and that no one tracks.
pre: Access to the inventory
steps: Ask for the inventory of trusted keys and certificates used to protect PAN in transit.
Scan the public and internal endpoints that carry PAN. Compare each certificate with the inventory.
Make sure each entry has an owner, an issuer and an expiry date.
Find certificates that expire within 30 days.
Make sure a process updates the inventory when a certificate changes.
tests.ex: nmap --script ssl-cert -p443 <host>; certificate lifecycle tool export; compare to the inventory
tests.exp: A current inventory lists all trusted keys and certificates for PAN in transit. Each has an owner and an expiry date, and none is missing.

tests.title: Check that PAN sent through messaging tools is protected or blocked
tests.obj: Find PAN in clear text in e-mail, chat, SMS or other end-user messaging.
pre: Test PAN
Test accounts on each channel
steps: Ask whether policy allows PAN in end-user messaging.
Make sure the policy forbids unprotected PAN, or requires strong cryptography.
Send a test message that holds a test PAN on each channel in use.
Make sure a data loss control blocks the message or encrypts it.
Search sent mail and chat archives for PAN patterns.
tests.ex: Mail gateway DLP rule test with 4111111111111111; chat DLP policy review
tests.exp: A control blocks PAN in end-user messaging or requires strong cryptography. No unprotected PAN is in messaging archives.

tests.title: Review the account lifecycle from creation to removal
tests.obj: Finds accounts that stay active after the person or service no longer needs them.
pre: Admin read access and a test account request process. Do not use real user accounts.
steps: List the account types: individual, group, role, service, guest, temporary and emergency.
Read the rules for who may approve, create, change and remove each account type.
Create a test account and follow the approval steps.
Change the roles of the test account and disable it.
Remove the test account and look for left-over sessions, tokens, keys and shared objects.
tests.ex: Compare the account export with the HR or ticket list: aws iam generate-credential-report; ldapsearch -b DC=corp -s sub '(objectClass=user)' lastLogon
tests.exp: Each account has an owner and an approval record. Disabled accounts cannot log in, and their tokens and sessions stop working at once.

tests.title: Check that temporary, emergency and inactive accounts end by themselves
tests.obj: Finds accounts and grants that never expire because only a person can remove them.
pre: Admin access to the user store and a way to move the system clock or wait.
steps: Find the accounts and grants that have a set end date.
Create a temporary account with a short life and wait until it ends.
Try to log in with the temporary account after the end time.
List accounts with no logon for the period that the policy sets.
Make sure the system disables each inactive account within the policy time.
tests.ex: Check last logon: aws iam get-credential-report; Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate; psql -c 'select rolname,rolvaliduntil from pg_roles'
tests.exp: Temporary and emergency accounts stop working at the end time. Inactive accounts are disabled within the policy time and the system records the change.

tests.title: Check that every account management action is written to the audit log
tests.obj: Finds account changes that leave no record, so misuse cannot be traced.
pre: Admin access and a test account. Use a test system.
steps: Create, change, enable, disable and remove a test account.
Add and remove a role of the test account.
Read the audit log for each of the actions.
Make sure each record names the actor, the target account, the time and the result.
tests.ex: Search the audit log for the test account name; for example grep -i TESTUSER /var/log/audit/audit.log; aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=TESTUSER
tests.exp: Each account management action has one audit record with the actor, the target, the time and the result.

tests.title: Review how privileged roles are assigned, watched and revoked
tests.obj: Finds privileged accounts with no owner, no review or no alert on role changes.
pre: Admin read access and a test account.
steps: List all accounts that hold a privileged or security role.
Compare the list with the approved list of people for each role.
Add a test account to a privileged role.
Look for an alert or a record of the role change.
Remove the role and make sure the access ends.
tests.ex: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide; aws iam list-entities-for-policy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess; net localgroup administrators
tests.exp: Only approved people hold privileged roles. Each role change creates a record and an alert, and a removed role ends the access at once.

tests.title: Check that each process and service runs with least privilege
tests.obj: Finds services that run as root or administrator or hold more rights than their task needs.
pre: Shell or console access to a test host with read rights.
steps: List the processes and services of the system and the account of each.
Read the file, network and system rights of each account.
Find rights that the documented task does not need.
Run a function that needs a high right as an ordinary user.
Make sure the system refuses the function.
tests.ex: ps -eo user,pid,cmd | grep -v '^root' ; sc qc SERVICE; systemd-analyze security UNIT; getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
tests.exp: No process runs with more rights than its task needs. Ordinary users cannot start privileged functions or raise their own privilege.

tests.title: Check the logon failure limit and the way to unlock an account
tests.obj: Finds logons that allow unlimited guesses, or a lockout that an attacker can use to block users.
pre: A test account. Do not run on production. Agree the lockout effect with the owner.
steps: Read the failed logon limit and the lockout or delay rule for each logon interface.
Send wrong passwords for one test account until the limit is reached.
Send the correct password after the limit and look at the response.
Try the alternate factor or the unlock path that the system offers.
Make sure the unlock path has its own limit of tries.
tests.ex: hydra -l TESTUSER -P short.txt -t 1 https://HOST/login; check Retry-After headers and the lockout events in the log
tests.exp: The system limits consecutive failed logons and then delays or locks the account. The unlock path has a limit and a record.

tests.title: Check the system use notice before logon
tests.obj: Finds logon screens that show no required legal, privacy or monitoring notice.
pre: Approved notice text from the owner of the system.
steps: Find the notice text that the policy requires for each logon interface.
Open each interface: web, console, SSH, API portal and admin tool.
Look for the notice before the credential fields.
Make sure the user must accept the notice, or can read it, before access starts.
tests.ex: ssh -v HOST (look for Banner text); curl -s https://HOST/login | grep -i notice; sshd_config: Banner /etc/issue.net
tests.exp: Each logon interface shows the approved notice before access. The text is the same as the approved text.

tests.title: Check that the user sees the last logon date and time
tests.obj: Finds systems that cannot show a user that someone else used the account.
pre: A test account and two devices.
steps: Log in with a test account and note the time.
Log out and log in again.
Look for the time and the place of the last successful logon on screen.
Look for the count of failed logons since the last success.
Make sure the data is correct when you log in from a second device.
tests.ex: SSH: PrintLastLog yes in sshd_config; web: look at the account security page; Windows: policy DisplayLastLogonInfo
tests.exp: After logon the user sees the correct time and place of the last logon. The user can see failed logons since then.

tests.title: Check the session lock and that it hides the screen content
tests.obj: Finds sessions that stay open on an unattended device and show data to other people.
pre: A client that has a lock function. Use a test account.
steps: Read the idle time after which the session must lock.
Leave a test session idle until the lock starts.
Look at the screen and make sure it shows no application data.
Try to use the session without new credentials.
Unlock with valid credentials and make sure the work state is kept.
tests.ex: Windows: InactivityTimeoutSecs; Linux: gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay; web client: leave tab idle and send a request
tests.exp: The session locks after the set idle time and hides the content. Access returns only after the user proves identity again.

tests.title: Check the timeout warning and the logout message
tests.obj: Finds sessions that end without a warning or leave the user unsure if the session is closed.
pre: A test account.
steps: Read the idle limit and the overall limit of the session.
Use a test session and wait for the warning time.
Look for a message that tells the user when the session ends.
Let the session end and look for an explicit logout message.
Log out with the logout button and look for the same message.
tests.ex: Browser: wait for the idle limit with the developer tools open; look for a 401 response and the logout page text
tests.exp: The user gets a warning before the session ends and an explicit message when it ends. The session cannot be used after that.

tests.title: Check the audited emergency override of access control
tests.obj: Finds break-glass paths that bypass access control with no approval, limit or record.
pre: Agreement of the system owner. Do not run on production.
steps: Find the break-glass or emergency access paths of the system.
Read who may start each path and under which condition.
Start the path with a test case.
Make sure the system limits the time and the scope of the override.
Look for audit records and an alert for the start and the end.
tests.ex: Check break-glass accounts in the IdP; kubectl auth can-i --list --as=EMERGENCY-USER; read the vault emergency policy
tests.exp: Only named people can start the override. It ends by itself, and the system records and reports each use.

tests.title: Check that sharing and delegation of access follows the policy
tests.obj: Finds users who can pass access to other people or change access rules for their own objects without limit.
pre: Two test accounts and one test object.
steps: List the functions that let a user share an object or grant rights to others.
Share a test object with a second test user.
Try to share the object with a user outside the allowed group.
Let the second user share the object again.
Look for audit records of the sharing and the changes of rights.
tests.ex: Test share links and ACL changes: curl -X POST https://HOST/api/files/ID/share -d '{"user":"OUTSIDER"}'
tests.exp: Users share only inside the limits of the policy. The system records each grant and each change, and the owner can revoke it.

tests.title: Check who can change which events the system logs
tests.obj: Finds logging settings that any admin or process can lower without a record.
pre: Admin read access and a test system.
steps: Read the list of event types that the policy requires the system to log.
Compare the list with the active logging settings of each component.
List the roles that can change the logging settings.
Change one logging setting with a test account and look at the audit log.
Make sure a role without the right cannot change the setting.
tests.ex: auditctl -l; kubectl get cm audit-policy -o yaml; aws cloudtrail get-event-selectors --trail-name TRAIL
tests.exp: Active logging covers all required event types. Only named roles can change the settings, and each change creates an audit record.

tests.title: Check the audit log storage size and the capacity warning
tests.obj: Finds logs that fill the disk and stop, or that lose old records with no warning.
pre: A test log volume. Do not fill production storage.
steps: Read the space set aside for audit logs and the rate of new records.
Calculate how long the space lasts at the peak rate.
Read the warning level for the storage and the receiver of the warning.
Fill a test log volume to the warning level and look for the alert.
Make sure the retention time still holds when the volume is full.
tests.ex: df -h /var/log; journalctl --disk-usage; check Elasticsearch disk watermark settings and alert rules
tests.exp: The storage holds the retention time at peak load. A warning reaches the named receiver before the storage is full.

tests.title: Check the response when audit logging fails
tests.obj: Finds systems that go on with no audit trail, or stop in a way that is easy to abuse, when logging fails.
pre: A test system. Do not run on production.
steps: Read the rule for what the system does when it cannot write audit records.
Stop the log agent or block the log target on a test system.
Do a security-relevant action and see if the system works as the rule says.
Look for an alert about the logging failure.
Restore logging and look for a gap record or a backlog.
tests.ex: systemctl stop auditd; iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 514 -j DROP; then look at the alert channel and the buffer
tests.exp: A logging failure creates an alert at once. The system follows the written rule and keeps a buffer, and no records are lost silently.

tests.title: Check audit record search and that reports keep the originals
tests.obj: Finds logs that cannot be searched for an incident, or reports that change the original records.
pre: Read access to the log platform.
steps: Pick a test event from the last day and note its time and actor.
Search the audit records for the event by user, time and event type.
Create a report from the search result.
Compare the original record before and after the report.
Make sure the time order of the original records is unchanged.
tests.ex: Search in SIEM: user=TESTUSER AND action=login earliest=-24h; sha256sum the raw log file before and after the report
tests.exp: The reviewer finds the test event with the search fields. Report tools read the records and do not change their content or order.

tests.title: Check the security impact analysis before a change
tests.obj: Finds changes that go live without an analysis of their effect on security.
pre: Read access to the change records.
steps: Pick five recent changes: one each of code, settings, infrastructure, dependency and access.
Find the change record of each change.
Look for a written security impact review with an approver.
Look for the test result that shows the security controls still work.
Look for a back-out plan.
tests.ex: Compare the change tickets with the deploy log; read the pull request checklist for security impact
tests.exp: Each change has a security impact review before approval. The record shows a test of the controls and a back-out plan.

tests.title: Review the authenticator lifecycle for issue, reset, revoke and expiry
tests.obj: Finds authenticators that are given with no identity check or that stay valid after loss or change of role.
pre: Admin access and a test account.
steps: List the authenticator types: password, key, token, certificate and API key.
Request a test authenticator and look at the identity check before issue.
Check that the first value must be changed or is single use.
Report the test authenticator as lost and make sure it stops working.
Look at the expiry date of each authenticator type.
tests.ex: Test the activation link twice; revoke an API key and call the API with it; openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in CERT
tests.exp: The system checks identity before issue. Lost or changed authenticators stop working at once, and every authenticator has an owner and an end date.

tests.title: Check that login names differ from public identifiers
tests.obj: Finds accounts whose login name is the public email or display name, which helps guessing attacks.
pre: Two test accounts.
steps: List the places where the system shows a user name, email or ID to other people.
Compare each public value with the login name of the test account.
Try to log in with the public value of another test account.
Look at how new identifiers are assigned and whether they are reused.
tests.ex: Compare the public profile page and API response with the login name; try login with the display name
tests.exp: The login name is not shown to other users. The system never reuses an identifier, and the public value does not log in.

tests.title: Check the security flaw tracking tool and its link to the build
tests.obj: Finds security flaws that are found but never tracked, assigned or fixed.
pre: Read access to the tracking tool.
steps: Find the tool that tracks security flaws for the system.
Pick five flaws from scans and reviews of the last quarter.
Look for each flaw in the tool with an owner, a severity and a status.
Make sure the build or release step can see open flaws.
Look for flaws that passed the fix time with no decision.
tests.ex: Compare scanner exports with the ticket system: jira JQL labels = security AND status != Done; defectdojo findings list
tests.exp: Each flaw has a record with an owner, a severity and a due date. The release step checks open flaws, and late flaws need a recorded decision.

tests.title: Check the dynamic and interactive security tests in the development process
tests.obj: Finds releases that only get static scans and never run tests on the running application.
pre: Read access to the pipeline and the test reports.
steps: Read the pipeline and find the dynamic analysis and interactive test steps.
Look at the last three runs and the code and API coverage.
Make sure the test target is a running build, not a mock.
Open the findings and check that the results are stored.
Check that high findings stop the release or need a signed exception.
tests.ex: Look at ZAP, Burp or IAST agent runs in the pipeline logs; check agent coverage reports and the exception list
tests.exp: Each release runs dynamic or interactive tests on a running build. The results are stored, and high findings block the release.

tests.title: Review the lifecycle of cryptographic keys from creation to destruction
tests.obj: Finds keys that are made weak, kept in clear text, never rotated or never destroyed.
pre: Read access to the key store. Do not copy key values.
steps: List all keys: TLS, signing, data encryption, token and backup keys.
Read where each key is created, who can read it and where it is stored.
Look at the rotation date of each key.
Revoke or rotate one test key and make sure the system keeps working.
Check how the system gets back data if a user key is lost.
tests.ex: aws kms list-keys; aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id ID; vault read sys/keys/encryption; keytool -list -v
tests.exp: Each key has an owner, a rotation date and protected storage. Rotation and revoke work, and the loss of a key does not cause data loss.

tests.title: Check that the system fails to a safe state when security fails
tests.obj: Finds systems that open access or lose protection when a security function or boundary device fails.
pre: A test system that copies production. Do not run on production.
steps: List the security functions: authentication, authorization, filtering, logging and encryption.
Stop or break one security function on a test system.
Send a request that the function normally blocks.
Make sure the system denies the request or stops, and does not allow it.
Look for an alert, restore the function and make sure it works again.
tests.ex: Stop the authorization service and call a protected API; stop the WAF or firewall rule engine; block the policy server
tests.exp: When a security function fails the system denies access or stops in a known state. It sends an alert and keeps data safe.

tests.title: Check that monitoring tools can see encrypted traffic where policy needs it
tests.obj: Finds encrypted paths where attack tools and data loss tools are blind.
pre: A monitoring tool in scope and approval for the test payload.
steps: Read which traffic the policy says the monitoring tools must inspect.
List where the system encrypts this traffic and who holds the keys.
Send a test payload that the monitor must detect through the encrypted path.
Look for the alert, or for the log of the decrypting proxy or host agent.
Make sure the decrypting point is protected and logs access.
tests.ex: Send the EICAR test string over HTTPS through the proxy; compare the IDS alerts with and without TLS inspection
tests.exp: The test payload raises an alert on every required path. The point that decrypts traffic is protected and audited.

tests.title: Check that old software versions are removed after an update
tests.obj: Finds old vulnerable versions that stay on the system and can be started after an update.
pre: A test host and an update package.
steps: Update a test component to the new version with the normal process.
List the installed versions of the component, images and packages.
Look for old binaries, libraries, containers and rollback copies.
Try to start the old version.
Read the rule that sets how long a rollback copy may stay.
tests.ex: dpkg -l | grep PKG; docker images; find / -name 'libssl*' 2>/dev/null; kubectl get rs -A
tests.exp: After the update only the new version stays active. Old copies are removed or locked after the set rollback time.

tests.title: Check that integrity violations create an audit record and a response
tests.obj: Finds changed files or software that raise no alert and start no action.
pre: A test system. Do not change production files.
steps: List the files, packages and settings that the integrity tool watches.
Change one watched test file on a test system.
Look for an audit record with the actor, the time and the file.
Look for the alert and the automatic action that the policy sets.
Restore the file and make sure the tool reports the clean state.
tests.ex: aide --check; tripwire --check; auditctl -w /etc/TESTFILE -p wa; sigcheck -h FILE
tests.exp: The tool detects the change and records it. It sends an alert, and the set response, such as restore or isolate, starts.

tests.title: Check the manual override of input validation
tests.obj: Finds override functions that let a user skip validation without a limit or a record.
pre: Two test accounts and source or admin access.
steps: Search the system for functions that skip or relax input validation.
List the roles that can use each override.
Use an override with a test account that has the right.
Try the same override with an ordinary account.
Look for an audit record of each use.
tests.ex: Search the code and settings for validate=false, skip_validation, force and import-without-check options
tests.exp: Only named roles can use an override. Each use is limited to defined inputs and creates an audit record.

tests.title: Check the self-test of security functions at start-up and on a schedule
tests.obj: Finds security functions that fail silently, such as a broken filter or a stopped log agent.
pre: A test system. Do not run on production.
steps: List the security functions that need a regular test, such as logging, filtering and encryption.
Read when the system tests them and who gets the result.
Break one function on a test system.
Wait for the next test run and look for the alert.
Make sure the result is stored and reported.
tests.ex: Stop the antivirus service; remove a firewall rule; look at the health check and the alert in the monitoring tool
tests.exp: The system finds a failed security function in the set time. It alerts the named receiver and keeps the test result.

tests.title: Check malicious code protection at the entry and exit points
tests.obj: Finds paths where files or messages enter or leave with no malware scan.
pre: The EICAR test file. Get approval from the security team.
steps: List the entry and exit points: upload, email, API, download and removable media.
Send the EICAR test file through each entry point.
Look for the block, the quarantine and the alert.
Check the date of the last signature or rule update of each scanner.
Make sure the update runs by itself.
tests.ex: curl -F file=@eicar.com https://HOST/upload; clamscan eicar.com; check the scanner update log
tests.exp: Every entry and exit point blocks or quarantines the test file and raises an alert. Scanners update by themselves.

tests.title: Review the incident response plan for personal data breaches
tests.obj: Finds response plans that skip privacy incidents.
steps: Ask for the incident response plan.
Look for privacy incident steps, owners and contacts.
Look for the 72 hour notice step to the authority.
Ask for the last test record of the plan.
tests.ex: Document review: plan, test protocol, contact list; check for a tabletop exercise in the last two years.
tests.exp: The plan names owners and steps for privacy incidents. It is tested and records of tests exist.

tests.title: Check that the breach register holds the required facts
tests.obj: Finds breaches that are not documented.
steps: Ask for the breach register.
Check each entry for facts, effects and remedial action.
Check entries that were not reported and the reason.
Compare with the incident tickets.
tests.ex: Compare register entries with the security incident tracker of the last year.
tests.exp: Every breach has an entry with facts, effects and action. The register allows the authority to check compliance.

tests.title: Check the draft user notice for a breach
tests.obj: Finds notices that are late, unclear or incomplete.
steps: Ask for the notice template.
Check for nature of the breach, contact point, likely effects and measures.
Check that the language is clear and plain.
Check the channel for fast delivery to all affected users.
tests.ex: Template review; send a test notice to a test group and measure the time.
tests.exp: The template has all required parts in plain language. The service can reach affected users without undue delay.

tests.title: Check that monitoring detects personal data leaks
tests.obj: Finds leaks that stay unseen because no monitoring covers them.
steps: List the monitoring rules for bulk data access and data export.
Create a test export of many records.
Check that an alert starts.
Check the response time of the team.
tests.ex: Run a bulk export in a test environment; check SIEM alert and ticket.
tests.exp: A bulk read or export raises an alert. The team starts triage within the agreed time.

tests.title: Check that processors tell the controller about a breach without delay
tests.obj: Finds contracts and channels that delay the breach message.
steps: Ask for the processor contracts.
Look for the breach notice clause and the contact.
Check the contact channel with a test message.
Check that the processor has a response plan.
tests.ex: Send a test alert to the processor breach contact and note the reply time.
tests.exp: Each processor must tell the controller without undue delay. The test message reaches a staffed contact.

tests.title: Check that consent is collected separately for each purpose
tests.obj: Finds consent that is bundled for several purposes, such as service use and advertising profiling.
steps: List all processing purposes in the privacy notice and the consent records.
Open the sign-up flow and the consent dialogs.
Count the consent choices shown for each purpose.
Try to finish sign-up while you refuse every optional purpose.
tests.ex: Evidence: screenshots of each consent dialog, consent database schema, list of purposes and legal bases.
tests.exp: Each purpose has its own consent choice. The user can refuse optional purposes and still use the core service.

tests.title: Check that optional consent is off by default
tests.obj: Finds pre-ticked boxes and opt-out defaults for purposes that the service does not need.
steps: Create a new account with default settings.
Look at every consent switch, tick box and cookie setting.
Look at the stored consent values after sign-up.
Record each optional purpose that is on without a user action.
tests.ex: Compare the consent table after a fresh sign-up with the list of necessary purposes.
tests.exp: All consent switches for optional purposes are off until the user acts. The stored value shows no consent.

tests.title: Make sure users can withdraw consent as easily as they give it
tests.obj: Finds consent that is easy to give but hard to withdraw.
steps: Count the clicks that give consent.
Count the clicks that withdraw the same consent.
Withdraw one consent and look at the stored consent record.
Watch network traffic for trackers after the withdrawal.
tests.ex: Burp Suite or browser developer tools: compare requests before and after withdrawal; check the consent log row.
tests.exp: Withdrawal needs no more steps than consent. Processing and tracker calls for that purpose stop after withdrawal.

tests.title: Make sure the service keeps proof of consent and its version
tests.obj: Finds services that cannot show who agreed to which text and when.
steps: Ask for the consent log of one test user.
Look for the timestamp, the purpose and the text version in each record.
Change the policy text and look for a new consent request.
Check that old records keep their original text version.
tests.ex: Document review: consent table export with user ID, purpose, version, timestamp, source.
tests.exp: Each consent record shows the user, purpose, text version and time. Users accept new versions of changed terms.

tests.title: Check that consent is voluntary and not a condition for unrelated service
tests.obj: Finds services that block use unless the user agrees to processing that the service does not need.
steps: List the data fields and purposes that the service needs for its core function.
Refuse every optional consent in the sign-up flow.
Try to use the core service.
Record any blocked feature and the reason that the service shows.
tests.ex: Walk through the flow with all optional consents refused; note any "accept to continue" wall.
tests.exp: The core service works when the user refuses consent for data that the service does not need.

tests.title: Test the access request process and the content of the answer
tests.obj: Finds access requests that fail, come late or leave out data.
steps: Submit an access request as a test user.
Note the identity checks that the service asks for.
Compare the answer with the data in the database.
Check the answer for purposes, recipients, retention and source.
tests.ex: Measure days from request to answer. Compare export with a database dump for the test user.
tests.exp: The answer arrives within one month and holds a copy of all data plus purposes, recipients, storage period and rights.

tests.title: Make sure access requests do not expose data to another person
tests.obj: Finds access processes that give data to the wrong person.
steps: Submit an access request for user A while you use a different e-mail address.
Try to change the user identifier in the request.
Check that the service checks identity before it sends data.
Check the channel that carries the export.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater on the export request; change the user ID parameter.
tests.exp: The service refuses requests that it cannot link to the data subject. The export goes only to the verified owner on a protected channel.

tests.title: Test the rectification of personal data and its spread to recipients
tests.obj: Finds data that users cannot correct or that stays wrong at third parties.
steps: Change a data field in the account.
Check that the new value shows in all features.
Check recipients and sub-systems for the old value.
Check the update process for critical actions.
tests.ex: Change a name or address; search downstream systems and exports for the old value.
tests.exp: Users can correct their data. The change reaches all systems and recipients.

tests.title: Test the portability export format
tests.obj: Finds exports that are incomplete or that use a format that others cannot read.
steps: Request an export of data that you provided.
Open the file.
Compare the content with the data in the account.
Check the format for structure and machine readability.
tests.ex: Check for JSON or CSV with a documented schema; compare field counts with the profile.
tests.exp: The export holds all data that the user provided in a structured, common, machine-readable format.

tests.title: Test the objection and the marketing opt-out
tests.obj: Finds marketing that continues after an objection.
steps: Subscribe a test user to marketing.
Use the opt-out link and the account setting.
Look for the stop of messages and profiling.
Check that the record shows the objection.
tests.ex: Check mail headers for a working unsubscribe link; check the marketing list for the user after 48 hours.
tests.exp: Marketing and related profiling stop after the objection. The objection stays on record.

tests.title: Check that rights requests have an owner, a tracker and a deadline
tests.obj: Finds missing process for the data subject requests.
steps: Ask for the request procedure.
Look at the request log of the last year.
Calculate the time to answer for each request.
Check for refusal records with reasons.
tests.ex: Document review: request tracker export; deadline of one month with a documented extension rule.
tests.exp: All requests are tracked. Answers or reasons for refusal go out within one month, or the extension is told to the user.

tests.title: Check that a record of processing activities exists and is current
tests.obj: Finds processing that nobody documented.
steps: Ask for the record of processing activities.
Check for controller, purposes, categories, recipients, transfers and time limits.
Compare with the data inventory and with traffic.
Check the date of the last update.
tests.ex: Document review; compare record rows with the systems list.
tests.exp: The record has all required fields for every processing activity and was updated after the last change.

tests.title: Check that a data protection impact assessment exists for high-risk processing
tests.obj: Finds high-risk processing with no impact assessment.
steps: List processing that uses profiling, large-scale sensitive data or monitoring.
Ask for the assessment for each item.
Check the assessment for description, necessity, risks and measures.
Check the review date after changes.
tests.ex: Document review: DPIA register with dates and owners.
tests.exp: Each high-risk processing has an assessment made before the start. It was reviewed after the last change.

tests.title: Check that privacy by design is part of development
tests.obj: Finds projects that add privacy late or never.
steps: Ask for the privacy requirements of the latest release.
Check design records for data minimisation and default settings.
Check for a privacy step in change control.
Check the privacy tests in the release checklist.
tests.ex: Document review: design review notes, release checklist, threat model with privacy threats.
tests.exp: Privacy requirements exist from the start. Change control includes a privacy impact check.

tests.title: Check the data quality controls for stored personal data
tests.obj: Finds old, wrong or duplicate personal data.
steps: Ask how the service keeps data up to date.
Look for periodic checks or prompts to the user.
Find duplicate or conflicting records in a sample.
Check that updates reach all copies.
tests.ex: SQL duplicate check on a sample; review of the reminder process.
tests.exp: The service has a process to keep data accurate. Old and wrong data is corrected or removed.

tests.title: Check the privacy of automated decisions and profiling
tests.obj: Finds profiling with legal or similar effect that has no human review or explanation.
steps: List automated decisions that affect users.
Check the notice for the logic and its effect.
Check for a human review path.
Check that users can object.
tests.ex: Document review: decision logic description, review procedure.
tests.exp: Automated decisions with significant effect have a notice, a human review path and an objection path.

tests.title: Compare the collected personal data with the documented purposes
tests.obj: Finds fields and telemetry that the stated purposes do not need.
steps: Ask for the list of purposes and the data inventory.
Open each form and API request that collects data.
List each field and map it to one purpose.
Mark each field with no purpose.
tests.ex: Data map: field, purpose, legal basis, retention. Tools: Burp Suite, API schema review.
tests.exp: Every collected field maps to a documented purpose. No field exists only in case it is useful later.

tests.title: Make sure the server accepts forms with only needed fields
tests.obj: Finds required fields that the service does not need.
steps: Open each registration and profile form.
Send the form with only the fields that the interface marks as required.
Send the form again with each required field removed one by one.
Check that the server accepts the minimum set.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: remove one parameter at a time and compare responses.
tests.exp: The server accepts a request that has only the data needed for the purpose. Each field shows its reason.

tests.title: Check that a new data purpose needs a new notice
tests.obj: Finds reuse of data for new purposes, such as marketing, without notice or consent.
steps: Ask for the list of data uses that were added after launch.
Compare the list with the purposes in the notice.
Look for a change record that shows a notice or consent step.
Check that users were told before the new use.
tests.ex: Document review: change log, DPIA update, notice versions.
tests.exp: Each new use of data has a documented purpose, a legal basis and a notice to the users before it starts.

tests.title: Check that test and analytics systems hold no clear personal data
tests.obj: Finds real personal data in test, analytics and marketing copies.
steps: List all systems that hold copies of production data.
Look at a sample of rows in each test and analytics system.
Look for names, e-mail addresses and identifiers in clear form.
Check the masking or pseudonymisation job and who holds the key.
tests.ex: Database sample query; masking tool configuration; key access list.
tests.exp: Test and analytics systems hold masked or pseudonymised data. The re-identification key is kept apart with limited access.

tests.title: Check that the default settings collect the least data
tests.obj: Finds privacy-invasive defaults for tracking, profiling and visibility.
steps: Create a new account.
List all privacy-relevant settings and their defaults.
Look at profile visibility and data sharing defaults.
Record each setting that is more open than the purpose needs.
tests.ex: Screenshot every settings page after fresh sign-up.
tests.exp: Defaults collect and share the minimum data. Personalised advertising and public profile visibility are off.

tests.title: Check that the privacy notice lists all required information
tests.obj: Finds privacy notices that miss controller identity, purposes, recipients, retention or rights.
steps: Find the privacy notice from the sign-up page and from the footer.
Make a list of the items in the notice.
Compare the list with the items in the checklist.
Mark each missing item.
tests.ex: Checklist items: controller and contact, purposes and legal basis, recipients, third-country transfers, retention period, data subject rights, right to complain, automated decisions.
tests.exp: The notice is easy to find and contains every required item. It is shown when the data is collected.

tests.title: Check that the privacy notice matches the real data flows
tests.obj: Finds processing, recipients and trackers that the notice does not mention.
steps: Record all requests of the application with a proxy during a normal session.
List all third-party hosts that receive data.
Compare the hosts and data types with the notice.
Report each recipient that the notice does not list.
tests.ex: Burp Suite or mitmproxy HAR export; compare hosts with the recipient list in the notice.
tests.exp: Every recipient and data category seen in traffic is named in the privacy notice.

tests.title: Check that the notice is readable and available in the user language
tests.obj: Finds notices that non-lawyers cannot read or that exist only in one language.
steps: Open the notice in each supported user language.
Check for a short summary and a long version.
Run a readability score tool on the text.
Look for a change history and a record of the version that each user accepted.
tests.ex: Readability score tool; compare language list of the product with the language list of the notice.
tests.exp: The notice is short, plain and in the user language. A change history and a per-user accepted version exist.

tests.title: Check the cookie list, its purposes and the opt-out
tests.obj: Finds sites that set cookies and trackers without a list or an opt-out.
steps: Open the site with a clean browser profile.
List all cookies and storage entries before any consent action.
Compare the list with the cookie list in the notice.
Use the opt-out control and list the entries again.
tests.ex: Browser developer tools Application tab; clear site data between steps.
tests.exp: Only necessary cookies exist before consent. The cookie list names each cookie and its purpose. The opt-out removes the others.

tests.title: Review the retention and deletion policy for each data category
tests.obj: Finds data categories that have no retention period or no deletion process.
steps: Ask for the retention schedule.
Compare it with the data inventory.
Mark each data category with no period.
Check that the period is in the privacy notice.
tests.ex: Document review: retention schedule, deletion concept, privacy notice section on storage period.
tests.exp: Each data category has a retention period and a deletion process. The periods are in the privacy notice.

tests.title: Make sure data is deleted when the retention period ends
tests.obj: Finds data that stays after its period, such as inactive accounts and old logs.
steps: Find records older than the retention period in the database.
Look at backups and archives for the same records.
Run the deletion job on a test set.
Check that the records are gone from all stores.
tests.ex: SQL count of rows older than the period; list of stores: database, search index, cache, object store, backup.
tests.exp: No record exists beyond its period in any active store. Backups have an expiry that follows the policy.

tests.title: Make sure account deletion removes data in all systems and at processors
tests.obj: Finds deleted accounts that stay in search indexes, caches, analytics or third-party systems.
steps: Create a test account with data in every feature.
Request deletion of the account.
Search for the test data in the database, indexes, logs and analytics after the deletion period.
Ask each processor to confirm deletion.
tests.ex: Use a unique marker string in the test data and search for it everywhere.
tests.exp: The marker string is not found in any active store or processor system after the stated deletion time.

tests.title: Check that deletion also covers backups, copies and shared data
tests.obj: Finds personal data that deletion leaves in backups, exports or third-party copies.
steps: Ask for the backup retention and restore procedure.
Check that a restore applies earlier deletion requests.
Look for exports and file shares that hold copies.
Check the process to tell recipients about an erasure.
tests.ex: Document review: backup policy, restore runbook, list of recipients with erasure notice process.
tests.exp: Backups expire on a set schedule. A restore re-applies deletion requests. Recipients get erasure notices.

tests.title: Check that the service keeps an erasure record without the deleted data
tests.obj: Finds services that cannot prove a deletion.
steps: Request deletion of a test account.
Ask for the deletion protocol of the request.
Check that the protocol shows date, scope and result.
Check that the protocol holds no more personal data than needed.
tests.ex: Deletion log row with request ID, time, systems cleaned, operator.
tests.exp: A deletion record exists. It shows what was deleted and when, and it holds no deleted personal data.

tests.title: Make sure URLs, logs and analytics hold no personal data
tests.obj: Finds personal data in places that many people and systems can read.
steps: Use the application with a test user that has unique data values.
Search access logs, application logs and analytics events for the unique values.
Look for personal data in URLs and query strings.
Check log access rights.
tests.ex: grep -r 'test.user@example.com' /var/log; compare analytics event payloads with the data map.
tests.exp: Logs, URLs and analytics events hold no clear personal data. Identifiers are masked or hashed.

tests.title: Check encryption of personal data at rest and the key separation
tests.obj: Finds personal data stored in clear form or with keys next to the data.
steps: List the stores that hold personal data.
Check the encryption setting of each store and each backup.
Find where the keys are kept.
Check who can read both keys and data.
tests.ex: Cloud console storage settings; database encryption status; key vault access policy.
tests.exp: All stores and backups are encrypted. Keys are kept in a separate key service with limited access.

tests.title: Check that access to personal data follows need-to-know
tests.obj: Finds staff and service accounts that can read more personal data than their role needs.
steps: Ask for the role list and the access matrix for personal data.
List the accounts with read access to the main data store.
Compare the list with the roles.
Check that access to personal data is logged.
tests.ex: Database grants export; IAM policy review; audit log sample.
tests.exp: Only needed roles can read personal data. Each access to bulk data is logged and reviewed.

tests.title: Check that personal data is encrypted in transit on every channel
tests.obj: Finds clear-text transfers of personal data, including internal and partner links.
steps: List all channels that carry personal data.
Capture traffic on each channel.
Look for clear-text protocols.
Check the TLS version and certificate checks.
tests.ex: Wireshark capture; nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 host.
tests.exp: Every channel uses current TLS with certificate checks. No personal data goes in clear text.

tests.title: Check that sessions end after inactivity and at logout
tests.obj: Finds sessions that stay open and let the service keep collecting data without user awareness.
steps: Log in and leave the session idle.
Check that the session ends at the documented time.
Log out and replay the old session token.
Check for a logout button on all pages.
tests.ex: Burp Repeater: replay the old cookie after logout and after the timeout.
tests.exp: The session ends at the idle limit and at logout. The old token is rejected. Tracking stops with the session.

tests.title: Check that users can see and end open sessions
tests.obj: Finds services that give users no control over open sessions.
steps: Log in on two devices.
Open the session list in the account.
End the other session from the first device.
Check that the second device lost access.
tests.ex: Two browsers; confirm the second token returns 401 after revocation.
tests.exp: The user sees all open sessions and can end them. Ended sessions stop at once.

tests.title: Check that the privacy assessment covers the web application vulnerabilities
tests.obj: Finds privacy reviews that ignore technical flaws such as injection and broken access control.
steps: Ask for the last penetration test and scan reports.
Check that the scope includes personal data stores.
Check the fix status of high findings.
Check the patch process for components.
tests.ex: Document review: pen test report, SAST/DAST results, patch SLA.
tests.exp: Regular tests cover personal data paths. High findings have a fix with evidence. Patches follow a set time frame.

tests.title: Find all third parties that receive personal data in application traffic
tests.obj: Finds trackers, widgets and SDKs that send data to third parties without notice.
steps: Start a clean browser profile and a proxy.
Load the main pages and log in.
List every third-party host in the traffic.
Look at the parameters sent to each host.
tests.ex: Burp Suite HTTP history filtered by host; browser developer tools Network tab; look for e-mail, user ID, location in parameters.
tests.exp: Only documented recipients receive data. No personal data goes to a tracker before consent.

tests.title: Make sure no tracker fires before consent or after refusal
tests.obj: Finds trackers that run without the required consent.
steps: Open the site with a clean profile and do not click the banner.
Record all requests.
Refuse optional cookies and reload.
Record the requests again and compare.
tests.ex: Browser developer tools Network tab with preserve log; compare host list before and after the consent action.
tests.exp: No analytics or advertising request exists before consent or after refusal.

tests.title: Check processor contracts and the list of sub-processors
tests.obj: Finds processors that have no contract terms for security and instructions.
steps: Ask for the list of processors.
Ask for the contract of each processor.
Check that each contract has the required terms.
Check the notice process for new sub-processors.
tests.ex: Document review: contract clauses on instructions, security measures, sub-processors, deletion, audit.
tests.exp: Each processor has a contract with the required terms. Changes of sub-processors need prior authorisation.

tests.title: Check that partner data feeds are minimised and pseudonymised
tests.obj: Finds partner feeds that hold more data than the partner needs.
steps: List the data feeds to partners.
Look at a sample payload of each feed.
Compare the fields with the contract purpose.
Check for pseudonymisation of identifiers.
tests.ex: Sample payload review; field list against the data processing agreement.
tests.exp: Each feed carries only the fields that the partner needs. Identifiers are pseudonymised where the purpose allows.

tests.title: Make sure external content does not leak the IP address
tests.obj: Finds third-party images and scripts that disclose the user IP address or page URL.
steps: List all external images, fonts and scripts on user pages.
Look at the Referer header sent to each host.
Check if users can block external content.
Check that user-supplied URLs are not loaded without a proxy.
tests.ex: Browser developer tools Network tab; check the Referrer-Policy header.
tests.exp: The application loads external content only from documented hosts. Referrer data is limited. Users can block external content.

tests.title: Check the notice and consent for automated profiling
tests.obj: Finds profiling that the user does not know about.
steps: List the systems that score, rank or predict habits, behaviour, interests or position of a user.
Look for the notice and consent for each system.
Check that the user can object to the profiling.
Check the effect on the user.
tests.ex: Review the model inventory and the notice text. Test the opt-out as a user.
tests.exp: Users know about profiling and consent to it. An opt-out exists and the controller can show the purpose.

tests.title: Check AI risk classification and purpose limits for personal data
tests.obj: Finds AI systems that use personal data beyond the stated purpose or with no risk class.
steps: List AI systems that process personal data.
Find the risk class for each system.
Check that the safeguards match the class.
Check the training data sources and the purposes.
Check that the system is not used to harm other people.
tests.ex: Review the AI inventory and the risk register. Compare training data fields with the purpose list.
tests.exp: Each AI system that uses personal data has a risk class and safeguards that match it. It uses data only within the stated purpose.

tests.title: Check that the breach process meets the 72-hour limit
tests.obj: Finds breach processes that cannot notify the authority in time.
steps: Read the breach procedure for the Vietnamese authority.
Find the step that starts the 72-hour clock.
Run a table-top case and record the time to notify.
Check that a late notice has the reason for the delay.
tests.ex: Table-top: simulate the leak of 1000 records. Use form Mau so 03 of the Decree.
tests.exp: The procedure notifies the authority within 72 hours. A late notice includes the reason for the delay.

tests.title: Check the content of the breach notice to the authority
tests.obj: Finds breach notices that omit required facts.
steps: Get the template or a sample notice.
Look for the time, place, act, parties, data types and amount of data.
Look for the contact of the person in charge of data protection.
Look for the possible effects and the steps taken.
Check that the process allows a notice in stages.
tests.ex: Use the four groups of Decree Art. 23(3) and form Mau so 03 as a checklist.
tests.exp: The notice has all required facts. The process allows a first notice and then more details in stages.

tests.title: Check that processors report breaches to the controller fast
tests.obj: Finds processors that delay the breach report.
steps: Read the contract with the processor.
Find the duty and the time limit to report a breach.
Ask the processor to run a test report.
Record the time from detection to the message to the controller.
tests.ex: Send a test incident alert to the processor contact and measure the response.
tests.exp: The processor tells the controller of a breach as soon as possible. The contact and channel are tested.

tests.title: Check the breach record and the reports of other violations
tests.obj: Finds breaches with no signed record or with no report of other violations.
steps: Find the record of each past breach.
Check that the record confirms the breach and the work with the authority.
Check the process to report unlawful processing, wrong purpose and failed rights.
Check who can send these reports.
tests.ex: Document review of the breach register and the report log.
tests.exp: A record exists for each breach. The organisation reports misuse of data and failures to meet data subject rights.

tests.title: Check the notice to users after a bank or credit data leak
tests.obj: Finds finance firms that do not tell users about a leak of account data.
steps: Read the user notice process for leaks of bank, financial and credit data.
Find who approves and sends the notice.
Run a test case and measure the time.
Check the notice text.
tests.ex: Table-top: leak of account numbers. Review the notice template.
tests.exp: The firm tells affected users about a leak of bank, financial or credit data.

tests.title: Check that the consent screen shows the four required facts
tests.obj: Finds consent that is not informed because required facts are missing.
steps: Open each form or screen that asks for consent.
Look for the types of personal data to be processed.
Look for the purpose, the name of the controller or other organisation, and the rights and duties of the user.
Compare the facts with the real processing.
tests.ex: Screenshot each consent screen and list the four facts in a table.
tests.exp: Each consent request shows data types, purpose, the organisation that processes the data, and the rights and duties of the data subject.

tests.title: Check that consent is clear, per purpose and never implied
tests.obj: Finds pre-ticked boxes, silent consent and bundled purposes.
steps: Open each consent form and look at the default state of each box.
Send the form with no choice and see what the service stores.
Accept one purpose and refuse the others, then examine the stored choices.
Try to give consent for part of the data or with a condition.
Look for consent that is a condition of service for an unrelated purpose.
tests.ex: Intercept the consent request and look for a consent flag per purpose. Burp Repeater: remove the consent field.
tests.exp: Consent is a clear action for each purpose. Silence is not consent. The service accepts partial consent and does not bundle unrelated purposes.

tests.title: Check the consent record and the proof of consent
tests.obj: Finds consent that the controller cannot prove in a dispute.
steps: Give consent as a test user and note the time, version and text shown.
Find the consent record in the data store.
Make sure the record can be printed or copied in a readable format.
Change the consent text and check that old records keep the old version.
Ask for the proof of consent for the test user.
tests.ex: Export the consent log for the test user. Check fields: timestamp, purpose, text version, channel, user ID.
tests.exp: The service keeps a verifiable record for each consent. The controller can show it and can print or copy it.

tests.title: Test the withdrawal of consent and its spread to processors
tests.obj: Finds withdrawals that do not stop processing at the controller or at processors.
pre: A test user whose data is in scope as data of a Vietnamese citizen.
Written permission to send data subject requests.
steps: Withdraw consent for one purpose as a test user.
Check that the service tells the user about the possible results of the withdrawal.
Check that the service stops the processing for that purpose.
Check that processors and third parties receive the withdrawal.
Check that data from before the withdrawal stays valid as history.
tests.ex: Look at processor API calls, queue messages and batch jobs after the withdrawal. Compare the data flow before and after.
tests.exp: The service accepts a withdrawal in a recordable format and tells the user the results. The controller, processors and third parties stop the processing.

tests.title: Check the processing notice before the first processing
tests.obj: Finds processing that starts with no notice or with an incomplete notice.
steps: Open the first data collection step as a new user.
Look for a notice before the service collects data.
Look for purpose, data types, method, other parties, possible harm, and start and end time.
Check that the notice is in a form that can be saved or printed.
Check the exception when the user already knows and agrees with all items.
tests.ex: Capture the notice text and compare it with the six items in the list. Check the timing against the first network request that carries data.
tests.exp: The user gets one complete notice before processing starts. The notice can be saved or printed.

tests.title: Check the legal basis for processing without consent
tests.obj: Finds processing without consent that has no documented legal exception.
steps: List the processing activities that run without consent.
Find the legal ground for each activity in the register.
Check that the controller can show the emergency or the legal duty.
Look for the oversight process: rules, risk checks, periodic audit and a complaint channel.
tests.ex: Document review: register of processing with a column for legal ground and a column for owner.
tests.exp: Each processing without consent has a named legal ground and an owner. The controller can prove an urgent case, and an oversight process exists.

tests.title: Review the controller dossier for the impact of processing
tests.obj: Finds dossiers with missing items or no dossier.
steps: Get the dossier of the controller.
Check the details of the controller and the data protection staff.
Check the purpose, data types, recipients (also foreign ones), transfers and the storage period.
Check the description of the safeguards and the impact assessment with the risk reduction steps.
Check that a legal document holds the dossier.
tests.ex: Use the nine items of Decree Art. 24(1) as a table. Compare the dossier with the real data flows.
tests.exp: The dossier exists from the first day of processing and holds all required items. It matches the real data flows.

tests.title: Review the processor dossier for contracted processing
tests.obj: Finds processors that keep no impact dossier of their own.
steps: Get the dossier of each processor.
Check the contact details of the processor and its staff.
Check the description of processing and data types in the contract.
Check the storage period, transfers, safeguards and the risk list.
tests.ex: Document review of the processor dossier against the processor contract.
tests.exp: Each processor keeps a dossier that matches the contract and lists safeguards and risks.

tests.title: Check the 60-day filing and the updates of the dossier
tests.obj: Finds dossiers that were not filed or that are out of date.
steps: Find the date of the first processing.
Check the filing receipt for an original dossier within 60 days.
Compare the dossier with the current system and vendors.
Check the change notices and the review dates.
tests.ex: Document review: filing receipt, change notices, system change log. Law: update every 6 months on change.
tests.exp: The dossier is filed in 60 days and updated when the system or business changes. The date of the last review is on record.

tests.title: Check consent for marketing and proof of its use
tests.obj: Finds marketing that uses data with no consent or with no proof.
steps: Sign up as a test customer without marketing consent.
Check that no marketing message arrives.
Check that the consent states content, method, form and frequency.
Ask the marketing team for proof of consent for the test user.
tests.ex: Review the sign-up flow and the campaign tool segments. Check against the consent log.
tests.exp: Marketing uses personal data only with consent that names content, method, form and frequency. The team can prove it.

tests.title: Test the way to refuse advertising and the stop of it
tests.obj: Finds advertising that continues after a refusal.
steps: Find the way to refuse advertising in the product and in each message.
Use it as a test user.
Record the time until the advertising stops.
Check that partners stop to use the data.
tests.ex: Click the unsubscribe link. Check the suppression list and partner sync.
tests.exp: The user can refuse advertising at any time. The service stops it at once and tells the partners.

tests.title: Check consent and controls for behavioural advertising and tracking
tests.obj: Finds tracking for advertising with no consent, no refusal or no storage limit.
steps: Open the site in a new browser with no consent.
Check for tracking cookies and SDK calls before the choice.
Refuse tracking and check that tracking stops.
Look for a do-not-track option.
Check the storage time of the profile data and its deletion.
tests.ex: Browser developer tools network and storage tabs. Compare with the cookie list in the notice.
tests.exp: The service tracks behaviour only after consent, offers a refusal and a do-not-track option, and sets a storage time with deletion.

tests.title: Check account verification and tracking rules for social platforms
tests.obj: Finds platforms that ask for ID images, read messages or collect beyond the agreement.
steps: Register an account on the platform as a test user.
Check the verification step and whether it asks for an image of an ID document.
Check app permissions for call, SMS and microphone access.
Look for the privacy settings, the way to report a violation and the privacy policy.
tests.ex: Walk through registration. Review the permissions in the mobile manifest.
tests.exp: The platform does not ask for an ID image for verification. It does not read calls or messages without consent and it offers privacy settings and reports.

tests.title: Check that a processor contract exists before data transfer
tests.obj: Finds processors that receive data with no contract.
steps: List all processors and the date of first data transfer.
Find the signed contract for each processor.
Check that the date of the contract is before the first transfer.
Check that the contract states the rights, duties and security measures.
tests.ex: Compare the processor list with the contract register and the date of first API call.
tests.exp: Each processor has a signed contract that is older than the first transfer. The contract states the duties and the measures.

tests.title: Check that processors return or delete data when the work ends
tests.obj: Finds processors that keep data after the contract ends.
steps: Read the exit clause of the contract.
Close a test project with the processor.
Ask for proof of deletion or return of the test data.
Look in the processor systems for the test data.
tests.ex: Request a deletion certificate. Look at storage buckets and backups at the processor.
tests.exp: The processor deletes or returns all personal data at the end of the work and gives proof.

tests.title: Check the consent for data given to another organisation
tests.obj: Finds data that goes to third parties without consent.
steps: List the third parties that get personal data.
Find the consent or other ground for each flow.
Run a test user flow and look at the outgoing traffic.
Check the notice to users for the same parties.
tests.ex: Proxy capture on a test user session. Compare with the consent log.
tests.exp: Data goes to third parties only with consent of the data subject or another ground in law. The notice names the parties.

tests.title: Test that a data access request gets an answer within 72 hours
tests.obj: Finds access (provision) requests that are late, incomplete or hard to submit.
pre: A test user whose data is in scope as data of a Vietnamese citizen.
Written permission to send data subject requests.
steps: Send an access request for the test user through each channel the service offers.
Use the fields of the Vietnam form: name, identity number, data requested, format, purpose.
Record the time from the request to the answer.
Read the answer for the cost, place, format and period of delivery.
Compare the delivered data with the data in the database.
tests.ex: Request form fields follow Mau so 01 (individual) and Mau so 02 (organisation) in the Decree annex. Use a stopwatch or ticket timestamps.
tests.exp: The service answers a valid request within 72 hours and delivers the data in the stated format. It states any cost and the delivery details.

tests.title: Check requests from a representative and requests to third parties
tests.obj: Finds service that hands data to a wrong representative or gives it to others without consent.
pre: A test user whose data is in scope as data of a Vietnamese citizen.
Written permission to send data subject requests.
steps: Send an access request for the test user from an authorised representative with a written authorisation.
Send the same request with no written authorisation.
Ask the service to send the test user data to another organisation. Try with and without consent.
Check that the service refuses each request that has no consent or authorisation.
tests.ex: Use a signed authorisation letter and an unsigned copy. Check the audit record of each request.
tests.exp: The service acts for a representative only with written authorisation. It gives data to another party only with the consent of the data subject.

tests.title: Test the correction of personal data and the 72-hour answer
tests.obj: Finds correction requests that fail, come late or do not reach other recipients.
pre: A test user whose data is in scope as data of a Vietnamese citizen.
Written permission to send data subject requests.
